US cross-source trend synthesis v1

The NBER fertility and remote-work record adds a work-care conversion boundary: fertility reduces mothers’ labor-force participation; an additional child increased remote-work likelihood before 2020 but reduced it after remote work became common. Read beside labor-force exit and firm/AI work evidence, the implication is that a work-location option is not the same as usable flexibility: employer practice, care intensity, occupation, housing, schedule, and period norms shape whether it expands agency.

The NBER multinational tax-planning record adds a firm-structure and public-revenue layer: structures adopted by 18% of US multinationals accounted for 36% of foreign profits in 2016, while the model finds tax-revenue and economic-activity tradeoffs amplified by global R&D. Read beside firm investment, AI organization capital, and cross-border services evidence, the implication is that legal/tax architecture can shape where profits, investment, R&D, and public capacity appear without directly revealing worker or consumer gains.

The NBER labor-force-exit record adds a labor-supply and household-room boundary: persistent exit is concentrated among low-income and low-skill workers, especially low-skilled unmarried men, and self-employment replaces roughly 25% of lost W-2 income. Read beside minimum-wage hours effects and AI productivity evidence, the implication is that employment status alone misses income replacement, flexibility, care, health, and social engagement. The tax panel does not identify a single cause or measure informal work and wellbeing fully.

The NBER SNAP restriction record supplies the policy counterpoint to P-EBT expansion: restricted spending fell 11%, purchased calories and sugar fell 5–8%, and substitution was asymmetric across fruit drinks and snacks; shelf prices barely moved, tax-inclusive prices rose 1.9%, and online response remained large. Read beside the 16% P-EBT sugary-item purchase increase, the cross-source implication is that policy direction changes purchase composition, but neither result alone establishes diet, health, food security, or welfare. Modeled national gains remain separate from observed household outcomes.

The NBER P-EBT purchase-response record adds a direct consumer allocation layer: disbursement was associated with a 16% increase in weekly sugary-item spending among eligible households with school-aged children, exceeding the overall food-spending increase, with no placebo response. Read beside SNAP purchase restrictions and food-security measures, the implication is that assistance, restrictions, purchases, consumption, nutrition, and household security are different stages; purchase response alone cannot settle the welfare question.

The NBER long-term PM2.5 record adds a cumulative-exposure mechanism: in roughly 150,000 initially healthy US soldiers, sustained PM2.5 exposure increases circulatory disease, particularly hypertension, while shorter exposure has little detectable effect. Read with household energy, weatherization, infrastructure, and public-health evidence, the implication is that short-run exposure or savings measures can miss health-capital erosion that accumulates over years. The Army design strengthens internal comparison but does not directly generalize to civilian households or identify the full cost pathway.

The NBER roommate peer-effects record adds a resident-placement mechanism: across 2.6 million stays, a roommate with Alzheimer’s disease or related dementia raises 90-day mortality by 2.1 percentage points relative to a private room, while cognitively healthy roommates help patients with dementia. Read with Medicaid allocation, ownership, inspection, and staffing evidence, the cross-source implication is that outcomes depend on who is placed together as well as which facility is chosen. A modeled 0.8-point overall mortality reduction is not an implemented policy and leaves privacy, preference, staffing, and quality of life open.

The NBER Medicaid nursing-home record adds the public-payment mechanism: matching grants reward verifiable volume rather than quality; in Indiana, Medicaid dementia volume rose 12%, expansion concentrated in the lowest-quality facilities, patients shifted toward worse providers, and one-year survival fell. Read with related-party finance, mergers, inspections, and threshold avoidance, the cross-source implication is that public money can expand access on a volume measure while worsening provider selection and clinical outcomes. The evidence is anchored in federal audits and Indiana administrative data; it does not prove a universal state-level effect.

The NBER related-party finance record adds a hidden-finance layer: 68% of nursing-home profits are estimated to be tunneled to commonly-owned real-estate and management companies, increasing implied typical investment IRR from 4.83% to 13.11% after adjustment. Read with mergers, inspection timing, and threshold avoidance, the cross-source implication is that reported profitability, regulatory compliance, labor input, and resident health can be separated by ownership and accounting structures. The abstract does not establish illegality or a causal care effect.

The NBER nursing-home merger record adds the ownership mechanism: acquisitions reduce deficiency citations by 8% over three years, with persistence of at least five years, but direct-care hours decline and resident health does not meaningfully improve. Low-severity citation changes suggest compliance can improve without equivalent clinical gains. Read with inspection timing, threshold avoidance, and financial tunneling, the cross-source pattern is a measurement-and-incentive split: firm cost efficiency, regulatory compliance, labor input, and resident health can diverge.

The NBER nursing-home inspection record adds a persistence and measurement challenge. Facilities improve several observed dimensions around inspections, then nearly all responses fall immediately afterward; ratings therefore may not measure absolute quality, even though higher-rated facilities have lower patient mortality. Read with threshold avoidance, mergers, and related-party financial evidence, the cross-source implication is that compliance, facility quality, resident access, and financial incentives can move on different clocks. The abstract does not disclose effect sizes or fully identify the mortality mechanism.

The NBER nursing-home threshold record adds a firm-avoidance layer to the care-quality chain. At California’s 100-bed threshold, facilities bunch and low-staffing homes manipulate size to avoid additional staffing requirements; higher staffing above the threshold is nearly entirely selection, and access is limited particularly for disadvantaged patients. Read beside inspection-timing, merger, and tunneling evidence, the cross-source pattern is that measured compliance, staffing, ownership, and resident access can move through different mechanisms. The abstract does not disclose effect sizes or clinical outcomes, so this is not a complete quality or welfare estimate.

The NBER immigrant minimum-wage record adds a worker-status boundary to the minimum-wage comparison. Hours fall without a reported employment response for immigrants, especially recently arrived, likely undocumented workers in high-turnover industries, while native workers show no comparable response. Read beside the poor-family SIPP result, this suggests that the outcome unit matters: employment can remain present while hours, schedule control, legal-status leverage, and household room change. The abstract does not disclose effect sizes or the complete identification design; the subgroup pattern is not proof that legal status alone causes the difference.

The NBER poor-family minimum-wage record adds a household-positioned counterexample to simple wage-floor narratives. SIPP evidence reports adverse employment, hours, and earnings effects for initially-employed low-wage workers in poor and low-income families, without a stronger adverse gradient for the poorest workers. Read beside overtime-coverage evidence with no detected employment decline, this makes the key comparison the policy design, worker starting position, firm adjustment, and outcome unit—not a single universal minimum-wage effect. The working-paper abstract does not disclose effect sizes, sample count, or the full identification strategy; it does not measure prices, profits, automation, benefits, consumption, or worker voice in the same episode.

The South Africa Census Cultural Dynamics record adds a population-structure layer beneath social-participation measures. Multiracial households rose from 1.3% in 2001 to 11.4% in 2022, multilingual households from 3.5% to 9.4% between 1996 and 2022, while legal marriage fell from 35.6% to 23.8%. The same census analysis reports 84.5% Christian affiliation and 9.5% traditional African religious affiliation in 2022. The pattern is cultural and household reorganization, not proof of increasing trust or cohesion; the next test is language access, housing and migration pathways, service usability, and lived intergroup contact.

The Singapore SG Culture Pass record adds a policy-designed audience-conversion route. More than 1.2 million citizens registered, and seven in ten had not attended a local arts or culture programme in the previous five years; among users, nine in ten expressed interest in another programme. The NAC survey shows why this is a meaningful but incomplete signal: physical attendance was 59%, digital arts consumption 66%, and active participation 28%, while childhood exposure was associated with substantially higher later engagement. The sharper test is redemption and repeat attendance by income, neighborhood, age, disability, and cultural background; registration and stated interest do not establish durable access or causal program effect.

The Open Banking Limited 2026 activity and fraud record shows digital financial infrastructure becoming routine while risk remains uneven. Payments rose 45% year over year and cumulative payments passed 1 billion, but more than two-thirds of reported fraud cases were authorised push-payment fraud. The signal is a conversion problem: infrastructure scale can increase convenience and access while shifting protection and loss-recoupment questions into the consumer layer. OBL’s aggregate and provider-covered measures do not identify unique users, switching, reimbursement, or causal safety.

The Australian ACCC Consumer Data Right data-quality record adds a concrete data-portability-to-choice test. The CDR had more than 1.3 million users by July 2026, but the ACCC’s 16 stakeholder respondents still described stale or misclassified product fields, inconsistent loan-to-value presentation, missing transaction identifiers, uneven update timing, bespoke workarounds, and issue tickets that could remain open for more than six months. The synthesis implication is that interoperability is not the endpoint: usable consumer power requires semantic consistency, current data, visible escalation, and timely correction. This is a small stakeholder survey and regulatory observation, not a representative consumer or causal adoption study; the next test is whether repeated data-quality and resolution measures predict actual switching, savings, fraud exposure, and distributional access.

The Fundação Itaú/Datafolha cultural-habits record adds a demand-side hybrid-access test to the Brazilian cultural-economy evidence. In 2025, 90% reported virtual cultural activity and 84% in-person activity, but in-person access was 70% among respondents with elementary education versus 96% among those with higher education, and 71% among D/E classes versus 93% among A/B. The cross-source implication is that digital reach can coexist with persistent physical cultural inequality; cultural conversion still depends on education, income, mobility, place, and venue access.

The Brazil IBGE SIIC 2013-2024 record adds the cultural-production side of the audience story. Brazil counted about 5.9 million cultural-sector workers in 2024, with 44.6% in informal occupations versus 40.6% across all sectors; among people with culture-related degrees, 74.6% worked outside the cultural sector. The cross-source implication is that cultural agency and cultural access depend on a labor and supply system whose workers may have weaker formal protection and whose educational capacity does not reliably convert into cultural employment.

The World Bank Digital Progress and Trends 2025 record adds the infrastructure-capacity layer beneath digital access. In 2024, internet use reached 54% in LMICs and 27% in LICs, 5G coverage reached 35% and 4%, and data traffic per capita was approximately 100 GB in LMICs versus 5 GB in LICs. The cross-source implication is that connectivity can spread while bandwidth, speed, affordability, skills, and compute remain stratified; “online” is not a common consumer or cultural experience.

The GSMA Mobile Gender Gap 2026 record adds a non-Western digital-participation counterweight to platform adoption stories. Women in LMICs were 12% less likely than men to use mobile internet in 2025, with about 200 million fewer women users; female use ranged from 35% in Sub-Saharan Africa to 77% in Latin America and the Caribbean. The cross-source implication is that network coverage and aggregate adoption can coexist with gendered participation, affordability, skills, awareness, and safety constraints. Mobile access is an opportunity condition, not proof of equal agency, cultural reach, or consumer benefit.

The England SACE 2025-26 record adds an official care-to-capacity bridge. Among carers known to local authorities, 16.8% could spend time on things they valued, 19.5% were out of paid employment because of caring, 34.7% provided at least 100 hours of care per week, and only 26.2% always felt involved or consulted about support services. The cross-source implication is that household cultural and consumer optionality is partly produced by unpaid care infrastructure: time, work, social contact, health, financial pressure, and service voice are linked stages, not one “carer wellbeing” endpoint.

The UK CMA Annual Report 2025-26 record adds a regulator-side remedy stage to the consumer-power pattern. The CMA reports a three-year average of £3.3bn in direct consumer benefits, 14 new-regime investigations, more than 80,000 learner-driver refunds averaging about £9, and a 33% year-over-year increase in public correspondence. The cross-source implication is that consumer voice can reach enforcement and direct-redress machinery, but institutional output, estimated avoided harm, refund receipt, and durable household recovery remain different endpoints.

The Creative Australia National Arts Participation Survey 2025 record supplies the current cultural-connection layer beneath the historical migrant baseline. Engagement through arts with one's own cultural background, language group, or community rose from 32% in 2022 to 40% in 2025; live arts attendance reached 74%, but 60% named cost as the biggest barrier and 55% missed a wanted event because of cost. The cross-source implication is culturally connective participation under constrained conversion: identity and community meaning can strengthen while price still blocks realization. The public summary does not identify migrant or country-of-birth subgroups, so it cannot close the current migrant cross-tab gap.

The same Creative Australia 2025 record adds a creative-AI legitimacy split: 40% report using AI tools to create art or generate ideas, while 82% want AI use disclosed and 93% report at least one concern about AI and creativity. The cross-source implication is selective delegation with provenance demand, not automatic substitution of human cultural production.

The full Creative Australia 2025 report adds a current CALD creative-agency layer: general-sample CALD respondents reported creative participation at 51% versus 39% overall, with higher participation in music, dance, theatre, and creative writing; a separate translated CALD sample reported still higher rates but was explicitly non-representative. The cross-source implication is that cultural inclusion cannot be inferred from attendance alone: a group can show strong creative production while household room, housing, language access, and public recognition remain uneven.

The report also adds direct audience conversion: 49% of CALD respondents attended arts events to engage with their own cultural background, language group, or community, compared with 32% of non-CALD respondents; music and festivals were prominent channels. The cross-source implication is culturally specific demand and participation, not a generic assimilation measure, and it still does not identify visa stream, country of birth, affordability, or repeat attendance.

The ABS historical migrant cultural-attendance baseline supplies a direct culture-by-migrant comparison that current settlement releases lack. In 2005–06, at least one cultural venue/event was reported by 90% of migrants born in main English-speaking countries, 76% of migrants born in non-main-English-speaking countries, and 86% of people born in Australia; cinema and library attendance also differed by migrant grouping. The finding is useful as a historical measurement anchor, not as evidence of present-day participation or a continuous trend. It makes the missing current cross-tab itself visible.

The existing ABS General Social Survey 2025 record now adds a migrant social-connection and discrimination comparison: weekly outside-household face-to-face contact was 46% among migrants versus about 53% for adults overall, while reported discrimination was 20% among migrants versus 17% among people born in Australia. This extends the new migrant-settlement route from economic and housing room into social friction and connection. It remains a broad cross-sectional self-report comparison, not a measure of cultural attendance by migrant status, isolation, or causal integration.

The ABS Migrant Settlement Outcomes 2026 record adds a migration-linked household-room and institutional-contact layer. Skilled-stream permanent migrants had 82% employment and A$83,466 median income in 2023–24, compared with 46% employment and A$43,910 median income among humanitarian-stream migrants; rent burden above 30% of household income was also higher among recent humanitarian arrivals. English proficiency varies by stream and arrival cohort while GP contact is relatively high, so service contact cannot be treated as equivalent to communicative or cultural participation capacity. The cross-source implication is that migration is not one consumer or cultural segment: visa stream, arrival cohort, housing pressure, language, and service access can create different conversion paths. This linked-data release is observational and does not directly measure cultural participation, discretionary spending, causality, or equal service quality.

The Spain INE Household Budget Survey 2025 record adds a direct budget-room layer beneath cultural attendance and transaction data. Average household spending on recreation, sport, and culture reached €1,772, up 4.7% in current prices, but the lowest-spending quintile devoted 61.5% of its budget to housing/energy plus food while the highest quintile devoted 33.6% to transport, restaurants/accommodation, and recreation/culture combined. The cross-source implication is that aggregate cultural-spending growth can coexist with sharply unequal conversion capacity; the survey does not establish real volume, attendance, or causal affordability.

The ABS Monthly Household Spending Indicator August 2026 record provides the next observed-consumption checkpoint. Total Australian household spending was flat month over month but 6.8% higher year over year; recreation and culture fell 1.4% after July's increase, while transport rose 2.3%. The cross-source implication is selective rotation rather than uniform consumer recovery: annual nominal resilience can coexist with immediate leisure contraction and mobility-cost exposure.

The ABS Monthly Household Spending Indicator July 2026 record adds observed transaction behavior beneath cultural-attendance and financial-stress surveys. Australian household spending rose 1.1% month over month and 7.0% year over year in current prices; recreation and culture rose 1.5% month over month and 7.8% year over year, with cinema, major sporting events, and gambling contributing. In real chain-volume terms, recreation and culture rose 1.7% in the June quarter versus 0.7% for total spending. The cross-source implication is observed leisure resilience with unresolved distribution and price boundaries: transaction growth is not equal household welfare, unique-user access, or cultural participation.

The Statistics Norway immigrant-background cultural-use record adds a subgroup conversion test beneath the national Norwegian barometer. Among 1,331 completed interviews, 60% visited a public library, 53% a museum, and 58% a cinema; the report says immigrant-background participation was higher in libraries and museums but lower in theatre and concerts than the total population. Sixty-two percent wanted to attend cinema more often and 61% concerts more often, with time, money, and selection recurring as barriers. The cross-source implication is venue-specific inclusion and unmet demand, not a single assimilation or exclusion score; the survey does not identify causal language, income, supply, or discrimination mechanisms.

The VisitBritain Domestic Sentiment Tracker September 2026 record adds a mobility-and-discretionary-consumption test. UK overnight-trip intention recovered to 78%, but 53.8% identified costs and finances as a barrier, 28.5% rising cost of living, and 27.2% rising holiday/leisure costs; among intended domestic trips, 62.1% were short breaks of one to three nights versus 34.3% holidays of four or more nights. The cross-source implication is demand recovery with constrained conversion and possible trip compression. The tracker measures stated intention, not completed travel, spending, cultural participation, or household welfare.

The England Community and Engagement Survey Quarter 2 record adds a current culture-and-community conversion test. From January–March 2025 to January–March 2026, in-person arts engagement fell from 90% to 83% while digital arts engagement moved from 34% to 36%; library use rose from 27% to 31% physically and 16% to 18% digitally, while monthly formal volunteering rose from 16% to 18% and local-official contact from 13% to 15%. The cross-source implication is selective hybridization and civic activation rather than one overall engagement trend. The release is a redesigned repeated cross-section and does not establish substitution, causality, institutional response, or durable cohesion.

The European Commission Consumer Conditions Scoreboard record adds a 29-country consumer-protection baseline beneath the platform cases. Online buying reached 76% in 2024, but 26% of online buyers reported a legitimate complaint problem versus 16% of offline buyers; 45% encountered online scams, 66% fake reviews, and 61% misleading discounts. Meanwhile, only 61% trusted public organisations to protect consumer rights, and environmental purchasing fell 13 percentage points since 2022 to 43%. The cross-source implication is an adoption-with-protection-gap pattern: reach and choice expand faster than trustworthy execution, remedy confidence, and sustainable conversion. The survey does not establish causal fraud loss, platform attribution, or household welfare.

The Australian ACCC Dendy Cinema record extends the late-fee pattern from platforms and live-event ticketing into a physical cinema venue. Dendy paid an A$19,800 infringement-notice penalty after an unavoidable per-ticket booking fee was excluded from the prominently displayed online price until late in checkout; the ACCC also said it was examining cinema pricing more broadly. The cross-source implication is that cultural access can be distorted by price-interface timing even when the cultural service is physical and local, because consumers spend time selecting a film and session before seeing the minimum payable amount. The ACCC notes that the notice is based on alleged conduct and is not an admission; the case does not quantify attendance loss or consumer harm.

The European Commission/CPC Vinted record supplies an implementation case alongside the commitment-only Viagogo evidence. Following complaints, Vinted modified its EU/EEA website and app to disclose total price including the automatically added buyer-protection fee, clarify refunds for nondelivery and counterfeits, improve seller identity and review information, and remove misleading free-purchase impressions; however, the Commission still identifies an unresolved request about early delivery-fee disclosure. The cross-source implication is that platform governance can produce real interface and remedy changes while leaving a late-stage price gap intact. The source does not quantify harm, refund completion, affordability, or consumer behavior.

The European Commission/CPC Viagogo record broadens the UK ticketing cases into an EU/EEA platform-governance layer. Viagogo committed to disclose seller identity and marketplace role, clarify total-price and delivery-fee conditions, explain search ranking, display seat information, reduce countdown pressure, improve fraud/cancellation handling, extend refund windows, and preserve local legal routes. The cross-source implication is that cultural access is governed by a stack of platform surfaces—identity, price, ranking, pressure, contract, and remedy—not only by ticket supply or headline affordability. The Commission says implementation would be actively monitored, but also records unresolved asks around upfront delivery-fee amounts and consumers' additional rights against sellers or organizers; the commitments therefore do not yet verify implementation, compliance, consumer outcomes, or participation effects.

The UK CMA Ticketmaster/Oasis record adds a second linked live-event pricing episode and distinguishes remedy types. After investigating dynamic-pricing, labeling, queue-pressure, and price-information concerns, the CMA accepted undertakings requiring 24-hour advance notice of tiered pricing, better price information during online queues, no misleading labels, and two years of reporting; unlike the StubHub case, the case page states no direct refund total. The cross-source implication is that consumer protection can convert harm into either retrospective monetary redress or prospective information and monitoring controls, depending on whether individual loss is measurable and recoverable. The case does not establish future compliance, restored affordability, or attendance effects.

The UK CMA StubHub hidden-fees record adds a linked consumer-culture episode beneath the participation surveys. Mandatory ticket fees were added at the final checkout stage during 6 April-7 December 2025; the CMA ordered automatic refunds to 51,350 customers totaling more than £590,000, fined StubHub UK £889,200, and recorded that the conduct ended. The cross-source implication is that cultural access is partly a price-interface and recourse problem: a nominally available event can become less comparable and less affordable at the point of purchase, while remedy design determines whether consumers must spend additional time and effort to recover. The case does not establish attendance exclusion, complete refund receipt, deterrence, or equal access.

The France Ministry of Culture/CREDOC cultural-outings record adds a recovery-with-stratification test. In 2024, cinema reached 60%, live performance 49%, monuments 64%, and libraries 37%, broadly returning to pre-pandemic levels; however, museum attendance was 25% among people below the baccalaureate versus 62% among those with bac+3 or more, and 30% among low-income people versus 54% among high-income people. The cross-source implication is that aggregate cultural recovery can coexist with durable inequality in conversion capacity: restored supply and headline participation do not equal equal access. The survey does not identify causal price, time, transport, or educational mechanisms.

The England DCMS Participation Survey 2024/25 record adds a physical-digital conversion test to the Spain findings. Ninety-one percent of adults engaged with the arts, but only 1% did so exclusively digitally; 34% engaged both physically and digitally, while libraries reached 31% overall with 26% physical and 16% digital engagement. The cross-source implication is that digital cultural access usually layers onto institutions and embodied participation rather than replacing them, and that digitization changes the task mix by sector. The survey does not identify causal affordability, time, or platform-substitution mechanisms.

The Spain Ministry of Culture cultural-habits record adds a mature direct-participation and platform layer. Among people aged 15 and above, 64.9% read a book in the previous year, 47.6% visited a museum, exhibition, or gallery, 47.1% attended a live cultural performance, and 48.5% went to the cinema; 74.1% had a household subscription to at least one digital platform, while paper reading, digital/audiobook reading, physical library visits, and online library access overlapped. The cross-source implication is that cultural recovery is not simply physical or digital: participation is broad, but the access system is hybrid and platform-mediated, with content-type and sex differences in practice. The survey does not identify causal affordability, subscription burden, frequency intensity, or substitution.

The Stats SA South Africa Volunteer Activities Survey 2024 record adds an unpaid social-capacity layer. South Africa counted 3.1 million volunteers and a 6.9% volunteer rate; direct volunteering exceeded organizational volunteering, 91.3% cited a cause they believed in, and rates varied by sex, population group, labor-market status, and province. The cross-source implication is that cultural/social agency can be widespread while formal organizational infrastructure remains thinner; food reciprocity and labor-market position also complicate a simple altruism story. The release does not establish causal cohesion, institutional durability, or welfare.

The DANE Colombia CSECC 2025 preliminary record adds a supply-and-labor layer beneath direct cultural participation. Real cultural/creative value added grew 2.6% in 2025, with arts and heritage up 4.3% and functional creations up 2.9%, but cultural industries fell 1.1%; total employment rose 1.7% while cultural-industry employment fell 2.3%. The cross-source implication is that cultural abundance and sectoral labor security can diverge: functional and heritage growth does not guarantee expansion across audiovisual/editorial industries or stable work. The satellite account does not measure household attendance, earnings distribution, or consumer welfare.

The INEGI Mexico MODECULT 2025 record adds direct cultural-participation evidence. Comparable adult attendance reached 61.2% in 2025, up from 52.5% in 2024 but still 2.8 percentage points below 2016; the redesigned 12+ data show strong age, education, Indigenous-language, disability, time, cost, online-consumption, artistic-activity, and organizing gradients. The cross-source implication is that cultural recovery is a conversion problem: attendance, household room, digital access, artistic agency, and institutional organizing are separate stages. The survey does not establish causal barriers or cultural welfare.

The INEGI Mexico ENIGH 2024 record adds a direct household-budget and cultural-conversion layer. Average monthly monetary household expenditure was 15,891 pesos, up 7.9% from 2022 in 2024 pesos; education and recreation represented 9.6% of spending, but education remained 21.0% below 2016, while the first-to-tenth income decile gap, gender gap, Indigenous-language gap, and state differences remained substantial. The cross-source implication is that aggregate retail or expenditure recovery can coexist with constrained cultural room and unequal conversion capacity. ENIGH is a household survey, not a real-time 2026 panel or causal cultural-participation study.

The IBGE Brazil July 2026 retail record adds a Latin American category-and-region layer. Retail volume fell 0.8% month over month but rose 1.2% year over year; food retail rose 2.9% year over year and pharmaceuticals/cosmetics 4.7%, while clothing fell 4.7% year over year and books/stationery fell 4.2% month over month. The cross-source implication is selective consumer adaptation: essential and health-related categories can expand while apparel, household durables, and cultural-goods retail weaken. The enterprise series does not measure households, cultural attendance, online commerce, or causal substitution.

The Statistics Canada July 2026 retail record adds a Canada channel-and-region divergence layer. Retail sales were C$73.7 billion, down 0.7% month over month but up 5.1% year over year, while volume fell 1.1%; e-commerce fell 3.5% to C$5.5 billion and 7.5% of retail trade, Ontario fell 2.0%, and Alberta rose 1.4%. The cross-source implication is that nominal annual resilience can coexist with immediate volume, online-channel, and regional pullback. The release does not identify household welfare, unique consumers, causal substitution, or durable retrenchment.

The India UPI infrastructure record adds a payment-rail layer beneath online commerce. In FY2025–26, UPI processed 24,161.69 crore transactions worth ₹314 lakh crore, with volume up 30.0%, value up 20.59%, 85% of India’s digital payments, and 703 live banks. The cross-source implication is that digital payment infrastructure can become dominant while the consumer-level questions remain open: unique-user access, repeated low-value use, fraud, fees, device capability, and remedy are not contained in throughput. The primary monthly NPCI page was access-limited in this pass, so the record uses the accessible PIB retrospective for the cited annual figures.

The South Korea July 2026 online-shopping record adds a mobile-commerce and convenience-service layer. Online-shopping transaction value rose 7.3% year over year and mobile value 6.4%, but mobile’s share slipped to 78.0%; food services, groceries, auto goods, and travel/transport grew while clothing declined. The cross-source implication is that digital commerce can expand through essential, delivered, or mobility-linked services without representing uniform discretionary or cultural expansion. The release does not identify households, unique users, or causal platform substitution.

The Hong Kong July 2026 retail record adds an Asian category-polarization layer. Nominal retail sales rose 4.5% and real volume 2.3%, while online sales rose 9.5%; jewellery, watches, and valuable gifts rose 19.7%, but books/newspapers/stationery/gifts fell 2.8%, apparel 1.8%, vehicles 18.2%, and fuel 18.0%. The cross-source implication is that headline retail growth can coexist with sharply different cultural, mobility, and status-consumption paths. The data do not identify households, visitors, or causal polarization.

The Statistics South Africa July 2026 retail record adds an African real-retail counterpoint. Real retail sales rose 3.4% year over year and 2.5% month over month, led by general dealers, other retailers, clothing/footwear/leather, and specialized food/beverage/tobacco. The cross-source implication is that retail growth can coexist with very different household and cultural conditions: category growth may be essential, general-dealer, or place-specific rather than broad discretionary expansion. The series does not identify household trajectories or equal access.

The Japan Statistics Bureau Household Economy record adds a channel-conversion layer to the household contraction finding. In July 2026, online-shopping expenditure fell 0.7% nominally year over year, the household use rate fell 2.4 points to 55.6%, and tickets contributed −0.53 percentage points to the spending change. The cross-source implication is that “consumer decline” can occur at multiple gates—household room, channel reach, and cultural-ticket conversion—and each needs separate evidence. The release does not measure attendance, individual trajectories, or causal substitution.

The Japan Statistics Bureau household-account record adds the household-level counterpoint to aggregate and establishment data. In July 2026, average two-or-more-person household consumption fell 3.6% in real terms year over year and workers’ household income fell 3.8% in real terms. The cross-source implication is that observed retail or national-account growth in one market cannot be generalized into global consumer recovery; household composition, prices, income, and measurement unit change the conclusion. The survey does not isolate cultural spending or establish causal mechanisms.

The ONS Great Britain retail-sales record adds an establishment-based channel and mobility-cost layer. Retail volume rose 0.5% month over month and 2.4% year over year in August, while online sales value rose 8.9% year over year to 28.8% of retail sales; fuel volumes fell as retailers reported some motorists partially filling tanks under price pressure. The cross-source implication is selective consumer adaptation: online convenience, cultural/sport categories, and mobility can move in different directions, so a single “consumer recovery” headline is too coarse. ONS retail data do not identify household trajectories or causal behavior.

The BEA August 2026 Personal Income and Outlays record adds an aggregate consumption-flow layer beneath household surveys and card/footfall indicators. Current-dollar PCE rose 0.9% month over month and real PCE 0.6%, while real disposable personal income was flat and the saving rate rose to 4.1%; goods supplied 59.8% of the monthly current-dollar increase. The cross-source implication is that consumer expansion can coexist with flat real income and selective household protection, so aggregate growth must be joined to distribution, debt, price, and cultural-participation evidence. These national accounts do not identify household trajectories or causal substitution.

The GSMA ASEAN Consumer Scam record adds a digital-consumer recourse test across Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam. The report says 8% experienced a scam in the prior year, 68% of victims lost money, 82% of money-losing victims recovered none, and 45% of reported cases remained unresolved; victims were more than twice as likely to switch accounts or providers. The cross-source implication is that digital trust depends on visible resolution, recovery, and coordinated institutional response—not only awareness or protective behavior. The source is industry-commissioned and not administrative prevalence data.

The EU Special Eurobarometer sport record adds a routine-and-social-infrastructure layer to cultural and consumer participation. In 2026, 39% reported never exercising, while active commuting reached 37% and fitness-centre attendance 39%; 93% believed activity improves mental health and 86% believed it helps community building, with inactivity reaching 68% in Portugal. The cross-source implication is that social meaning and stated benefit do not automatically convert into accessible routine behavior; transport, time, price, place, and country context remain open mechanisms.

The MBIE New Zealand Domestic Visitor Survey record adds the resident-side conversion test. In the October 2025 wave, 61% took an overnight trip and 47% a qualifying day trip; 36% of overnight trips included a museum/gallery visit and 13% a Māori cultural site, while 32% of planned overnight travellers cited cost as a barrier. The cross-source implication is that international tourism recovery cannot stand in for domestic cultural access: realized travel, future intention, cost, social motivation, and cultural activity are separate stages.

The MBIE New Zealand IVS record adds an observed international-mobility and cultural-experience layer. For the year ending June 2026, visitor volume reached 94% of 2019 and inflation-adjusted spend 98%; holiday travel was 53% versus 51% in 2019, while Australia and USA volumes reached 105% of 2019. The cross-source implication is that recovery is composition-sensitive: arrivals, real spend, purpose, market, cultural experience, and regional benefit are distinct stages.

The MHRC Poll 29 record adds a Canadian bridge from material pressure through social connection to institutional continuity. In the July-August 2026 weighted online survey, 46% said cost of living negatively affected mental health, 37% had difficulty fully paying household bills, and 35% had difficulty affording or maintaining stable housing; among those accessing support in the past five years, 52% ended care earlier than planned or needed, while only 29% of recent support users said needs were fully met. The cross-source implication is that access, adequacy, and continuity are distinct stages, with social connection and time scarcity surrounding them; all relationships remain associative and survey-based.

The England CES loneliness record adds the social-consequence test beneath household room and cultural participation. The national often/always-lonely rate held at 7%, but it was 14% for disabled people versus 3% for non-disabled people, 11% in the most deprived areas versus 4% in the least deprived, and ranged from 13% to 2% across local authorities. The cross-source implication is that national stability can coexist with sharply unequal exposure and place capacity; the survey does not establish causal pathways or intervention effects.

The ONS real-time consumer record adds a UK administrative/card-payment contrast to annual surveys and payment diaries. In August 2026, retail footfall fell 2% month-on-month, total Revolut debit spending fell 1%, entertainment spending rose 14% year-on-year, and sampled Direct Debit failures rose from 2.3% to 2.4%; fuel quantity demanded per transaction also weakened as fuel-price growth accelerated. The cross-source implication is that “consumer weakness” is not one scalar: physical presence, category spending, recurring-payment reliability, and mobility-cost exposure can move differently. These are experimental aggregated indicators, not household trajectories.

The China NBS August 2026 retail/CPI record adds a high-frequency non-Western consumer-composition layer. Total retail sales rose only 0.4% year-on-year in August, while online service retail rose 5.1% year-to-date, telecom equipment rose 27.3%, and motor vehicles fell 18.5%; education/culture/recreation prices rose 1.4% and residence prices fell 0.3%. The cross-source implication is that aggregate consumer growth and lived consumer room require category, channel, and price decomposition. These are national aggregates, not household trajectories.

Checked: 2026-09-30 Status: living cross-source synthesis; no single causal chain claimed Scope: the current machine-readable trend/case registry and its linked analysis layers

The current registry contains 2003 machine-readable records, 5972 observations,

The latest US wage-and-consumer rotation adds the NBER sticky-wage record: 43% of same-firm workers experienced real-wage decline across 2021–2024, 37% of all workers did, and job changers' wages rose nearly one-for-one with inflation. The cross-source implication is that firm wage rules are an upstream part of household room and consumer sentiment, but the payroll source does not observe the same workers' spending, debt, care, trust, or political action.

The latest US industrial rotation adds the NBER creative-destruction record: rival innovation passes asymmetric downside into incumbent-worker earnings and job-destruction risk, while the model allows upward mobility for lower-income workers and concentrated downside for high-income workers. The cross-source implication is that innovation policy must track firm gains, worker losses, mobility, household room, and voice separately.

The latest US firm-insurance rotation adds the NBER firm-insurance and labor-income-risk record: higher risk premia erode firm insurance, bad-times pass-through of firm shocks into earnings rises, and lower-paid workers near separation are especially exposed. The cross-source implication is that financial conditions can become worker risk before they appear as household hardship; the next test must connect a named firm or sector to pay, hours, separation, household room, and remedy.

The latest US labor-rule comparison adds the NBER overtime-coverage record: expanded coverage raises earnings without a detected employment decline, while employers raise salaries above the threshold rather than reduce base pay or substitute more workers for fewer hours. Together with firm-insurance and creative-destruction evidence, this shows that worker risk is not one direction: financing shocks can pass risk into earnings, while a labor rule can raise pay without the expected job loss. The missing test is whether the overtime result changed paid hours, time control, household room, and durable worker bargaining.

The latest US firm-structure rotation adds the NBER dynamic-investment and product-market-rivalry record: product rivalry drives investment and capital allocation, cost-of-capital shocks generate heterogeneous markup and investment responses, monopoly rents take a rising share of firm value, and mergers since 1995 are associated with modestly lower aggregate capital formation but uneven firm-level markup changes. The cross-source implication is that financial conditions can alter both worker insurance and firm concentration, but firm value is not consumer welfare; the next test must follow a named industry or merger into prices, suppliers, workers, and remedy.

The latest US measurement correction adds the NBER monopsony framework record: firm-specific residual labor-supply elasticity is the organizing measure of labor-market power, while search frictions, worker preferences, employer concentration, and wage-setting practices are distinct sources. The cross-source implication is that a wage markdown or concentration statistic cannot stand in for worker power; the named-industry test must observe outside options, mobility, wage-setting, voice, and welfare together.

The latest US AI-firm rotation adds the NBER organization-capital record: AI-skilled employment and job-description-based organization capital are associated with recent productivity growth, while the existing project summary reports a 6.2 percentage-point sales-per-worker association for 2018–2024. Together with the investment, monopsony, and worker-risk records, this separates firm productivity from worker control and household benefit; the next test must follow AI investment into workforce composition, pay, monitoring, prices, and customer outcomes.

The latest US payment-infrastructure rotation adds the NBER payment convenience record: faster transfers are associated with more transfers and lower deposit growth, while delays raise deposit demand. The cross-source implication is that payment speed is also a bank-funding and monetary-transmission mechanism; the next test is whether that infrastructure change alters household liquidity, completion, fraud exposure, and recourse.

The latest US consumer-finance rotation adds the NBER Credit Card Banking record: broad card coverage and household borrowing coexist with an average rate near 22%, an 18-point spread over the short rate, and reported 6.8% lender ROA after expenses. The cross-source implication is that consumer access, lender profitability, and household welfare are different stages; the next test is a borrower-weighted link from product terms and credit tier to payment burden, remedy, alternatives, and exit.

The Brazil BCB Pix-conversion record adds a Latin American diary-and-preference test to the South African payment findings. Cash fell from 76.6% of recorded payments in 2019 to 40.5% in 2023, while Pix reached 24.9%; however, 17.3% had not used Pix in the prior year and 37.3% of nonusers cited lack of knowledge, while 24.2% sometimes chose another method because of internet-access difficulty. The cross-source implication is that infrastructure growth, stated preference, observed transactions, and executable capability must be separated.

The South Africa SARB Payments Study record adds a payment-diary test to the Kenya digital-finance and ICT layers. In 2023, cash represented 56% of estimated payment volume but 21% of value, while debit cards represented 34% of volume and 55% of value; low-income consumers were 36% of the diary population but 16% of payment value, while high-income consumers were 14% of the population but 28% of value. The cross-source implication is that payment adoption, transaction value, and realized frequency are different consumer stages, and recall surveys can overstate short-window observed use.

The Kenya FinAccess record adds the downstream financial-consumer stage to the prior connectivity finding. In 2024, mobile-money usage reached 82.3% and daily use 52.6%, while credit use reached 64.0% and savings use fell to 68.1%; 16.6% of borrowers completely defaulted and 9.8% of mobile-money users reported losses. The cross-source implication is that digital reach converts into high-frequency financial behavior, but access does not guarantee suitability, resilience, or remedy. The survey is descriptive and uses different conditional denominators for users, borrowers, and the adult population.

The Kenya KNBS ICT record adds a digital-funnel distinction beneath cultural and consumer access. In 2024, 64.9% of individuals used a mobile phone but only 35.0% used the internet; household internet connection was 54.1% urban versus 25.1% rural, and county internet use ranged from 64.7% in Nairobi City to 9.1% in West Pokot. The cross-source implication is that mobile reach should not be treated as equivalent to household digital optionality: device ownership, shared use, fixed access, geography, and privacy can determine whether online cultural or consumer behavior is executable.

The India MoSPI HCES record adds an observed consumer-budget layer beneath cultural supply and time constraints. In 2023–24, average monthly per-capita consumption was ₹4,122 rural versus ₹6,996 urban; non-food items represented 53% versus 60% of MPCE; and the top-to-bottom-5% average MPCE ratio was about 6.0× rural and 8.6× urban. The cross-source implication is that cultural and discretionary “choice” should be read through household resource distributions, not only supply, access, or stated interest. The survey does not isolate entertainment spending or cultural attendance.

The Colombia DANE ENUT record adds a direct time-budget test beneath cultural and consumer choice. In the preliminary October 2024–March 2025 results, 90.0% of women aged 10+ participated in unpaid work on the reference day versus 65.5% of men; among participants, women averaged 7h35m versus 3h12m for men. Foreign-born women averaged 9h31m versus 7h30m for Colombia-born women. The cross-source implication is that “participation” needs a time-conversion layer: cultural supply or digital access cannot be interpreted as equal optionality when unpaid work consumes different amounts of household time. The release is preliminary and its averages are conditional on participation.

The Indonesia BPS socio-cultural record adds a nationwide non-European participation test. In 2025, 88.87% of residents aged 10+ participated in neighborhood social-community activity, but only 11.06% were registered in an organization outside work or school; meeting participation was 43.22% for men versus 24.81% for women, and 41.13% of meeting participants gave a suggestion or opinion. The cross-source implication is that social cohesion cannot be inferred from one participation rate: recurring community activity, formal affiliation, access to a meeting, and voice within it are separate conversion stages. The survey is descriptive and self-reported, and high activity participation may include periodic religious or life-event obligations.

The Eurostat leisure-affordability record adds the household-room boundary beneath cultural and digital supply. In 2025, 27.5% of EU residents could not afford a week away from home and 12.1% could not afford regular leisure participation; holiday exclusion ranged from 61.4% in Romania to 10.6% in Luxembourg. The cross-source implication is that more cultural supply and online access do not automatically yield more participation when households cannot finance mobility or recurring leisure.

The Eurostat cultural-employment record supplies the production-side counterpart to online ticketing and streaming. Europe’s cultural sector employed 8.9 million people, or 4.3% of employment, in 2025; 61.9% had tertiary education, and cultural employment ranged from 5.7% of total employment in the Netherlands to 1.8% in Romania. The cross-source implication is that cultural consumption depends on a large but credential-intensive and place-stratified labor system; employment does not by itself establish output, access, or cultural welfare.

The Eurostat online event-ticket record adds a transaction-stage bridge between digital access and cultural attendance. In 2025, 26.8% of EU individuals bought event tickets online in the prior three months, up 3.8 points from 2024, but country rates ranged from 51.5% in Ireland to 11.4% in Bulgaria. The cross-source implication is that digital cultural consumption is not simply “online versus offline”: payment, platform, place, and event supply determine whether interest converts into an acquired ticket and then into attendance.

The Eurostat social-network record adds a population-use layer across Europe. In 2025, 89.3% of 16–29-year-olds used social networks versus 67.3% of the general 16–74 population; youth use ranged from 80.3% to 98.3%, and age gaps varied from 7.2 to 29.2 percentage points across selected countries. The cross-source implication is that platform sociality is near-default for youth but remains nationally and generationally differentiated; usage alone does not establish connection quality or benefit.

The Ofcom telecom switching and remedy record connects household cost pressure to actual exit and firm response. More than 3.43 million people started the One Touch Switch process, but Ofcom also found millions of likely mishandled Virgin Media cancellation calls, over one million callers forced to repeat requests, and a £28 million fine. The cross-source implication is that competition is a lived process: consumer power requires a usable exit route, not just nominal alternatives or advertised savings.

The UK Financial Ombudsman record adds a recourse-stage test to the consumer-harm chain. New complaints fell from 305,700 to 214,600 in 2025/26, but professional-representative cases fell from 50% to 18% after charges were introduced, while withdrawal/abandonment fell from 35% to 18%; only 30% of resolved complaints were upheld overall. The cross-source implication is that complaint counts are jointly produced by harm, awareness, representation, fees, preparation, and institutional routing—not a clean measure of consumer harm alone.

The Ofcom protective-defaults record adds an experimental platform-governance layer. In mock-platform trials, safer defaults were retained at high rates across age groups; prior experiments found reduced-sensitive-content selection at 15% under a permissive default versus 42% under a protective default, and children retained a no-harmful-recommendations setting at roughly 70% with a default versus 50% without one. The cross-source implication is that user safety is partly a starting-state problem, not only a matter of individual literacy or vigilance. The experiment does not establish live-service harm reduction or long-run behavior.

The Statistics Canada time-use record adds a long-run behavioral layer to the program's time-and-social-capacity chain. High time pressure rose from 15.0% in 1992 to 24.2% in 2022; the share seeing friends on an average day fell from 47.9% in 1986 to 19.3% in 2022; and among those who did see friends, average contact fell from 5.0 to 3.8 hours. The cross-source implication is that cultural and social participation face a hidden time price, while the series cannot identify causal displacement, digital substitution, or loneliness.

The Philippines PSA NICTHS cybersecurity record adds the protection layer beneath the social-commerce finding. Among ICT-device users, 62.5% experienced at least one cybersecurity incident in 2024, but only 33.4% of people aged 10+ were aware of cybersecurity/data privacy and just 1.9% of victims reported incidents to authorities; SMS fraud affected 57.1% of victims. The cross-source implication is that mobile-first commerce is also a trust, fraud, and recourse system, with awareness stratified by education and place. This is not forensic incident evidence or a causal platform-liability finding.

The Philippines PSA NICTHS e-commerce record converts the access-and-intensity pattern into observable consumer behavior. In 2024, 36.7% of internet users purchased online, 15.4% sold goods or services for income, and 94.4% of online goods sellers used social media; however, 97.6% of buyers preferred cash on delivery, 42.9% cited security concerns around electronic payment, and 71.7% of non-buyers preferred in-person shopping. The cross-source implication is that digital consumer adoption is not a single funnel: connectivity, attention, commerce, seller livelihood, delivery, payment trust, and offline habit are separate stages.

The Indonesia BPS telecommunications record broadens the mobile-first pattern beyond Ghana, South Africa, and the Philippines. Internet use reached 72.78% of the population, 99.08% of internet users used mobile cellular devices, computer ownership was 18.52% of households, and fixed-line telephony only 0.99%; public-place and in-vehicle access were also material. The cross-source implication is that digital cultural and consumer life is increasingly organized around handsets and movement, with “home internet” often meaning mobile use at home rather than stable fixed broadband.

The Ghana NCA Q2 2026 telecom record adds an administrative market check to the Philippines and South Africa household access layers. Ghana's mobile internet subscriptions rose from 23.2 million to 30.5 million and penetration from 71.6% to 89.5% since Q4 2023, while mobile voice minutes per subscription fell 11.7%; fibre broadband reached only 294,626 subscriptions. The emerging cross-source pattern is mobile-first digital reach with a possible shift from voice to data-mediated connection, but subscription counts cannot establish unique-person use, cultural behavior, or welfare.

The Philippines PSA NICTHS 2024 record adds a use-intensity layer to South Africa's mobile-first access finding. Home access rose to 48.8%, 67.3% of people aged 10+ used the internet, 98.8% of users used a cellphone, 76.9% used it daily, and average use was 4.6 hours per day. But home access ranged from 68.7% in NCR to 27.7% in BARMM. The cross-source implication is that mobile connectivity can produce high attention intensity without equal household reach, stable quality, or equal cultural and consumer optionality.

The South Africa GHS 2025 record adds the infrastructure layer beneath Brazil's mobile-first cultural use and the wider digital/home shift. Internet access reached 85.6% of households somewhere, but fixed-home access was only 20.6%; provincial any-access ranged from 93.8% to 74.5%, and fixed-home access from 49.7% to 5.9%. The cross-source implication is that “online access” is not one consumer condition: mobile affordability, fixed reliability, public access, privacy, food security, and household structure can produce very different cultural and social experiences behind the same headline connectivity rate.

The France INSEE cultural-leisure spending record supplies an observed-spending counterpart to the French attendance barometer. Within the cultural, sports, and leisure basket, cultural services rose from 8.6% of spending in 2021 to 12.4% in 2025, while books/press/stationery fell from 13.6% to 9.9% and durable cultural/recreational goods from 11.3% to 9.0%. Combined with South Korea's attendance-to-active-participation divergence and China's cultural-enterprise channel shift, the emerging hypothesis is a broader move from ownership and one-off attendance toward services, subscriptions, active participation, and platform-mediated access. The data do not prove that mechanism.

The China NBS cultural-enterprise H1 2026 record adds the missing production-side counterpart to household and attendance data. Cultural enterprises above designated size grew 4.6% overall, but information and creative-design services grew 9.2%, cultural communication channels contracted 3.2%, and consumer-terminal production was nearly flat. The cross-source implication is that a cultural economy can expand while distribution and value capture move between production, design, information, channels, and platforms; revenue growth alone cannot stand in for audience reach or cultural welfare.

The South Korea MCST 2025 culture and leisure record complicates a simple participation-decline story. Direct cultural attendance fell to 60.2%, with film attendance down 6.4 points, but active cultural/arts participation rose to 5.8%, cultural-arts education to 8.6%, and broader leisure continuity rose to 43.2% while satisfaction reached 64.0%. Alongside France's place and income gradients and Brazil's home-first consumption, this suggests that cultural change is occurring across modes—commercial attendance, active making, education, routine leisure, and digital/home use—rather than on one attendance axis.

The French Ministry of Culture 2025 outings barometer sharpens the physical-access side of the digital-to-place question. Cinema, monuments, and live shows remained broadly near pre-pandemic attendance levels, but cinema ranged from 76% among 15–24-year-olds to 45% among people aged 70+, from 71% among high-income groups to 46% among low-income groups, and from 64% in large urban centres to 48% in dispersed rural areas. Museum and festival attendance also frequently involved overnight travel. Across France, Spain, Norway, Mexico, Brazil, and England, the emerging pattern is not simply digital versus physical: cultural optionality is sorted by age, education, income, place, time, and mobility.

The Brazil Ministry of Culture habits and policy record adds a digital-domestic cultural-consumption and symbolic-legitimacy layer. In the last 30 days, music, films, and series reached 53%, 52%, and 40%, while lack of time (33%) exceeded lack of money (24%) as a reported barrier; intended return to cinema (33%) and music shows/festivals (27%) shows that home-first access does not eliminate demand for shared venues. Approval of CEUs da Cultura (81%) and Paulo Gustavo/Aldir Blanc (73%) coexisted with 74% reporting no awareness of the named laws, suggesting that cultural policy can be socially valuable as a symbolic state-capacity signal even when its detailed mechanisms are poorly understood. This is not a causal legitimacy estimate.

The Chile ENPCCL 2024 cultural-participation record adds a useful hidden-price finding: cultural access can fail through time scarcity and fatigue before it fails through money. Overall participation was 75.4%, but 28.7% reported unmet cultural demand; among that group, lack of time/fatigue (30.9%) exceeded economic reasons (20.1%), alongside large SES and disability gradients. This supports a bounded bridge from time, care, work, and accessibility to participation—not a causal claim.

The Statistics Canada accessibility-and-travel record extends that bridge from desire and time into mobility realization. Among people with disabilities or long-term conditions who considered an out-of-town trip, 29% reported possible accessibility barriers discouraging or preventing it; the share was 46% with greater daily-activity difficulty versus 19% with less. The source supports a transport/interface bottleneck hypothesis, not a cultural-trip or provider-fault conclusion.

The England DCMS Participation Survey 2024/25 record adds the realized mode split: 90% engaged physically with the arts and 35% digitally, with 56% physical-only. Deprivation gradients appeared in both modes—81% versus 95% physical and 31% versus 39% digital from most to least deprived—so digital culture is not yet a general replacement for place-based access. This is cross-sectional participation evidence, not a causal account of transport, price, or preference.

The ONS August 2026 social-trends record adds a current adaptation layer: reported cost pressure translated into non-essential cutbacks, shopping-around, and some reductions in food or essentials, while drought and restrictions produced widespread water-saving routines. The useful bridge is pressure -> household action -> time, quantity, quality, and welfare, with the survey unable to observe the final outcomes.

The ONS Family Spending FYE 2025 record supplies the observed-spending counterpart: real average household expenditure increased 5% and recreation/culture rose £6.70 per week, yet the richest fifth spent 2.7 times the poorest and increased weekly spending by £98.10 versus £18.10. The cross-source implication is selective recovery, not uniform consumer relief; prices, quantities, household composition, debt, and actual use remain open links.

The CFPB Bilt transition record adds an observed remedy stage to the voice-and-trust chain. A named bank-partner transition generated fee-related consumer harm; the CFPB reports proactive outreach, more than $264,000 in reimbursement to over 2,000 eligible consumers, technical remediation, monitoring, and closure. This is stronger than a stated intention to remedy, but it remains an agency-reported single episode: individual receipt, residual burden, retention, satisfaction, and durable trust change are still unobserved.

The Credit Acceptance Corporation settlement record adds a mobility-specific consumer-remedy layer. The New York Attorney General reports more than $630 million in debt relief for more than 55,000 consumers, $60 million in restitution, and distinct treatment for borrowers whose vehicles were repossessed versus retained; future qualifying loans receive risk disclosures and a possible 95%-debt-waiver off-ramp. The cross-source implication is that financial harm becomes cultural and social through transportation access and household room, while payment receipt, credit repair, mobility continuity, and compliance remain open.

The China NBS 2025 household-consumption record widens the cultural-consumer comparison beyond the recent U.S./European expenditure layers. Education, culture, and recreation spending rose 9.4% to 3,489 yuan per person, but urban spending was 4,298 yuan versus 2,322 yuan rural. The signal is rising cultural-consumption room with persistent place stratification; it does not identify actual participation, price-adjusted quantities within the category, or cultural meaning.

The Saudi GASTAT household culture and entertainment record supplies the missing participation denominator conceptually: 81.6% visited a cultural event or activity and 85.3% visited entertainment, but only 39.0% practiced a cultural activity. The venue mix—parks and gardens 65.8%, cinemas 24.9%, museums 13.4%, literary or poetry events 2.5%—suggests broad everyday participation alongside a steep formal-venue gradient. The source cannot identify whether cost, supply, transport, preference, or social meaning creates that gradient.

The Norwegian Cultural Barometer 2025 record adds persistence and unmet-demand evidence. Cinema attendance was 62% in 2025 versus 72% in 2016, theatre 37% versus 50%, while library participation stabilized near pre-pandemic levels and roughly eight in ten 9–15-year-olds visited a library. The cross-source pattern is not “culture recovered” or “culture collapsed,” but venue-specific recovery shaped by age, time, money, and competing attention.

The Spain Ministry of Culture habits record adds a digital-to-place bridge: monthly audiovisual and music use were 80.4% and 77.3%, while annual monument, museum/exhibition/gallery, live-event, and cinema participation ranged from 48.3% to 54.3%; photography, painting, and video creation were also common active practices. This suggests digital reach and physical participation can coexist, while the provisional sample and cross-sectional design do not identify substitution or causal recovery.

The Mexico INEGI MODECULT 2025 record sharpens the inequality layer: 64.7% of people aged 12+ attended a cultural event, but the rate was 80.9% among 12–24-year-olds, 82.8% among people with higher education, and 48.3% among people with disabilities. Fairs and cinema were major gateways, while audiovisual creation accounted for 61.0% among people reporting artistic activities, not all residents. The source makes the access gradient measurable without claiming that education, age, disability, or language status alone causes it.

The India Time Use Survey 2024 record makes the hidden time price observable: 93.0% participated in the broad culture/leisure/media/sports category during the reference day, but women carried much more unpaid domestic and care time, while culture/leisure/media time per person was 148 minutes for women versus 169 for men. This does not prove that unpaid work caused the gap, but it shows why participation rates alone cannot establish equal cultural optionality.

The ECB Consumer Expectations Survey August 2026 record adds the forward-looking layer: euro-area consumers expected nominal spending to grow 3.6% against nominal income growth of 1.0%, while lower-income households expected materially worse unemployment and mortgage-rate conditions. The combined ONS/ECB signal is a widening gap between aggregate spending recovery, perceived future room, and distributional capacity—not a single confidence trend.

The European Commission September 2026 consumer-survey record adds a broader EU timing signal: consumer confidence reversed after four months of recovery, while inflation expectations, uncertainty, and major-purchase components deteriorated. Across the ONS, ECB, and Commission layers, the open question is whether reported adaptation and sentiment become delayed purchases, substitution, or continued selective spending.

The Eurostat July 2026 retail-trade record provides an observed category check: food retail volume rose while non-food and fuel fell month-over-month, and annual growth was stronger for food than non-food. This is consistent with selective demand protection, but prices, household distribution, and cultural-category behavior remain unobserved in the aggregate index.

The IMF Japan 2026 household-consumption record adds the balance-sheet channel: high debt and high loan-to-value exposure amplify consumption responses to fiscal tightening, and deleveraging can itself suppress current consumption. This makes “weak demand” compatible with active financial repair, not only low confidence or low cultural interest.

The Eurostat online-event-ticketing record adds a transaction-stage cultural signal to the atlas. In 2025, 26.8% of EU individuals aged 16–74 bought event tickets online in the previous three months, up 3.8 percentage points from 2024; the reported country range ran from 51.5% in Ireland to 11.4% in Bulgaria. The cross-source implication is that digital cultural access should be tracked as a gateway with its own price, fee, accessibility, discovery, resale, and intermediary-power conditions. The purchase measure does not establish attendance, affordability, repeat participation, or cultural belonging. The next bridge is ticket transaction -> event use -> repeat participation -> provider and audience value.

The Eurostat paid-streaming subscription record adds the recurring-payment side of that gateway. In 2025, paid film, series, or sports streaming reached 32.7% of EU internet users, ahead of music streaming at 23.0%, online news at 7.2%, and gaming streaming at 6.1%; city access was 35.6% versus 29.0% in rural areas. The cross-source implication is that digital culture is organized through different payment models and unequal place-based access, not one generic “online participation” trend. Subscription presence does not establish actual use, affordability, cancellation power, content quality, or creator income; the next bridge is recurring payment -> use and exit -> discovery and provider value capture.

The ONS creative-industries jobs record adds the production side of the cultural-consumer system. Creative work is estimated to be 13.7% of London jobs versus 5.9% elsewhere, with strong credential and self-employment patterns. This suggests that cultural consumption and cultural production may be organized by the same place, housing, skills, and labor-power constraints—but the APS extract does not measure earnings, job quality, consumption, or causality. The next bridge is creative work -> household room and cultural supply -> local participation and value capture.

The Census HTOPS arts-production and local-opportunity record adds the missing practice and perceived-supply stages. Personal art creation, practice, or performance is higher among younger adults in the four-week window, while perceived local opportunity is much lower in the lowest household-income group. The cross-source implication is that cultural access is organized by both the ability to make culture and the ability to recognize or reach local supply; the release does not establish professional production, venue counts, affordability, or causality. The next bridge is practice -> local supply -> attendance -> repeat participation.

The ONS real-time arts-payment-flow record adds a near-real-time production-network signal. Scottish arts organisations’ payments to other UK arts organisations rose 73% in August versus July while equivalent rest-of-UK payments fell 40%, with recurring August peaks associated with festival activity. This is administrative payment activity, not ticket sales, attendance, jobs, or artist income; the useful bridge is production network -> festival place -> footfall and audience use -> value distribution.

The Eurostat generative-AI use record adds an official population baseline beneath the more speculative AI and consumer records. EU use is sharply age-stratified, and private, professional, and formal-education purposes form different adoption routes. The cross-source implication is that AI’s cultural and consumer effects will depend on who can convert access into reliable tasks, learning, work leverage, or discovery—not on aggregate adoption alone.

The Eurostat enterprise social-media record adds the firm-side counterpart to individual digital adoption. Large enterprises are 28.5 percentage points more likely than small enterprises to use social media, and the country range is 46.7 points. The cross-source implication is that consumer discovery is shaped not only by who uses platforms, but by which firms have the resources to enter, maintain, and benefit from those platforms.

The Eurostat hostile-online-content record adds the user-experience counterpart: exposure to hostile or degrading content declines from roughly 54% among younger adult internet users to 28.1% among ages 65–74, and young women report higher exposure than young men across several identity targets. The cross-source implication is that platform access, enterprise presence, and platform safety form one social infrastructure—but exposure is not yet evidence of harm, moderation failure, or exit.

The Eurostat youth-overcrowding record adds a material-capacity counterpart to the digital-experience lane. Young people are more likely than the total population to live in overcrowded households, with extreme country variation. The cross-source implication is that cultural and consumer autonomy may depend on room, privacy, rest, study, care, and digital capacity before platform choice or cultural preference is observed; the housing indicator does not prove those downstream effects.

The Eurostat parental-home exit record adds a transition-stage measure beneath overcrowding. The age of household exit varies by more than ten years across the EU and broadly tracks youth employment, creating a route from work and housing conditions to privacy, spending control, care exchange, and cultural participation. The release reports an association, not an individual-level causal pathway.

The Census Monthly State Retail Sales record adds a place-by-category consumption layer: June 2026 modeled total retail growth ranged from -7.6% in Alaska to +11.3% in Louisiana, while sporting-goods/books/music retail ranged from -9.6% in D.C. to +24.8% in Alaska. This widens the consumer trend lens beyond national averages, but the product is experimental, nominal, modeled, and subject to revision; it does not identify welfare, preference, or individual behavior.

The ABS General Social Survey 2025 record adds a cultural-social-material tension: cultural attendance and participation were 79% and 48%, and weekly outside-household contact recovered from 41.3% in 2020 to 52.2% in 2025, while cash-flow problems and dissaving rose to 25.3% and 25.7%. The result argues against using social or cultural participation as a proxy for household security; the repeated cross-sections do not establish individual change or causality.

The Statistics Canada National Culture Indicators record adds a production-side tension: real culture GDP rose 0.6% in Q1 2026 while culture jobs fell 0.3%; broadcasting GDP rose 1.6% while broadcasting jobs fell 1.8%, and film/video jobs fell 2.3%. This separates cultural-sector output from worker outcomes and audience experience; the national accounts do not identify the causal mechanism.

The Japan Statistics Bureau CTI record adds a real-consumption composition layer: July 2026 nominal household consumption was nearly flat at -0.1% year-over-year while the real index fell 2.4%, with especially sharp real declines in education (-11.8%) and utilities (-8.7%). This is a modeled aggregate index, not a household-level welfare estimate, but it makes category-specific purchasing-power pressure visible.

The Statistics Canada disability-accessibility record adds a usable-access layer beneath nominal digital availability: 13% of Canadians with disabilities reported barriers to government information/services online, 11% to booking online, and 9% to banking/shopping online, with a severity gradient from 28% to 9% for Internet-use barriers. It does not establish completed transactions, consumer loss, or institutional remedy.

The New Zealand cultural-participation record adds an audience-to-production tension: attendance rose to 88% in 2025 while active creation fell to 40%, and 72% named accessibility or convenience as an enabler. Digital tools and generative AI are already inside creator practice, but skills remain a barrier for nonusers; the online panel does not establish causal conversion or creator outcomes.
