The World Bank energy-crisis social-protection record adds a global policy-tracking route from energy shocks through uncertainty, instrument choice, delivery readiness, household room, political attribution, and exit. The paper records 256 planned or implemented responses across 104 countries, with subsidies nearly half of current responses and more than three times the share of cash transfers from 2022–2026. The cross-source implication is that crisis protection is a capability problem: governments need delivery infrastructure, financing, triggers, communication, and a credible withdrawal path. The review is descriptive and does not establish household receipt, welfare, or causal legitimacy effects.

Latest geopolitical-investment rotation: global shocks scar the investment pipeline unevenly

The World Bank global-growth-shocks FDI-scarring record adds a route from adverse global growth shocks through investor uncertainty, project announcements, country safety, strategic sectors, geopolitical positioning, and future local opportunity. The paper estimates scarring in FDI announcements for about three years, with more subdued effects in safer countries and buffered fluctuations in strategic sectors. The cross-source implication is that geopolitical fragmentation can be experienced as a quieter future of fewer expected projects and narrower bargaining options before realized jobs or capital visibly fall; announcements remain an early-warning measure, not realized welfare.

Latest housing-resilience rotation: climate adaptation becomes a household and fiscal-capacity problem

The World Bank housing-hazard-resilience record adds a long-horizon route from demographic and household change through housing demand, construction standards, hazard exposure, resilient-cost tradeoffs, household wealth, displacement, and public fiscal obligations. The study projects 4.1–4.5 billion housing units globally by 2100 and identifies 46 countries facing a triple burden of high demand, severe hazard exposure, and limited fiscal capacity. These are scenario projections, not realized affordability or adaptation outcomes.

Latest education-gender rotation: schooling parity does not guarantee equal capability

The World Bank Sub-Saharan Africa education-convergence record adds cross-cohort evidence from roughly 736,000 people across 35 countries: female attainment gaps narrowed sharply, and females exceed males in secondary attendance and years of education in a majority of countries among cohorts born after 1999. Yet learning gaps move inconsistently, some convergence reflects boys' stagnation, and wider attainment gaps persist among rural, poorer, and Muslim populations. The cross-source implication is that attendance parity is an incomplete capability signal; the next conversion stages are learning, work, earnings, health, household bargaining, and voice.

Latest regional-integration rotation: formal openness becomes usable through enforceability and mobility

The World Bank AfCFTA deep-integration record adds a route from agreement depth through legal enforceability, trade-defense discipline, visa mobility, firm entry, worker movement, services, and consumer choice. AfCFTA is classified as medium in the baseline; a deep-integration counterfactual produces an estimated average GDP gain of about 0.7% for the African economies in the sample. The cross-source implication is that regional integration is experienced through rules, movement, and remedy rather than tariff language alone; the estimate remains model-based and does not establish realized jobs, wages, prices, or equal welfare.

Latest public-sector reform rotation: reform models diffuse faster than institutional capacity can sustain them

The World Bank Africa public-sector reform record adds project-review and case-study evidence that more than one-third of reviewed World Bank-financed public-sector reform projects included New Public Management interventions, but only 40% of interventions were fully implemented. Performance-based public financial management performed comparatively better than agencification and performance-based pay. The cross-source implication is that reform adoption is not state capacity: implementation resources, authority, coalitions, institutional fit, and durability determine whether citizens experience better service, feedback, correction, and trust.

Latest growth-and-jobs rotation: economic growth is becoming a weaker promise of work

The World Bank Bangladesh employment-elasticity record adds macro-labor evidence that Bangladesh has weaker support for a conventional growth–employment relationship than six Asian comparison countries. Agriculture’s employment elasticity rises from 0.29 to 0.98 across the compared periods, while industry falls from 0.84 to -0.04; accommodation/food and transportation/storage show the strongest subsector responses, while manufacturing turns negative. The cross-source implication is that growth must be traced through sector, job quality, wages, hours, formality, migration, and household room rather than treated as employment or welfare.

Latest household-nutrition rotation: salience can change feeding habits, but cannot manufacture food access

The World Bank Bihar food-accounting record adds randomized evidence that a wall-mounted food journal increased caregiver attention, habit formation, and the likelihood of minimum dietary diversity among children, while not changing food quantity or mid-upper arm circumference. The cross-source implication is a salience-within-constraint mechanism: behavior tools can complement frontline care and nutrition programs, but food availability, household income, implementation relationships, and time limit what attention can convert into health. The study is a Bihar cluster RCT with short follow-up and does not establish long-run nutrition or food-security effects.

Latest AI-institutionalization rotation: government use is broad, but organizational scaffolding is shallow

The World Bank 60-economy government-AI record adds survey evidence that government AI use is broad but shallow and uneven: 44% of internal use is reported as individual public servants using AI for ad hoc tasks, while many governments provide generative-AI access before formal guidelines. The cross-source implication is that AI adoption can become a shadow workflow before it becomes accountable public infrastructure; data, skills, budgets, organizational capacity, privacy, ethics, and remedy need to be treated as complementary conditions. The survey does not audit systems or establish citizen outcomes.

Latest agency-measurement rotation: voice is culturally situated and cannot be safely inferred from one universal scale

The World Bank Tunisia women's-agency record adds mixed-methods evidence that questions performing well in India and Tunisia overlap minimally, and that rural and urban Tunisian contexts can require different agency measures. Machine learning performed well against a qualitative benchmark, while current generative-AI approaches did not and did not reduce the work of validation. The cross-source implication is that measurement is part of institutional voice: a context-blind score can make populations look comparable while erasing how goals, constraints, and action are locally expressed. The study concerns instrument performance, not population agency prevalence or causal empowerment.

Latest labor-market participation rotation: application inactivity can be an initiation-cost problem

The World Bank Pakistan job-search record adds randomized evidence that changing the default process for initiating applications increased applications by 600%, with a pattern consistent with psychological costs of starting the search. The cross-source implication is that observed inactivity can reflect system friction rather than low motivation: defaults determine whose latent interest becomes visible. Applications are not employment, however; the paper does not establish effects on interviews, offers, wages, job quality, retention, or employer welfare.

Latest small-firm market-access rotation: the first buyer can matter more than another training module

The World Bank Georgia digital-market record adds randomized evidence that supply-side training did not increase digital participation, while a conditional purchase order increased market access by 26 percentage points; a payment six times larger produced only a modest additional increase. The cross-source implication is that digital inclusion is partly a demand and coordination problem: a credible buyer, first transaction, and organizational routine can make a platform usable, but the effect largely dissipated as control firms caught up and persisted more among firms already ready for e-commerce. The study is specific to the Georgian experiments and does not establish durable profits, employment, productivity, firm survival, or consumer welfare.

Latest digital-fiscal rotation: digital reach becomes a condition of fiscal capacity and social protection

The IMF Middle East and Central Asia digitalization record adds a route from digital identity, connectivity, financial inclusion, interoperable social registries, tax e-services, and digital payments through revenue capacity, targeting, poverty and inequality reduction, household access, privacy, and trust. The cross-source implication is that digital readiness is becoming a distributional institution: a system can improve fiscal reach and reduce leakage while excluding people without accounts, connectivity, usable documentation, or correction and appeal routes. The IMF note combines comparative indicators, cases, and associations; it does not establish a uniform causal welfare effect or show who is actually reached in each country.

Latest geopolitical-cultural rotation: election salience fuses security, identity and social repair

The JPPI September 2026 Israeli Society Index record adds a geopolitical-cultural legitimacy layer. Eight in ten respondents describe the coming election as the most important or especially important; security leads decisive issues at 31%, followed by government–judiciary relations and unity. Yet 52% describe the past year as poor socially, while 30% do so economically and 37% in security. Security and territorial preferences, antisemitism attribution and education judgments divide sharply by Jewish/Arab identity, ideology and religiosity. The cross-source implication is that geopolitical legitimacy is a bundle of security, authority, unity, identity, social repair and education—not one national mood. The mixed survey frames and public summary do not establish objective conditions, turnout, policy delivery, conflict outcomes or causal polarization.

Latest household-shortage rotation: availability becomes a search and spending tax

The ONS Great Britain shortages record adds a concrete household-material layer. In the 5–30 August 2026 window, 45% of responding adults said they had to spend more than usual to obtain usual purchases, 23% saw less variety, 18% visited more shops and 5% shopped online. Thirty-seven percent said they were buying less. Eleven percent reported essential food items unavailable or inaccessible, 17% reported this for other food, 4% for medicine and 3% for fuel. The cross-source implication is that continued shopping can conceal different household costs: money, search time, substitution, reduced quantity and unmet availability. ONS notes a May 2026 wording change for the availability item, so historical comparisons require caution.

Latest supply-chain power rotation: formal compliance can coexist with thin supplier room

The UK Groceries Code Adjudicator supplier-survey record adds a firm-sector contestability layer. Average perceived compliance across the 14 designated retailers remained 92%, and more than half of suppliers reported no issue, but the share reporting a Code issue rose from 30% to 32%. Invoice-discrepancy resolution, inaccurate forecasting, de-listing without reasonable notice and payment delays were each reported as supplier problems. The cross-source implication is that supply-chain power is experienced through timing, information and practical exit, not only through formal code compliance. The release does not establish monetary loss, remedy, consumer-price effects or causal retailer power.

Latest care-and-labour rotation: care converts infrastructure into unequal time

The Statistics South Africa Gender Series XIII record adds a gendered care-conversion layer. The official summary reports a rise in the 65+ population share from 5.9% in 2015 to 7.3% in 2026, female-headed households rising from 41.3% to 42.6% between 2015 and 2025, and 8.4% of girls aged 7–18 who were not attending an educational institution citing family commitments, compared with 0% of boys in the reported comparison. Women dominated several paid-care occupations, while female-headed households were less likely to spend under 30 minutes fetching water. The cross-source implication is that care infrastructure changes the time and labour-market option set, but formal access does not settle who supplies remaining care or who absorbs its educational and employment cost. The report uses proxy indicators because recent time-use data are unavailable; it does not estimate unpaid-care hours or causal effects.

Latest public-safety rotation: security is partly privately supplied

The Statistics South Africa GPSJS 2025/26 record adds a public-safety conversion layer. Housebreaking affected 5.3% of households and home robbery 0.9%, but only 48.2% and 51.6% of affected households respectively reported some or all incidents to police. Personal-property theft affected 2.6% of people aged 16 and older, with 37.3% reporting; only 37.9% felt safe walking alone after dark, and 46.6% reported taking some protective action, up from 43.3% in 2024/25. The cross-source implication is that exposure, reporting, perceived safety and self-protection are different stages: households may privately absorb the time, movement, spending and avoidance costs of security while formal remedy remains partial. The one-page release does not establish reporting causes, police effectiveness, protective costs or causal safety change.

Latest comparative consumer-legitimacy rotation: routine spending persists while political-economic confidence fractures

The Ipsos Thailand September 2026 record adds a non-Western consumer-legitimacy layer. Corruption is the leading concern at 52%, crime and violence rises to 34%, unemployment reaches 30%, 52% say the country is heading in the wrong direction, and 61% describe the economy as bad. Yet 64% feel more comfortable making everyday purchases than six months earlier, versus 50% for major purchases. The cross-source implication is that routine consumption can persist through necessity, substitution or short-horizon adaptation while public legitimacy deteriorates. The public country analysis does not establish objective conditions, realized purchases, subsidy incidence, or causal trust effects.

Latest care-and-energy rotation: targeted warmth joins material relief, information reach and social recognition

The Small Acts of Kindness/Ipsos older-people record adds a support-encounter layer. Among 618 nominated gift-bag recipients, four in five reported negative cost-of-living and energy-cost effects; 74% said heating was affected, 68% food purchases were affected, and 64% reported some isolation. The printed information pack was useful to 88%, while 95% said printed organizational information was important and open-ended responses often described being cheered or cared for. The cross-source implication is that small targeted interventions operate across warmth, information and recognition, but recipient gratitude and usefulness do not prove reduced bills, improved food security, better health, or durable loneliness reduction. The opt-in recipient feedback is not population prevalence or causal evaluation.

Latest cultural-institution rotation: club heritage turns place-based attachment into fan voice

The Ipsos–Independent Football Regulator club-heritage record adds a cultural-institution layer. Among 1,904 supporters of men's clubs in England and Wales's top five divisions, 32% would feel high distress if their club were dissolved, 56% would consider at least one response, and club history, stadium location, matchday traditions, community presence, fan engagement and team name rank as personally important. The cross-source implication is that a club can function as local identity and social infrastructure, with institutional threat converting symbolic attachment into prospective organized voice. The hypothetical survey does not establish actual mobilization, club survival, regulator effectiveness, or policy influence.

Latest household-expectations rotation: aggregate stability conceals an income-positioned credit map

The ECB Consumer Expectations Survey August 2026 record adds a distributional expectations layer. Across the approximately 19,000-adult, 11-country monthly survey, expected nominal income growth was 1.0% and expected spending growth 3.6%, while lower-income respondents reported higher inflation and unemployment expectations and expected mortgage rates of 5.7% versus 4.4% among the top income quintile. The cross-source implication is that aggregate consumer stability can coexist with sharply unequal anticipation of prices, job risk, housing cost, and credit access. These are expectations and perceived conditions, not realized spending, borrowing, employment, or causal household outcomes.

Latest cultural-AI rotation: adoption is broad, but authority remains relational and domain-specific

The NPR/Ipsos Religion and AI record adds a cultural-meaning layer. Sixty-one percent of U.S. adults report using AI, but among AI users only 11% have used it for spiritual or religious guidance, while 69% say they would never seek such guidance from AI. For difficult personal topics, family and friends remain more trusted than AI, even though AI's availability, information access, and low fear of judgment create a practical opening. The cross-source implication is selective delegation: AI can absorb instrumental tasks without acquiring authority over conscience, identity, or emotionally consequential judgment. The source is a probability-sample attitude survey, not observed substitution or wellbeing evidence.

Latest financial-capacity rotation: measured security can improve while felt insecurity worsens

The Equifax Q2 2026 Market Pulse record adds a balance-sheet layer. The index rose from 60.9 to 61.3 while University of Michigan sentiment fell to 49.5 and late payments improved; assets, rather than income or credit score alone, were described as the clearest dividing line between Thrivers, the Middle, and Strivers. The cross-source implication is that consumer insecurity cannot be inferred from sentiment or credit behavior alone: asset buffers create different option sets, and aggregate stabilization can conceal unequal exposure. The release is proprietary aggregate analysis, not causal household evidence.

Latest cultural-belonging rotation: cultural visibility does not guarantee recognition or safety

The STAATUS Index 2026 record adds an AAPI cultural-politics layer. Cultural influence is visible in food, digital culture, entertainment, and fashion, yet only 7% of U.S. adults say AAPI communities have a great deal of influence overall and 49% say they have little or none. That recognition gap coexists with contested definitions of Americanness, geopolitical threat framing, race-based harassment, and reported unsafety on public transit and online. The cross-source implication is that consumption and visibility can coexist with weak collective credit and unequal protection; education, media, local business, and cultural programming remain proposed bridges rather than demonstrated remedies.

Latest care-and-career-pipeline rotation: near-parity at entry can become senior attrition

The UK Women in Research Charter record adds an institutional-career layer. Women are near parity in STEM entry, science-related undergraduate study, and junior/mid-level research but fall to 31% of professors; the charter links the narrowing to caring responsibilities, short contracts, long-hours and mobility norms, biased productivity measures, and an enactment gap between formal flexibility and usable flexibility. The cross-source implication is that care is not only a household or welfare variable: institutions convert time, leave, and dependency support into promotion and status outcomes. The charter's voluntary commitments create a measurement route, not evidence of implementation or causal effect.

Latest reproductive-politics rotation: public autonomy is broader than unconditional access

The Afrobarometer East Africa reproductive-autonomy record adds a cultural-legitimacy layer. Across seven countries, support for women’s marriage and childbearing autonomy and sexuality education is broad, while support narrows for age-neutral contraception and abortion outside specified circumstances. The cross-source implication is that formal principle, public legitimacy, institutional delivery, and usable reproductive agency are separate stages; high support for autonomy does not prove safe, affordable, confidential access.

Latest care-legitimacy rotation: support for public responsibility coexists with weak system knowledge

The Health Foundation social-care and NHS record adds a care-system legitimacy layer. Public pessimism about social-care standards, preference for state or non-profit provision, misconceptions about funding, weak financial preparation, and unresolved tax/provider trade-offs coexist with durable support for universal NHS principles. The cross-source implication is that public consent depends on both service performance and a usable map of who pays, who provides, and what households can expect; perceptions are not equivalent to care quality or reform feasibility.

Latest geopolitical-cultural rotation: African publics seek integration without surrendering agency

The Afrobarometer African Insights 2026 record adds a 38-country public-agency layer. Support for trade, free movement, multi-partner relations, greater African voice, and climate action coexists with weak awareness of continental institutions, difficult border crossing, labor-competition concerns, neutrality preferences, and household-cost limits. The cross-source implication is that openness is conditional on visible benefit, fair exposure, and decision-making power; stated attitudes are not realized integration or geopolitical leverage.

Latest justice-capacity rotation: formal rights depend on resource geography and adjacent services

The IFS Resources and the justice system record adds a public-capacity layer. Tribunal delays, civil legal-aid contraction, court and police infrastructure, management, provider viability, and prevention services shape whether a formal right becomes reachable remedy. The cross-source implication is that justice performance cannot be read from headline spending or completed cases alone: lower observed use may reflect lower access, and pressure can be exported across welfare, housing, youth, early-years, police, courts, and prisons. The report synthesizes multiple studies and preserves their different causal boundaries.

Latest digital-life rotation: screen time becomes a negotiated household and platform-governance problem

The EU Flash Eurobarometer 579 record adds a paired adolescent/parent layer. Across all 27 Member States, adolescents reported more screen time than parents estimated, earlier social-media entry was associated with higher weekend use, and distress, harmful-content exposure, support demand, and restriction preferences coexisted. The cross-source implication is that digital time is not only an individual quantity: it is shaped by platform design, household visibility, offline opportunity, content exposure, and access to support. The survey is descriptive and cross-sectional, not a clinical or causal evaluation.

Latest institutional-transition rotation: pathway parity can fail at the household budget

The SSAC post-16 benefit cliff-edge record adds an institutional-incentive layer. The report shows how benefit rules, information gaps, transition delays, and weak tracking can make officially equal academic, technical, and apprenticeship routes financially unequal. The cross-source implication is that “choice” is mediated by household room and administrative visibility: a pathway can be formally available yet practically unaffordable, especially for disabled young people, carers, care leavers, and estranged young people. The report uses worked scenarios and mixed-methods evidence; it does not estimate prevalence or prove a population-level causal effect.

Latest youth-service rotation: trusted access requires partnership and measurement infrastructure

The Young Futures Hubs interim evaluation record adds an implementation-capacity layer. Eight early-adopter hubs were beginning to connect open-access youth work, targeted and specialist support through trusted spaces and warm handovers, but partnership time, co-design authority, referral pathways, sustainable funding, consent, identifiers, and common measures constrained what could be learned. The cross-source implication is that reach and attendance are not durable outcome; service connection and evaluation infrastructure are part of the intervention. This is an interim process and feasibility evaluation, not a causal impact study.

Latest food-information rotation: consumer confidence can rise while source credibility remains fragile

The EIT Food Trust Report 2026 record adds a European food-information layer. Across 18 countries, confidence in making good food choices rose from 60% in 2024 to 66% in 2025, yet fewer than half considered food information reliable and 53% said they knew where to find trusted sources. The cross-source implication is that food literacy requires source navigation, transparency, validation, and usable information—not simply more claims. The report is self-reported consumer-observatory evidence, not an objective accuracy test or causal intervention evaluation.

Latest health-information rotation: practical judgment is an unequal care-capacity resource

The LSHTM health-misinformation record adds a health-specific information-to-capacity route. Confidence in judging health claims varies sharply by income and education; social media is the dominant reported exposure route; young adults report more regretted decisions and known harms; and the public prioritizes education, penalties for profiteering, and platform warning labels. The cross-source implication is that trustworthy information must be reachable before harm and connected to clinicians, public services, and correction routes. This is an online-panel survey with self-reported exposure and harm, not verified clinical or causal evidence.

Latest consumer-recourse rotation: affordability can expand exposure while remedy remains conditional

The UK IPO Counterfeit Goods Wave 5 record adds a consumer-authenticity layer. Price and perceived comparable quality sustain counterfeit purchasing, marketplace and social-media routes increase exposure, younger adults report more unintentional purchases, and negative consequences are common among affected purchasers while reporting remains low and often depends on the possibility of financial recovery. The cross-source implication is that consumer agency requires verification, payment protection, reporting, refund, and safety routes—not only disclosure or enforcement messaging. The source is self-reported mixed-method evidence, not a market-size or causal estimate.

Latest youth-civic rotation: formal voice requires information and readiness infrastructure

The UK Votes at 16 research record adds a youth political-socialization layer. Young people distinguish relatively robust trust in elections from low trust in politicians, encounter politics through family, television, and algorithmic feeds, want more school preparation, and see earlier voting as a possible route to being heard while remaining uncertain about readiness and external influence. The cross-source implication is that formal voice is usable only when registration, civic knowledge, media judgment, identity access, and representative responsiveness travel with it. This is a mixed-method baseline, not a turnout or causal evaluation.

Latest beyond-GDP rotation: headline progress does not guarantee lived capacity

The ONS September 2026 national well-being record adds an official beyond-GDP measurement layer. GDP per head and low-carbon energy improved, while mean life satisfaction remained below its pre-pandemic level, good health remained weaker than five years earlier, youth NEET remained elevated, and government trust stayed low. The cross-source implication is that progress must be tested through usable health, opportunity, local belonging, and institutional voice rather than aggregate output alone. The bulletin combines different samples, periods, geographies, and measures; it is not causal evidence.

Latest consumer-room rotation: precautionary saving does not equal comfortable consumption room

The INSEE France September consumer-confidence record adds a monthly consumer-expectations layer. Confidence remains below its long-term average, major-purchase intentions remain weak, and saving intentions remain elevated while perceived price increases accelerate. The cross-source implication is that saving sentiment can represent caution, unmet security demand or unequal balance-sheet protection rather than broad household abundance. This is a repeated cross-sectional opinion survey with synthetic indexes, not realized spending or saving.

Latest mobility-capacity rotation: labor mobility is neither frictionless nor directly observed between censuses

The Statistics Canada interprovincial labour-mobility record adds an institutional and measurement layer to regional inequality. Only about 1%–2% of working-age people move between provinces annually; licensing and recognition barriers remain, while experimental occupation-level predictions can diverge substantially from observed rates. The cross-source implication is that mobility policy must connect legal recognition, housing, care, worker voice and reliable measurement to realized movement rather than treating predicted mobility as outcome evidence.

Latest cultural-consumer rotation: physical arts participation falls without digital replacement

The England Community and Engagement Survey arts record adds official cultural-participation evidence: overall arts engagement fell to 84%, physical engagement to 83%, digital engagement remained near 36%, and deprivation and local-authority gaps were large. The cross-source implication is that cultural access is a household-room and place system, not only a preference system. The report explicitly warns that the decline may partly reflect survey-method changes, so the apparent withdrawal remains an open measurement question.

Latest migration-and-work rotation: certification does not complete labor-market integration

The Statistics Canada childhood-immigrant journeyperson record adds a longitudinal administrative-data layer. Childhood immigrants remained below Canadian-born journeypersons in earnings before, at and after certification, while trade composition, union and pension coverage, regional mobility, sex and post-certification progression altered the pattern. The cross-source implication is that integration must be followed through occupational sorting, bargaining institutions, household room and mobility—not inferred from schooling, certification or employment alone. This is observational linked administrative data, not a causal policy estimate or complete measure of belonging.

Latest care-infrastructure rotation: nominal affordability does not guarantee usable child care

The Statistics Canada home-based child-care record adds a provider-side care-capacity layer. Nearly four in five home-based services were at maximum capacity in April 2024, waitlists were common, nonstandard hours were rare, and disability accommodations differed sharply by licensing status. The cross-source implication is that fee policy must be joined to capacity, schedule, accessibility, provider capability, and institutional monitoring before it can become released household time or employment continuity. This is a nationally representative provider survey and descriptive snapshot, not a parent-level unmet-demand or causal reform estimate.

Latest comparative consumer rotation: confidence rebounds before present household room does

The Bank of Korea September consumer-survey record adds a recurring non-U.S. consumer-expectations layer. The composite sentiment index rose 2.1 points to 106.6, but current living-standards assessment was unchanged while prospective household income rose two points and prospective spending one point. Past-year inflation perception was 3.0%; one-, three-, and five-year expected inflation were 2.7%, 2.6%, and 2.6%, while housing-price outlook remained high and the interest-rate outlook strengthened. The cross-source implication is that confidence about direction can coexist with flat present room and persistent housing/financial-cost exposure. This is a monthly repeated cross-section and expectation index, not realized spending, affordability, debt stress, housing mobility, or causal policy evidence.

Latest comparative consumer-infrastructure rotation: payment choice becomes a liquidity and trust system

The Stitch South Africa consumer-payments record adds a non-U.S. commerce-interface layer. In the publisher's digitally active sample, 93.3% tried a new payment method, while wallet speed, BNPL, payday timing, international low-cost platforms, and checkout failure made payment architecture part of household room and consumer optionality. The report also places AI product research ahead of an unresolved agentic-commerce middle: discovery can move into AI interfaces before authentication, fraud controls, APIs, returns, and liability are interoperable. This is sponsor-produced commercial intelligence with mixed survey and platform denominators, not national prevalence, repayment, market-share, or causal welfare evidence.

Latest comparative political-ecology rotation: nature attachment is broader than climate-policy identity

The More in Common Strong Roots record adds a cross-party place-and-stewardship layer. Its survey and swing-voter focus groups describe nature and wildlife as a shared source of pride, reject an abstract nature-versus-development binary, and report that known politician positions on nature protection shape voter perceptions. The cross-source implication is that environmental legitimacy may travel through local identity, stewardship, recreation, health, and future security even when voters disagree about net-zero politics. The study does not establish willingness to pay, local project acceptance, vote change, or conservation delivery.

Latest global information-environment rotation: intermediary convenience can outrun trusted source access

The IPIE 2026 expert-survey record adds a global information-governance layer. Among 470 experts covering 71 countries, 76% expected deterioration in the next year; 78% rated lack of platform accountability a big or extreme threat; and the report separates viewpoint findability from trusted accuracy. AI summaries are expected to speed answer-finding while reducing news-site visits and narrowing viewpoint diversity. The cross-source implication is that information quality is a conversion chain involving intermediary design, source visibility, public trust, civic understanding, and the capacity of researchers and institutions to contest errors. This is expert assessment, not observed public behavior or platform-causal evidence.

Latest U.S. place-and-participation rotation: geography changes civic route more than civic level

The Pew urban/suburban/rural public-life record extends the existing engagement typology into place. Urban, suburban, and rural adults have broadly similar distributions across engagement groups, but differ in group membership, religious attendance, in-person versus online interaction, protest, signage, and other political expression. The cross-source implication is that place is a route variable: local institutions, transport, digital access, and social visibility may shape how engagement becomes participation without making urban, suburban, or rural residence a civic identity. This is cross-sectional survey association, not a causal place effect or measure of political efficacy.

Latest comparative citizen-futures rotation: resilience is imagined as capacity to act across linked crises

The JRC Our Futures citizen-resilience record adds narrative evidence from more than 4,000 citizen-authored future stories. In the 340-story EU-focused subset, democracy/governance appears in 41% and nature/climate in 29%; the stories connect those themes to migration, affordability, technology, work, human connection, and geopolitical risk. The cross-source implication is that public meaning is formed before policy preferences are separated into departments: the same anxiety can produce hope or collapse depending on perceived institutional capacity and personal agency. This is self-selected narrative evidence, not representative prevalence, forecast, or causal policy evidence.

Latest social-pressure rotation: mental-health concern is filtered through material exposure and permission to seek help

The St Patrick's Irish mental-health and stigma record adds a social-pressure layer to the mental-health route. The survey links wellbeing concerns to loneliness, housing, climate change, and wider economic uncertainty; it also shows that public concern and perceived stigma progress can coexist with private silence around suicidal thoughts and self-help-seeking. The cross-source implication is that mental-health legitimacy has at least three gates: pressure, permission to disclose, and reachable care. This is descriptive public-attitudes evidence, not clinical prevalence, causal evidence, or a service-capacity audit.

Latest consumer-media rotation: professional audience models can drift away from public attention

The thinkTV/Ipsos Ad Nation 2026 record adds a consumer-media translation layer. Canadian media professionals estimated public TikTok use at 89%, versus 30% reported by Canadian adults in the public sample; the release also finds persistent advertising distrust, concern about data and AI-generated fake content, and continued value placed on live television as a shared experience. The cross-source implication is that cultural and consumer systems can misread the public when professional exposure becomes the implicit audience model. This is a two-sample descriptive comparison, not a causal campaign-performance or platform-adoption estimate.

Latest youth-cultural rotation: high AI adoption can coexist with low delegated trust and delayed independence

The Pacsun/GlobalData Drawbridge Generation record adds a youth selective-delegation layer. In the publisher's 6,126-person U.S. sample, family and friends dominate trust, 85% used AI in the past year, but only 2% trusted it for fashion advice and 5% for financial advice. The same release reports a decline in self-described financial independence from 41.3% to 34.9% and a rise in full parental reliance from 23.8% to 29.1%. The cross-source implication is that youth are not simply pro- or anti-technology: they allocate authority by domain while material dependence reshapes adulthood, aspiration, and the meaning of a successful future. This is sponsor-reported repeated-survey evidence, not causal evidence of economic dependence or AI quality.

Latest AI-trust rotation: content abundance is weakening authenticity signals

The Gartner consumer-authenticity record adds a broader consumer trust layer. In a 1,006-person U.S. survey, 35% said they rely less on influencers because of AI-generated content, 43% said they rely more on real people, 65% said brands produce too much AI marketing content, and 57% said it makes them less trusting of brand messaging. The cross-source implication is that AI changes not only content production but the social heuristics through which people decide who deserves attention and authority. This is publisher-reported descriptive survey evidence, not a content audit, causal trust estimate, or sales outcome.

Latest multilateral-legitimacy rotation: a necessary institution faces a visibility and delivery test

The UN Foundation/GeoPoll Secretary-General mandate record adds a leadership-transition layer. Across the 5,000-person, 20-country poll, 84% say the UN remains necessary, but 52% say it is struggling to deliver; 58% trust the UN and other international institutions to make progress, with a Global South/Global North difference of 65% versus 44%. Conflict prevention is the leading priority, while the public wants an outward-facing diplomat, crisis manager, or moral voice and 85% have heard little about the selection race. The cross-source implication is that institutional legitimacy depends on the combination of necessity, delivery, public visibility, and representation—not institutional survival alone. This is commissioned public-opinion evidence, not a performance evaluation or causal leadership study.

Latest local-consent rotation: national AI ambition meets concentrated community costs

The UMass AI data-center poll record adds a siting-legitimacy layer. In a 1,000-person U.S. poll, 65% oppose an AI data center in their local community and 11% support one; opposition remains majoritarian among Democrats and Republicans. Open-ended responses center on environmental resources, utility bills, land use, noise, and community fit, while supporters invoke jobs, economic development, and competition with China. The cross-source implication is that technological legitimacy has a local-cost conversion problem: national enthusiasm or strategic necessity does not settle who bears the physical and household price of infrastructure. This is cross-sectional opinion and publisher-reported coding, not realized impact or permitting behavior.

Latest diaspora-cultural rotation: heritage identity travels through media and contact, not one universal language pathway

The Frontiers ethnic-Chinese cultural-identity record adds a diaspora-identity mechanism across Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand. In an online panel of 1,298 second-generation-and-beyond ethnic Chinese respondents, Chinese-content exposure and visits to China were positively associated with cultural identity across all three countries, while language proficiency mattered significantly only in Malaysia and media exposure mediated several relationships. The cross-source implication is that cultural identity is reproduced through a distributed system of content, contact, language, and national context rather than through heritage or screen format alone. This is comparative panel association evidence, not causal proof, a representative estimate of all ethnic Chinese, or evidence of political allegiance to the PRC.

Latest consumer-governance rotation: financial-services AI needs visible human fallback

The YouGov financial-services AI record adds a consumer-protection mechanism to the AI-trust route. In a weighted Great Britain survey of 8,220 adults, 53% said greater AI use would make financial-services firms less likely to act in customers' best interests, versus 11% who said more likely; 68% attributed adoption to cost reduction and 60% to profit, compared with 10% to better customer outcomes. Confidence is conditional rather than absent: 51% said access to a human when needed would increase confidence, alongside company accountability and personal-information protection. The cross-source implication is that automation becomes legitimate when customers can see reversibility, responsibility, and benefit—not merely speed or firm efficiency. This is stated public perception, not observed deployment, harm, compliance, or causal trust evidence.

Latest work-and-family meaning rotation: the good life is socially reproduced through children and work

The YouGov values-of-children-and-work record adds a social-reproduction mechanism. Across two September Economist/YouGov poll waves, childrearing ideals split between self-reliance and obedience, consideration and good behavior, independence and elder respect; work ideals split between shorter hours and standard schedules, remote-work rights and employer discretion, and passion versus pay. These preferences vary by age, ideology, education, gender, parenthood, and labor-force position. The cross-source implication is that political and consumer conflict often concerns the life model that institutions should make possible—security, autonomy, respect, time, care, and purpose—not only the policy instrument. This is weighted stated-preference evidence from opt-in panels and forced-choice items, not observed parenting, work behavior, or causal value change.

Latest family-time conversion rotation: desired care becomes an unequal option set

The New America National Parent Survey record adds lived-constraint evidence to the work-and-family meaning route. In a nationally weighted survey of 5,472 parents and primary caregivers of children ages 0–5, 72% wanted more quality time with their children, 55% said post-birth time was less than wanted, and 75% said their current work arrangement did not fully match their ideal. Money is the conversion bottleneck: 52% cited a financial barrier to using time as desired, 54% of parents with a child-care mismatch cited cost, and 28% also regularly cared for an older adult. The cross-source implication is that family policy is not choosing between one universal work/care model; it is expanding or narrowing a plural, unequal option set. This is weighted mixed-panel self-report evidence, not causal policy or independently verified hardship evidence.

The Carers UK work and unpaid-care record adds a harder employment-continuity measure to that family-time route. In a weighted 4,000-adult UK survey, 20% of workers were combining paid work and unpaid care, while reported consequences ranged from reduced hours and stress to leaving employment; the report estimates about 1.1 million people left work to care in the prior two years. The cross-source implication is that care infrastructure is also a labour-market retention system: the relevant outcome is not only care hours, but whether people can remain employed without converting care into income loss or hidden exhaustion. This remains repeated cross-sectional, self-reported advocacy evidence, not causal proof of a paid-leave effect.

The Catawba College–YouGov Ballots & Bots record adds an election-specific version of the information-authority problem. The survey finds broad commitment to secure, fair elections and stated acceptance of unfavorable results alongside weaker confidence in the overall system, high concern that AI will make political content harder to authenticate or correct, and stronger trust in friends, state election websites, and local officials than in social media or AI assistants. The cross-source implication is that synthetic-media risk is also a verification-and-legitimacy problem: disclosure, rapid correction, and locally credible explanation may matter as much as content removal. This is cross-sectional, self-reported survey evidence, not verified exposure or causal policy evidence.

The SOCi Local Discovery Index record adds a consumer-scale version of the same verification shift. SOCi reports that 52% of surveyed U.S. consumers used AI to find a local business in the previous 30 days, but 81% still took a verification step before contacting the business; reviews and responsive business replies become a conversion and remedy layer. The cross-source implication is that AI-mediated discovery does not eliminate intermediaries—it redistributes them across search, social, maps, reviews, and direct information, with different routes by income, generation, and category. This is vendor-sponsored, self-reported directional evidence, not observed clickstream or causal sales evidence.

The Public First cross-party education record adds a pathway-legitimacy route to the work-and-meaning evidence. UK voters across parties express demand for technical education, apprenticeships, life skills, and adult readiness, while only 47% are confident the tested policies can be delivered and 42% are not. The cross-source implication is that a shared social ideal can become a delivery test: political legitimacy depends on whether education reform produces visible work pathways, local capability, and transparent explanations when promises change. This is commissioned mixed-method political research, not a causal education or employment evaluation.

The WorldSkills UK/Public First Ready to Work record adds the employer-side test to that education pathway. Employers report that youth entry is harder, while 95% say the right mindset matters in hiring and 70% believe young people with the right employability skills could increase revenue. The cross-source implication is that pathway legitimacy requires a translation layer between public demand for technical routes and firm-level hiring: skills demonstrations, work experience, and competitions must become observable access mechanisms rather than symbolic credentials. This is commissioned, self-reported employer evidence, not observed hiring or productivity data.

The IKEA Life at Home 2026 record adds a household-cultural counterpart to the material-room evidence. Across the report’s global sample, security, comfort, and control are more important than people regularly experience, while home satisfaction is associated with greater future optimism; saving money and health benefits are stronger climate-action motivators than abstract obligation alone. The cross-source implication is that the household is not only a site where external shocks land—it is an agency infrastructure where people attempt to regain control through routines, repair, reuse, and sustainable consumption. This is retailer-commissioned, self-reported, mostly-2025-fieldwork evidence, not causal housing or climate evaluation.

The IKEA Store & Organise 2026 record adds a distinct household-coordination route. The source frames mess as a possible indirect negotiation over who notices and performs domestic work, while clutter also creates conflict, preserves memory, and consumes search time. The cross-source implication is that household room is simultaneously material infrastructure, identity infrastructure, and a bargaining surface: the same object can be a sentimental anchor, a storage burden, and a signal about unpriced labor. This is retailer-commissioned, cross-sectional online self-report evidence; it does not establish gendered labor allocation, intentional protest, or causal conflict effects.

The Nextdoor/Harris Poll neighborhood-trust record adds a local social-infrastructure counterpoint to the broader trust-decline narrative. Practical neighbor reliance and recommendation trust remain visible, but younger adults report a sharper gap between desired interaction, loneliness, and feeling welcomed. The cross-source implication is that social cohesion may depend less on generalized attitude than on repeated, low-stakes contact routes that convert proximity into help, information, and belonging. This is platform-commissioned, cross-sectional online-panel evidence; it does not establish actual aid, recommendation accuracy, or app-driven trust.

The England Community and Engagement Survey 2025/26 record adds an official place-based comparator. In England, monthly neighbor contact and willingness to pull together are broader than reported neighborhood trust; intergroup coexistence can coexist with a judgment that the local area is getting worse; and belonging varies by age, disability, deprivation, and local authority. The cross-source implication is that cohesion is a conversion chain whose weakest link may be local conditions and access—not simply an absence of social goodwill. This is official self-report evidence, descriptive at subgroup and local levels, and not a causal evaluation of community policy.

The DWP education-professionals record adds an education-to-work route that complements the employer-side readiness evidence. Educators describe opportunity as a readiness ecology: work-readiness, confidence, local jobs, transport, health, SEND support, family context, networks, and work experience determine whether academic preparation can become a usable transition. The cross-source implication is that “skills” are not only an individual asset; they are a conversion problem involving institutions, place, and support. This is professional-perception evidence from a commissioned online panel, not observed youth transition or employer outcome data.

The DfE Parent, Pupil and Learner Voice record adds the learner-side route. Young people report high confidence in named plans, but alternative pathways can remain invisible or reputationally weak, while student-finance anxiety and the gap between mental-health-support awareness and use constrain the usable option set. The cross-source implication is that education-to-work opportunity requires both system readiness and learner-facing legibility: a plan is not yet a reachable route. This is official, self-reported panel evidence, not confirmed enrollment, completion, or outcome data.

The KFF/AP Rural Voters record adds a rural political-economy route. Cost of living and health-care exposure organize the issue agenda, local provider shortages make care capacity politically legible, and partisan loyalty can persist even as performance dissatisfaction lowers turnout certainty among some rural Republicans. The cross-source implication is that political alignment, delivery judgment, attribution, and participation must be modeled as separate conversions rather than one partisan preference. This is cross-sectional registered-voter evidence, not observed vote choice or causal policy evaluation.

The IFS Devout Difference record adds a relational-social-infrastructure route. Among the groups studied, regular religious practice and shared marital norms are associated with stronger reported marital quality and sexual satisfaction even as religious participation declines. The cross-source implication is that social institutions can shrink at the population level while retaining concentrated relational capacity among those who remain engaged. The source is institutionally sponsored observational research with incomplete public methodology; it does not establish causal faith effects or universal religious advantage.

Latest U.S. religious-social infrastructure rotation: communal trust persists through internal change

The Pew Latter-day Saints community/trust/diversity record adds a religion-as-social-infrastructure route. Current Latter-day Saints remain highly religious, with 72% saying religion is very important, while 72% report recent volunteering and 48% say most people can be trusted, compared with 41% and 34% among all U.S. adults. Yet retention among people raised Latter-day Saint fell from 70% in 2007 to 54% in 2023-24, and 28% are now religiously unaffiliated. The community is more racially diverse, and its Republican members are more supportive of racial and religious diversity than Republicans nationally. The cross-source implication is that institutional continuity is not static inheritance: dense routines can preserve trust and family cohesion while membership boundaries, demographic composition, and political meaning change. This is survey association and historical comparison, not a causal estimate of religious membership, family wellbeing, volunteering, or political action.

Latest comparative wellbeing rotation: broad wellbeing coexists with loneliness, anxiety, and material issue salience

The ONS Great Britain wellbeing and loneliness record adds a repeated official-survey layer that keeps wellbeing measures distinct. In August 2026, average life satisfaction was 6.9, worthwhile 7.2, happiness 7.2, hope 6.4, and anxiety 3.9; among 16-to-29s, anxiety was 4.1 and 32% reported loneliness often, always, or some of the time versus 25% overall. Young adults also had high hope (69%), so aspiration and distress coexist rather than forming one generational mood. Cost of living was named by 89% overall and 90% of 16-to-29s; housing by 64% of young adults versus 53% overall; immigration and international conflict were much more salient among older adults. The cross-source implication is that subjective wellbeing, material exposure, issue salience, and cultural-political meaning are linked but non-equivalent surfaces. This is repeated cross-sectional self-report evidence, not a clinical, causal, behavioral, or policy-effect estimate.

Latest comparative cohesion rotation: belonging is materially and locally uneven

The Helen Clark Foundation New Zealand cohesion record adds a material-belonging route. In its 2025 survey, 84% felt they belonged to New Zealand, but only about half felt a strong local community; two in five trusted the government, and nearly two-thirds of under-30s felt isolated at least sometimes. Financial stress predicted low belonging, low trust, high isolation, and more negative immigration attitudes, while homeowners reported higher neighbourhood belonging and civic participation than renters. The cross-source implication is that national identity and social cohesion are not one variable: housing, food security, friendship, safety, age, media, and household room mediate whether belonging becomes participation. This is weighted cross-sectional survey association evidence, not a causal account of loneliness, civic behavior, or policy effects.

Latest comparative nation–state cohesion rotation: national pride can survive institutional weakening

The AthenaLab Chile identity-and-cohesion record adds a nation–state gap. In an August 2025 survey, 68% reported the highest pride in being Chilean, while 87% said one must be very careful dealing with other people and 89% said society was more divided than ten years earlier. Trust was much higher in police and armed forces than in Congress and political parties, and 58% described attitudes toward foreigners as divided between inclusion and rejection. The cross-source implication is that symbolic belonging, interpersonal trust, institutional legitimacy, and everyday cooperation are distinct currencies: crisis solidarity can activate cohesion without institutionalizing it. This is a Chilean survey plus qualitative study, not a causal account of migration, violence, or democratic decline.

Latest comparative care-legitimacy rotation: the public trusts care quality more than the route to reach it

The BSA 43 NHS waiting record adds an access-time mechanism beneath health-system legitimacy. In the latest survey, 50% were satisfied with NHS care quality, but only 16% with the time before a hospital appointment, 14% with A&E waiting, and 27% with GP appointment waiting. Overall NHS satisfaction was 26% in 2025 after 21% in 2024, while the chapter’s historical comparison shows a much stronger recovery when earlier governments made improvements visible through shorter waits and service performance. The cross-source implication is that funding, staffing, targets, and technology become legitimacy only when converted into reachable appointments, continuity, and lower household waiting costs. This is longitudinal survey and comparative service-indicator evidence, not a patient-level causal evaluation; definitions and geographies vary.

Latest comparative consumer-culture rotation: confidence rebounds while meaningful occasions remain fragile

The PwC UK consumer-sentiment record adds a household-meaning layer beneath sentiment. The index rose from -13 in April to +1 in August 2026 and 39% said their finances were healthy, yet 68% still planned some cutback and cost of living and the UK economy remained top concerns for 85% and 86%. Christmas spending was partly protected: 25% expected to spend more and 21% less, with “keep Christmas special” the leading reason among those spending more. The cross-source implication is that household confidence is not a single spending throttle; people rank cultural occasions and may protect them until rent, food, energy, or job pressure overwhelms the ritual. This is a nationally representative cross-sectional survey of intentions, not receipts, debt, social connection, or causal household welfare evidence.

Latest comparative welfare-culture rotation: deservingness sorts public care inside an anti-welfare climate

The BSA 43 welfare record adds a cultural-political boundary beneath welfare spending. In 2025, 49% supported more spending on benefits for disabled people who cannot work and only 7% supported less; 63% named disability benefits among their top two priorities for extra spending, above retirement pensions at 53%. Even among respondents opposing more welfare spending overall, only 11% favored less spending on disabled people, versus 67% favoring less spending on unemployed people. The cross-source implication is that “welfare opinion” is not one bloc: claimant prototypes, perceived deservingness, fiscal context, political identity, media framing, and reform salience sort which recipients remain legitimate. This is four-decade survey evidence, not a causal account of media effects, policy outcomes, benefit adequacy, or durable attitude change; the report also flags a 2024 wording discontinuity.

Latest U.S. energy-infrastructure rotation: household affordability is increasingly coupled to data-center demand, grid investment, and geopolitics

The EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook record adds a macro-to-household transmission route. EIA forecasts U.S. electricity sales of 4,135 billion kilowatthours in 2026 and 4,211 billion in 2027, with data centers and manufacturing activity driving much of the growth and the West South Central region carrying the largest share of forecast growth. The same outlook embeds geopolitical exposure: global oil prices averaged $91 per barrel in August, inventories were estimated to have fallen by 400 million barrels year to date, and the model assumes Middle Eastern production remains below pre-conflict averages until the second quarter of 2027. The generation transition is uneven: energy-related CO2 emissions are forecast to fall 1.7% in 2026, while natural-gas generation rises 2% and coal generation falls 8%. The cross-source implication is that the energy transition is no longer separable into “household cost” versus “technology investment”: data-center and manufacturing demand, grid reinforcement, global fuel flows, local rate design, and emissions are coupled. The open arrow runs through who pays for capacity, who receives jobs and tax revenue, which communities bear environmental exposure, and whether climate or affordability claims translate into visible public legitimacy. This is an EIA model forecast and scenario analysis, not realized household bills, local reliability, or causal welfare evidence.

Latest U.S. institutional-legitimacy rotation: trust is fragmented by alignment and place, not simply absent

The Weidenbaum Center institutional-trust record sharpens the U.S. political layer. Across Waves 6-8, the report finds relatively low but stable federal-government trust, while trust in specific institutions is sorted by partisanship, geography, and personal economic security. In Wave 8, 75% of Republicans versus 9% of Democrats reported high trust in the presidency; the pattern reversed for news media, at 55% versus 23%, while military trust was 87% versus 54%. Place matters selectively: rural residents reported more trust than urban residents in the military (73% versus 64%) and presidency (42% versus 37%), while urban residents reported more trust in news media (42% versus 34%); the report found no comparable urban-rural gap for Congress and local government. The cross-source implication is that “trust decline” is too coarse: legitimacy is institution-specific and filtered through identity, geography, and perceived economic position. The open arrow is from differentiated trust through attribution, information choice, compliance, participation, and institutional response. This is repeated-survey association evidence, not a causal account of democratic stability or political behavior.

Latest U.S. consumer-infrastructure rotation: payment digitization changes the interface, not the need for redundancy

The Federal Reserve Diary of Consumer Payment Choice record adds a consumer and infrastructure layer to the U.S. spine. In the 2025 diary wave, consumers made about 47 payments per month, including six with cash, and four out of five used cash at least once in the prior 30 days. Cash is not merely a preferred legacy instrument: about 70% of in-person cash payments came from people whose stated preference was another method, indicating a fallback role when cards or digital channels are unavailable or impractical. Cash also functions as stored liquidity: 76% carried cash and 45% stored it elsewhere, with average stored holdings of $364. The transition is uneven: adults 55 and older averaged 10 cash payments per month versus two among those under 25; rural residents averaged nine versus six in urban and suburban areas; and households under $100,000 averaged seven versus five among higher-income households. The cross-source implication is that payment modernization is not a clean replacement story. Consumer technology can expand options while cash remains a resilience, privacy, acceptance, and access layer whose importance varies by place, age, and household resources. This is weighted diary and repeated-cross-sectional evidence, not a causal estimate of financial inclusion, exclusion, or welfare.

Latest U.S. working-family rotation: paid-work expansion does not remove care scarcity; it relocates the bargaining problem

The Pew working parents record gives the U.S. spine a strong current household-to-work mechanism. In 2025, 52% of different-sex couples with children under 18 had two full-time working parents, up from 31% in 1975, while the full-time-dad/not-employed-mom arrangement fell from 42% to 23%. The institutional gap is visible in the 2026 survey: more than eight in ten non-self-employed working parents say paid leave would be highly helpful, but only about half report access; 71% say work-from-home or control over when required hours are worked would be highly helpful, while only 23% report substantial work-from-home flexibility. Childcare is similarly a coordination problem: 48% of parents with a child age five or younger say cost makes suitable care difficult, 39% use multiple arrangements for the same child, and 59% say onsite childcare would be highly helpful while only 7% say it is available. In dual-full-time different-sex couples, 52% say the mother does more day-to-day parenting, 43% say she does more household chores, and 70% say the more flexible worker is a major factor in deciding who takes unexpected time off. The cross-source implication is that the U.S. working-family trend is not simply “more women working” or “remote work solves care”: paid-work expansion increases the importance of employer flexibility, childcare infrastructure, and household bargaining over time. This is a descriptive survey and CPS synthesis, not a causal estimate or a same-family time diary.

Latest comparative migration-governance rotation: control signalling can substitute for capacity building

The MPI Europe control-signalling record adds a political mechanism beneath migration headlines. The report argues that visible toughness can respond to public anxiety without improving migration or integration outcomes, while cutting language training and housing support can delay employment and prolong welfare dependence. It also emphasizes that many publics prefer a combination of control and compassion, and that trust is more likely to improve when migration levels, housing, education, health, employment, rights, obligations, and community resource allocation are made explicit and contestable. The cross-source implication is that migration governance is a capacity-allocation problem as much as a border-control problem: symbolic control may gain visibility while shifting costs into households, local services, family separation, and longer-run integration. This is a heterogeneous policy synthesis, not a pooled causal estimate or implementation evaluation.

Latest comparative household-consumption rotation: essential pressure and cultural spending do not move as one block

The Eurostat household expenditure record adds a comparative consumer-budget layer beneath inflation narratives. In January 2026, food, housing/water/energy, and transport accounted for 46% of EU household consumption expenditure. Yet between January 2025 and January 2026, the shares devoted to recreation/sport/culture, restaurants/accommodation, and education rose, while transport and information/communication shares fell. The cross-source implication is not that households were uniformly better off or more culturally active: share changes can reflect relative prices, seasonality, substitution, or composition. The useful question is which households preserve social and cultural occasions, which cut mobility or information access, and whether rising shares reflect more participation or simply higher prices. This is EU aggregate expenditure evidence, not household-level welfare or behavioral causality.

Latest comparative demographic rotation: population change is a household, labor, and territorial systems problem

The European Commission JRC Demographic Transformation 2026 record shows the demographic transition as a connected systems problem. The EU population is projected to decline from a current peak of 450.6 million to 398.8 million by 2100, while nearly one in three residents may be 65 or older by 2050 and the population needing support may rise from 36 million to 48 million by 2070. The response therefore runs through care, housing, skills, women’s and older-worker participation, youth transitions, skilled migration, rural and regional policy, and public finance. The cross-source implication is that demographic “decline” does not have one remedy: increasing labor participation without care and housing capacity can transfer pressure into households, while migration without regional and social infrastructure can redistribute rather than resolve the constraint. This is official projection and policy-synthesis evidence, not an evaluation of EU implementation or a forecast of any single country.

Latest comparative identity-infrastructure rotation: adoption can rise faster than legitimacy

The UK Digital Identity Sectoral Analysis 2026 record shows digital identity becoming an infrastructure layer across finance, employment, healthcare, public services, and age assurance. Reported use and understanding are high, but income-linked gaps remain: 65% of respondents in households under £19,999 reported use versus 87% among households earning £40,000 or more. Preferences are also context-specific: digital identity is more acceptable for online purchases and public services, while physical proof remains preferred in many in-person and healthcare settings. Most strikingly, 71% expect digital identity to be important within five years, while only 43% view its current direction positively. The cross-source implication is that infrastructure can become practically inevitable before it becomes normatively legitimate; access, non-digital alternatives, data control, and visible remedy will determine whether convenience becomes capability or dependency. This is a UK market assessment and weighted consumer survey, not evidence of improved service outcomes or causal trust change.

Latest comparative political-voice rotation: voting is not enough when citizens cannot see the feedback loop

The canonical OECD Trust Survey political-voice record extends the U.S. Pew finding beyond one national civic culture. Across participating OECD and accession-candidate countries, 68% say voting influences government decisions, but only 31% are confident that the political system allows people like them to have a say. Public consultations and townhalls are seen as influential by only 39% and 35%, respectively. The dominant reported barrier is not simply lack of time or resources: 40% say elected officials do not care about people like them. The cross-source implication is that trust depends on a visible conversion of participation into institutional response. Information and low-cost expression can widen the voice funnel, but without feedback, remedy, and evidence of responsiveness they may coexist with low legitimacy. This is comparative perception and participation evidence, not observed policy impact or a causal trust estimate.

Latest U.S. civic-culture rotation: public participation is a portfolio, not a single scale

The Pew-Knight public-life engagement record shows why “engaged” versus “disengaged” is too blunt for the atlas. The report identifies Mobilizers (9%), Connectors (28%), Spectators (31%), and Outsiders (31%) by combining news attention, voting, volunteering, religious participation, donations, and direct political action. News attention is relatively broad, but direct institutional contact and repeated collective action are concentrated: 65% of Mobilizers contacted an elected official in the prior year versus 13% of Connectors, 7% of Spectators, and 3% of Outsiders. The socioeconomic pattern matters too: Outsiders are more likely to have lower education and income, while remaining politically mixed rather than simply partisan or apathetic. The cross-source implication is that public voice depends on the conversion of attention into organization, time, resources, and reachable institutions; electoral participation alone is not a sufficient measure of civic capacity. This is a descriptive, period-specific aggregate survey classification, not a longitudinal causal account of participation.

Latest U.S. housing-structure rotation: supply, mobility, migration, and affordability are one system

The Harvard JCHS State of the Nation’s Housing 2026 record shows why new construction does not automatically become accessible housing: only 23% of listings in March 2026 were affordable to households earning $75,000 or less, down from 49% in 2019. Residential mobility fell to 11.2% in 2024, the lowest point in the ACS’s 20-year history, while first-time buyers fell to 21% of buyers and reached a median age of 40. The report also links declining immigration to slower household formation and regional population growth. The cross-source implication is that housing is a gatekeeper for labor mobility, family formation, demographic renewal, and access to opportunity—not merely a monthly expense. This is a secondary public-data synthesis, not a causal land-use evaluation or household panel.

Latest comparative urban-cohesion rotation: migration becomes a projection surface for unresolved insecurity and state-capacity failure

The KAS South Africa migration, rule-of-law, and social-cohesion record shows how unemployment, inequality, housing pressure, service deficits, spatial segregation, and weak institutional trust can be translated into anti-migrant attribution. Migrants become a projection surface for conflicts whose deeper causes are domestic economic and state-capacity failures. Gauteng and Cape Town also show that the same belonging conflict takes different forms depending on labor markets, housing, visibility, organization, and institutional reach. This is a qualitative urban case with cited statistics and event series, not representative public opinion or a causal estimate of migration effects.

Latest U.S. administrative-trust rotation: formal access can remain available while perceived enforcement risk makes public systems practically unusable

The Urban Institute immigrant-families record adds a U.S. survey route from immigration concern through non-use of work, health care, schools, police, community events, and safety-net programs. The route is household-wide: mixed-status families reported much higher worry about ordinary public contact than immigrant families made up entirely of U.S. citizens, including worry about work, care, and police contact. The cross-source implication is that administrative capacity depends on perceived safety and data trust as well as formal eligibility; a program can exist on paper while becoming unreachable in practice. This is 2025 repeated-cross-sectional survey evidence, not a causal estimate of enforcement effects or proof of durable withdrawal.

Latest U.S. AI-work rotation: adoption is broad, but time benefit is not automatically worker-controlled time

The Census HTOPS AI task/time record adds task-level evidence beneath the existing AI-exposure and AI-attitudes layers. Fifty-six percent of workers reported using AI for at least one job task; among recent users, 31% reported saving one to two hours, while 10% reported no time saved and 4% reported additional time. Access and frequency vary by education, sex, and age. The cross-source implication is that the next question is not whether AI is spreading, but whether saved time becomes lower workload, higher output, learning, bargaining power, or employer capture. This is weighted cross-sectional self-report, not verified productivity or realized worker gain.

Latest comparative cultural-infrastructure rotation: culture is social infrastructure, but cost and welcome determine who can convert participation into belonging

The Canada Arts and Heritage Access survey record shows that culture is valued as a source of enjoyment, socializing, local identity, cross-cultural connection, and economic vitality. Yet cost is the leading participation barrier, only 56% report feeling welcome in cultural facilities, and fewer than half say arts and culture help them feel part of their local community or Canada. The cross-source implication is that cultural abundance and cultural belonging are different outcomes: participation becomes social infrastructure only when people can afford entry, feel welcome, and have routes to contribute. This is a national survey summary, not causal evidence that culture produces cohesion.

Latest comparative political-voice rotation: participation is not the same as influence, and influence is not the same as responsiveness

The OECD political voice and trust record shows a persistent legitimacy gap: 68% view voting as influential, but only 31% feel people like them have a say in government. Public consultations and town halls are viewed as less influential, while 40% say elected officials do not care about people like them. The cross-source implication is that voice is an institutional chain: access to participation must be followed by visible responsiveness, adoption or explanation, and feedback. Material constraints also matter—low-income people report more time barriers and more perceived official indifference. This is a cross-national survey synthesis, not evidence that participation caused trust or that consultation outcomes were actually changed.
