The mechanism is mobility-to-place conversion. Easier access, stronger cultural assets, and digital discovery can turn heritage, food, festivals, and local traditions into visitor demand and jobs. But the same growth phase can raise prices, expose workforce and skills gaps, intensify crowding, and distribute benefits unevenly. The WEF estimates 1.5 billion international arrivals, USD 11.6 trillion in total tourism contribution, and 366 million supported jobs in 2025, but its index measures enabling conditions rather than resident welfare or inclusive outcomes.

Rotation finding: follow a mobility signal from borders and affordability through digital discovery, cultural demand, transport, hospitality work, local income, crowding, environmental pressure, and political legitimacy. The open arrow is whether managed growth converts cultural and natural assets into broad local capability or concentrates value while residents absorb the costs.

Consumer polarisation: inflation can hollow out the mainstream while households switch between premium and value modes

The NIQ/World Data Lab consumer-polarisation record adds a global consumption route across FMCG prices, basket trade-offs, premiumisation, value choices, private label, cultural relevance, and regional income mobility. The report says global FMCG prices rose 26% from 2021 to 2025; it projects affluent consumers to account for USD 35.9 trillion of 2026 spending versus USD 31.6 trillion for the much larger core-consumer group. It also projects North America and Europe's share of the global core-consumer population to fall from 41% to 13% by 2036, as volume growth shifts toward emerging markets.

The mechanism is price-pressure-to-selective-basket conversion. Households do not simply become “premium” or “value” consumers: they trade up when trust, function, convenience, identity, or cultural relevance earns the premium, and trade down where it does not. That can hollow out mainstream products while making private label, precise claims, local distribution, and category-specific value more important. This record uses commercial market analysis and projections, not individual household budgets, respondent purchase histories, causal welfare estimates, nutrition outcomes, or proof that commercial classes map cleanly onto social classes.

Rotation finding: follow a consumption signal from inflation and wages through price tiers, trust, cultural fit, private label, social commerce, regional income mobility, household trade-offs, and firm market power. The open arrow is whether selective upgrading preserves meaningful choice or whether polarization leaves households and products stranded between unaffordable premium and eroded value.

AI-mediated participation: scaling voice can broaden access while shifting representation into systems that need oversight

The OECD AI citizen-participation record adds a technology-to-democracy route based on 50 use cases across 22 countries. The report identifies nine application types, with sense-making, virtual assistance, and translation among the most widespread; deliberative processes are a prominent site of experimentation. These tools can improve design, accessibility, interpretation at scale, communication, and process cost, but the reviewed government use remains mostly ad hoc or pilot-based, with local governments driving much of the emerging practice.

The mechanism is mediated-voice conversion. AI can help more people enter, translate, summarize, or navigate a participatory process, while also deciding which inputs are legible, grouped, prioritized, or omitted. The OECD flags ethical, operational, exclusion, public-resistance, skills, scaling, and vendor lock-in risks. This record uses public use-case analysis, not respondent-level records, representative participation rates, individual political histories, causal effects on turnout or trust, proof of policy influence, or evidence that every deployment has the same effect.

Rotation finding: follow a voice signal from access and language through AI mediation, deliberation, data governance, human oversight, civic space, policy uptake, trust, and institutional legitimacy. The open arrow is whether low-tech alternatives, transparent guardrails, citizen co-governance, skills, and procurement controls make AI a participation amplifier or a new gatekeeper.

Private finance: public risk-sharing can expand capital while concentrating development finance away from the most fragile and social sectors

The OECD private-finance mobilisation record adds a development-finance route across guarantees, direct investment, syndicated loans, recipient-country risk, sector allocation, climate finance, multilateral development banks, and data/coordination capacity. OECD reports more than USD 600 billion in private resources mobilised by official development finance from 2012 to 2024, with a 2024 peak of USD 77 billion. About 70% of mobilised finance reached middle-income countries that were not least-developed countries, while only 8% reached low-income countries; 70% went to economic infrastructure and business activities versus 6% to social sectors.

The mechanism is public-risk-sharing-to-investment conversion. Guarantees, development-bank intermediation, and blended instruments can make projects look more investable to private capital, but the resulting portfolio can still favor larger markets, infrastructure, and mitigation over fragile settings, social provision, and adaptation. This record uses OECD aggregate DAC statistics and report synthesis, not individual investments, firm-level causal outcomes, household welfare, jobs or skills effects, technology transfer, project additionality, or proof that mobilisation is inclusive.

Rotation finding: follow a capital signal from public guarantees and country risk through private investment, infrastructure, climate mitigation/adaptation, social sectors, jobs, services, and political legitimacy. The open arrow is whether better data, standardised instruments, country platforms, and multi-stakeholder coordination broaden finance toward low-income, fragile, social, and adaptation needs or reinforce investability bias.

Latest workplace meaning rotation: purpose can improve firm performance while shifting who stays

The current BLS ATUS flexibility record anchors the route in U.S. official statistics. In 2024–25, 57% of wage-and-salary workers could vary when they began and ended work, 69% said an hour or two off for personal or family matters would not be difficult, and 9% knew their schedule one day or less ahead. Parents with children under 18 were more likely to work at home, while workers with less education were more likely to receive short notice. This is access and exposure, not a causal estimate of care adequacy or welfare: nominal flexibility can coexist with low pay, high workload, or unpaid care transfer.

The NBER meaning-at-work record adds a randomized worker-centered firm route to the workplace-control lane. In a two-year rollout among 2,976 white-collar employees, the intervention increased performance; low performers either improved or left; the meaning–pay tradeoff flattened as low-meaning/high-pay workers exited; and parental-leave behavior and bonuses changed. This is stronger than a stated firm purpose or AI-adoption measure because it observes worker-level performance and retention paths. It still does not show whether workers gained durable control, bargaining power, household security, or political voice. Firm performance and worker welfare can move together, diverge, or redistribute risk through exit.

The comparative IZA job-flexibility record extends the worker-control lane into the household. In 464 Dutch couples with children, a collective structural model links parent-specific schedule and telecommuting flexibility to market work, childcare, chores, household resources, and modeled child well-being. Simulations generally reduce gender gaps in paid and domestic work, yet the child-well-being result is not uniform: lower wages accompanying flexibility reduce household resources, and the parent targeted matters. The comparison shows why “more flexibility” cannot be treated as a single welfare outcome; the open U.S. test is whether control is usable without transferring pay risk or unpaid care back into the household.

The NBER autonomy-of-labor record adds a more tightly identified task-control mechanism. In a randomized online labor experiment with 476 U.S.-located workers, high autonomy increased preventative effort by 9.7 percentage points because workers could distribute skippable work across two task sets. The result shows that discretion can alter risk management and later effort, not merely reported job satisfaction. It is still a short task experiment: the open questions are earnings, schedule control, household time, health, bargaining, and whether autonomy was usable in the worker's broader labor market.

The next decisive workplace test should follow the same worker from purpose or system exposure through actual task/schedule control, pay and care tradeoffs, voice or appeal, retention/exit, and later household security. The intervention should not be coded as universally beneficial merely because average performance or bonuses rise.

Latest cultural rotation: stable aggregate arts engagement can conceal a public/private shift

The ATUS arts-engagement record adds a national cultural baseline to the meaning, time, and participation lanes. A 2026 analysis of 236,270 nationally representative American Time Use Survey respondents covering 2003–2023 found that daily arts engagement was stable overall, while participatory activities such as dancing, performing, arts, crafts, and writing rose slightly and receptive activities such as attending performing arts or museums and watching dancing declined slightly. People also increasingly did arts activities alone at home, with differing trends by sex, age, and income.

The usable claim is therefore about composition and setting, not cultural collapse: an unchanged daily aggregate can contain a movement from public or receptive settings toward private or participatory ones. The diary design does not identify whether the shift reflects access, cost, time pressure, technology, health, or preference, and it does not measure durable belonging, organizational continuity, trust, or political action. The next end-to-end test should retain activity type, setting, companionship, and subgroup position, then join them to local cultural infrastructure, social connection, and later collective or political behavior.

Cultural-to-civic bridge: positive associations are real but context-sensitive

The NEA Great Connector record tests the open middle between cultural participation and civic action using three national surveys. In the July 2022 SPPA analytic sample, arts participation was associated with a 4.86 incidence-rate ratio for civic/community engagement after demographic and socioeconomic controls; in the February 2025 HTOPS analytic sample, the corresponding estimate was 1.17. The report also finds stronger SPPA relationships for consuming art (IRR 2.77), creating art (1.35), and multi-mode participation, with educational attainment remaining a major predictor.

The important counterweight is the GSS Arts Module: the adjusted overall arts participation relationship was effectively null (IRR 0.999), while creating or performing art remained positively associated (IRR 1.17). The cross-survey spread means the program can retain a cultural-to-civic association without claiming a universal mechanism or causal mobilization effect. Survey frames, measurement windows, analytic samples, education, local opportunity, prior social networks, and selection may all matter. The next end-to-end test should follow a named arts setting and participant exposure through repeated participation, companionship, local institution, civic behavior, and later political or policy feedback.

Public engagement is plural: action, attention, community, and trust diverge

The Pew public-life engagement record adds a recent national map of the action endpoint without treating “engagement” as a single ladder. Pew’s late-2025 Cross-Sectional Engagement Survey classified adults from 19 political, civic, religious, and news measures into Mobilizers (9%), Connectors (28%), Spectators (31%), and Outsiders (31%). Mobilizers reported the highest political action: 65% contacted an elected official and 77% volunteered. Connectors reported 87% 2024 voting and 65% group membership but much less direct political action. Spectators followed national news at 84% while only 7% contacted an elected official, and Outsiders followed news at 41% while 41% still reported voting.

The pattern is important for the broad material-to-meaning chain because it separates attention, community participation, institutional action, and voting. The follow-up ATP analysis also found roughly one-in-five trust in the federal government across all four groups, while trust in national news ranged from 64% among Connectors to 45% among Outsiders. These are cross-sectional cluster associations, not causal types or evidence that hardship produced withdrawal. The next end-to-end test should attach a dated public-system, workplace, consumer, or household episode to a distinct action route, then retain the actor, attribution, response, recovery, and persistence variables.

Read this synthesis first

Latest household-room rotation: assistance can coexist with pressure, and the pooled pattern can reverse by context

The new SIPP housing-transition timing audit adds a real public-use person-month backbone to the housing, work, and household-room lanes. The streamed 2025 SIPP file retains 379,215 person-month rows for 32,052 people in 13,910 households across all 12 months. Its key finding is a timing boundary: the main housing-assistance fields are reference-period or residence-spell measures, not monthly receipt histories. The genuinely monthly EOTHAS_MNYN field supports a narrower same-person descriptive screen.

That screen observes reported next-month rent/mortgage payment difficulty of 9.15% among month-t assistance-exposed pairs and 4.17% among unexposed pairs, while job-count and poverty-band movement are close. The result is compatible with assistance reaching people already under greater pressure; it is not an assistance effect. The follow-up tenure and resource counterexample audit shows why: among renters below twice the poverty line, exposed cells have lower reported next-month difficulty than unexposed cells, while the direction reverses in higher renter resource bands. Owner exposed cells are small and imprecise.

Evidence layer What it adds to the cross-source map What it does not establish
SIPP public person-month timing audit A lawful same-person clock for assistance context, work, resources, and reported housing difficulty Monthly HUD receipt, benefit amount or adequacy, application effort, landlord response, recovery, trust, or political action
SIPP weighted assistance/work screen Assistance context beside a following-period household-security measure Causation, program identity, arrears, eviction, homelessness, or verified protection
SIPP tenure/resource stratification A direct counterexample to treating the pooled contrast as one universal effect Why the direction differs, because exposure remains a combined clothing/housing-assistance field
HUD–LEHD and HEARS linked records Separate linked evidence on labor trajectories and exit-type outcomes A valid join to the SIPP person-months or one combined household story

The cross-cutting implication is stronger than “assistance works” or “assistance fails.” Support and pressure can coexist, and the meaning of a support route depends on starting resources, tenure, timing, and the form of assistance. This connects four atlas themes: household room, public-system access, housing/place, and unequal exposure/status. It also sharpens the broader subtheme of usable help: a program indicator is not the same as an adequate amount, a reachable alternative, or a durable reduction in risk.

The result also reinforces a general measurement rule. A field's presence is not enough; the atlas must preserve its clock. Reference-period assistance, residence-spell status, monthly work, and next-month reported difficulty cannot be silently treated as one dated benefit episode. The correct broad-program finding is therefore a distributional and methodological one: public support can appear alongside continuing constraint, and aggregate contrasts can hide protective, neutral, and adverse paths in different resource contexts.

The next cross-source test is not another assistance percentage. It is a program-specific or matched route that retains amount, adequacy, alternatives, notice or application effort, institutional response, and a later housing or security outcome. Until that exists, keep the SIPP bridge, HUD–LEHD trajectory, and HEARS exit-type evidence as layered records rather than a pooled causal claim.

Latest cross-scale rotation: dependence is shared, but leverage is conditional

The new dependence, control, and leverage synthesis connects labor-market concentration, platform defaults and exit, connected- vehicle data control, large-load infrastructure, and U.S. arms-transfer concentration. These sources do not share a unit or causal design. Their cross-source value is structural: each shows an actor facing a route whose cost of refusal, switching, delay, or non-use may be unevenly distributed.

The comparison supports a bounded distinction:

dependence = exposure to the cost of refusal
control = ability to shape another actor's available route
leverage = observed change in that actor's behavior, decision, or autonomy

The worker and platform sources show that dependence can enter political meaning, beliefs, and behavior. The PJM and Virginia records show that infrastructure dependence can produce operating and regulatory response before household incidence is visible. SIPRI shows supplier concentration without proving delivery, sustainment, recipient obedience, or deterrence. The search experiment is a counterexample to permanent lock-in: temporary exposure to an alternative can update quality beliefs and produce some continued preference.

The cross-cutting subtheme is unequal replaceability. Formal choice is not equivalent to practical agency when alternatives require losing income, time, information, safety, service quality, local belonging, or strategic readiness. The next decisive evidence is therefore not another concentration or use-rate measure; it is an attributed response, correction, substitution, refusal, acceptance, or durable change for the affected actor.

Latest linked housing-route rotation: assistance entry and exit have different labor clocks

The HUD–LEHD trajectory record adds a genuine longitudinal administrative bridge. Census CES links HUD assistance records from 2005–2022 to LEHD earnings records from 2000–2023 and follows employment and earnings around entry and exit over 14-year windows. Among 2.086 million first-time entrants, the earnings slope changes from -$112 per year before entry to +$174 after entry; the $286 slope break exceeds the adjusted ACS comparison by $228 per year, while the employment slope rises 1.45 percentage points per year. Among 1.233 million final leavers, the post-exit employment and earnings slope changes are -1.05 percentage points and -$244 per year, respectively, relative to more stable adjusted stayers.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Linked HUD participant and LEHD employment/earnings records 2.086 million first-time entrants and 1.233 million final leavers; longitudinal entry/exit trends and adjusted comparisons housing-assistance transition → same linked unit's employment/earnings path → possible household-room change causal effect, assistance amount/timing, rent burden, housing quality, alternatives, exit reason, remedy adequacy, health, trust, and action

This is stronger than a participation total because the linked units are followed across time, but it is not a complete household recovery episode. Entry and exit are selected events; the next test must add housing conditions, assistance details, work/care trade-offs, and the reason and consequences of exit before interpreting the labor trajectory as program effect or security.

Latest housing-exit rotation: exit type separates stability from loss of support

The HUD HEARS exit-type record adds the missing housing-side comparator. In linked data from Seattle Housing Authority and King County Housing Authority, only 13.5% of 8,266 heads of household had positive exits, while 31.6% had negative exits. Within one year, homelessness or unstable housing was recorded for 3.1% of people with positive exits, 14.5% with neutral exits, and 25.4% with negative exits. Negative exits were also associated with about twice the odds of a behavioral-health crisis versus neutral exits; positive exits had lower emergency-department-use odds than negative exits.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Linked PHA exit, wage, Medicaid, behavioral-health, homelessness-service, and HMIS records 8,266 heads of household and 16,301 linked individuals; classified exit type and one-year outcomes assistance exit reason/type → same linked person's housing stability, health, behavioral-health, and wage outcomes national generalization, causal exit effect, assistance adequacy, rent burden for every unit, later trust/action, and durable security

This is the crucial correction to treating “exit” as a single success or failure endpoint. It is a regional observational study, and the categories are partly constructed from administrative reasons, but it demonstrates that the same institutional transition can transfer either autonomy or residual risk.

Latest consumer-pressure rotation: budget exposure differs before hardship is visible

The BLS Consumer Expenditures record adds a population-level composition and distribution layer. In 2024, average annual expenditures were $78,535 per consumer unit; housing was 33.4% of the average budget, and the published average housing expenditure increased 3.3% from 2023. BLS's grouped comparison also shows that income-before-tax and expenditure changes varied across income quintiles, with the lowest-quintile expenditure increase concentrated in housing.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey consumer-unit annual averages and income-quintile groupings Nominal average budget composition, component changes, and grouped income/expenditure changes resource position and budget composition → different observed spending movement and potential exposure to essential costs a dated bill or price, quantity change, substitution, liquidity, debt, food/housing adequacy, time cost, trust, and action for the same unit

This is a distributional consumer-budget signal, not a hardship rate or a causal price effect. A larger expenditure can reflect income, quantity, quality, household composition, or price; a large housing share does not establish that any particular consumer unit faced an unaffordable payment. The record becomes more informative when held beside SHED's reported adaptations and food-security sources, but those surveys remain separate populations rather than a common household trajectory.

Latest consumer-recourse rotation: removing a fee is not the same as restoring financial room

The NBER bank-fee record adds a transaction-level policy-change bridge. Its study of staggered large-bank NSF-fee eliminations and overdraft-policy relaxations finds immediate reductions in the targeted fees, but later reductions in late fees, interest payments, account-maintenance fees, and alternative-financial-service use are observed only among more liquid households. The source reports no substantial reduction in financial stress among more vulnerable households.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Individual transaction data around staggered large-bank fee-policy changes Targeted fee changes and liquidity-differentiated subsequent account/alternative-credit outcomes fee rule → immediate charge reduction → unequal later financial-room indicators original bill or need, merchant/service result, household trade-off, family support, welfare, trust, switching, and durable recovery

This is stronger than a generic fee complaint because it observes a policy change and later account outcomes, but it is not a full consumer-recovery episode. The safe recurring trend is that a visible cost can be removed while the underlying liquidity gap continues to shape who gains later room.

The payment-resilience evidence adds a distinct disruption version of the same problem: during outage conditions, digital payment can become unavailable and cash access is associated with more completed transactions. The fee-policy and outage studies use different populations, shocks, and outcomes, so they do not form one common resilience rate. Their shared implication is narrower: financial fallback capacity—liquidity, cash, credit, and practical access—is a distributed condition for continuity, not a property of a payment system alone.

Latest usable-option rotation: formal routes fail at timing, visibility, and correction

The recent public-system records converge on a mechanism that is broader than any one program. A formal option becomes usable only when the affected person can identify it, reach it in time, and obtain a meaningful result:

Route What is visible What remains open
Federal reentry GAO found earned time was not fully applied toward RRC or home confinement for 21,190 of 29,934 reviewed people; capacity and late contractor payments constrained the route Person-level transfer receipt, housing/work continuity, treatment, later justice contact, and trust
Community supervision BJS counted 3.6819 million adults under probation or parole at year-end 2024 and distinguished completion, incarceration, absconding, and other exits Supervision intensity, condition burden, service use, household effects, and durable inclusion
Accessibility complaints GAO recorded 41 GSA-building complaints, 25 closed and 16 in process; stakeholders reported low public awareness of the route Barrier prevalence, route discovery, correction quality, restored access, and later participation
Digital public contact Census Household Panel evidence suggests text can accelerate initial response, while consent and access differ across demographic groups Accurate representation, privacy cost, trust, policy use, and civic action

Across these routes, the institution can report an eligibility rule, a contact channel, a complaint closure, or a population decline while the person still experiences delay, uncertainty, or no practical alternative. This is a working interpretation, not a pooled causal estimate: the records use different units, agencies, and outcomes. The next decisive test is a same-person route ledger that retains notice or eligibility, attempted access, time and effort, usable alternative, institutional response, verified correction, protected or sacrificed outcome, and later trust, action, switching, or exit.

Latest administrative-contestability rotation: procedure distributes access, voice, and legitimacy

Several recent records make the procedural layer more specific than a general “friction” concept. They show different ways that an institution can decide who reaches a benefit, who can inspect or correct a record, who contests an assessment, and who receives a remedy:

Source unit Observed or estimated stage Safe cross-source connection Still open
NBER SNAP administrative records using ABAWD age exemptions and waiver periods Work requirements associated with higher procedural and overall denials; study interprets administrative burden as participation deterrence policy rule/exemption → paperwork or compliance burden → denial → reduced participation notice, claimant effort, appeal, restored benefits, food security, work quality, trust, and action
U.S. property-tax field experiment Information about average peer tax payments increased perceived fairness and reduced tax appeals comparative information → fairness interpretation → institutional contestation payment, service quality, compliance, durable legitimacy, resignation versus acceptance, and household welfare
DOD/VA toxic-exposure record system Claims staff, clinicians, and researchers use ILER while service-member and veteran access/correction functions roll out institutional visibility → affected-person access and correction → possible claim/care consequence verified exposure, correction success, claim approval, treatment, health, appeal, and trust
Medicare Advantage skilled-nursing authorization review Denials, appeals, and high reversal among appealed requests initial administrative decision → contestation → formal reversal interim care, admission timing, functional recovery, caregiver burden, and plan switching
FTC/Amazon Prime redress program Automatic payment design and aggregate issuance reduce some claim-form burden remedy design → payment reachability → possible receipt eligible-person denominator, acceptance, account correction, adequacy, and recovery

These records do not measure one common administrative-burden rate. Their value is comparative: procedure is not merely an interface around policy; it is a distribution mechanism that can create or remove practical voice. The same formal right can have different meaning depending on notice, documentation, time, information, representation, reversal, and the availability of an alternative. A denial, appeal, correction, or payment should therefore be read as a stage in an actor's route, not as the final state of eligibility, care, food, privacy, or financial recovery.

The cultural and political implication remains conditional. Comparative fairness information can reduce contestation; administrative burden can deter participation; personal record access can make institutional decisions more contestable; and a reversal can signal responsiveness. None of these stages by itself proves trust, legitimacy, political action, or durable use. The decisive next evidence is a same-person or same-account ledger that joins notice, attempt, effort, alternative, institutional response, verified receipt or correction, and later interpretation or action.

The FAA simulator-oversight workload record adds a physical-safety capacity version. The simulator inventory grew by more than 500% from 1990 to 2025 while National Simulator Program staffing stayed steady and evaluation activity was relatively steady in 2019–2024. The Extended Evaluation Interval program can lengthen qualifying simulator review intervals from 12 to 36 months; six of ten selected sponsors raised communication concerns, two cited potential safety concerns, and GAO found unaddressed mission-critical skills gaps. Workload, interval design, sponsor communication, and oversight staffing are visible system conditions—not an accident-risk, simulator-error, pilot-performance, or causal safety estimate. Risk-based extensions may be efficient for high-performing simulators, and the selected-sponsor concerns cannot establish unsafe determinations.

Latest health-record rotation: administrative visibility precedes personal control

The GAO toxic-exposure record adds a data-governance stage to the health and benefits route. GAO reports that the Individual Longitudinal Exposure Record links DOD and VA exposure information for clinicians, researchers, and disability-claims staff, with use increasing after the PACT Act. Service members gained access and could add self-reported updates in March 2026, while veteran access and correction were still in rollout.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
ILER staff-use data, VA screening estimate, and selected stakeholder interviews About 3.2 million of 6.8 million screened veterans were estimated to have a potential exposure; claims staff were the largest user group; access/correction rollout was reported exposure/screening → linked record → claims/clinical use → possible personal access and correction verified exposure, correction success, claim approval, treatment, health improvement, household effect, appeal, trust, and action

This makes “having a record” and “having practical control over the record” separate currencies. It does not show that ILER is inaccurate or that access changes improve benefits. The next decisive test is a named record followed through access, correction, verification, claim or care decision, treatment, health, and later appeal or trust.

Latest same-household meaning rotation: cash changes relationships without a uniform stability result

The guaranteed-income intrahousehold record reports a randomized experiment in which 1,000 recipients received $1,000 per month for three years and 2,000 controls received $50 per month. The experiment found no aggregate household-stability effect, while other household income fell by about $1,700 per year; partners were less likely to be promoted or move to a better job, transfers to friends and family increased, and relationship quality and trust in partners improved suggestively. Other household members were more likely to pursue education or training, and recipients were more likely to report that someone forwent healthcare, an ambiguous measure that may reflect newly visible unmet need rather than a confirmed care loss.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Randomized recipient/control households over three years Household income, partner advancement, transfers, relationship/trust measures, education/training, and healthcare reports cash exposure → intrahousehold redistribution and changed relationship signals → mixed work, care, and meaning outcomes political action, post-payment persistence, actual healthcare receipt, durable security, household decision power, and which person experienced each trade-off

This is a same-household bridge, not a political-action result. It shows why the atlas keeps material improvement, household stability, trust, and action as separate endpoints: a transfer can alter relationships and perceived support without producing a uniform improvement in work or security.

The transitory-income durable-purchase record adds a consumer-finance conversion route. Using variation from the 2008 Economic Stimulus Act, an NBER study estimates that households spent about 80% of a payment on durable goods within three months, largely motor vehicles, and borrowed on average about 40 cents for each stimulus dollar to finance those vehicle purchases. A temporary income gain can therefore become both a durable good—potentially preserving mobility, work, or care access—and a future loan obligation. The study does not establish purchase necessity, loan terms, delinquency, insurance/fuel/repair burden, later cash margin, or whether the purchase improved or weakened household security. Its 2008 policy and vehicle market setting should not be used as a current consumer-credit forecast.

The ACS state transportation-context record adds an ecological counterexample to a single mobility-burden scale. When states, DC, and Puerto Rico are pooled into quartiles by state median household income, zero-vehicle household shares run 6.90%, 6.77%, 11.52%, and 8.16%; the corresponding shares of workers not working from home with commutes of 30 or more minutes are 33.43%, 35.48%, 41.22%, and 42.31%. State median income is a place context, not household income: higher no-vehicle shares can reflect dense urban form and transit availability, while longer commutes can coexist with higher income. These aggregate tables do not identify affordability, service quality, trip success, care access, missed activity, or whether a commute is chosen or required.

Latest causal material-to-politics rotation: income does not automatically become civic action or institutional trust

The guaranteed-income political-attitudes and behavior record analyzes the political outcomes of the same broad guaranteed-income experiment. Among 1,000 low-income treatment participants receiving $1,000 per month for three years and 2,000 controls receiving $50, the study finds no detectable effect on political participation or engagement, largely no change in political preferences, and no detectable change in trust in government, polarization, or support for democracy. It reports small improvements in affect toward racial groups and some politicians, alongside evidence that treated participants viewed work as more important or as a requirement for accessing government programs.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Randomized low-income adults receiving three years of differentiated cash transfers Political participation, engagement, preferences, institutional trust, affect, and work-attitude outcomes cash/resource increase → tested political endpoints; no automatic mobilization or trust shift detected household mediation, attribution and fairness, subgroup mechanisms, post-payment persistence, other transfer designs, and political effects of more salient shocks

This is one of the strongest current causal boundaries in the atlas. It rejects a simple “more resources produce more participation” rule without rejecting the possibility that material conditions matter through other mechanisms, contexts, or politically attributed events. The political outcomes must remain separate from the experiment's intrahousehold work, relationship, and healthcare outcomes.

Latest fairness-to-institution rotation: comparative information can change contestation without proving compliance

The property-tax fairness and appeals record uses a U.S. property-tax field experiment that disclosed the average tax rate paid by other households. Higher perceived peer contributions increased perceived fairness and reduced the likelihood of filing a tax appeal. The authors estimate that each additional dollar paid by the average household increased an individual taxpayer's willingness to contribute by $0.43.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Property-tax households receiving comparative tax-rate information Experimental fairness perception and tax-appeal outcomes; contribution estimate comparative public burden → fairness judgment → administrative contestation payment, compliance, ability to pay, public-service quality, durable legitimacy, political participation, and household security

This adds a concrete action endpoint between material obligation and public meaning. It also prevents an overclaim: appealing a tax assessment, declining to appeal, paying, complying, trusting government, and participating politically are different behaviors with different costs and meanings.

Latest policy-uncertainty rotation: expected relief can change behavior before relief exists

The student-loan policy-uncertainty record studies the 2022 forgiveness and payment-pause uncertainty using an information experiment linked to credit, employment, and nondurable-consumption records. Borrowers more optimistic about future forgiveness reduced loan payments by $40 per month and increased nondurable spending by $80 per month. Those more optimistic about future pauses were 7.5 percentage points more likely to be delinquent after payments resumed; the paper's calibrated model estimates a possible cost of up to 6.9% of the initial loan balance for overly optimistic beliefs.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
U.S. student-loan borrowers in an information experiment linked to administrative records Beliefs, payments, spending, employment linkage, and post-resumption delinquency policy uncertainty → belief → household payment/spending adaptation → later payment risk actual relief, spending purpose, housing/health/family trade-offs, attribution, trust, political action, and durable security

This is a strong belief-to-material-behavior bridge, but it is not evidence that borrowers received forgiveness or changed political identity. An expected policy, a payment decision, a spending shift, a later delinquency, and realized relief must remain separate clocks.

Latest contested-safety rotation: shared goals can produce different political tools

NBER Working Paper 34962 surveys more than 5,400 U.S. respondents and runs randomized information treatments about firearm costs, safe storage, and non-lethal alternatives. Owners and non-owners can share a goal of protecting themselves or their families while reporting different safety perceptions and preferring different means. Information about private costs increased concern about harms and support for safe storage; information about non-lethal tools increased willingness to pay for alternatives and support for incapacitating tools, but did not increase current owners' stated willingness to give up lethal firearms.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
U.S. firearm owners and non-owners in survey and randomized information arms Shared safety goal, divergent perceptions, tool preferences, storage/alternative attitudes, and persistence patterns common protection objective → different risk interpretation and tool choice → bounded attitude movement actual acquisition/use/storage, injury or crime, durable policy support, public safety, and political action

This is a cultural-political correction to treating policy disagreement as a simple disagreement about goals. People may agree on the desired outcome while disagreeing about the safety possibilities they believe different tools create. Stated willingness, storage preference, ownership, and realized safety remain separate endpoints.

Latest disaster-liquidity rotation: credit can protect against collapse without proving recovery

NBER Working Paper 32845 links Federal Disaster Loan applications from households with uninsured disaster damage to pre- and post-shock credit records. Exploiting the program's debt-to-income approval discontinuity, the study reports that approved liquidity reduced bankruptcy likelihood by 61% over the following three years and increased car purchases even three years after receipt. This is a stronger shock-to-financial-outcome bridge than an aggregate disaster-loan total, but it remains a selected applicant route and a debt-based intervention.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Federal Disaster Loan applicants with uninsured damage linked to credit records Quasi-experimental approval effect on bankruptcy and later car purchase disaster damage → liquidity approval → financial-collapse avoidance and possible mobility preservation repayment burden, repairs, insurance and other aid, work/care continuity, non-applicant access, housing security, protected versus displaced needs, trust, and action

The result sharpens the program's hidden-trade question: a loan can preserve mobility or prevent bankruptcy while moving future repayment risk into the household. A later car purchase is not by itself proof of repair, adequacy, or durable recovery.

Latest attribution rotation: people can share the hardship judgment while splitting on cause and remedy

NBER Working Paper 32497 uses a U.S. online survey with conjoint and information experiments to distinguish perceived inflation harm from perceived causes, policy trade-offs, and remedies. Respondents could regard inflation as harmful while assigning responsibility to government, firms, supply chains, labor markets, oil prices, or the Federal Reserve; partisan differences shaped those attributions, and the tested beliefs were difficult to move with information.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
U.S. survey respondents in conjoint and information experiments Perceived harm, cause ranking, trade-off beliefs, policy preferences, partisan contrasts, and experimental belief movement price pressure as publicly understood → attribution/fairness/remedy judgment → possible political meaning respondent-specific price exposure, messenger trust, durable belief change, spending, policy implementation, turnout, vote choice, and whether perceived responsibility matches the economic cause

This closes an interpretive middle that generic inflation or hardship measures cannot supply. It does not establish that a stated cause is correct or that a policy preference became political action; those remain separate links.

Latest work-security rotation: safety has a price, and insurance can change who can move

NBER Working Paper 35580 combines a representative survey of employed U.S. workers with a general-equilibrium search model. Workers require an average 1.63% pay increase for each additional percentage point of annual unemployment risk in a new job. In the model, complete markets raise job mobility by 12% and productivity by 0.19%; unemployment insurance encourages acceptance of riskier, more productive offers while also increasing modeled job loss and unemployment.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Employed-worker survey plus calibrated job-search model Stated wage-for-risk trade-off and modeled mobility/productivity/UI mechanisms job opportunity → security premium → constrained mobility; insurance can expand practical outside options actual offer, acceptance, switching, layoff, household liquidity, benefits, care/health, worker voice, and realized security

This makes “mobility” a conditional resource rather than an unqualified good: moving can improve wages or productivity, but workers with little ability to insure unemployment may rationally remain in safer jobs. The survey result is observed preference evidence; the macro effects are model-dependent and do not establish a universal realized UI effect.

The Census race/context/job-mobility record adds a social-composition condition to that practical-option question. In a restricted ACS analysis across commuting zones, Black and Hispanic workers were less responsive than White workers to changing job opportunities, while their responsiveness rose when opportunities were in destinations with a higher share of their own race. The result does not identify a simple preference for same-race locations: networks, expected discrimination, safety, information, family support, job matching, and moving costs remain competing mechanisms. Nor does it show that a move occurred, that the destination offered better job quality or earnings, or that any later household security, belonging, or political outcome changed.

Latest platform-agency rotation: a choice screen can change use, but implementation determines how much choice becomes real

The NBER browser-choice record studies browser usage around the European Union's Digital Markets Act choice-screen mandate. From month 15 onward, Firefox usage was 91% higher on iOS and 13% higher on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual. The platform difference is consistent with rollout: iOS reached existing users, while Android primarily reached new devices; market shares also moved away from Safari on iOS and Chrome on Android.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
EU browser usage and market-share data around DMA choice-screen rollout Difference-in-differences estimates and platform-specific market movement default/choice architecture → observed alternative-browser use U.S. generalization, comprehension, accessibility, privacy/data-sharing outcomes, durable switching, welfare, and whether users experienced practical exit

The result corrects a simple “more options means more agency” story: regulation can weaken a default, but the effect depends on when and to whom the intervention is delivered. Browser use is still not proof of informed choice or improved privacy.

Latest U.S. platform-learning rotation: active choice is weaker than learning by trying an alternative

The NBER search-engine learning record uses a randomized field experiment with approximately 2,300 U.S. desktop Google users. Requiring active choice increased Bing's share by only 1.1 percentage points. By contrast, users paid to try Bing for two weeks updated positively about its relative quality, and 33% preferred to continue using it. The paper's model estimates larger market-share and consumer-surplus effects if demand frictions and incorrect quality beliefs were removed, but those estimates are counterfactual rather than observed universal outcomes.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Randomized U.S. desktop-user search experiment plus demand model Active-choice effect, paid-trial behavior, quality-belief updating, continued preference, and modeled friction-removal counterfactuals incumbent default → choice or temporary exposure → use, learning, and continued preference durable switching, privacy/security, accessibility, consumer welfare, data-sharing, complaint route, and political action

This separates nominal choice from practical agency: an interface can ask a person to choose without changing behavior, while actual exposure can teach some users that an alternative is better for them. Continued preference is still not verified durable exit or proof of improved privacy.

Latest platform-ownership rotation: removing a platform-owned product can reduce short-run consumer surplus

NBER Working Paper 34135 reports a field experiment that hides Amazon-owned brands in selected product categories. Shoppers choose similar products along observable dimensions, without increased search effort or increased shopping on other retail websites. Model-based counterfactuals estimate a 5.4% short-run consumer-surplus reduction when private labels are removed, with substantial category heterogeneity; demoting Amazon brands in search did not produce a detected welfare gain in the tested setting.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
U.S. Amazon shoppers and selected categories in a field experiment plus calibrated model Product choice, search effort, cross-platform substitution, and category-specific short-run surplus estimates platform-owned availability/placement → observed product choice and search effort → heterogeneous short-run consumer welfare long-run seller entry/exit, ranking fairness, future price/quality, data use, durable dependence, household welfare, and political response

This is a useful counterexample to a one-directional anti-platform story: removing a platform-owned option can harm some current consumers even if the same platform may possess longer-run gatekeeping power. Short-run product choice and long-run competitive structure must remain separate endpoints.

Cross-source platform-agency synthesis: choice has at least four different clocks

The current platform evidence supports a more precise practical-agency model. The sources do not measure one common consumer or one common welfare outcome, but they separate four mechanisms that are often collapsed into “choice.”

Mechanism Evidence surface What changes What remains unproven
Prompted choice EU browser choice-screen rollout Alternative-browser use changes, with strong iOS/Android rollout heterogeneity comprehension, accessibility, privacy, durable switching, U.S. transferability
Learned choice U.S. paid search-engine trial Temporary exposure updates quality beliefs and produces continued preference for some users durable exit, privacy/security, broad welfare, complaint or correction route
Consent friction Cookie-banner field experiment and structural model Click burden, defaults, dismissal, and repeated decision time shape data-sharing behavior informed consent, actual downstream data use, equal accessibility, realized privacy
Owned-option value Amazon private-label field experiment Removing a platform-owned option can reduce short-run consumer surplus without increasing search or cross-platform substitution long-run seller competition, ranking fairness, future prices/quality, platform dependence
Data-access governance Platform data-neutrality model Equal data quantity and price can widen seller access and downstream competition while reducing modeled data-production incentives actual market implementation, data quality, privacy/security, enforcement cost, seller survival, and consumer welfare

The synthesis implication is that practical agency is not a single binary state. A person may receive more nominal options, learn that an alternative is better, remain inattentive to consent, or value an incumbent-owned product—all at different clocks. The decisive missing design is a protected user-level panel that joins interface exposure, comprehension and accessibility, actual use, data-sharing, support/complaint, retention, switching, and welfare. Until then, market-share movement, click behavior, continued preference, and consumer-surplus estimates must remain separate endpoints.

The platform data-neutrality record makes the governance tradeoff explicit. In the model, a weak rule requiring only equal data amounts can be offset through discriminatory pricing. A stronger rule equalizing both data quantity and price broadens access and intensifies downstream competition, but can lower the platform's incentive to refine and produce data; the reduced-data effect can outweigh competition benefits in the modeled consumer-welfare comparison. This is a theoretical mechanism, not an observed U.S. platform result or a rule recommendation. It does not measure data accuracy, privacy, security, compliance cost, actual seller outcomes, or consumer welfare in any particular market.

Latest property-mobility rotation: mortgage lock-in makes staying an active constraint

The mortgage-lock-in and housing-mobility record combines individual mortgage data with a spatial housing-ladder model. It reports a 25% causal reduction in borrower mobility associated with mortgage lock-in, with disproportionate reduction in moves down the housing ladder. The separate model counterfactual estimates house-price and rent increases of 4.4% and 1.5% relative to no lock-in; those price estimates are not observed household payments.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Individual mortgage data plus spatial housing-ladder model Study-specific lock-in/mobility evidence and modeled equilibrium effects rate change and low-rate mortgage → constrained sale/buy option → staying or altered move desired move, replacement housing, repair/insurance, care/work, household security, trust, and exit

This complements managed-retreat evidence: an official buyout can produce a move, while a financial condition can make staying the adaptation. Neither endpoint alone proves durable housing security.

Latest workplace-control rotation: request, grant, and job structure are different stages

BLS reports that 5.9 million wage and salary workers requested or made a change to help them do their job better in July 2024. Schedule requests were fully granted 70.1% of the time, partially granted 21.9%, and not granted 7.5%; full-grant shares were lower for training and workplace accessibility. Separately, the 2025 Occupational Requirements Survey reports pause control for 53.5% of workers, self-paced workload for 18.5%, and employer-driven schedule variability for 48.3%.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
CPS worker requests/grant outcomes plus ORS job requirements Worker-request and employer-grant distributions; establishment-based job-structure estimates need or desired improvement → requested change → full/partial/no grant; job-level control context same-worker usability, persistence, pay, health/care, voice, retention, household security, and exit

This advances the implementation-to-control arrow without treating a request, a grant, or a job-level requirement as a complete worker outcome.

Latest remedy rotation: cashing and reissue are a middle stage between formal payment and recovery

The FTC's 2024 Annual Report on Refunds to Consumers documents a six-step refund process and reports that 2,794,012 of 4,350,411 consumers in its first-distribution table had cashed a payment to date (64.2%). In programs closed during 2024, 1,162,743 of 1,770,214 consumers sent a payment had cashed at least one (65.7%). A named Amazon Flex reissue using Zelle produced 2,806 successful payments and raised reported participation from 90.3% to 92.3%.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
FTC 2024 refund distributions and Amazon Flex reissue Administrator-reported payment, cashing, reissue, additional-distribution, and closure stages formal remedy → payment usability and administrative reach individual adequacy, underlying correction, continued work/service, trust, switching, exit, and durable household recovery

This is stronger than a settlement order or check-sent count, but cashing is not the same as full compensation or restored practical options.

Latest material-to-action rotation: hurricane exposure can move policy and create electoral risk

NBER Working Paper 25835 uses the universe of federal disaster declarations from 1989–2014 and reports that representatives from hurricane-hit districts were more likely to support environmental regulation and control in the next year. The agenda change persisted and was associated with an electoral penalty in following elections, with stronger responses among safer districts, more experienced representatives, and representatives with stronger environmental records.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Hurricane-hit congressional districts, representatives, legislative records, and subsequent elections Study-level disaster exposure, lagged representative response, persistence, and electoral association material disaster → institutional agenda/action → later electoral consequence household damage, aid/insurance, attribution, trust, voter awareness, turnout/vote reason, implementation, and recovery

This is one of the clearest current event-to-institution-to-political-outcome routes, but it is not a same-voter household-to-ballot chain.

Latest capability-to-external-response rotation: agreement commitments are not replaceability

The USTR fact sheet on the February 2026 U.S.-Taiwan Agreement on Reciprocal Trade reports Taiwan tariff and non-tariff commitments, a Taiwan-linked plan for U.S. semiconductor, electronics/AI, and energy clusters, and named planned purchases for 2025–2029. The new Taiwan response record keeps those commitments separate from the prior record's TSMC Arizona production and workforce observations.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
USTR agreement and referenced AIT-TECRO MOU Officially reported bilateral terms and plans; the $84.8 billion total is a transparent sum of three planned categories domestic strategic-capacity pressure/alignment → external partner trade, investment, and procurement commitments approval, contracts, payment, delivery, output, supplier switching, local burden, persistence, and changed strategic behavior

This advances the external-response stage without calling a negotiated plan a realized capability or a concession that proves durable U.S. leverage.

Latest property-risk rotation: assistance does not guarantee a reachable housing route

GAO-26-108154 reports more than $3 billion in FEMA Individual Assistance to 1.2 million individuals and households affected by selected recent disasters. The program can cover temporary lodging, rental housing, and home repairs, but the review also reports long helpline waits, confusing eligibility letters, constrained post-disaster housing, direct-housing setup delays, and access concerns after delivery changes toward state/local centers and away from door-to-door canvassing.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
FEMA assistance totals plus selected helpline, letter, housing, and institutional evidence Agency-reported assistance scale and selected implementation barriers disaster need → assistance route → possible lodging/rental/repair support → housing-reach constraint survivor eligibility, notice, application, award, receipt, repair, safe occupancy, move/stay, durable security, trust, and action

This advances the property-risk lane from protection and hazard toward a named public recovery route. It does not turn aggregate dollars or selected official accounts into a survivor-level recovery rate.

The GAO FEMA assistance/housing-reach record preserves the delivery and federalism boundary behind that route. GAO reviewed FEMA data and 56 interviews or written responses and reports that officials in four Helene- and Milton-affected states lacked their own individual-assistance programs. Federal and state officials also emphasized that state and local governments need preparation time because they rely on significant federal support. This is evidence of selected institutional dependence, not a representative measure of local capacity or an argument that federal pooling is ineffective. It does not link a survivor through eligibility, contact, application, award, payment, repair, occupancy, or durable housing security.

Latest disaster-capacity rotation: federal support meets uneven local capability

The state/local disaster-response capability record adds an upstream institutional layer to the FEMA assistance route. GAO's selected-state review found wide variation in response capability and reported particular challenges for rural or less-resourced jurisdictions, even inside otherwise well-resourced states. Officials emphasized clear guidance, time to prepare, and federal coordination when responsibilities change; federal officials also described a continuing federal-support floor for catastrophic disasters.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Selected state preparedness assessments plus federal, state, and local official interviews Capability variation, federal-support dependence, rural/resource constraints, and role-transition requirements hazard → jurisdictional capability and federal support → coordination and implementation conditions → possible assistance reach response speed, survivor contact, eligibility, receipt, repair, safe housing, local economic recovery, trust, and political action

This sharpens the distinction between formal program availability and usable capacity. It does not establish that federal dependence is inherently harmful: federal pooling may be efficient, and variation may reflect hazards or local responsibilities. The next decisive test is a named jurisdiction and event linking capability, support, role transition, response timing, survivor reach, repair, and durable recovery.

Latest service-route rotation: work requirements can become procedural denials

The SNAP procedural-denial record uses SNAP administrative data and difference-in-differences comparisons around age-based exemptions for ABAWDs aged 50 and older and periods of work-requirement waivers. The study reports significant increases in procedural and overall denials under work requirements and interprets the result as participation deterrence through administrative burden.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
SNAP administrative records in study-selected jurisdictions and ABAWD age/waiver comparisons Policy-associated procedural and overall denial changes work requirement/exemption → administrative burden → denial → participation deterrence claimant notice, effort, appeal, restoration, food security, health, work, later trust, and political action

This advances the public-system route toward remedy without treating denial as the same thing as ineligibility, final loss, or household recovery. The public abstract does not disclose a full denominator or every jurisdiction and does not provide a claimant-level follow-up.

Latest experimental rotation: surveillance effects depend on managerial clarity

NBER Working Paper 33348 randomizes digital-surveillance use and whether its use is explained according to workers' baseline productivity in an online labor market. The study reports no statistically significant average performance effect from surveillance alone, but a significant output reduction when the presence or removal of surveillance is not explained on the basis of worker performance.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Randomized online-labor-market workers in surveillance and explanation arms Randomized monitoring, rationale, worker-performance grouping, and output response surveillance implementation → managerial explanation/worker interpretation → output response national exposure, pay, autonomy, voice, appeal, remedy, health, retention, exit, household security, and long-run effects

This gives the broader GAO review a causal mechanism without treating online labor-market output as ordinary employment quality. It also makes transparency and rationale an observable implementation variable rather than a soft interpretive add-on.

Latest workplace-implementation rotation: surveillance changes the stakes of measurement

The GAO digital-workplace-surveillance record reviews 122 studies published from 2020 through 2024 and interviews stakeholders from 11 organizations. It describes digital-surveillance tools as capable of improving safety or identifying health problems while also pressuring workers to move faster, increasing injury risk, creating anxiety, and exposing workers to flawed benchmarks or incomplete task measures. Those implementation failures can feed into low evaluations, lower pay, discipline, or termination. GAO identifies EEOC, NLRB, and DOL OSHA as relevant investigative routes and reports that several agencies had rescinded or were reassessing prior guidance in 2025.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
GAO review of 122 studies plus 11 stakeholder organizations Reviewed worker-effect patterns and agency roles; no worker-level prevalence estimate monitoring design/transparency/targets → possible safety, mental-health, evaluation, and employment-risk pathway → institutional oversight route named worker exposure, consequential decision, appeal, remedy, pay or health outcome, job exit, household security, later trust, and collective action

This is an implementation bridge, not proof that surveillance is uniformly harmful. The same technology can support safety, while opaque or inaccurate measurement can transfer uncertainty and contestation costs to workers. It therefore advances the work-control lane without collapsing tool adoption, worker exposure, employer authority, voice, and realized household outcomes into one observation.

Latest trust rotation: care-seeking depends on which institution is trusted

NBER Working Paper 32028, revised in April 2026, uses a nationally representative U.S. adult survey and a model of care-seeking through perceived usefulness, expected disutility, out-of-pocket cost, and claim denial. The study separates trust in doctors, nurses, hospitals, insurers, public-health authorities, and the health-care system overall. It reports that higher trust is associated with more retrospective and anticipated preventive and elective care-seeking and less care avoidance, with an association comparable to education and income gradients. Structural estimates describe trust as more substitutable across entities overall but more complementary within provider domains; the reported simulations assign the largest effect to losses of trust in doctors.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Nationally representative U.S. adult trust and care-seeking survey Entity-specific trust, retrospective/anticipated care, mechanism associations, structural estimates, and counterfactual simulations health need/care decision → institutional trust → perceived value, disutility, cost, and denial → seek, delay, or avoid care dated trust shock, appointment/treatment receipt, affordability, health, debt, later trust, remedy, switching, and political action

This supplies a behavioral middle to the trust-and-meaning lane. It also prevents institutional trust from being treated as one pooled attitude: provider, hospital, insurer, and public-health trust can have different routes. Because the evidence is survey and model based, it does not prove that a trust change caused a later decision; access, resources, prior experience, and health need remain alternative explanations.

Latest public-capacity rotation: disaster assistance depends on workforce reach

GAO-26-108427 reports that FEMA averaged about 25,134 employees in FY2025, while more than 4,300 separated, a 55% increase over FY2024. GAO also reports that FEMA rescinded its strategic plan and did not base key 2025–2026 workforce decisions on a workforce analysis; FEMA officials described lost institutional knowledge and longstanding staffing challenges. During the Helene and Milton response, FEMA deployed 13,500 employees, and only 4% of the incident-management workforce was available to deploy in November 2024 afterward. Anticipated DHS surge support for the 2026 hurricane season fell to about 240 personnel from 600 in 2025. GAO connects reduced surge and call-center staffing to long waits and unanswered calls reported for Texas flood survivors.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
FEMA workforce, cadres, deployment, and selected disaster-assistance cases Staffing counts, separations, planning condition, deployment, anticipated surge capacity, and selected contact evidence concurrent disaster demand → workforce/planning constraint → surge/call-center/grant reach → access friction representative contact failure, application/notice, assistance receipt, housing and income continuity, health, trust, and action

This adds an upstream public-capacity mechanism to the flood and wildfire records. Federal dollars and private firm capacity can exist while the route to an answer remains constrained by staffing, institutional memory, and competing disasters. The selected GAO cases do not prove that staffing reductions caused any individual survivor outcome; demand, communication systems, policy, and application complexity remain alternative explanations.

Latest disaster-capacity rotation: federal finance can change which firms survive a flood

The flood disaster-aid, firm-reallocation, and productivity record studies large federally declared floods with confidential plant-level Census data, business credit, and county-income measures. It reports that exits were concentrated among the least productive plants; machinery released by exits moved toward more productive entrants; surviving plants upgraded machinery and productivity; and federal disaster spending expanded financing access for young and small firms. The recorded estimates include a 3.6-percentage-point increase in shutdown within two years, more than 11% higher survivor productivity by year six, about 14% higher entrant productivity, and about a 3.1% increase in bank loans after declared floods. In contrast, severe non-declared floods had higher exits and about a 0.73% decline in aggregate TFP without the same productivity selection.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Flood-affected plants, firms, credit, and counties in CES-26-52 Event-study estimates of exit, capital reallocation, productivity, lending, and county income across declared, non-declared, and denied-request floods flood shock → federal finance → firm selection, credit, and productive capacity → local-income signal worker continuity, wages and job quality, firm ownership, relocation, customer/service continuity, housing and insurance recovery, trust, and political action

This adds a firm-and-public-finance realization stage to the disaster lane. It is important because emergency capacity is not only a dollar total: finance can affect which organizations remain and which machines move. But selective exit and higher productivity are not the same as universal local recovery, and the study's manufacturing and infrequent-inland-flood setting limits the generalization.

Latest infrastructure rotation: broad water coverage coexists with uneven household responsibility

The EPA/CDC drinking-water coverage and replacement-risk record reports $625 billion in public drinking-water needs over 20 years, including $422.9 billion for distribution and transmission. EPA's approximately four million lead-service-line estimate combines three million reported lead or galvanized lines requiring replacement with one million lines predicted to be lead from unknown-material reporting; neither count is completed replacement or household exposure. CDC reports that about nine in ten Americans receive water from community systems, while about one in eight use private wells; private-well owners are generally responsible for safety, and about one in five sampled private wells had a potentially health-affecting chemical.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
EPA infrastructure assessment and CDC coverage indicators National need, projected service-line inventory, public/private coverage, governance responsibility, sampled-well contamination infrastructure need → exposure/governance route → public replacement or household testing responsibility named household exposure, notice, replacement, cost, remediation time, health, mobility, trust, and action

This adds a domestic-capability boundary: broad public coverage and large public investment needs can coexist with private responsibility for testing and safety. The units are national systems and sampled wells, not a common household panel.

Latest time-and-care rotation: care capacity is a differentiated time buffer, not one shared route

The Census 2023 SIPP working paper examines first-time parents who worked before and after their first biological child's birth. Among the 2014–2023 cohort, any leave was reported by 89.2% of mothers and 63.9% of fathers; paid leave was reported by 51.6% and 49.3%. Paid leave, no-leave shares, and return within less than one month differed across race/ethnicity-by-sex groups.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
2023 SIPP first-time-parent work/leave universe Descriptive leave, paid-leave, no-leave, and return-timing comparisons birth/work-family need → leave route and timing → differentiated care/work option employer/job mechanism, leave adequacy, wages, childcare, job retention, caregiver/child outcomes, security, trust, and action

This strengthens the time/care lane by separating nominal leave from a paid, usable, and timely option. It remains a selected employed-parent comparison, not a causal racial or gender explanation and not an all-parent access rate.

The dependent-coverage and parental-job-retention record adds a causal benefit-to-work bridge. Exploiting the ACA's birth-month discontinuity in the duration of dependent eligibility, the employer-claims study finds that extra eligibility increased dependent take-up and a proxy for parental job retention. The effect was strongest among parents nearer a job-exit margin, families placing more value on dependent coverage, and workers at firms offering a broader set of insurance options. The result shows that a child's coverage can shape a parent's labor-market decision; it does not show whether staying was desired or harmful, the retained job's pay, safety, schedule, or quality, plan affordability or network adequacy, actual care continuity, or family wellbeing. Coverage-related retention is therefore neither automatically coercive job lock nor automatic household security.

The newer Census child-care and BLS eldercare layers extend the same conversion problem beyond first birth. Census reports that some households with children ages 0–13 had an adequate-care problem that prevented more work; among affected households, reported adaptations include paid or unpaid leave, reduced hours, non-search, job quitting, and supervision while working. BLS separately estimates 38.2 million eldercare providers age 15+ in 2023–24 and reports care-day time among employed providers. The leave, childcare, and eldercare records have different populations, clocks, and measures, so they do not yield one national care-shortage or work-loss rate. Together, they support the narrower trend: care capacity is a time buffer whose practical availability varies with workplace terms, income, household resources, and care arrangements.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Census households with children 0–13; BLS eldercare-provider population; BLS wage-and-salary leave module Child-care work-prevention and reported adaptations; eldercare prevalence and care-day time; formal leave access and unmet leave need care requirement → differentiated time, work, and leave adaptations across separate source units common household trajectory, care quality/safety, verified work loss, earnings, recipient outcome, wellbeing, and durable security

Latest place rotation: redevelopment can improve children's opportunity without adult earnings gains

The Census CES HOPE VI record examines $17 billion of redevelopment across 262 distressed public-housing developments. Using matched difference-in-differences with anonymized tax records, plus movers-exposure and sibling comparisons, it reports lower neighborhood poverty, no causal earnings effect for adults living in public-housing units, and better long-run earnings, college attendance, and incarceration outcomes for children raised in revitalized units. Increased interaction with surrounding peers—especially higher-income peers—is reported as an important mechanism.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
HOPE VI developments and linked tax outcomes Matched redevelopment comparison, adult earnings null, child long-run outcomes, movers/sibling mechanism tests place redevelopment → social interaction and changed neighborhood exposure → intergenerational opportunity resident retention/displacement, housing quality, rents, safety, services, adult security, resident control, trust, and political action

This is a stronger place-to-long-run-outcome bridge than a neighborhood poverty snapshot, but a lower aggregate poverty rate and improved child outcomes do not establish that every original household stayed, benefited, or gained control.

Latest platform rotation: AI choice is task-specific, while privacy action depends on knowledge and replaceability

Jennifer Zou's June 2026 preprint surveys 1,999 U.S. adult AI-assistant users with population-weighted estimates and an embedded choice experiment.
