The reported market is concentrated, but smaller assistants occupy task niches; about 43% of respondents intentionally route different tasks to multiple platforms. Trust rankings differ between users and aware non-users, consistent with trust being learned through use rather than reputation alone. Privacy concern is widespread, but the study reports a knowledge/action gap and higher stated willingness to pay to avoid human review than several other data-use features.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
U.S. AI-assistant survey and choice experiment Weighted platform/task shares, reported multihoming, trust comparisons, privacy knowledge and tools, hypothetical feature valuations task exposure → provider choice and replaceability → experiential trust/knowledge → stated or reported protective behavior verified settings, actual data exposure, causal knowledge effect, durable switching, provider response, wellbeing, and practical exit

This adds a current U.S. task-level agency layer between platform use and privacy control. It complements the account-exit, collective-exit, and DROP records without treating their different users, systems, or outcomes as one longitudinal history.

Latest platform rotation: privacy control becomes more observable without becoming fully durable

California's Delete Request and Opt-Out Platform (DROP) adds an implementation route for data-broker privacy control. CalPrivacy reports more than 325,000 consumer sign-ups/submissions and more than 600 active brokers. A single verifiable request is hashed, brokers must match it against their records, and the public status vocabulary distinguishes deleted, exempted, opted-out, not-found, and pending. Brokers must access the mechanism at least every 45 days, while status updates can take up to 90 days to appear.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
California DROP implementation Program scale, hashed request architecture, broker clock, status categories, and optional matching fields privacy concern/right → centralized request → matching and processing → visible partial-success states consumer-level match and deletion distribution, residual data, re-collection, exemption fairness, trust, switching, and durable control

This complements the account-exit and collective-exit studies by showing a formal privacy route whose administrative status is more visible than before, while the lived outcome still depends on matching, waiting, exceptions, and persistence.

Walmart's company-reported California metrics supply a named firm-level processing layer: access, deletion, and sale-opt-out requests are separately counted as received, completed, or denied, with separate median completion times. The FTC's review of nine large social-media and video-streaming companies is a different system-level counterweight: it reports broad sharing, potential indefinite retention, and that some reviewed companies did not delete all user data after deletion requests. These sources cannot be converted into a shared consumer completion or failure rate. They sharpen the pattern instead: submission, matching, administrative completion, and durable data control are different stages, and a visible status or completed request is not proof of full deletion, non-recollection, trust, or practical exit.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
California DROP system; Walmart's California request metrics; FTC review of nine companies Centralized request/status route; company-reported request processing; platform-practice retention and deletion findings privacy concern/right → request and administrative processing → bounded, observable control status individual deletion verification, downstream copies, re-collection, exemption fairness, trust, switching, and durable control

Latest platform rotation: individual exit can help while collective exit remains costly

The social-media deactivation and collective-exit record retains two separate U.S.-anchored study layers summarized by the World Happiness Report 2026. In the Allcott et al. Facebook experiment, 2,743 users were recruited and eligible participants were randomized to four weeks of paid deactivation or continued use; the chapter reports higher happiness, life satisfaction, and lower anxiety and depression after deactivation, alongside lower later use and more app deletion. The continuing-use group had higher political knowledge on the reported measure. Separately, a U.S. college-student Instagram/TikTok study found stated willingness to pay to eliminate the platform from one's academic community even while individual deactivation was assigned a positive stated exit cost.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Facebook randomized deactivation experiment 2,743-user recruitment, four-week treatment/control design, measured wellbeing and later-use outcomes individual deactivation → short-run wellbeing improvement and lower later use, with a political-knowledge trade-off account closure, data erasure, durable non-use, social/information loss, and political behavior
U.S. college-student Instagram/TikTok valuation study stated individual and community-wide willingness-to-pay judgments summarized by WHR individual exit cost plus social dependence → stated preference for coordinated community exit actual coordination, collective deletion, persistence, substitution, and durable welfare

This is a product-trap and coordination mechanism, not a single pooled study. It complements the Korean qualitative non-use source by adding a U.S.-anchored experiment and a stated collective-exit contrast.

Latest platform rotation: practical non-use is not the same as durable exit

The social-media non-use and practical-exit record adds a lived-experience bridge to the platform-exit lane. In interviews with 20 young Korean adults, participants described time, app, account, and routine-level strategies for limiting or stopping Instagram use. The sample included 11 active users, 2 deactivated accounts, 5 deleted accounts, 1 inactive account, and 1 partially deactivated account at interview. The authors report UX, psychological, and social challenges, nonlinear and reversible non-use, exclusion, incomplete disconnection, and compensating use of other platforms alongside relief and greater control for some participants.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
20 Korean interview participants Account-status composition and reported non-use strategies, frictions, and consequences platform utility and connectivity norms → non-use attempt → experienced friction → reversible non-use, exclusion, or platform substitution population prevalence, verified deletion/data erasure, durable non-use, wellbeing, remedy, U.S. generalization, and collective action

This is comparative qualitative evidence, not an account-deletion rate or proof that Instagram deliberately obstructed exit. It complements the platform-use, privacy, age-restriction, and AI-companion records by adding the user-experience middle between formal exit availability and durable practical exit.

Latest geopolitical rotation: dependence can produce negotiation before coercion

The international-power and negotiation record adds a dependence-to-bargaining mechanism. It constructs a model-implied international-power measure from asymmetric bilateral import dependence weighted by sectoral trade elasticities, then combines it with bilateral engagement events and high-frequency geopolitical relationships. The paper reports more engagement and negotiation when measured power rises, and trade adjustment when geopolitical relationships worsen, consistent with countries building future leverage before a dispute.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
NBER international-power panel Model-implied dependence measure combined with country-pair engagement and geopolitical data asymmetric dependence → bargaining condition → negotiation and anticipatory trade adjustment named demand, threat, concession, firm/public incidence, retaliation, alliance response, and strategic result

This is a comparative model-and-panel mechanism, not proof that a particular country successfully coerced another. It complements the conflict-risk paper’s trade-disruption pathway by adding what may happen before open sanctions or retaliation.

Latest geopolitical implementation rotation: partner capacity can fail before capability is usable

The GAO Section 333 partner-capacity record adds a planning-to-use stage beneath security-assistance funding. In GAO’s selected review of 46 train-and-equip proposals, 42 did not fully document partner absorptive capacity, sustainment, or measurable objectives. The program had allocated nearly $5.6 billion across FY2018–2022, but that total is not evidence of delivery, partner use, or strategic effect. GAO also found uneven State participation and an unresolved joint DOD–State planning process in its April 2026 follow-up.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
GAO Section 333 review Selected proposal documents, allocation totals, interagency process, and recommendation status authorization/funding → planning and partner-fit requirements → documented implementation risk named-project delivery, training completion, operational use, sustainment, partner response, local legitimacy, and deterrence

This is a process-risk finding, not a partner-failure rate. It complements the international-arrangements record by showing that even after an assistance authority exists, the missing middle can be partner fit, sustainment, measurable objectives, and a defined interagency owner.

The GAO human-rights training record adds a legitimacy stage that capability records cannot supply. DOD initially did not systematically track mandated human-rights training, and DOD and State had not evaluated whether the training was effective. Follow-up documented new tracking fields, quarterly Section 333 status reports, and DOD/State monitoring and evaluation plans. These are administrative reforms, not evidence of changed conduct or civilian protection; the composite chain must keep rights oversight, equipment reliability, partner use, and external strategic effect separate.

The GAO Northern Triangle police-training record adds a local institutional endpoint. In 22 State/USAID police-training projects across El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras, none of the reviewed State or USAID project documents had explicit human-rights objectives, and State lacked reliable consolidated training counts. Later follow-up added human-rights language and indicators, but neither reform establishes changed police conduct, civilian safety, complaint resolution, or public legitimacy. The geopolitical chain therefore distinguishes security-assistance funding, planning, delivery, reliability, rights oversight, local policing, and lived legitimacy.

The companion GAO Section 333 delivery record extends the route to delivery and evaluation. GAO found 75% of Section 333 deliveries late relative to DOD estimates as of FY2022. Of six reviewed project evaluations, four reported capability improvement and two reported no improvement because equipment was unsuitable or unreliable, while the evaluation evidence generally failed GAO's quality criteria. The safe composite is therefore: funding and planning can coexist with delay, reliability problems, and weak learning systems. It remains open whether a named partner used the capability continuously, sustained it, or changed an external actor's choices.

Latest technology-security rotation: export controls create compliance capacity before strategic effect

The GAO advanced-semiconductor export-control record adds a technology-security implementation layer to the domestic-capability and geopolitical-dependence routes. GAO reviewed three 2022–23 rules and found Commerce working with six other federal agencies on technical review, licensing, foreign-partner outreach, border verification, investigations, and enforcement. Affected firms updated compliance programs and self-reported potential violations; GAO identified ten reported compliance challenges, including unclear classifications, and documented BIS outreach, briefings, definition changes, and rule updates.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
GAO advanced-semiconductor export-control review Rules, interagency implementation, reported firm compliance, and administrative clarification national-security rule → multi-agency and firm compliance surface → implementation learning partner adoption, shipment/substitution response, domestic incidence, PRC capability change, deterrence, and U.S. leverage

The implementation stage matters because a control can become administratively real without producing the intended external result. The review itself points to later enforcement and foreign-partner engagement work; it does not establish that China substituted away from controlled technology, that allies aligned, or that another actor changed its choices. This is a capability-to-response bridge, not a strategic-effect claim.

The BIS foreign-fab VEU record adds a second technology-security stage: policy can preserve current operation while narrowing future expansion. BIS required former VEU foreign-owned fabs in China to obtain licenses, intended to permit existing-fab operation, and stated that it would not license capacity expansion or technology upgrades. The cross- source implication is not that the control succeeded; it is that a transition clock and an expandable-capability boundary can be observed before firm-level production, sourcing, partner alignment, or external behavior.

Evidence Observed stage Still open
GAO implementation review plus BIS VEU closure interagency/firm compliance, policy revision, license transition, existing-operation continuity, and stated expansion restriction affected-fab license outcomes, shipments, production, substitution, partner response, PRC capability change, deterrence, and U.S. leverage

The formal endpoint is now partly observable: BIS's September 2025 final rule removed Intel Dalian, Samsung China Semiconductor, and SK hynix Semiconductor (China) from the VEU authorization list, effective December 31, 2025. This closes the administrative loop for authorization status while leaving the operational loop open. A removed general authorization is not the same as a denied individual license, stopped fab, changed production line, or altered external behavior.

Company-side certification adds a limited continuity signal: Samsung's Xi'an site is certified for 12-inch flash-memory manufacture and related packaging/testing through October 14, 2026, while SK hynix's current quality page lists Wuxi 12-inch integrated-circuit manufacture through August 2, 2027. These are not output series or license records. They support the narrower claim that formal authorization revocation can coexist with a currently listed operational scope; they do not show unchanged production, technology access, or external response.

The first external-response signal is now directly attributed rather than inferred. China's Ministry of Commerce opposed the VEU removals, warned of serious global semiconductor supply-chain harm, urged U.S. correction, and said it would take necessary measures to protect Chinese enterprises. This advances the rule → formal revocation → official response chain, while leaving enacted countermeasure, firm behavior, production, negotiation, and strategic effect open.

The EU dual-use list record adds a partner-alignment stage after the U.S. implementation and Chinese response layers. The European Commission adopted common EU controls covering semiconductor manufacturing/testing equipment and advanced-computing items, with a stated basis in multilateral regimes and member-state commitments. This supports list-level coordination, not identical policy, national enforcement, firm adaptation, or strategic leverage.

The Commission's 2026 implementation report adds a system-level enforcement stage: €77.6 billion in EU-authorized dual-use exports and 487 security-risk denials in 2024, with China and the United States representing 25% and 21% of authorized-export value. Because the report summary does not isolate semiconductor items or member-state cases, this cannot be treated as a measured effect of the 2025 list update or as proof of strategic alignment.

The Commission's underlying 2024 dataset adds a category-level authorization stage. For 3EC4 equipment for manufacturing and testing semiconductor devices or materials, the listed Member State rows sum to €721.1 million and 156 individual authorizations, with the largest reported values in Austria and Germany. This improves measurement of semiconductor-specific licensing exposure, but it still does not identify destinations, denials, exporters, shipment completion, firm adaptation, or strategic effect.

The same Commission dataset also reports 415 full-time-equivalent control staff, 154 outreach events, 1,353 compliance audits, 270 reported infringements, and 144 penalties or fines in 2024. This adds a system-capacity and enforcement endpoint after list adoption and authorization, while keeping item category, destination, firm, shipment, deterrence, and geopolitical effect unresolved.

The Applied Materials settlement record adds a named enforcement route: BIS reported approximately $126 million in illegal semiconductor-equipment shipments through Korea to China, imposed an approximately $252 million penalty, and required continuing audits and annual certifications. This is a realized violation-and-remediation stage after the general EU and U.S. implementation layers; future compliance, production, substitution, deterrence, and leverage remain unmeasured.

The Cadence enforcement record adds a second named firm route at the semiconductor-design layer: 56 BIS- admitted violations and at least 59 DOJ-described exports through a PRC alias to NUDT and related entities. The coordinated civil/criminal resolution included a $95 million BIS penalty, DOJ penalties and forfeiture, a net amount above $140 million, account freezes, an export hold, and remediation. This shows enforcement reach across equipment and design tools, not a measured change in Chinese capability or deterrence.

The Alpha and Omega BIS order adds a power-semiconductor route involving approximately 1,650 items across 15 unauthorized occasions sent through an AOS China facility for Huawei after the Entity List addition. The $4.25 million penalty was tied to continued export-privilege eligibility, while the order separately reports later elimination of the Digital Power business unit. This adds a firm-operational endpoint without attributing the exit to enforcement or inferring deterrence.

The Bosch settlement record adds the foreign-produced and allied-firm layer: approximately $72.4 million in MEMS sensors and automotive software exported from abroad to Huawei under the Foreign Direct Product Rule without authorization. Bosch self-disclosed and cooperated; BIS imposed a $36.18 million penalty and DOJ disgorgement was approximately $3.6 million, credited against the BIS penalty. This shows cross-border enforcement reach and remediation, not a measured change in Huawei capability, supply, or deterrence.

The BIS H200/MI325X licensing record adds a policy-reversal/conditional-opening layer. Certain advanced-computing exports to China or Macau can receive case-by-case review when applicants meet U.S.-supply, foundry-capacity, end-use, comparative-TPP, and independent-testing requirements. No application approval or shipment is reported; the rule is a formal conditional route, not evidence of market reopening or capability gain.

The NVIDIA H200 license realization record then supplies a realized administrative transition: NVIDIA reported a U.S. license for small H200 shipments to specific China-based customers in February 2026. The same filing reports zero H200 licensing-program revenue to date and uncertainty over whether China would allow any imports; U.S. inspection and a 25% tariff condition remain. The evidence therefore moves the chain from formal conditional policy to license approval, while preserving the gap between approval and shipment, import, revenue, capability, or market recovery.

The NVIDIA partial H200 shipment record provides the subsequent endpoint. In its fiscal Q2 2027 filing, NVIDIA reported that PRC restrictions prevented all licensed sales, yet a fraction of permitted H200 shipments had occurred and represented less than 1% of quarterly Data Center revenue. The company continued to report a $0.4 billion H200 inventory and purchase-obligation charge, tariff absorption, and no China data-center compute revenue in its forward outlook. The chain therefore reaches physical delivery while remaining commercially and politically constrained.

The MOFCOM H200 non-confirmation record adds a state-side information boundary rather than a new substantive control. When asked on July 16, 2026 about U.S. claims that a small number of H200s had been sold to China, a Ministry of Commerce spokesperson said he did not know about the situation. The response neither confirms nor denies NVIDIA's filing; it leaves Chinese import clearance, customer authorization, and official acceptance of the reported shipments unresolved.

The SAMR NVIDIA-Mellanox investigation continuity record adds a parallel state-capacity clock: SAMR's September 2025 notice initiated further investigation after a preliminary finding, and SAMR's April 2026 review continued to list the NVIDIA case. The sources do not report a final decision, penalty, or remedy. This supports regulatory continuity and unresolved institutional exposure, not a measured causal effect on H200 shipments, customers, competition, or Chinese capability.

The Hygon DCU competitive-adaptation record adds the competitor-response stage. Hygon said H200 entry would intensify domestic high-end-chip competition and described a response centered on performance, ecosystem compatibility, security compliance, cost-performance, submarket focus, and domestic customer cases. It also reported existing DCU applications and expected 2026 share gains. The record advances from state and firm constraint to adaptation, while leaving actual substitution, customer switching, market share, and capability effects unmeasured.

The Hygon realized growth and deployment record then supplies a firm outcome: Hygon reported RMB 9.099 billion in first-half 2026 consolidated revenue, 66.52% year-over-year growth, and DCU deployment in multiple key industries and hundreds of application scenarios, with more than 400 mainstream large models adapted. The report strengthens the domestic adaptation-to-deployment bridge, while leaving DCU-specific revenue, customer switching, displacement, and causal export-control effects unresolved.

The Hygon large-model cluster realization record extends the chain from deployment to reported operation: Hygon said a 10-trillion-parameter model had achieved preliminary stable operation on a cluster of tens of thousands of Hygon DCUs, alongside a DTK stack with more than 2,000 operators and 100-plus framework components. The evidence is useful as an operational milestone, but lacks independent benchmarks, customer acceptance, utilization, cost, or substitution evidence.

The Hygon Kimi K3 adaptation record adds a model-specific realization stage: a 2026 listed-company interim report states that Hygon completed full-process Kimi K3 adaptation, deployment, and performance verification on its DCU platform. The report does not supply independent benchmark values, a named customer or site, production duration, utilization, or evidence that the model displaced another accelerator.

The Hygon Kimi K3 performance-claim record adds a quantitative performance-claim stage: a technical-news report relayed an official Hygon figure of performance loss within 12 percent and described a Sugon 8000 distributed training and multi-card inference path. Because the baseline, metric definition, test configuration, and artifacts are absent, this is a vendor-reported result rather than independent parity evidence.

The Hunan public-system integration record adds an external infrastructure endpoint. Hunan's provincial platform reported trial operation, Hygon DCU compatibility within a multi-accelerator scheduler, and first-batch resource access for the Changsha National Supercomputing Center, operator compute centers, and Changsha AI Innovation Center. The evidence moves the chain toward public-system acceptance while leaving utilization, procurement value, workload success, and substitution unmeasured.

The Changsha AI-center workload record adds a named application endpoint. Hunan's inventory describes a 200P mixed Ascend/Hygon center whose Hygon-based module sits alongside an Ascend module, and lists support for a visual foundation model, an agricultural Q&A model, and a tourism model. This is stronger than compatibility alone, but still does not isolate Hygon workload share, production duration, performance, or substitution.

The MOFCOM analog-IC investigation record adds a formal trade-remedy stage after the attributed response. China opened an anti-dumping investigation into specified U.S. analog IC imports following a domestic-industry application and reported preliminary claims of rising import quantity and falling import prices. This is not evidence that the VEU removals caused the investigation; it is a separate institutional response in the same semiconductor conflict. Final ruling, duty, import, firm, and strategic effects remain open.

The MOFCOM anti-discrimination investigation record adds a broader legal-contestation stage after the VEU objection and analog-IC trade-remedy initiation. China opened a formal investigation into U.S. integrated-circuit measures, specified a legal basis, and invited affected parties to participate. This is observable institutional action, but not a finding, remedy, direct causal response to the VEU removals, or strategic effect.

Latest care rotation: a work incentive can create an unfilled care gap

The EITC parent-care-gap record adds a policy-to-care substitution test. Using Health and Retirement Study data and simulated EITC generosity, it estimates that a $500 increase in EITC generosity reduces care from eligible daughters to older parents by 13–24 hours per month, driven by less intensive care. The study reports no increase in financial transfers and finds that other children, spouses, or paid providers do not fill the measured gap.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
NBER EITC-parent-care study Simulated policy variation, family-care measures, and tested replacement channels work-contingent benefit → daughter care allocation → reduced intensive care → no measured replacement in tested channels care quality, unmet need, health, safety, daughter earnings, formal services, and total household welfare

This is a bounded U.S. mechanism, not proof that every work incentive harms older parents. It complements the family-care, paid-leave, and childcare records by showing that the missing middle can be substitution failure rather than simply insufficient time measurement.

Latest redistribution rotation: similar cash does not imply similar recovery currency

The NBER parental-investment record adds a randomized cash-to-adaptation comparison. A large multisite U.S. study reports similar treatment effects on net household income, earnings, and total expenditures across racial and ethnic groups, but different child-investment routes: Latino families increased child-focused spending by nearly one-third of the transfer without detectable changes in maternal employment or time with children, while Black families reduced maternal work hours and increased time with children on early-learning activities without higher child-focused expenditures.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
NBER unconditional-cash study Randomized monthly transfer with subgroup-specific money/time outcomes cash support → subgroup-specific spending or time reallocation → distinct care/investment route treatment amount, compliance, care quality, stress, durable employment, broader household welfare, trust, and action

This is a counterexample to treating redistribution as a single recovery currency. The subgroup pattern should not be read as a racial mechanism or generalized to all cash programs; it shows why the same transfer can buy goods, buy time, or leave measured child time unchanged depending on household context and the income source's meaning.

Latest household-room rotation: immediate relief is not balance-sheet recovery

The NBER consumption/balance-sheet record adds a two-state randomized test of cash support and durability. Assignment to $1,000 per month rather than $50 per month for three years increased household expenditures by at least $300 per month, with the largest effects in housing, food, and car expenses. Housing-unit and neighborhood mobility, self-reported financial health, and credit scores also increased. Yet asset gains were offset by higher debt, producing a near-zero net-worth effect; credit limits, delinquencies, utilization, bankruptcies, and foreclosures did not change.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
NBER two-state cash-transfer study Random assignment, spending, mobility, credit, assets, and debt transfer → short-run spending/room and financial-health improvement → no clear durable net-worth gain bill-level relief, care/time substitution, adequacy, stress persistence, trust, political action, and exit

This is a direct warning against collapsing consumption, mobility, credit, financial health, and net worth into one recovery variable. The transfer can create usable room now while leaving the household's longer-run balance sheet largely unchanged.

Latest care-quality rotation: better inputs can coexist with reported stress

The NBER parenting/stress record adds a care-quality counterexample from a randomized three-year transfer of $1,000 per month versus $50. The treatment increased spending on children and reported parenting behavior, with the largest parenting improvements among the lowest-income families and increased use and quality of non-parental childcare. At the same time, parents reported more child developmental difficulties and stress; the authors note that closer monitoring may partly explain that result. Parental satisfaction and several other household outcomes did not change.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
NBER parenting/cash study Random assignment with parenting, care, child-stress, mobility, and household outcomes cash → spending/supervision/formal-care inputs → mixed observed care and wellbeing signals clinical meaning of reported stress, care quality measurement, persistence, household time, trust, and political action

This prevents “more parenting,” “more childcare,” or “more spending” from being treated as interchangeable with improved wellbeing. A policy can improve an input, increase detection of problems, and leave satisfaction or downstream outcomes unchanged at the same time.

The cash-transfer recovery-currency crosswalk now consolidates this redistribution branch. Across the retained U.S. studies, cash can become consumption, mobility, credit, child spending, maternal time, formal childcare, or reduced unpaid care; these currencies cannot be pooled as one recovery score. The common missing middle is still same-household adequacy and persistence, followed by fairness/attribution, trust, political action, or exit.

The NBER family-income/voting record adds the first retained U.S. cash-to-voting bridge in this redistribution rotation. Exogenous unconditional cash transfers increased adult children's voting propensity among those raised in initially poorer families, while parents and children from initially better-off families showed no effect. The effect is therefore delayed and intergenerational: it supports a resource, human-capital, or social-capital route into later participation, not a claim that a current payment immediately changes the adult recipient's turnout, trust, approval, or vote choice.

The APSR Moving to Opportunity record adds a place-based counterexample. Random housing-voucher offers reduced neighborhood poverty and improved some child socioeconomic outcomes, but later children's turnout did not increase, adult effects were null, and teen voting and registration declined under both voucher conditions. This shows that material/place improvement is not sufficient for political participation: developmental stage, disruption, dosage, social integration, and persistence remain part of the mechanism.

The Social Problems welfare-participation record adds a contemporary program-design counterexample. In nationally representative young-adult data with fixed-effects models, cash assistance showed little association with participation; food stamps were positively associated with registration but had countervailing voting associations by political attentiveness. This is not a causal transfer estimate, but it prevents the political endpoint from being coded as one welfare effect: benefit type, administrative experience, attention, registration, turnout, and trust remain distinct.

The NBER welfare-reform voting record adds a positive adult-voting contrast: greater exposure to 1990s reform was associated with roughly a four-percentage-point relative voting advantage among low-income women, concentrated in presidential elections and stronger in Democratic states and states with stronger work incentives. The proposed path runs through employment, education, and income. This should not be averaged with the NBER EITC employment-instrument negative estimate: benefit retraction, work-incentive design, exposure, comparison group, election type, and estimand differ.

The Health Affairs Scholar safety-net stigma record adds direct trust/meaning measurement to this political branch. SNAP participation and EITC receipt were associated with greater reported social stigma, overall government perceptions did not differ, and food-insecure SNAP respondents additionally showed program stigma and discrimination. The study is cross-sectional and convenience/snowball based, so it is not a causal or national trust estimate. Its cross-source value is the boundary itself: material support, stigma, government perception, and political action are different currencies and should not be inferred from one another.

The Oregon Medicaid voter-participation record adds a causal public-system-to-action contrast. Randomized coverage access raised November 2008 presidential turnout by 2.5 percentage points, but did not raise turnout in later elections through November 2010. The early effect is consistent with a route through registration, administrative contact, health or financial security, or election-specific mobilization; the study does not identify which route and does not show a generalized trust change. It therefore strengthens the action endpoint while preserving the open meaning and durability arrows.

The UAS economic-insecurity record adds an observational mobilization counterexample. Greater income-history insecurity predicted higher reported voting probability and Trump support in the 2016 U.S. election context, conditional on current resources, while other surfaces show lower contact or action under hardship. Because the insecurity index uses modeled income bands and the outcomes are reported probabilities, this does not identify causality or a uniform response. It does establish that the material-to-action arrow can point toward mobilization or polarization as well as withdrawal, depending on timing, identity, attribution, and outcome.

The urban-poor government-contact record adds a local encounter mechanism: among 462 low-income respondents, severe hardship and formative contact with government agents were associated with greater willingness to participate, while resources and demographics also structured activism. This is not a causal or national estimate, but it makes the interface visible. Hardship does not carry one political meaning apart from the institution, agent, explanation, and efficacy experience through which it is encountered.

The Social Security and intergenerational-migration record adds a distinct historical causal setting. Using early Social Security coverage variation across industries within occupations and linked parent--child records, the study estimates that greater predicted parental coverage led sons to move farther from childhood homes, earn more, and later live in better neighborhoods; the corresponding migration, earnings, and neighborhood effects were not found for daughters, whom the authors describe as providing less easily replaceable support. The historical design does not observe every exchange of care, money, or obligation and cannot establish a present-day national Social Security effect, a single migration mechanism, or that moving itself produced each later outcome. It nevertheless shows that family support can shape the practical mobility margin rather than merely offset a contemporaneous care gap.

Latest platform rotation: formal access restriction does not equal complete control

Australia’s eSafety implementation record adds a policy-to-platform-action bridge. Platforms reported about 4.7 million age-restricted accounts removed or restricted by mid-December 2025 and more than 300,000 additional accounts prevented from signing in by early March 2026. In eSafety’s pulse survey of 898 parents and carers, reported account ownership among children aged 8–15 fell from 49.7% before the restriction to 31.3% afterward. Yet among children with pre-existing accounts, substantial platform-specific retention remained, and eSafety flagged five platforms for age-assurance and new-account-prevention concerns.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Australian eSafety implementation Platform-reported account actions, parent pulse survey, regulator testing and compliance concerns legal rule → platform process → reported access change and residual retention → enforcement unique-child exposure, privacy and false-positive cost, migration, safety, wellbeing, trust, and durable cultural effect

This is comparative implementation evidence, not a U.S. estimate or a causal child-safety result. It complements the existing platform-use and control records by showing that aggregate action counts and lived access can diverge.

Latest infrastructure rotation: emergency reserve capacity is conditional on operation

GAO-26-106918 adds an operational state-capacity layer to the atlas. As of December 2025, DOE estimated effective Strategic Petroleum Reserve drawdown at 61% of design rate and fill at 56%. The reserve had met drawdown directives to date, but aging infrastructure, construction outages, low inventory, and limited commercial pipeline and storage spare capacity constrained the route from nominal reserve to realized emergency market effect.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
GAO SPR capability review Point-in-time effective fill and drawdown estimates, reserve operating history, and reported infrastructure/market constraints reserve asset and maintenance → effective emergency operating capability → conditional distribution capacity release-specific prices, refinery receipt, household/firm incidence, replenishment, deterrence, and geopolitical effect

This is an operational-capability finding, not evidence of a current shortage or of energy-security success. It complements the Puerto Rico grid and transmission-capacity records while preserving different infrastructure, commodity, and downstream units.

Latest geopolitical rotation: economic coercion can become a trade and retaliation pathway

NBER Working Paper 35077 adds a comparative state-to-market bridge. Its GDELT-based monthly bilateral indicator separates kinetic fighting, military posture, sanctions-context hostility, and routine diplomacy. The paper reports that the trade-weighted share of hostility routed through sanctions contexts nearly doubled over the past decade. In its gravity-trade estimates, kinetic and trade-context hostility reduce bilateral trade, routine diplomacy has no detected aggregate trade effect, and directed retaliation compounds losses over several months. A pre-escalation counterfactual places roughly $334 billion of bilateral trade at risk, with the U.S.–China pair accounting for about half.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
NBER bilateral conflict-risk panel GDELT events calibrated to human-curated ground truth; decomposed hostility and gravity-trade estimates sanctions-context hostility → bilateral trade disruption → lagged retaliation U.S.-specific firm and household incidence, product substitution, alliance behavior, legitimacy, and strategic success

This is a comparative mechanism and counterfactual estimate, not an episode-level proof that a particular U.S. coercive action worked. It complements the CRS timeline of 2025 foreign retaliation while keeping government response, firm compliance, public cost, and political outcome as separate stages.

Latest public-systems rotation: public benefit can coexist with incomplete individual recovery

The Los Angeles shelter study adds a public-good layer to the atlas. Shelter availability and unsheltered exposure are connected to neighborhood crime, psychiatric emergency-room visits, and short-run mortality, while future homelessness does not improve relative to outreach or other non-shelter services. The result prevents a single “shelter success” endpoint from hiding different beneficiaries and clocks.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Los Angeles shelter availability Daily shelter beds/occupancy linked to crime, hospital, and mortality records; availability shocks used for comparison shelter capacity → public safety and short-run health benefits; shelter entry → short-run mortality access, safety, service quality, durable housing, future homelessness, trust, and collective response

This is a public-capacity and health realization finding, not evidence that temporary shelter is adequate or that all residents receive equal benefit.

Latest depth rotation: average recovery can hide a negative subgroup

The Nevada job-search-assistance experiment adds a durable work-to-housing route. A randomized offer combining counseling, search planning, enforcement, and referrals is followed through administrative employment, earnings, UI, disability, tax, and homeownership outcomes for up to eight years. Average outcomes improve, but roughly 40% of the sample is estimated to have negative long-run employment treatment effects.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Nevada randomized UI intervention 4,673 offers in a 32,751-person UI population; later employment, earnings, UI, tax, disability, and homeownership outcomes bundled public employment route → heterogeneous long-run work and housing-related outcomes component effects, job quality, health, care burden, housing adequacy, coercion, trust, and action

This is a durable outcome bridge, not proof that counseling alone caused the gain or that aggregate employment gains equal welfare gains for every person.

Latest depth rotation: emergency assistance can reach a later work outcome without proving housing recovery

The NBER emergency-financial-assistance record adds a stronger same-study bridge than a cross-sectional association: Chicago homelessness-prevention hotline callers experiencing a housing crisis are linked to federal tax records, and quasi-random variation in funding availability supports a comparison of families receiving and not receiving roughly $900–$1,000 in one-time rent or utility help. The study reports about 5,300 eligible callers referred to funds versus about 2,800 not referred, with estimated receipt of 71% versus 12%; employment and earnings gains are reported up to four years later, especially among the lowest earners.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
NBER emergency financial assistance Hotline callers linked to tax records; assistance availability used for comparison; later employment and earnings gains reported housing-crisis assistance route → later labor-market outcome housing continuity, same-job retention, job quality, adequacy, displacement, household security, trust, and action

This is an important open-middle advance, but earnings are not a recovery score. Address-change evidence is suggestive but not robust, and the source does not establish that the housing break was prevented or that the same household's housing, health, debt, or meaning stabilized.

The emergency-rental-assistance lottery record adds a pandemic-era intervention counterexample. Across five lottery-based programs in four cities distributing more than $200 million, assistance increased rent payment and reduced reported eviction concerns; self-reported mental and physical-health improvements were suggestive. Yet the study detected little effect on its housing-stability and financial-distress measures. That is not evidence that assistance failed: eviction moratoria, expanded safety-net programs, and tenant-favoring market conditions may have weakened the usual link between rent payment and displacement, while rent payment or reduced anxiety can matter on their own. The evaluation does not establish national eviction prevention, durable tenure, subsequent bills, debt, health, or household recovery beyond the program-specific follow-up.

Latest cultural rotation: local social infrastructure is a resource, not a guaranteed outcome

The American Neighbor Survey adds a place-level meaning and capacity layer to the atlas. It reports regular neighbor conversation and neighborhood problem-solving alongside trust, third-place access, and emergency childcare comfort, with visible education and housing gradients. This supports a bounded proposition: social infrastructure can create opportunities for contact and mutual aid, but usable support is distributed unevenly and cannot be inferred from amenities or stated goodwill alone.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
American Neighbor Survey 40% report regular neighbor conversation, 40% neighborhood problem-solving, and 72% fair/great neighbor trust; 27% with no listed third places versus 43% with six or more report weekly neighbor conversation place resources and proximity → contact/trust → stated informal capacity and belonging selection, actual aid, time/money burden, adequacy, recovery, and collective or political action

This is a weighted cross-sectional panel survey, not a causal neighborhood experiment or a household crisis episode. It complements the existing Pew neighbor-trust layer without pooling the two surveys.

The Census 2023 SIPP child-wellbeing report adds a family-time and cultural opportunity distinction. Reference-parent reading and family-dinner measures were broadly similar to their 2014 comparison values, while organized activity participation was uneven: among children ages 6–17, 1.2% of those in families below poverty participated in sports, lessons, and clubs versus 8.8% of those at 200% of poverty or higher. This supports a bounded proposition: relatively stable routine does not make access to organized social and cultural opportunity equal.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Census 2023 SIPP child-wellbeing report Age-specific parent-child routine, outings, organized activity, school-engagement, material-hardship, and poverty-gradient measures household resources and time context → reported routine and access to organized activities → unequal opportunity surface activity cost, transport, supply, preference, quality, belonging, confidence, educational attainment, and same-child later outcome

The measures use different child-age universes and reference periods; stable dinner or reading rates do not establish equal relationship quality or support, and the activity gradient does not identify why participation differs. See the SIPP child cultural-participation record.

The CDC Community & Connection indicators add a measurement correction to the social-infrastructure lane. The page reports that 58% of youth in its 2021–2023 indicator received needed social and emotional support, 82% of adults did so in a separate 2021 indicator, and 12% of adults reported health-related difficulty participating in social activities in 2024. The usable proposition is not an age trend: perceived support and practical ability to participate are different social outcomes, and neither is interchangeable with loneliness, delivered help, or belonging.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
CDC Community & Connection summary indicators Separate youth and adult self-reported support indicators and an adult health-related social-participation-difficulty indicator perceived support and participation constraint as distinct community-connection surfaces common-year/person comparison, adequacy or reciprocity of help, loneliness, invitation/access barrier, delivered support, belonging, civic action, and recovery

The summary page does not retain one linked survey sample or full denominators. Higher adult reported support than youth support is not a valid age comparison, and participation difficulty does not identify a particular barrier or prove isolation. See the CDC community-connection record.

The CIRCLE youth political-homes record adds a civic-belonging version of the social-infrastructure lane. Young people reporting access to a political home had about 20-percentage-point higher civic action and civic self-efficacy than peers without reported access. CIRCLE describes those settings as potentially supplying safe third spaces, belonging, civic information, food, financial compensation, and transportation, while also reporting a relationship between strong connections and lower mental-health costs of political involvement. The result makes practical support, belonging, self-efficacy, wellbeing, and action visible as separate but adjacent surfaces; it is not a randomized assignment, a turnout estimate, or evidence that a political home caused later participation, durable trust, or policy influence.

The CDC loneliness/social-support record adds a single analytic sample with a different social-connection surface. In the 2022 BRFSS analysis of 218,915 adults in 26 states, 32.1% reported always, usually, or sometimes feeling socially isolated and 24.1% reported sometimes, rarely, or never receiving needed social and emotional support. Isolation was 43.3% among ages 18–34 and 47.9% among households below $25,000; reported prevalence was also higher among bisexual and transgender subgroups. Adjusted associations with frequent stress, frequent mental distress, and depression history do not show that isolation caused those outcomes, nor do they identify the social disruption, help received, care route, belonging, civic action, or recovery path for any person.

The standardized ATUS eldercare-provider comparison adds an everyday time profile rather than a survey attitude. In both 2024 and 2025 diary samples, providers had about 64 more eldercare minutes than matched-cell nonproviders, plus more household-work, care-for-people, and travel time and less socializing/communicating time. The age, sex, and labor-force-status standardization preserves the profile across two annual samples, while the paid-work difference remains imprecise.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
ATUS 2024 and 2025 standardized diary comparisons Provider/nonprovider differences in eldercare, household work, care for people, travel, socializing/communication, secondary childcare, and paid-work minutes eldercare-provider status → distinct one-day time allocation/social-participation profile care onset, recipient need, health, family structure, schedule control, employer accommodation, causal displacement, adequacy, wellbeing, recovery, trust, or action

The years are separate samples, not a panel; residual selection can reflect family, health, occupation, diary timing, or recipient need. Lower socializing/communication time does not by itself show isolation or worse wellbeing. See the standardized eldercare-provider record.

SHED's 2025 care/living-arrangements tables add the household organization layer that neither the Census child-care problem screen nor one-day ATUS diary can supply. Thirty-three percent of adults reported living with at least two adult generations. Among parents of children under 13, 25% reported paid childcare in the prior week and 44% reported unpaid childcare; paid-care use was lower in the lowest income group, but that difference cannot distinguish unaffordability from unpaid support, nonemployment, availability, or preference. The same source reports an 18% adult unpaid-caregiving prevalence and an association between regular adult care and not having paid work among prime-age adults. Care arrangement, gendered caretaker role, work status, and meaning are separate surfaces, not a causal household trajectory.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Federal Reserve 2025 SHED care/living-arrangements tables Co-residence, paid/unpaid child care, child-care payment comparison, caretaker-role and adult-care/work-status distributions household composition and resource position → reported care-arrangement and work-status surface dated need, provider availability/quality, hours, schedule control, employer response, causal work displacement, family reciprocity, recovery, and later trust/action

The SHED, Census, and ATUS records use different recall windows, units, and conditional bases. Their combined implication is limited but important: care capacity is assembled through co-residence, paid services, unpaid networks, and time adaptation; none is a direct proxy for adequate, chosen, or durable care. See the 2025 SHED care/living-arrangements record.

The GAO unpaid-household-work record adds a national accounting surface beneath those arrangements. GAO estimates that most people spent almost four hours a day on unpaid household work in 2021–2024; using selected 2024 wage proxies, it values that work at roughly $70 per day and at least $5.6–$6.0 trillion annually (19.2%–20.2% of GDP). Women made up 54% of people performing unpaid work versus 51% of the population, and women and married people spent more time on childcare in the reported comparisons. Replacement-value accounting makes a large hidden productive capacity visible, but it does not measure care quality, exhaustion, reciprocity, choice, bargaining, paid-work displacement, health, household security, or whether outsourcing would improve wellbeing.

The work-control corpus adds an upstream opportunity layer. An NBER field experiment connecting college students with 10,000 working professionals found that female students received substantially more work-life-balance information than male students in broad career exchanges, with a gap that persisted when they explicitly asked about work-life balance; the paper links this information pattern to career intentions. This is direct evidence that career information can be gendered before a job, wage, care arrangement, or employer policy is observed—not evidence of later labor-market inequality by itself.

Two different AI/work records sharpen the next stages. SHED reports that AI use among workers differs by education and reported task control, alongside softer job-mobility measures; an NBER occupation-level framework separates potential AI exposure from adaptive capacity and retains revised working-paper versus published-chapter counts separately. Neither establishes individual displacement, retraining success, job quality, or bargaining power.

Evidence unit What is directly visible What remains open
Randomized career-information exchange Requester-gender differences in work-life information and a reported career-intention mechanism Actual occupational choice, employer practices, pay, hours, care, discrimination, and later wellbeing
2025 SHED employment/AI/control tables Labor-market friction, mobility, schedule, and education/control-stratified reported AI use Employer policy, task exposure, productivity, pay, displacement, and causal control effect
Occupation-level AI exposure/adaptive-capacity framework Exposure/capacity overlap and clerical/support concentration under stated coverage versions Person-level resilience, job loss, retraining, earnings, care constraints, and usable transition options

The supported subtheme is anticipated work is socially and institutionally mediated before it becomes a realized career outcome. The studies do not share a sample or a causal chain. See the career-information/advice record, SHED employment/AI-control record, and AI exposure/adaptive-capacity record.

The ILO/ETF Changing Landscape of Skills in the Age of AI record extends this route from exposure to capability. The report argues that AI is raising the value of contextual judgment, oversight, hybrid expertise and socio-emotional skill; it also frames AI literacy—technical, analytical and ethical—as a foundational capability for agency in AI-mediated work and public life. The open test is whether education, workplace training and institutional guardrails convert that capability frame into usable control, inclusion and better job quality rather than individualized adjustment pressure.

The ILO AI systems @ work record adds the downstream psychosocial-work endpoint. It connects AI-enabled surveillance, work intensification, reduced autonomy, dignity, data collection and transparency to mental and social working conditions, then argues that labour law, equality, occupational safety and health, and privacy governance must be coordinated. The open test is whether workers can actually see, contest and remedy AI-mediated decisions and workload pressure.

The World Bank livable and resilient cities record adds the place-and-infrastructure endpoint. It reframes resilience as a planning problem: hazard and climate information should shape where housing, services, transport, infrastructure and economic growth occur, using a Restrict–Condition–Promote framework and multi-level governance. The open test is whether risk analytics become enforceable, equitable and participatory land- use decisions rather than technical maps that leave displacement and access trade-offs unresolved.

The World Bank What a Waste 3.0 record adds the consumption-to-infrastructure endpoint. It shows municipal waste as a joint signal of rising consumption, uneven collection, public-health exposure, flooding and climate costs, municipal finance, employment and circular-economy capacity. The open test is whether waste prevention and service investment improve household and worker conditions without exporting pollution, unsafe work or fiscal burdens to weaker communities.

The ITU/Global E-waste Monitor record extends the waste route into digital infrastructure. In 2022, 62 billion kilograms of e-waste were generated, but only 22.3% was properly collected and recycled; the stream contained an estimated $91 billion in valuable metals and formal recovery avoided substantial primary-ore extraction and emissions. The policy contrast is sharp: countries with e-waste legislation reported about 25% collection/recycling versus rates close to zero where no legal instrument existed. The open test is whether digital circularity includes repair, safe work, producer responsibility and accessible recovery—not only device growth.

The IEA Key Questions on Energy and AI record adds an AI-to-energy-system endpoint. Global data-centre electricity demand grew 17% in 2025 and AI-focused data-centre consumption 50%, while announced 2026 capital expenditure by leading hyperscalers and neo-clouds reached $715 billion. The IEA also shows why efficiency alone is insufficient: simple AI tasks are getting cheaper in energy terms, but video, reasoning and agentic tasks can use hundreds or thousands of times more energy per query. The open test is whether grid connections, prices, emissions, siting and cost allocation are governed so AI infrastructure creates shared energy benefits rather than concentrated risk.

AP-NORC's State of the Facts comparison adds an information-legitimacy layer. Reported trust in federal-government information fell between its 2024 and 2026 issue-specific estimates for inflation/cost of living, health care, and elections/politics, while separate 2026 measures reported difficulty evaluating candidate claims and low confidence in the reliability or easy verification of AI-generated information. This places institutional information trust, candidate claim evaluation, and AI-information judgment on separate surfaces.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
AP-NORC 2024/2026 State of the Facts survey comparisons Issue-specific reported government-information trust change; 2026 perceived candidate-information/claim difficulty and AI-information reliability/verification attitudes institutional information environment → reported trust and evaluation-difficulty surface factual accuracy, source exposure, search time, AI use, correction attempt, persuasion, turnout, vote, policy action, or causal explanation for trust change

The items do not measure government performance or factual accuracy directly. Question context, salience, political interpretation, and composition can shape the comparison; perceived difficulty may reflect volume, interest, access, or scrutiny. See the AP-NORC information-trust record.

The Gallup/With Honor anniversary survey adds a distinct national-meaning route. Among adults who planned to celebrate the 250th anniversary, 66% said they intended to spend time with family or friends, 32% intended to join a neighborhood or community event, and 17% intended to attend an official America250 program. In the separate civic-or-educational recognition subgroup, history learning and listening to personal stories were more common than arts, service, or travel routes. Together with the local-infrastructure evidence, this supports a bounded subtheme: cultural legitimacy can be practiced through ordinary relationships and local stories as well as through official ceremony.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Gallup/With Honor 250th-anniversary survey Planned recognition: 66% of all adults planned some celebration; activity intentions among planner subgroups, including family/friends, community event, official program, learning, and personal stories national commemoration → intended relational, local, educational, or formal ritual route → stated meaning/pride surface completed participation, cross-group contact, learning, agreement about history, institutional trust, civic action, and durable identity

These are nonexclusive plans, not a participation count or a measure of shared political belief. Family celebration can coexist with disagreement about history, institutions, or policy; official-program nonattendance is not civic withdrawal. See the Gallup anniversary meaning record.

AP-NORC's separate America 250 survey sharpens the distinction between shared ideals, perceived threat, and expected opportunity. Respondents widely named speech and voting rights as important to national identity while differing on whether those rights face a major threat; only 33% said the hard-work pathway of the American Dream still holds. These are attitudes about meaning and security, not a legal-rights audit, mobility measure, or action record. See the AP-NORC America 250 identity/rights record.

Latest trust-and-care rotation: institutional meaning can enter a care decision without proving access

The NBER health-care trust study makes a specific behavioral middle stage visible. In a nationally representative adult survey, higher trust in the health-care system was associated with greater reported and anticipated preventive and elective care seeking and with less care avoidance. Its model also distinguishes trust in doctors, nurses, hospitals, insurers, and public-health entities rather than treating trust as a single attitude. That supports a bounded social/institutional theme: the meaning people assign to particular care institutions can be associated with whether they approach or avoid care.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
NBER nationally representative health-care trust survey Entity-specific trust, retrospective and anticipated care-seeking/avoidance, demographic and political heterogeneity, and model-based counterfactuals institution-specific trust/expected usefulness → reported or anticipated care-seeking versus avoidance causal trust change, appointment completion, affordability, provider availability, treatment quality, health outcome, remedy, durable trust, and political action

This is survey-and-model evidence, not a trust intervention. Lower reported care seeking may also reflect cost, time, transport, provider supply, health need, or prior care quality; anticipated care is not completed treatment. See the health-care trust record.

Pew's separate source-use and influencer studies make the upstream information environment visible. In the 5,111-adult source-use survey, 85% said they got health information from providers at least sometimes, 66% from people with a similar health issue, 36% from social media, and 22% from AI chatbots. Half reported at least some difficulty judging accuracy and 54% reported at least some difficulty knowing what to trust when information conflicted. The influencer study separately found that 40% of adults ever got health/wellness information from influencers or podcasts; the profiles mix self-described health professionals, coaches, and entrepreneurs. Read with the NBER result, these sources identify a source landscape → credibility judgment → possible care-seeking route, not a same-person causal chain.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Pew health-information source survey Source-use frequency, perceived accuracy, conflicting information, and difficulty judging/trusting information provider, peer, platform, or AI information environment → reported credibility problem particular claim, verification, clinical discussion, decision, care, spending, adherence, or health result
Pew health/wellness influencer profile and audience surveys 6,828 prominent influencer profiles; self-described professional/coach/entrepreneur identities; audience reach, trust, and perceived understanding platform authority cues and commercial/professional identities → audience interpretation verified credentials, sponsorship, accuracy, individualized advice, purchase, clinical decision, and health result

The records must not be pooled with the NBER trust survey: their samples, questions, and measures differ. Provider information may be more highly rated yet still costly, delayed, or inaccessible; use of peer, social, or AI sources does not establish misinformation or harm. See the health-information source record and health/wellness influencer record.

Pew's topic-diversity survey broadens that information-route result beyond health. The main reported source differs by subject: news media lead for foreign policy, immigration, the economy, and technology/media regulation; government sources are jointly most common with news media for Social Security; social media and friends/family remain visible but smaller primary routes in the published topic distributions. The atlas can therefore treat information infrastructure as topic-specific: a person may encounter different authorities when deciding about a consumer, public-benefit, political, or geopolitical question.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Pew topic-specific information-source survey Self-reported primary information source for health care, elections, immigration, economy, Social Security, foreign policy, and technology/media regulation topic → declared information route among news, government, social, personal network, school, other, or none actual exposure, accuracy, ranking, trust, persuasion, consumer choice, policy understanding, civic action, or legitimacy

Naming a main source is not exclusive use, agreement, or decision reliance. Different topic bases and cross-sectional self-report prevent a claim that one route caused a later belief or behavior. See the topic-diversity information source record.

The AI-assistant choice study adds a platform-choice and privacy-control surface. In its weighted U.S. adult AI-user sample, about 43% reported intentionally routing different tasks to more than one assistant; platform choice and trust varied by task and user experience. More than 80% reported concern about conversation-data use, while the study's regression associated knowledge of a training policy more strongly with reported protective-tool use than an incremental increase in concern. Its embedded choice experiment also measures stated willingness to pay for different data-handling conditions.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Weighted AI-assistant-user survey and embedded choice experiment Task-specific primary assistant, reported multihoming, trust rankings, privacy concern/knowledge/tool use, and hypothetical data-handling preferences task and platform environment → stated routing, trust, knowledge, and privacy preference/action surface telemetry, actual payment, privacy disclosure/loss, causal protective behavior, durable switching, provider retention, dependence, wellbeing, or productivity

Reported multihoming can coexist with a dominant default assistant, and stated willingness to pay is not a purchase. The cross-sectional survey cannot show whether use caused trust or policy knowledge caused protective behavior. See the AI-assistant choice, trust, and privacy record.

The comparative NBER cookie-consent experiment adds a causal interface mechanism, not a U.S. prevalence estimate. It randomized consent-banner design and found that placing options behind extra clicks shifted users toward more accessible alternatives; the associated structural analysis treats repeated site-specific consent decisions as an attention/time cost. This shows why a formal data choice can be shaped by the route through which it is presented.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Comparative cookie-consent field experiment and structural model Randomized banner/interface effects on acceptance, dismissal, and accessible alternatives; modeled site-versus-browser consent/time comparison consent design/default/friction → observed interface choice and repeated-attention-cost mechanism U.S. prevalence, informed consent, comprehension, actual data use/protection, service trade-off, fraud, welfare, or durable exit

An acceptance or dismissal is not an informed privacy choice, and the modeled browser-level benefit relies on preference, time-cost, and data-value assumptions. See the cookie-consent choice-architecture record.

The GAO digital-homebuying record adds a housing-market version of that interface problem. Its review spans online home search, automated valuations, automated underwriting, and electronic closing: these tools may supply information, financing options, lower costs, or faster mortgage approval. But the same route can collect sensitive data for personalization and marketing, enable algorithmic advertising or chatbots that may steer protected-class consumers, and make valuation inputs or errors hard to inspect or contest. GAO also found product-specific oversight concentrated at FHFA while other reviewed agencies generally had not conducted it, alongside an open recommendation to clarify enterprise fair-lending expectations. This is not an estimate of discriminatory treatment, privacy loss, loan approval, affordability, completed purchase, or stable housing; it establishes that transaction speed and information access do not close the contestability and fairness stages.

The federal AI privacy-guidance record adds a public-system version of the same control gap. GAO's expert panel identified ten selected challenges spanning security, transparency, secondary use, consent, privacy technology, performance measurement, impact assessment, workforce capability, and privacy-performance tradeoffs. In its January 2026 comparison, OMB's government-wide guidance fully addressed two of the ten; GAO found it did not specify the known privacy-risk types agencies should consider in policy development and issued two open recommendations. This is a guidance-coverage result, not a score for agency compliance or a count of breaches, misuse, affected people, privacy harm, trust change, or successful remedy. Agencies may use controls that the government-wide guidance comparison does not capture.

The privacy and digital-safety records now add a fuller contestability middle. California's DROP reports system reach, broker-level statuses, processing clocks, and deletion by at least one broker for nearly all reported registrants; Walmart separately reports received, completed, denied, and median-time privacy-request metrics. GM/OnStar, the TAKE IT DOWN Act, and Google Search make formal data/removal, exception, deadline, tracking, and escalation routes visible. The common result is not that every user has recovered control: it is that request visibility and administrative completion are now observable stages that must remain separate from verified deletion/removal, no recurrence, safety, trust, and exit. See the DROP deletion record, DROP contestability record, Walmart privacy-request record, GM/OnStar control record, TAKE IT DOWN Act record, and Google image-removal record.

Gallup's financial-guidance survey adds a social and consumer-information route. Among U.S. adults who sought guidance, internet research was the most commonly reported source, while family, professional advisors, and AI were separate nonexclusive routes. Financially stressed guidance seekers reported family and AI use more often than financially fulfilled seekers, yet reported confidence in AI's financial expertise remained low. This identifies guidance seeking as a mixed human-and-digital support system rather than evidence that AI has replaced human advice.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Gallup/Edward Jones U.S. financial-guidance survey Reported source mix, financial-fulfillment subgroup differences, and confidence comparisons financial-guidance need/status → reported family, professional, internet, or AI guidance route → stated confidence surface question, recommendation, advice quality, decision influence, fee, loss, financial improvement, human substitution, trust change, switching, or recovery

The guidance sources are nonexclusive and the status/use/confidence measures are cross-sectional. More family or AI use among stressed respondents may reflect greater need or multiple-source search, not source effectiveness. See the financial-guidance and AI-trust record.

A randomized Chilean consumer-credit trial supplies a mechanism comparator, not a U.S. estimate. Among 112,063 loan seekers, belief elicitation increased search and produced lower interest rates, while a regulator-linked comparison tool increased negotiation and lowered rates without increasing search; it also made participants more likely to borrow. This is a valuable consumer-power distinction: better price information can improve a term while increasing loan take-up, so lower rates do not by themselves establish lower total cost, repayment success, or household security. The experiment's products, market, and follow-up are not the U.S. guidance survey's population or outcome path. See the comparative consumer-credit search/negotiation record.

For the fuller source-by-source treatment across health, finance, AI, and public/political information, see information authority and practical judgment.

Latest rotation: capacity is filtered through selection, maintenance, learning, and validation

The latest rotation adds five different units without treating them as one population. Together they sharpen a cross-domain proposition:

A formal offer or resource becomes a lived outcome only after it passes through selection, operating capacity, feedback, and meaning. The same resource can expand one form of agency while leaving another burden or risk untouched.

Evidence unit Directly observed or estimated What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Federal duplication and fragmentation portfolio GAO identifies 610 remaining matters, 97 new matters, $774.3B reported cumulative savings/revenue gains, and >$100B potential additional gains fragmented responsibility → coordination and navigation cost → possible service and accountability consequence household benefit, service quality, transition cost, and legitimacy
AI public-finance model Two-stage framework models erosion of labor-income/consumption bases and possible taxation of autonomous production AI transformation → tax-base and redistribution problem → public capacity and political conflict realized adoption, revenue, ownership, incidence, feasibility, and legitimacy
Public-university admissions metrics In one large urban public system, high-school GPA predicts first-year outcomes and graduation better than SAT; separate Ivy-Plus evidence differs metric choice → institution-specific classification and gatekeeping → possible access and legitimacy consequence admissions reform, fairness, completion causality, earnings, and trust
K–12 AI diffusion gaps School-principal survey finds lower AI integration associated with student disadvantage; training, guidance, and policy lag adoption AI availability/use → institutional support capacity → unequal integration and possible student/teacher consequence causal learning, wellbeing, privacy, safety, and durable inequality
AI economic forecasts and policy preferences Five groups broadly expect capability advances; disagreement centers on economic consequences, while experts favor retraining and the public also supports broader income or job interventions capability expectation → perceived distributional risk → preferred insurance or redistribution → possible legitimacy and action realized AI effects, policy adoption, household security, and political behavior
