Cybersecurity-regulation harmonization Seven selected industry representatives reported overlapping controls, definitions, and incident-reporting burdens; 11 of 12 earlier federal coordination recommendations were implemented and one partially addressed private infrastructure exposure → regulatory burden and reporting capacity → possible security and service consequence national prevalence, compliance cost, breach reduction, consumer harm, and service outcome
Water-sector cybersecurity oversight Internet-connected operational technology expands remote access; systems vary in capability and face workforce, legacy, funding, and legal constraints; EPA has a risk plan but identified authority and requirement gaps digital infrastructure dependence → prevention capacity and governance gap → possible physical-service and public-health exposure named incident, outage, household burden, compliance, and remediation
Medicaid eligibility correction (selected states) States used training, guidance, and system updates; CMS did not consistently verify plan elements or learn which fixes worked across states administrative error → correction attempt → incomplete institutional learning loop individual coverage restoration, continuity, beneficiary time, health, trust, and appeal
DOD installation maintenance $285B estimated backlog; about 80% of identified needs funded against a 90% goal; department-wide effectiveness data are weak appropriations and maintenance capacity → facility/risk visibility → possible readiness and quality-of-life exposure realized readiness loss, personnel harm, recruitment/retention, and adversary response
Medical-school selection weak outside options shifted entry cohorts; later cohorts billed more per Medicare beneficiary and used more revenue-generating services without detectable health improvement labor-market selection → professional incentives and setting → service intensity and measured outcome patient-level welfare, household cost, coding, trust, and mechanism separation
Historical U.S. risk preferences crop-choice-derived risk estimates correlate with leverage, Liberty Bond participation, local risk sharing, and tractor adoption inferred risk orientation → different collective and technology choices preference versus constraint, contemporary transfer, and causal institutional trust
Comparative household employment experiment direct female work experience shifted later employment preferences, with unequal partner-wellbeing effects lived experience → norm revision and expressed preference U.S. transfer, durable employment, safety, care substitution, bargaining, and political action
AI measurement methodology AI can make structured variables from unstructured data cheaper, while plausible construct choices can support different conclusions; explicit criteria and validation are required scalable measurement → construct choice and validation → institutional visibility or allocation named-system accuracy, subgroup error, appeal, trust, and downstream resource effects
AI coding and software production coding activity rises much faster than projects, releases, and total marketplace usage tool exposure → task activity → project/release realization → use quality, review/security work, worker time and pay, firm profit, and consumer value
Housing-tax allocation model tax treatment can lower capitalized prices and young downpayments while raising older holding costs and changing tenure tax design → price and holding-cost changes → age- and wealth-conditioned housing access observed reform incidence, rentals, displacement, public services, and political response
Jail healthcare accreditation RCT standards, coordination, screening, and oversight improved in participating jails, with lower 12-month mortality and no added capital or labor inputs institutional route → operating practice → care and mortality post-release continuity, trust, detention exposure, vendor-wide performance, and generalizability
American Indian heterogeneity essay pooled averages and changing definitions can hide historical harm, tribal variation, and gains associated with self-governance historical policy and place → identity, governance, and measurement → observed human-capital and health outcomes tribal-specific causal mechanisms, current policy effects, privacy, and sovereignty-aware measures
Managed-LTSS cross-payer comparison Florida hospitalization and vaccination changes diverged from New York after managed-LTSS rollout Medicaid delivery design → preventive care and utilization → Medicare-financed health outcome individual quality, implementation mechanism, functional status, household burden, and generalizability
AI asset-management evidence AI hedge-fund adoption grows, early outperformance decays, and return comovement is lower than among non-AI peers disclosure and labor signals → firm capability → performance and strategy structure causal alpha, investor welfare, leverage, and systemic-risk consequences
Emerging-technology governance foresight GAO reviews neural implants, general-purpose robots, and orbital-debris removal as potentially transformative technologies and identifies unresolved privacy, autonomy, environmental, and legal questions emerging capability → governance timing, human oversight, and legal capacity → future public and infrastructure consequence adoption, distribution, realized harm, employment, public acceptance, and geopolitical response
Founder-tax risk-sharing model startup exit value is highly concentrated; accrual taxation trades successful-founder dilution against refundable-credit insurance venture ownership → tax timing → payoff distribution and entrepreneurial risk realized reform, employee ownership, innovation, public revenue, and household effects

The NBER AI-measurement/validation record grounds the table's methodological row. Its review distinguishes discovery, construct definition, and observation: AI can turn unstructured text or images into structured variables at lower cost, while shifting the hard question from whether a measure can scale to which plausible construct should be used and how it is validated. The framework requires explicit criteria and designed validation, but is not a population estimate or an evaluation of any named AI system. It does not establish accuracy, subgroup error, discrimination, appeal, trust, agency practice, or downstream allocation for a public or private user.

The AI public-finance tax-base record grounds the table's fiscal row as a two-stage theoretical mechanism. In the first stage, if AI displaces human labor, the model treats labor-income and human-consumption bases as vulnerable and makes consumption or differentiated commodity taxation more salient. In a later hypothetical stage where autonomous systems produce most value and absorb more resources, the model argues that taxing human consumption becomes inadequate and frames taxation of autonomous production as an optimal-harvesting problem. This is not a realized AI adoption path, revenue forecast, tax recommendation, incidence estimate, or feasible international policy design; its implications depend on assumptions about displacement, ownership, production, consumption, transfers, and political capacity.

The AI asset-management record grounds the table's finance row in an empirical adoption screen. Across 116,000 investment-adviser disclosures from 2012–2024, the paper identifies steadily growing AI-driven investing concentrated among hedge funds. AI hedge funds outperformed non-AI peers initially, but that advantage declined over time, including among early adopters; their reported return comovement was lower. The result describes adoption, reported performance, and strategy structure, not causal AI alpha, ordinary-household investment returns, productivity, leverage, or systemic-risk reduction. Disclosure classification, novelty, selection, changing strategies, hidden common exposures, and market adaptation remain plausible alternative explanations.

The water-sector cybersecurity-capacity record grounds the table's water-infrastructure row. GAO describes roughly 170,000 water and wastewater systems where operational technologies controlling valves and pumps are increasingly connected to internet-enabled devices and remote access. It identifies uneven system capability, workforce shortages, hard-to- update legacy technology, and limited resources; EPA completed a sector risk assessment and risk-management plan, while identifying gaps in assessment requirements and federal authority. This is a risk-governance and operating- capacity stage, not evidence of a successful attack, outage duration, household water-safety effect, operator failure, compliance rate, or remediation result.

The common pattern is not that capacity is absent. It is that capacity is converted unevenly and represented through contested measurement. A state program can correct an error without proving a beneficiary regained continuity; a funded installation can retain a backlog without a measured readiness failure; a medical profession can expand spending without detectable health gain; caution can reduce leverage while increasing local risk sharing; and a household can revise a gender-work preference after experience without yet changing durable employment.

This rotation therefore strengthens the atlas's middle layer—selection, maintenance, feedback, and interpretation—while preserving the end-to-end stopping rule. The next decisive evidence must follow named people, cases, facilities, or institutions across the open middle rather than infer the final outcome from an upstream allocation or reported response.

This atlas is currently strongest at showing how pressures and capabilities are distributed, how people and institutions adapt, and where the next link in the chain is still unmeasured. It is not yet a single model that explains political or geopolitical behavior from household conditions. The useful reader question is therefore: which stage is directly observed, which stage is compared across sources, and which stage remains an open test?

If you want to understand Start here The current safe conclusion
How pressure reaches daily life Material room and household findings and energy-room findings Income timing, assistance, prices, energy spending, disconnection, repair risk, and adaptation are connected questions, not one stress score.
How time and care enter the story The household calendar integration program Work, care, travel, health, and recovery run on different clocks; the same-family trigger-to-outcome chain is still the key acquisition target.
How institutions shape practical options The public-system and consumer route findings and CFPB route findings A complaint, notice, or benefit receipt is an institutional route, not by itself a remedy, recovered security, trust change, or exit.
How local economies and infrastructure matter The firm/place finding and infrastructure/state-capacity bridge Applications, openings, jobs, capacity, revenue, ownership, and replaceability are separate stages; entry or investment is not automatically broad prosperity or leverage.
How meaning, politics, and geopolitics enter The cost/trust/politics program and comparative capability context Surveys and international comparisons identify meaning, confidence, capability, and context; they do not by themselves prove attribution, collective action, or external behavior change.
How consumer participation becomes social power Consumer culture, trust, status, and everyday power and consumer recourse visibility/remedy Buying, sharing, reporting, help-seeking, switching, and staying are distinct participation surfaces; trust, visibility, remedy, dignity, and practical exit must not be substituted for one another.

The rest of this page moves in four passes: the joint proposition, the evidence by arrow, the segments that are genuinely end-to-end, and the next research cycle. Each section keeps a direct observation beside its limitation and next test so that a compelling theme does not silently become a causal claim.

Current broad-program rotations

The latest rotation cycle deliberately moved across the full program rather than deepening one household lane. The continuity ledger records 56 documented rotations; the 46 numbered entries below are the cross-source synthesis artifacts currently carried in this table. They are bounded syntheses, not estimates of one pooled phenomenon:

The new partisan-identity layer adds a caution about political coalitions. Pew's 2026 NPORS shows a small national Democratic advantage after leaners are included, but larger uneven differences by gender, race, and education. Many people call themselves independent before leaners are assigned. This supports the claim that political identity can organize belonging and interpretation without proving a vote, a policy position, a switch, or a durable realignment.

The common pattern

Across the 56 documented rotations, the strongest recurring theme is unequal optionality under institutional mediation. A condition or capability changes the options available to people, consumers, workers, firms, places, or states; an institution then routes, prices, classifies, delays, corrects, funds, or governs the response. The visible endpoint is often not the human or public outcome but the institution's own record: a complaint label, a benefit transition, a time measure, a tax receipt, a policy filing, a vote, or a production milestone.

The broad map therefore needs one discipline at every scale:

observed condition or capability
  -> available alternatives and control
  -> adaptation and redistribution of money, time, risk, data, or power
  -> institutional and firm response
  -> meaning, trust, action, switching, or exit
  -> sector, state, or geopolitical consequence

The rotations strengthen the middle of this chain and sharpen the open-arrow list. They do not prove one grand causal theory, and they do not make the unavailable PSID/UAS respondent files a program-wide dependency.

The newest cases make the same idea visible at different scales. Nursing-home inspections can change care effort without showing complete resident wellbeing; the CHPE line can operate without showing household affordability; a TAKE IT DOWN complaint route can exist without showing removal or safety; a USMCA labor remedy can report reinstatement and backpay without showing durable worker power; and a SNAP office closure can reduce participation without showing the full food-security consequence. These are not one causal sequence. Together they support a narrower subtheme: institutional visibility often arrives before usable control, adequate protection, or durable trust.

The safe-drinking-water investment and health record adds a public-infrastructure-to-health version. Across 266 million readings in 48 states, the share above current standards fell by about half from 2003 to 2019; the study nevertheless estimates that roughly 10%–20% of Americans still receive water violating standards. Safe Drinking Water Act loans were associated with lower pollution and lower mortality among older Americans in the study's estimates, at an estimated average cost of $46 per person per year to remove excess pollution. Local hotspots, household exposure, private treatment, monitoring, equal receipt, and each household's private cost remain separate from the system-level trend.

The water-resilience record adds the financing-and-place middle. Fourteen EPA, FEMA, and USDA programs provided about $35 billion in grants and $29 billion in direct loans, yet selected utilities still reported rate resistance, repayment burden, maintenance costs, and difficulty making results visible to the public. Service areas also did not line up cleanly with community boundaries. Federal capital can therefore expand infrastructure capacity while local affordability, maintenance, targeting, and dependable household service remain unresolved; funding and project counts do not establish resilience or equal protection.

The CBP port-partnership record adds a public-private border version. More than 1.15 million people and 88,500 containers entered daily through 328 ports in FY2024, while reimbursed overtime and donated lanes or equipment expanded the capacity route. Partnership dollars and equipment do not by themselves show a shorter queue, fairer inspection, lower trade cost, or preserved accountability.

The retained same-unit bridge matrix clarifies the strongest longitudinal evidence currently retained. MEPS closes an event-to-later-health/work bridge; SHED closes a pressure-to-adaptation and partial-reversal bridge; CCES closes a prior-disruption-to-later-judgment or action bridge. Read together, they produce a useful cultural result without a false join: adaptation, institutional approval, contact, political action, and recovery are different currencies. Hardship does not automatically become backlash, and continued use does not automatically mean satisfaction. The next decisive evidence must measure the person's perceived control, reason for the choice, institutional response, and later outcome in the same episode.

The case-level audit sharpens the boundary further: no retained episode has both a clearly observed alternative/non-use choice and recipient-level remedy receipt. Meadley comes closest on an official reported payment, but the worker's alternative is not recorded. Platform cases add reactivation, substitute earnings, or post-restoration work, but separate lost-pay receipt, durability, and later recovery remain open. This is why the atlas treats formal remedy, implementation, receipt, and durable recovery as separate clocks rather than one “resolved” outcome.

The latest SHED additions make the optionality pattern legible across three everyday institutions. Banking access shows that formal entry can coexist with nonbank substitution and incomplete fraud recovery; care and living arrangements show that households can convert cost into co-residence, unpaid care, and gendered work tradeoffs; employment and job quality show that weaker outside mobility coexists with unequal access to AI and task discretion. Read together, these are not one household-level causal sequence. They are three bounded demonstrations that the same visible behavior—using an alternative payment route, providing unpaid care, or adopting a work tool—can represent preference, support, constraint, or some mixture. The decisive missing fields remain the dated trigger, feasible alternatives, actor response, verified outcome, and later trust, action, recovery, or exit in the same unit.

The NASBO state-budget finding adds a public-capacity layer between macro conditions and household-facing services. Proposed fiscal 2027 general-fund spending grew only 0.6% at the median even as states reported targeted cuts, vacant-position reductions, and revenue increases; most states still expected dollar rainy-day balances to hold or rise while total balances declined as prior surplus was spent. This supports a sharper institutional subtheme: fiscal room can remain visible while adjustment is pushed into staffing, program choice, timing, or local delivery. It is not evidence of a service cut or household burden. The next test is a named state service or shock followed through enacted policy, implementation, access, and resident or firm outcome.

The Pew state rainy-day capacity record adds the state-buffer stock beneath that budget-planning surface. Fiscal 2025 rainy-day balances totaled $174.2 billion; the median covered 47.8 operating days (13.1% of annual spending), down from 54.5 days in FY2024. Capacity ranged from 320.2 days in Wyoming to zero dedicated rainy-day days in New Jersey, with 24 states increasing and 26 decreasing their cushion. Total rainy-day plus ending balances were $346.9 billion, yet median ending balances declined 17.4%. These descriptive reserve ratios do not show legal availability, program need, service quality, tax incidence, disaster response, household benefit, or trust.

Three currencies of everyday optionality

The three latest SHED-based findings are useful together because they expose different forms of room to maneuver without pretending that the respondents or episodes are the same. The comparison is a mechanism map, not a pooled index:

Lane Unit and measured surface What the evidence supports What it does not establish
Banking and fraud recourse 2025 SHED adult respondents; formal account status, overdraft, nonbank transaction routes, reported fraud loss/recovery, provider contact, and reported switching Formal entry can coexist with reliance on alternative payment routes and incomplete or uneven recourse; non-switching is an observed behavior, not proof of satisfaction A dated account event, provider fault, quality of the alternative, verified dollar recovery, usable liquidity, trust change, or practical exit
Care and living arrangements 2025 SHED adult respondents; multigenerational living, paid and unpaid childcare, childcare cost relative to housing, adult caregiving, gendered caretaker roles, and caregiving-related employment status Households may convert money pressure into co-residence or unpaid labor, and care responsibilities can coexist with employment differences; these are distinct resource and time allocations A same-family care trigger, available substitute, schedule control, displaced work/time, employer or public response, recovery, or political meaning
Employment and AI control 2025 Federal Reserve SHED workers/adults; young-adult job-finding difficulty, layoffs, voluntary exits, new-job starts, work location/schedule variation, AI use, perceived time saving, education, and task-control differences Outside mobility and workplace control are separate dimensions of the AI transition; adoption and perceived time saving can be distributed by education and decision latitude Causal AI displacement or productivity, pay or benefit change, task-level implementation, worker bargaining, household welfare, trust, or political response

The common analytical point is that an alternative is not just a second product or a second place to live. It can be a payment channel, a family member's unpaid time, a schedule accommodation, a job change, or the ability to refuse a tool. Each alternative carries a different price in money, time, privacy, status, dependence, or future bargaining power. The available data show the surfaces separately; they do not tell us which option a particular person considered, whether it was genuinely usable, or what outcome it protected.

This is why the atlas should code the following as distinct states:

formal access       != usable access
alternative route  != equivalent substitute
continued use      != satisfaction
AI adoption        != worker gain
co-residence       != voluntary preference
non-switching      != practical power

The next decisive design is therefore a same-unit event or repeated-person comparison that records the initiating need, the alternatives actually available, the choice and its money/time cost, the actor controlling the next step, and a protected or sacrificed outcome. Only then can the three lanes be connected to recovery, trust, action, or exit without converting population patterns into one synthetic household story.

The Amazon Flex tip-refund follow-up adds a named worker-remedy stage to the same distinction. The FTC publicly reports earlier payment rounds totaling more than $60.6 million and a current Zelle route for eligible drivers who did not cash their checks. This is stronger than a compensation obligation or reserved fund, but it still does not provide the complete eligible-driver denominator, every individual's receipt or remaining loss, continued platform work, alternative work, household recovery, or bargaining and exit outcomes. The worker remedy is therefore coded as administrator-reported distribution with downstream lived recovery open.

The CFPB Ombudsman redress-process trend adds a recipient-side middle stage to that distribution boundary. The FY2025 report records 2,584 Ombudsman inquiries, with questions and complaints as distinct categories, and names redress-list, address-update, and check-reissue problems among the recurring process topics. Its illustrative servicemember example documents an expired check, a correct reissue request, administrator friction, and Ombudsman facilitation. This makes effort and institutional escalation visible without turning inquiry volume into a failure rate or facilitation into verified receipt, cashing, recovery, trust, or exit.

The FTC refund-administration benchmark adds a route-specific receipt measure: its 2019 report gives average check- cashing rates of 64% for known-customer mailings, 93% for claims-process cases, and 89% when Consumer Sentinel supplied the recipient list. The rates are not one current remedy-success rate; they show that identification route, contactability, claims friction, and reissue rules shape what “receipt” means.

This is the current end-to-end reading of the atlas. It is deliberately a bridge across different units, not a merge of respondents, households, complaints, workers, places, or countries. The machine-readable trend registry is the source index; each record's boundary controls how far its evidence can travel.

The automatic-saving multi-currency bridge adds a policy-to-household sequence across NBER/CRI Auto-IRA studies, Federal Reserve SHED liquidity and credit, and BEA aggregate income and spending. It does not pool the estimates: the policy studies use different treatment designs and balance-sheet definitions, while the Federal Reserve and BEA layers are context rather than treatment outcomes. The surviving claim is that automatic saving can move current liquidity, future assets, and retirement timing on different clocks; the net-security and meaning/action arrows remain open.

The SIPP utility-credit-savings finding now adds a sharper household-room bridge inside the material and institutional route layers. In the same person-record/month diagnostic, reported utility payment difficulty co-occurs with more carried credit balances and less savings account ownership, while higher-resource respondents within the difficulty group are more likely to carry balances—an access counterexample, not evidence that they face less hardship. The separate following-month utility-to-work finding places utility difficulty or energy-assistance status beside next-month earnings and hours. These are adjacent descriptive stages, not a bill-to-credit-to-work causal estimate.

The directional SIPP work/resource finding sharpens the work/time bridge: earnings changes can rise or fall, while hours are unchanged for most adjacent-month pairs. Work-limitation and resource position condition the direction distribution, but no bill, health event, employer decision, care substitution, or later meaning/action is observed.

The new ATUS work-location finding adds a published 2025 work-location surface to the time architecture. Home and workplace indicators overlap, and their sex and education gradients are visible, but location does not identify schedule control, total workload, care conflict, or worker voice. The federal-shutdown coverage warning in the 2025 release is retained as a measurement caveat.

The new SIPP tenure/resource finding adds a replicate-weighted intersection to the household-room surface. Renters report more housing and utility-payment difficulty than owners within each displayed resource band, including at the highest band, while the food-hardship measure follows a different pattern and has its own universe. This sharpens the alternative-space question—resources do not erase tenure-linked exposure—but does not identify rent, local price, repair, insurance, debt, or a dated bill as the mechanism.

The new household-room layer puts that SIPP comparison beside the Federal Reserve's emergency-liquidity and linked-credit measures. It separates resource position, tenure, hypothetical emergency capacity, and realized card-balance exposure rather than treating them as one security index. The combined reading is that household room is about available alternatives when a dated cost arrives; the same-person event, time/care substitution, protected outcome, and later recovery are still open.

The new multi-clock material/time/care synthesis connects that open middle to the longitudinal evidence already acquired. SIPP shows monthly resource and work transitions for the same people; MEPS follows health spending, coverage, employment, wages, and perceived-health change in a panel; SHED and ATUS add emergency routes, care, and time allocation. The combined evidence supports distinct material, time, health, and work clocks, not a pooled household stress score. A complete dated trigger → alternative → protected/sacrificed outcome → recovery → meaning/action chain remains the program's acquisition target.

The SHED coverage-to-care-foregoing comparison adds an important condition inside that middle. In the recontact panel, stable insurance has the largest no-foregoing share (69.12%) and the lowest persistent-foregoing share (14.53%), while persistent uninsurance has the highest persistent-foregoing share (37.35%); coverage loss and gain remain smaller cells with different entry and exit profiles. The reproduction audit confirms these cells from the existing local artifacts. This is a route condition, not an insurance effect: the annual fields do not observe plan adequacy, network access, a dated need or bill, treatment continuity, or recovery.

The SHED care-foregoing/adaptation record adds a cross-sectional household-pressure surface. Among respondents reporting that they skipped at least one listed kind of care because of cost, 42.2% had medical debt, 64.0% reduced savings, 34.0% increased borrowing, 74.3% delayed a major purchase, and 33.0% worked more or got a job; the corresponding no-foregoing shares were 10.0%, 33.1%, 9.6%, 35.6%, and 11.5%. The respondent link makes the co-occurrence visible, but it does not establish a dated bill, direction of causation, care alternative, treatment outcome, coverage adequacy, remedy, or recovery. Prior scarcity, health need, access, coverage, and reverse timing can produce both care foregoing and adaptation.

The SHED coverage and care-skipping association record adds a coverage-conditioned snapshot. Among insured respondents, 23.8% reported skipping at least one listed care type because of cost; 42.6% of that foregoing group also reported medical debt, versus 10.0% of insured respondents reporting no listed foregoing. The corresponding medical-debt shares were 40.1% and 9.9% among uninsured respondents who did and did not report foregoing, respectively. Coverage therefore conditions the care-foregoing surface but does not eliminate concurrent debt. These are same-respondent, cross-sectional comparisons without replicate-weight standard errors, bill timing, plan generosity, care need, clinical outcome, or causal insurance effect.

The new MEPS expenditure-conditioned finding deepens the health-cost/work bridge without turning spending into a burden score. Baseline 2022 expenditure bands have different perceived-health and employment-continuity profiles, but the differences remain confounded by need, age, insurance, retirement, and service mix. The correct next question is not whether high spending “caused” work loss; it is which treatment, coverage, out-of-pocket, unpaid-care, and baseline-employment paths explain the distinct outcomes.

The new public-system route-to-judgment synthesis extends the safety-net chain through institutional meaning without pooling incompatible respondents. USDA/FNA measures administrative timeliness, WBNS measures recipient route barriers, SIPP measures following material hardship, and Gallup measures institution-specific confidence. Together they support a layered route/buffer/judgment architecture; they do not show that one notice caused one hardship or changed one person's trust or political action.

The Medicaid-expansion safety-net-spillovers record adds a cross-program route mechanism. In border-county and restricted-ACS comparisons, a typical 0-to-138%-of-poverty Medicaid expansion reduced uninsurance by about 2.2 percentage points and was associated with about 0.6 additional SNAP participants per 100 people (0.49 percentage points in the ACS) and higher TANF participation, particularly among single parents; the preferred EITC estimate was small and not statistically distinguishable from zero. The authors' leading interpretation is reduced information or transaction costs for participation conditional on eligibility. The repeated cross-section and county-pair designs do not follow a named household through notice, application, amount, food security, care use, trust, action, or recovery, and cannot make those downstream outcomes part of the expansion effect.

The LIHEAP reach/restoration record adds a public-capacity comparator to this route. HHS reports broad FY2024 program reach and distinct restored-energy instances, but those aggregate endpoints do not reveal whether service remained on, whether the next bill was affordable, or which food, medicine, housing, health, or work trade-off was avoided. Program reach, restoration, and durable household recovery therefore remain separate stages.

The Clean Energy Connector record adds a different eligibility-to-bill route. In six pilot jurisdictions, DOE and HHS describe identifying LIHEAP recipients for community-solar subscriptions; eligible households opt in, subscription managers complete enrollment, and the program requires at least a 20% difference between the household's financial benefit and participation cost. Clear communication, disclosure, data, and consumer-protection requirements are visible program design. The page does not report the number of eligible households, successful opt-ins, subscription fees, bill-credit timing, net savings, retention, service reliability, or energy security. A required discount is therefore a condition of a potential route, not a measured household outcome.

The new CFPB route-vintage audit adds a measurement-integrity result to the consumer-power lane. In live 2024/2025 product samples, timely does not substitute for elapsed routing time, and the returned has_narrative field is unavailable in the re-query. The public API therefore supplies a route/schema diagnostic, not a remedy or consumer-welfare trend; omitted fields remain missing rather than zero.

The CFPB complaint-publication record adds a later institutional consequence to that visibility boundary. The Bureau described two-factor and routing controls after concerns about third-party and AI-assisted complaint activity, then ended discretionary publication of unverified complaint narratives and visualizations while retaining collection, monitoring, response, and secure regulatory sharing. This is not evidence that the complaint route became less useful or more useful to any individual. It does establish that administrative integrity and public consumer voice can move in opposite directions: a more controlled intake can coexist with a less visible public narrative layer, while correction, payment, trust, switching, and exit remain unobserved.

The CFPB narrative-filter API record adds a narrower public-data boundary. In a live query of 21,425 matching credit-card complaints carrying the company label Closed with monetary relief, the capped returned payload exposed 15 administrative fields but no usable narrative field. Adding has_narrative=true returned the same total, count, and 25 IDs as the control query. This establishes only that the tested public API route did not expose a narrative/meaning stage; it does not show that consumers lacked narratives, that the filter fails everywhere, or that monetary relief was received, adequate, or associated with account correction, repeat effort, trust, switching, or exit.

The federal shared-services record adds a public-administration version of the same interface problem. Agencies can be offered centralized cybersecurity, financial, grants, and human- resources services while legal fit, legacy systems, integration, leadership, and performance data remain uneven. Centralization may reduce duplication, but the review does not establish government-wide savings, service quality, user experience, or mission improvement. A marketplace or shared platform is a route choice; it is not proof that the work became easier or better for the agency using it.

The GAO federal-cloud security-control record adds a system-level control test. Across eight selected cloud systems in four agencies, three fully performed continuous monitoring, five fully implemented the selected service-level-agreement practice, and three agreements lacked consistent performance metrics, measurement, and enforcement. The remaining five systems only partially implemented the three reviewed practices: continuous monitoring, incident response/recovery, and enforceable provider terms. GAO issued 12 open recommendations. This selected-system review does not establish federal prevalence, a breach, outage, data loss, provider fault, or public-user harm; it identifies the governance work that must exist before cloud capacity can be treated as monitored, recoverable, and accountable.

The NNSA Strategic Partnership Projects record adds a realized shared-infrastructure version. NNSA sites performed more than $15 billion in reimbursed partner work across FY2019–24, and GAO reports about $1.4 billion in FY2024 indirect costs reimbursed by partners while specialized facilities were used for mission and research work. This moves the evidence from available capability to operating use, staffing, maintenance, and cost allocation. It also exposes a reciprocal dependence: federal partners may lack substitutes, while NNSA programs may rely on partner-funded overhead and utilization. Some sites limited SPP growth because core mission work and facility or staffing capacity competed for the same resources. Net savings, facility condition, equitable allocation, substitute capability, delivered mission effect, and geopolitical leverage remain open.

The cross-agency performance-goals record adds the coordination layer. GAO participants said four-year shared goals can create ownership and energy across agencies, while implementation still runs into uneven leadership, limited resources, inconsistent measurement, and transition problems. Coordination is not only a shared objective; it requires stable authority, staff, data, and a way to survive administrative change. The report does not show that any specific goal improved service or public trust.

The USAspending supplier-concentration record adds a quantitative replaceability check to the geopolitical/state-capacity lane. One JASSM/LRASM subaward extract has 51 reported recipient names, but the top five receive 49.50% of returned amount and the top ten 74.60%. The result keeps component diversity, financial concentration, production, replaceability, and external leverage as separate stages.

The entity-parent-facility reconciliation adds an official identity layer to that supplier test. DLA CAGE records make the apparent BAE route legible from the Merrimack recipient to BAE Systems, Inc. and BAE Systems plc, and provide a parallel General Dynamics-OTS to General Dynamics Corp route. This improves the jurisdiction and facility denominator without resolving the central capability question: parentage is not facility-level assignment, production, acceptance, delivery, replaceability, or external leverage. The next evidence must join the exact identifiers to procurement and performance records.

The follow-up recipient-identifier ambiguity audit tests that missing join directly. A name search returns 17 BAE recipient rows across 10 UEIs and three General Dynamics-OTS rows, while the retained JASSM/LRASM subaward response exposes no UEI or CAGE. One General Dynamics UEI overlaps the selected DLA facility set, but that intersection does not assign the $80.55 million subaward to a plant. The evidence therefore strengthens the measurement boundary: legal identity, facility identity, award action, and production location remain separate until an identifier-bearing performance record appears.

The richer subaward-to-UEI and location finding then closes an important measurement step. The official award-search route returns UEI, recipient-location, and primary-performance-place fields for all 74 rows, including exact identifiers for the selected BAE and General Dynamics-OTS actions. The locations are Nashua and Niceville, not automatically the previously selected DLA CAGE facilities. This turns the next question into a real CAGE-to-site and production/acceptance/delivery join rather than a name search, while preserving the operational and geopolitical arrows as open.

The facility-capability context finding adds a meaningful middle layer. Official BAE quality material places military electronics design/production/servicing scope at the Nashua address, and official General Dynamics-OTS material names Niceville Operations and advanced-warhead capability. The sources make those locations plausible industrial sites without proving that the selected subaward work occurred there. Production, acceptance, delivery, alternatives, and external response remain separate gates.

The realization-stage milestone finding adds dated movement beyond procurement intent: a DoD JASSM/LRASM production-support IDIQ, Lockheed Martin capacity investment/ramp-up evidence, and a completed first phase of LRASM F-35C flight-science testing. The Air Force FY2026 exhibit adds a government-reported Troy, Alabama minimum sustained rate of 396 combined JASSM/LRASM missiles, allocated as 336 JASSM and 60 LRASM, attributed to a new operational production facility. These stages strengthen production-capacity evidence while preserving the missing realized throughput, accepted quantity, delivery, fielding, maintenance, replaceability, and external-response links.

The Poland JASSM-ER delivery non-observation keeps the foreign customer stage honest. The May 2024 agreement's 2026–2030 window and the later 2028–2030 schedule reference conflict without a verified amendment, and the reviewed official source set still lacks a delivery, acceptance, fielding, training, or inventory event for the order. The absence is bounded to public-source review; it is not evidence that no delivery has occurred.

The historical Polish audit-control finding adds an institutional-observability layer: NIK found that a JASSM-ER production-cost settlement relied on milestone/process material without a numeric value tied to the settlement. This is evidence about documentation and control of realization, not a missile quantity or delivery estimate. The separate 32-unit comparator is retained as a general Polish defence-contract example and is not attributed to JASSM.

The PSID 2023 field-audit finding closes a different acquisition gap. Official documentation confirms a large panel family file with work, unpaid labor, care, perceived time pressure, health, income, wealth, insurance, and utility fields. The fields make a longitudinal material/time/care test feasible, but they do not yet supply a dated event, attribution, recovery, trust, or political-action result.

The FMS timing-asynchrony finding shows why the realization arrow needs multiple clocks. NIK records four F-35 deliveries in December 2024 and January 2025 while the related settlement forms arrived in 2025, and states that FMS delivery schedules are estimates. The comparator improves the measurement design but does not establish a JASSM-ER delivery or operational capability.

The historical GSS finding adds a long-run meaning countercheck: financial dissatisfaction is associated with lower trust and fairness expectations in each selected anchor year, but the gap and overall trust level change across decades. This supports a relational meaning route without turning financial position into a stable causal explanation of social trust or political action.

What the evidence jointly supports

Stage Current evidence Safe cross-source reading Arrow still open
Material room and exposure BLS food-at-home prices; USDA food security; SHED food pressure, liquidity, credit, and financial paths; SIPP adjacent-month hardship and SNAP transitions; FTC reported fraud losses; LBNL national energy load; CFPB published complaints Material price pressure, household resource gradients, liquid-buffer and credit exposure, basic-security severity, reported consumer loss, and infrastructure demand are measurable, but each source sees a different unit and exposure surface. A dated household, customer, worker, or place event causing the next response and showing which buffer or institution absorbed it.
Adaptation and time SHED repeated adaptations; SHED care/work cells; SIPP SNAP-transition/child-care time-loss and child-care-work/hardship comparisons; USDA family-shielding and assistance observations; ATUS eldercare prevalence, care-day intensity, 2024–2025 recipient-roster comparison, provider/nonprovider time profiles, age/sex/labor-force-standardized contrasts, and richer child/education-standardized contrasts; AI workplace time findings People and institutions absorb pressure through substitution, borrowing, care, work, waiting, assistance, and other time or resource transfers. The SIPP SNAP/child-care time-loss record shows child-care work prevention is higher in the stable-SNAP comparison (7.43% versus 3.42%). The separate SIPP child-care/work-hardship bridge places annual work prevention beside following-month hardship within stable SNAP-status pairs: utility hardship is 16.9% versus 7.8% in the no-SNAP comparison and 32.4% versus 19.4% in the SNAP comparison. These are descriptive contrasts, not a care-to-hardship effect: the work-prevention cells contain 71 and 23 valid pairs, respectively, with wide intervals and separate hardship universes. ATUS adds that roughly four in five eldercare provider respondents list a non-household recipient and that care, household work, and travel differences remain after richer composition controls, while social-time ordering varies by year and paid-work differences are uncertain. Whether a specific exposure displaced paid work, health, rest, family time, or civic availability for the same unit, and whether the support route caused or relieved that displacement.
Institutional route CFPB case-route timing, response endpoint, and visibility through 2025, including six matched product slices and a student-loan timing-field audit; SIPP SNAP transitions; USDA assistance participation; BLS union membership/coverage Access and protection are shaped by the route through a firm, benefit system, or workplace institution—not just by the headline outcome. The CFPB annual record shifts toward explanation and lower narrative visibility in 2025, but product routes diverge sharply. The student-loan audit shows that the broad timely = No field and narrower company-response untimely category are different endpoints; these are institutional records, not verified consumer outcomes. Notice, effort, appeal, remedy adequacy, practical control, and later exit or trust in the same episode.
Unequal capacity and power BLS age/occupation/state variation; SHED financial paths; ATUS age/employment differences; SIPP transition cells; AI adoption and education-gap comparisons; NHTS mobility options The same shock or tool can land differently because cash, time, care capacity, skill, representation, transport, and institutional access are distributed unevenly. A valid matched or longitudinal design identifying which capacity changed the outcome.
Meaning and political action CPS schedule/health/administrative/transport/interest/candidate barriers; ANES/CCES layers including joint trust/action quadrants; Pew engagement/source/influencer measures; national ANES immigration cross-tabs; Chicagoland local immigration-attitude case Political participation contains distinct access and interpretation routes; material and institutional experiences can be relevant inputs without being treated as votes. The CCES joint layer shows that trust and civic action can diverge across material/work proxy cells, so distrust cannot be equated with withdrawal. Local and national surveys can measure meaning and policy preference without proving the local cause. Attribution, fairness, identity, trust, organizing, turnout, and vote measured after a defined exposure.
State and geopolitical consequence SIPRI military-resource allocation; IMF WEO defense-boom fiscal estimates and US projections; defense procurement and realization records; Prince William county fiscal-revenue series (TY2012–2025); Virginia large-load governance and reliability record; LBNL infrastructure scenarios; domestic large-load rate governance; Romania–Malaysia project milestones and ownership changes Digital capacity, public revenue, defense-resource allocation, fiscal/social-spending trade-offs, and physical dependence can create public/private control questions at the same time, while domestic regulators and alliances specify who carries financial, infrastructure, and strategic risk. Procurement intent, operating milestones, macro-fiscal estimates, local fiscal visibility, and regulatory response are separated as distinct stages. The TY2025 county-linked report records $465.9M in data-center tax revenue alongside 621 MW of new capacity, while SCC evidence records large-load events, a GS-5 framework, and a modeled Rider T1 allocation comparison. Verified production/delivery, actual utility cost allocation, observed household or community incidence, financing/social-spending incidence, practical replaceability, and an observed external response.

The CFPB product-response-routes record puts numbers behind the institutional-route distinction. In 2025 published records, explanation was the recorded endpoint for 84.5% of checking/savings complaints, 94.9% of mortgage complaints, and 73.3% of debt-collection complaints; monetary relief was respectively 10.6%, 1.7%, and 0.16%. The student-loan slice also separates two timing fields: 15.9% carried a company-response untimely label while 30.4% had the broader timely = No field. These are product-filtered published complaint records, not customer harm or remedy rates: product and issue mix, complaint propensity, publication, routing, firm coding, and the 2025 taxonomy can all shape the shares. An explanation, relief label, or timing field does not establish correction, payment receipt, debt or account restoration, residual loss, switching, or trust for a complainant.

The payment-resilience record adds an outage version of the material-room and infrastructure rows. In the source's disaster and outage evidence, digital payments fell and cash use rose; nearly half of surveyed consumers could not use their preferred electronic payment during an outage, and greater cash access was associated with more completed transactions. This shows a practical fallback route, not a complete household outcome: the record does not establish whether people obtained food, medicine, fuel, or care, avoided income loss, or recovered without debt strain.

The 2024 CFPB case-route sample deepens the institutional-route row only through the first handoff: receipt to company routing, channel, narrative/public-response visibility, and response labels. Its capped retrieval-order design cannot establish route probabilities or remedy; effort, verified outcome, repeat contact, trust, and exit remain open. The 25-case public event-ledger finding turns that handoff into an explicit case-level contract: receipt, routing, lag, channel, narrative presence, timeliness, and response labels can share a de-identified record, while verified correction and later choice remain absent. The public event-ledger acquisition audit now proves that a de-identified episode ledger can be built from the public API without overstating those fields. Its 25-record student-loan extract preserves receipt, routing, channel, narrative presence, timeliness, and response labels; it explicitly does not turn a company label into verified correction, recovery, repeat effort, switching, trust, or exit.

The SNAP data-governance finding extends the institutional route backward to control over the records that define eligibility, benefit levels, and program integrity. DOJ's 2026 lawsuit announcement reports a federal demand for five years of applicant data from four states after 29 jurisdictions reportedly shared data; the related 2025 court order temporarily restrained threatened funding disallowance for most plaintiff states and noted that the record did not show significant fraud or eligibility errors in compliant states. This creates a useful two-sided governance stage—oversight authority versus privacy, statutory, and state control—without converting either agency claims or a temporary order into applicant-level benefit, food-security, or trust outcomes. The June 2026 USDA system-of-records notice adds the implementation surface: FedRAMP High hosting, need-to-know access, authentication, encryption, and legally bounded routine uses were specified after more than 450 public comments, including roughly 132 privacy or mishandling concerns. Those are stated controls and public concerns, not observed privacy safety or applicant behavior.

The SHED annual fraud-comparison record adds a second annual household sample to the consumer-power row. In 2024, non-credit-card fraud exposure was 6.85% for respondents age 18--29 and 10.25% for those 45--59; in 2025 it was 7.13% and 8.38%, respectively. Among fraud reporters, the unrecovered-money share was 53.78% versus 22.57% in the $10,000--$24,999 and $100,000--$149,999 household-income bands in 2024, and 50.67% versus 28.29% in 2025. Separate weighted annual samples and unreproduced replicate-weight variance mean these are descriptive comparisons, not a panel trend or causal age/income effect. They do not join household loss to CFPB response or establish remedy, trust, or exit.

The 2024 SHED household-fraud recovery record separates the loss and recovery currencies in the underlying survey. Twenty-one percent of adults reported some financial fraud; among adults reporting non-credit-card fraud, 63% lost money, 32% said some money was not recovered, and about 30% spent ten or more hours recovering or dealing with the incident. The Federal Reserve estimated $84 billion in non-credit-card losses, $21 billion recovered, and $63 billion borne directly by consumers. Those are self-reported, conditional survey measures—not verified case outcomes, firm liability, remedy adequacy, or a common denominator with CFPB complaints.

The GAO fraud-risk finding adds an institutional-control layer to the household fraud evidence. GAO's recommendation count and open-status share show unfinished control work and its stated trust/mission link, but they do not measure fraud prevalence, beneficiary recovery, or person-level trust change. Administrative integrity, usable correction, and restored confidence therefore remain separate outcomes.

The GAO Ukraine-assistance monitoring record adds an international assistance-accountability stage. State's MEASURE contract covered oversight of $6.1 billion in nonhumanitarian, nonmilitary Ukraine assistance through September 2025, including police and border-guard training and nuclear-safety operations. GAO found that the department used some contract information for oversight and budgeting and made reports more analytical, but wartime data access and varied outcome clocks constrained evaluation; strategic outcome indicators and cross-project evaluations were still incomplete in November 2025. Better reporting and administrative use are therefore visible state-capacity outcomes, not proof of program effectiveness, Ukrainian public legitimacy, institutional resilience, nuclear-safety result, deterrence, or changed Russian behavior.

The domestic capacity and state-leverage bridge now integrates SIPRI resources, procurement transactions and modifications, realization milestones, ownership context, and international infrastructure cases. The resulting cross-source chain is staged rather than collapsed: resource allocation and commitment can precede operation, and operation can coexist with external control or weak replaceability. Leverage remains open until another actor changes behavior.

The state-capacity synthesis now makes that distinction concrete in the data-center lane. LBNL's 176 TWh 2023 estimate and 649 TWh 2030 reference scenario describe national modeled demand; Prince William County's $465.9M reported TY2025 tax revenue describes local fiscal capacity; Virginia filings describe modeled residential-incidence illustrations and reported large-load drop events. These are not one benefit/cost estimate. Together they show the political economy of infrastructure: growth can create public revenue while leaving customer allocation, interruption risk, inspection, portability, and community incidence unresolved. The missing state-capacity test is not another load forecast; it is observed cost allocation, local experience, control or switching rights, and an external actor changing behavior.

Two current infrastructure records make the stage distinction more concrete. NYPA reports Smart Path Connect completed and energized, with physical corridor and substation outputs plus projected system/customer savings; its public accounting and tariff materials separately expose a revenue-requirement and formal cost-allocation surface. PJM reports that about 4,000 MW of data-center load disconnected in a July 2026 event, requiring backup generation and grid management, followed by proposed ride-through controls and further regulatory standard-setting. Completion and live stress response are stronger evidence than a forecast, but neither record supplies retail bills, customer-class incidence, local environmental burden, outage experience, or durable affordability.

Infrastructure stage Direct observation Still open
Completed transmission Project completion/energization, physical assets, reported or modeled system savings, and formal revenue/cost-allocation artifacts Retail pass-through, household bill/reliability result, geographic and class incidence, acceptance, and persistence
Large-load grid event Approximate load disconnection, operator/backup-generation response, proposed connection controls, and regulatory process Facility attribution, final rule/compliance, residential interruption, bills, emissions, and local burden

The records should not be combined into one grid-benefit number: one is a named transmission realization with distinct reported and modeled value surfaces; the other is a PJM operating and governance episode. See the Smart Path Connect realization record and PJM large-load disconnection-response record.

The state-accountability records add a related but distinct implementation pattern: being able to count funding, reach, a current baseline, or a process does not establish that the intended problem changed. GAO found an estimated $1.2 billion across roughly 470 State/USAID projects intended to counter Chinese influence while agencies lacked readily available reliable portfolio data and had no portfolio-wide results assessment. In a separate DHS review, 18 of 19 baselined major acquisitions met their current goals even though 15 had revised baselines and collective projected costs had risen $11.4 billion from initial baselines. GAO's broader program-performance synthesis identifies the same measurement boundary across federal programs and also documents a counterexample: a DHS program improved its tracking/management process without yet demonstrating preparedness impact.

Administrative surface What is visible What remains open
Geopolitical funding portfolio Funding, estimated project count, data/process gaps, and early/paused evaluation framework Project result, partner consent, changed Chinese behavior, legitimacy, or strategic effect
Major acquisition baseline Current-plan milestone status, revised baseline history, projected cost movement, staffing/oversight changes Fielded capability, user performance, mission result, safety, or external consequence
Federal performance management Goals/data/process coverage and selected tracking improvement Recipient adequacy, problem resolution, durable effect, trust, or political response

The sources do not show that funding, rebaselining, or performance management is meaningless; they show why outcome claims need a later compatible measure. See the GAO countering-China-influence record, DHS acquisition-baseline record, and federal program-effectiveness record.

The NYC Universal Access to Counsel study provides a stronger, causal consumer/housing-court middle. Using staggered zip-code rollout and detailed court records, its main instrumental-variable specification estimates that tenant counsel reduced possession judgments by about 33.4 percentage points, monetary judgments, and eviction-warrant issuance by about 34.0 percentage points. The executed-warrant result was smaller and not consistently statistically significant in the full sample. This is a valuable correction to calling all legal access merely formal: representation can alter a court process. It is not a completed housing-recovery chain—the study does not follow rent arrears, later moves, homelessness, credit, work, health, schooling, or whether the underlying rent problem was solved.

Evidence unit What the atlas can safely connect Still open
NYC housing-court records with staggered counsel rollout low-income tenant court case → counsel → lower modeled possession-judgment and warrant-issuance stages payment/arrears, physical eviction, later stay/move, housing quality, debt/credit, household wellbeing, and generalization outside the setting

The court-record effect is not a national eviction rate or a claim that every represented tenant remained housed. See the NYC tenant legal-representation record.

The eviction-order consequence record adds the downstream counterpart. Linked administrative data from Cook County and New York City show tenants' earnings/employment decline and financial distress/hospital visits rise before court; using random assignment to judges with different leniency, the study then estimates that an eviction order adds homelessness and hospital visits and reduces earnings, durable-goods consumption, and credit access in the first two years, with later indebtedness and lower credit scores. Reported housing and labor effects were driven by female and Black tenants. An eviction order is therefore an additional causal shock, not simply a label for the prior crisis. The two-city study does not reconstruct the initial shock, aid and counsel route, landlord response, move destination, household care network, later housing quality, or the effect of preventing an order on durable housing security.

The carbon-tariff model adds a geopolitical economic-policy boundary. In its counterfactual, a U.S. tariff alone raises modeled U.S. emissions while lowering foreign emissions and achieves about half the global emissions reduction of a combined tariff-plus-domestic-carbon-tax policy; it can nevertheless improve modeled U.S. GDP and welfare. The result distinguishes domestic, foreign, global, and welfare surfaces, and its multilateral tariff-only result is not monotonic in membership. It is not an implementation study: actual tariff incidence, firm relocation, household bills, retaliation, partner acceptance, and leverage remain unobserved. See the carbon-tariff/global-coordination record.

The new Poland reciprocity and co-production finding adds an official response-stage layer: Poland's 2026 announcements describe potential buyer/seller access in a US-linked UAS/C-UAS arrangement and planned regional Barracuda B500M co-production with the US, Estonia, and Latvia. This is evidence of institutional and industrial response around a procurement relationship, not evidence of output, delivery, public reception, replaceability, or bargaining leverage. The next test is to observe the named transaction, plant, workforce, component-control, delivery, or switching event.

The July 6 Bydgoszcz implementation account adds a more specific stage inside that response: assembly followed by production at PGZ/WZL-2, reported PGZ exclusivity for a Polish version, and technology/know-how/competence transfer language. Those are agreement terms, not commissioned output or independently verified control rights. An August 19 BBN follow-up with Anduril adds a dated senior-level governance checkpoint focused on the Barracuda-500M program and Polish implementation competencies. It still does not establish a production milestone, output, delivery, or amended contract. The Ministry of State Assets' detailed production page adds reported targets of thousands of systems and staged Polish/European supplier localization. These make scale and local-content denominators testable, but remain plans rather than completed units or observed supplier shares. The September 9 Polish-US FMF agreement adds a broader financing checkpoint: Poland reports $4 billion in Foreign Military Financing and acceleration of existing contracts, including Apache helicopters. It is not Barracuda-specific and therefore belongs to the resource/implementation stage, not the production, delivery, or leverage stage. The September realization watchpoint records the current public-source non-observation: no first assembly, commissioning, completed quantity, acceptance, delivery, or measured local-content share was located in the checked primary-source set.

The new public-system buffer-and-credit bridge adds a financial-coping stage to the public-system row. SIPP shows that SNAP transitions can sit beside declining resources, stable job counts, and following hardship; Federal Reserve SHED shows that liquid capacity, revolving balances, linked balance growth, student-loan difficulty, and retirement actions are distinct coping layers. This is a cross-source mechanism map, not evidence that a public-system transition caused credit use or that financial pressure produced political action.

The follow-on route-and-buffer synthesis and public-system route-security triangulation record add the WBNS lived-route and charitable-food layers. Across 51 state/DC aggregates, SNAP participation has near-zero simple correlation with application timeliness (0.033) and only 0.211 with recertification timeliness, so it cannot stand in for route quality. Separately, among 182 people reporting a recertification-related interruption, 40% reported too little time after notice, 32% not receiving notice, and 22% difficult paperwork (overlapping responses). These sources place notice, recertification, interruption, cash/credit capacity, supplemental food, and unmet need in one staged public/private safety-net map without pooling state, respondent, person-month, and conditional-credit denominators. The result is stronger evidence for incomplete protection and route substitution, not a same-household causal chain or a political-trust finding.

The SNAP reason-to-food-security record adds a narrower same-person adjacent-month arrow: classified entry and exit reasons lead to distinct following-month low/very-low food-security profiles, with 26.12% after entry and 18.87% after exit in the aggregate classified comparison. It strengthens the route-to-material-condition stage while preserving the missing notice, effort, benefit amount, gap-day, remedy, and recovery fields. Exit is therefore not treated as restored security, and the reason cells are not ranked as program performance.

The care-cost/time/work cross-source finding extends the care/health row by putting MEPS, SIPP, and SHED beside one another without merging their samples. The layers jointly support a bounded social- reproduction pattern: health and care costs can be transferred among system spending, out-of-pocket payment, unpaid time, work capacity, borrowing, and saving. The same-person dated event through household recovery, institutional response, trust, or politics remains an open arrow.

The IMF geopolitical fiscal-shock record adds the April 2026 WEO defense-boom estimates. Across its historical cross-country episodes, a typical defense-spending boom raised outlays by 2.7 percentage points of GDP over about two and a half years, with 67% financed through deficits; the analysis reports a 2.6-point deficit increase and a 7-point public-debt increase within three years, with social spending falling in wartime booms. The macro layer shows that fiscal and social-spending trade-offs can appear between resource allocation and usable capacity, but these cross-country estimates and the IMF's U.S. aggregate projections do not establish a U.S. household burden or realized geopolitical leverage. The required leverage test remains an observed refusal, switch, concession, regulation, or external behavior change.

The defense resource-to-capability finding now aligns that macro stage with SIPRI spending estimates, a bounded USAspending JASSM/LRASM supplier extract, and the Poland-US procurement and co-production sequence. It makes contract, supplier, implementation, and realization stages more explicit while preserving the missing tests for production, delivery, domestic incidence, replaceability, and external response.

The strongest current composite proposition

The long-form reader version is Unequal optionality is the recurring structure behind pressure, adaptation, and power. It carries this proposition through the household, institutional, work, cultural, place, infrastructure, and geopolitical scales and records the counterexamples and tests required before it can become a causal claim.

Across the current evidence, a defensible provisional proposition is:

US social and political change is often organized by unequal optionality: households, workers, customers, public agencies, and states respond to pressure through different combinations of money, time, care, representation, institutional route, and ability to switch or refuse. The same visible outcome—continued consumption, benefit receipt, employment, care, voting, or infrastructure growth—can therefore coexist with unresolved burden or dependence.

This is a synthesis of recurring measurement patterns, not a causal estimate. The current registry contains 1539 machine-readable records, 4445 observations, and 164 source packets across 14 program themes. It does not claim that the records describe separate evidence units rather than the same people or that one mechanism explains all domains. The counterexamples are part of the proposition: financial improvement can coexist with worse health; SNAP exit can coexist with hardship; continued receipt can coexist with utility burden; assistance participation can coexist with very low food security; adults and children can experience different food-security states; care can occur across work and financial paths; a reported response is not a verified remedy; and infrastructure scale is not state leverage.

New government-AI signal: adoption is outpacing operational accountability

The OECD Digital Government Outlook 2026 adds a public-sector technology and governance route distinct from household or firm AI-use evidence. AI is used in at least one government area in 35 of 36 OECD countries (97%), and 32 of 36 (89%) report government AI training programmes. Yet the enabling layer is less complete: only 21 of 36 (58%) provide central AI-procurement support, and only 13 of 36 (36%) offer training for public-service use or policymaking. The pattern is consistent with adoption concentrating first where processes are structured and easier to standardize.

The accountability endpoint is thinner still. All 36 countries report at least one AI guardrail, but only 14 (39%) require pre-deployment risk assessments, 11 (31%) conduct post-deployment audits, and 10 (28%) measure any financial or non-financial impact of government AI use cases. Only 15 (42%) engage service users and 8 (22%) have citizen feedback or complaint mechanisms. These are country-level institutional indicators, not proof that any specific system is unsafe or ineffective; they identify a recurring test for public-service adoption: whether deployment is matched by procurement capacity, enforceable controls, evidence of realized value, and a usable route for affected people to contest or repair outcomes.

The state-administered-programs review adds a public-delivery version of the same pattern. GAO's 20-program sample represents about $1.1 trillion in FY2025 obligations, but funds and responsibility can pass through states, Tribes, local governments, subrecipients, and contractors. Local flexibility may improve fit and reach; the same chain can reduce visibility into risk and correction. Only 5 of the 20 selected programs had documented evidence of identifying and assessing fraud risks for action. This does not establish fraud or service failure. It adds a cross-source test: when a public benefit travels through more layers, ask whether the final recipient, the accountable agency, and the repair route remain visible to one another.

The DHS acquisition review adds a geopolitical version of target movement. Eighteen of 19 baselined programs met their latest goals, while 15 revised those goals and collective projected costs rose $11.4 billion from the initial baselines. Eight programs also lost at least 20% of staff, and department-level acquisition oversight was reorganized. This is not evidence of failed defense capability; it is a reason to keep original promise, revised target, resources, oversight, and fielded use as separate evidence stages.

The older-worker review adds a person-level version of usable capacity. Older adults were a substantial share of participants in six federal workforce programs, yet used training less often and had lower post-exit employment than younger groups in the selected comparisons. This does not establish age discrimination or program failure. It shows why enrollment, service use, exit, employment, job quality, and durable household security must remain separate stages in the cross-source map.

The UI/concentration study adds a firm-power test to the work-and-benefit lane. Extra search time lengthened nonemployment by about a week, but its earnings response was weaker in more concentrated local labor markets. This does not measure current household welfare. It shows why a benefit's practical value depends not only on its duration but also on the worker's available employers, alternatives, and bargaining room.

The Census AI diffusion at firm, function, and task record adds a measurement and control split inside the technology lane. In the 2026 BTOS supplement, 18% of firms reported AI in a business function (32% employment-weighted), while 23% reported workers using it in work tasks (41% employment-weighted). Firm adoption, functional deployment, and worker task use did not always coincide. Most adopting firms reported narrow scope—57% used AI in three or fewer business functions and 65% in three or fewer tasks—and 66% reported augmentation only; AI-related employment decreases appeared in 2% of firms. Broader functional deployment and operational investment were associated with reported employment decreases, while worker-task integration was not significantly linked to headcount reduction after controls. These are cross-sectional firm associations, not causal worker-level displacement, productivity sharing, or control. AI capacity, worker use, and worker power remain separate stages.

The Pew health-information survey adds an information-legitimacy layer. People still rely most on clinicians, but also combine peer experience, websites, social media, and AI; many struggle with conflicting claims. This is not a measure of misinformation or medical harm. It extends the atlas’s recurring split between available capacity and usable trust: an information source can be available, convenient, or familiar without being judged accurate or converted into care.

The influencer study adds a more personal authority mechanism. Large health accounts mix professional credentials, coaching, entrepreneurship, and lived experience; their audience may trust only part of the message while still finding it useful. This does not establish misinformation or harm. It shows that platform reach and relatability can generate practical legitimacy before accuracy, sponsorship, and health effects are visible.

What the latest broad rotation adds

The congestion-pricing and EMS rotation adds a public-service version of the same pattern: a city policy can measurably improve emergency travel time while patient outcomes, household charge exposure, and distributional fairness remain separate questions. System speed is not automatically equal usable benefit.

The Free Association compact implementation/oversight record adds the geopolitical version. The amended Compacts with the Federated States of Micronesia, Marshall Islands, and Palau commit more than $6 billion through 2043 for grants, trust funds, health, education, and infrastructure while providing U.S. military access and security rights. GAO also reports delayed fund disbursement, rising construction costs, labor shortages, most required reports arriving late, and all three countries' single audits late since FY2019; delayed U.S. appointments further constrained committee work. Formal access and funding commitment can therefore coexist with implementation and oversight lag. The source does not establish completed projects, service quality, durable self-sufficiency, local acceptance, migration effects, or U.S. strategic success.

The rural-housing service-coordination rotation adds a social version: a housing unit can become more usable through a local person who helps residents cross paperwork, distance, and service barriers, while the official data system cannot reliably count the people or evaluate the results. Visible housing capacity and usable social support therefore also move on different clocks.

The GAO rural-housing service-coordination record supplies the institutional evidence behind that claim. GAO reports roughly 56,000 federally subsidized affordable-housing properties with more than four million units, of which about 19% of properties and 9% of units were rural in the reviewed inventory. FY2025 appropriations for two HUD coordinator programs totaled $152 million; in 2024, ROSS funded 50 coordinators at 49 rural-headquartered entities and the multifamily program funded about 113 rural grant recipients. Site stakeholders reported help with eviction avoidance and Medicaid applications, but four of five reviewed studies had mixed effects and HUD could not accurately determine how many multifamily properties had coordinators or routinely analyze required performance reports. Funding, coordinator presence, navigation help, eviction prevention, enrollment, health, and durable housing stability are thus distinct stages, not one measured outcome.

The remote-work residential-sorting rotation adds a place-choice version. A quasi-random office-lease exposure design links remote work to more migration, more space and ownership, different school use, and movement away from income-taxing jurisdictions.
