This does not turn moving into wellbeing: the paper does not follow the same household to later security, belonging, displacement, or political action. It shows that removing one constraint—the need to live near work—can make housing supply, money, schools, tax rules, and the ability to move more important.

The Instacart rotation adds a consumer-market version: convenience and platform access can coexist with hard-to-see fees, subscription consent, and refund routes. The FTC announced $60 million in consumer refunds to settle its allegations concerning fee disclosure, paid-membership enrollment, and cancellation/refund access; its later inquiry extends the question to marketwide food-delivery fees. This makes an alleged design → enforcement → announced redress route visible, not a customer-level recovery rate. See the Instacart fees/refunds record.

The FTC AT&T data-throttling refund record adds a service-quality version of that distinction. The FTC reports more than $5.6 million in initial refunds in April 2024 for eligible former unlimited- data customers and an August 2026 Zelle reissue route for people who did not cash a check or accept a PayPal payment. The enforcement account describes post-threshold speeds so slow that ordinary browsing and streaming were difficult or impossible. A refund route and a service-access injury therefore belong to different clocks: the public page does not disclose an eligible or paid-recipient denominator, individual receipt, restored past connectivity, substitute service, current provider choice, switching, or trust.

The DC Solar for All crediting/remedy record adds a public-utility version of the same recovery problem. A DCPSC reconciliation audit could not determine whether subscribers had been properly credited because the billing data needed for that core question were not provided in time. Consumer-side parties proposed $5.70 per subscriber per month during the audit period as an error-rate remedy, and separate customer guidance described front-loaded June/July credits and a planned September bill adjustment. Program enrollment, a customer notice, a proposed remedy, and a planned adjustment are not evidence of final commission adoption, a correctly credited individual bill, actual savings, arrears avoided, energy security, trust, or practical exit. The proposed average can over- or under-compensate individual accounts when the account-level billing record is unresolved.

The DCPSC monthly-credit-receipt record adds an intermediate, project-level billing endpoint. Four listed community-renewable-energy project rows reported every listed subscriber receiving a monthly credit: 309/309, 303/303, 297/297, and 260/260. This is stronger than a program promise but remains a selected four-row project slice: it does not reveal an individual credit amount, Pepco bill line, subscription charge, arrears, billing error, net savings, or continued receipt. It cannot resolve the earlier account-level reconciliation gap or validate the later program-wide savings estimate.

The DC Solar for All reach/savings record adds a program-level endpoint that should remain separate from that audit. DOEE reports nearly 10,000 households served and about $500 average annual bill savings, or roughly $5 million annually across participants; the community- solar subscription is free and credits are intended to appear on Pepco bills. The route nevertheless begins only after enrollment is updated in Pepco's system, credits are anticipated after about 60 days, and continuity depends on income eligibility and an active account. Reported reach and average savings are stronger than a design-only claim, but not evidence of a particular bill line, correct credit timing, net savings after other charges, arrears avoided, continued enrollment, energy security, or household recovery. These program figures and the crediting-audit record are different source units, not a common household outcome series.

The FleetCor/Corpay fee-redress record adds a small-business recourse route with a stronger legal finding but the same recovery gap. A federal district court found FleetCor liable on all counts in 2023 and an appeals court upheld summary judgment in 2026; the FTC then announced a proposed $100 million redress allocation and prospective controls against billing without express informed consent and clear unavoidable-charge information. The fund remains a proposed allocation subject to a final Commission decision, with no published customer denominator, claim/distribution ledger, receipt, restored liquidity, alternative fuel-card access, switching, or business-survival outcome. A legally confirmed fee practice and a large nominal redress pool are therefore not an account-level recovery measure.

The randomized meal-delivery customer-service study adds a different middle stage. AI suggestions reduced response time and improved automated sentiment in 256,934 chats, but were least effective for repeat complaints where the underlying issue was systemic; customers handed from an incomprehensible chatbot to an AI-assisted human also had lower sentiment. Faster response and warmer language can therefore improve an interaction without correcting the delivery, billing, account, or product problem that generated it.

Evidence unit What is visible What remains open
FTC Instacart case and fee inquiry Alleged price/consent/cancellation practices, announced $60M redress, and marketwide rulemaking question Exposure prevalence, individual fee, refund receipt/adequacy, grocery affordability, continued use, switching, and trust
Randomized meal-delivery customer-service experiment Response time, automated sentiment, intent-specific AI performance, and chatbot-to-human handoff contrast Actual refund/correction, repeat-contact resolution, retention, switching, and household welfare

These sources do not describe the same firm, customers, or event. Their shared consumer subtheme is narrower: response quality is not remedy quality. See the AI customer-service/recourse record.

The SNAP sugary-drink rotation adds a direct policy-to-consumption and policy-to-meaning contrast: excluded purchases fell, but recipients' perceived stigma rose. A policy can therefore be behaviorally effective while imposing a social cost that a health or fiscal model does not fully count.

The Urban WBNS food-insecurity persistence record adds a population hardship surface. Its weighted working-age series fell from 24.0% in 2019 to 19.9% in 2021, then rose to 27.7% in 2025; the brief's values are unadjusted for sample-composition differences and its 2025 methodology update means this is not a seamless causal time series. In the 2025 working-age cross-section, food insecurity was 32.0% among adults in households with children, 51.0% below 200% of the poverty line, and 52.1% among adults with disabilities. The cross-sectional pattern identifies unequal hardship, not the cause of any annual change, SNAP receipt, food price, charitable-food use, dietary adequacy, health, or later political judgment.

The charitable-food access record adds an informal-support route that public-program measures can miss. In 2025, 16.1% of adults reported household receipt of free groceries or meals, rising to 39.5% among food-insecure adults; 8.0% of adults and 28.8% of food-insecure adults reported needing or wanting charitable food but not receiving it. Among recipients, 51.6% reported at least one access difficulty. Among people with unmet need, closed hours (45.5%), not knowing where to go (42.8%), discomfort getting help (39.9%), unavailable needed variety (37.6%), and transportation (35.2%) were all reported, with overlapping answers. Charitable food is thus a real but incomplete buffer governed by time, information, comfort, transport, variety, safety, and treatment—not a binary service-exists measure. The cross-sectional survey does not establish food quantity or adequacy, provider capacity, the causal effect of stigma, SNAP loss, later trust, or political action, and it cannot show that charitable food substitutes for public aid.

The California fast-food wage/small-chain record adds a firm-side version of uneven adjustment: aggregate employment can look modestly changed while small-chain entry slows and exit rises. The incidence of a policy is therefore not visible in one statewide average; it can move through firm survival, worker opportunity, prices, and local choice on different clocks.

The Healthy Diné Nation food-price and health record supplies a place-specific counterexample to the price-to-health route. The policy exempted healthy foods and beverages from sales tax while raising tax on unhealthy foods and beverages, a reported 7--8% price wedge, but did not produce a detectable improvement in the studied maternal and newborn diet- and weight-related outcomes. The estimates could rule out gestational- diabetes improvements as large as those reported for U.S. city sugary-drink taxes. That null does not mean no one changed purchases; it points to the missing middle of retailer implementation, cross-border shopping, cultural fit, and exposure. It is not a universal test of fiscal nutrition policy or a measure of store pass-through, purchases, household budgets, or trust.

The 989 rotation adds a crisis-care version: implementation improved the front-door operation, but population mortality and broader mental-health outcomes did not move detectably in the short run. The missing middle is the care, housing, safety, and social-support system after the call.

The peer-loss rotation adds a social-network version of the same gap: a shared event can produce more formal care for some young people and more offending for others. Exposure, diagnosis, help-seeking, and recovery are therefore distinct paths shaped by prior history and reachable support.

The comparative elite-network rotation adds a political-access version: in historical Buenos Aires, Jockey Club membership was associated with a higher chance of legislative office, while the advantage weakened after a democratizing reform. Social connection can therefore become political access when institutions reward personal networks, but the finding is not a present- day U.S. estimate and does not show representative governance.

The organized-interests rotation adds a U.S. policy-responsiveness version. A state-level NBER study links campaign contributions, party trifectas, a Gun Law Index, and estimated constituent sentiment from 2000 through 2024. Contribution and policy associations differ by party control, while the study's instrumental- variable estimates do not find constituent sentiment itself causally predicts policy change. Public preference, organized political capacity, party control, enacted policy, implementation, safety, and legitimacy are therefore separate stages; the study does not show that money always defeats public opinion or that any individual constituent was represented or ignored.

The whistleblower-disclosure rotation adds an accountability-and-risk version. GAO finds that selected agencies use different combinations of confidentiality, retaliation investigation or relief, and awards, while workers may face fear, identity exposure, or restrictive employment agreements and agencies may face high report volume. Information, voice, protection, investigation, correction, and trust therefore move on separate clocks; the presence of a reporting route does not establish reporter safety, adequate remedy, or durable institutional learning.

The Public Buildings Service rotation adds a reorganization-and-capacity version. GAO reports that a 45% workforce reduction occurred without prior strategic workforce planning, while performance measures and two-way feedback were missing and selected tenant agencies reported service delays. Centralized design, staffing, communication, service delivery, measurement, correction, and customer confidence are therefore separate stages; later agency plans do not yet show operational recovery.

The DOE nuclear-cleanup rotation adds an early-framing and contestability version. GAO found that most of 21 reviewed large-project mission statements named a particular solution before the full option set was tested, and selected projects did not pursue cheaper technically sound alternatives after legal, regulatory, or contractor-linked constraints entered the process. Need, option generation, independent review, approval, construction, cost, safety, and public consequence are therefore distinct stages; formal review does not prove that realistic alternatives remained open.

The international-commitment rotation adds a geopolitical visibility version. GAO found that 90 of 311 agreements and qualifying instruments reported to Congress were late, while estimated public publication was about 86% overall but about 53% within the 120-day deadline. Separate pages, identifiers, and missing searchability further increased the work of finding and matching the records. Formal commitment, congressional visibility, public usability, partner understanding, implementation, and legitimacy are therefore separate stages; delayed reporting is not by itself proof of concealment or invalidity.

The federal performance-review rotation adds a government-learning version. GAO found that none of four selected agencies fully addressed new strategic- review requirements in 2025, while OMB guidance covered 10 of 15 assessed requirements. Formal goals, performance sites, and review rules therefore do not yet demonstrate completed review, stakeholder learning, changed decisions, cross-agency coordination, or improved public results.

The gig-work rotation adds a practical-exit version: access to one competing platform made Uber drivers more responsive to conditions at the first platform and lowered the study's implied monopsony markdown. A second option can create worker leverage, but formal access is not the same as usable switching, better net pay, or household security.

The dementia-coverage rotation adds a care-transition version: older adults with probable dementia were more likely to have Medicare without supplemental coverage before onset, while Medicaid eligibility rose without higher take-up. Eligibility, enrollment, complete coverage, and actual care therefore remain separate stages.

The neighborhood-opportunity rotation adds a place-market version: childhood neighborhoods can shape later outcomes, while credit limits, search friction, social spillovers, and behavioral barriers can prevent families from reaching opportunity. A voucher or mobility service is therefore an offer that still has to become a workable move.

The market-participation rotation adds a financial-culture version: investors who leave markets are more pessimistic and see greater crash risk, and that belief-driven sorting can concentrate risk among the investors who remain. Participation, exit, realized wealth, and household security are still different outcomes.

The consumer-credit rotation adds an information-and-bargaining version: a comparison tool changed beliefs, negotiation, and loan rates, but also made people more likely to borrow. Consumer power and consumer exposure can rise together; a lower interest rate is not automatically a lower total burden.

The historical competition-and-consumer-discrimination record adds a different consumer-power mechanism. Using historical local-market data from the decades before the Civil Rights Act, the study finds that increases in nondiscriminatory businesses were concentrated in the least competitive markets. Across more than 25,000 establishment prices, nondiscriminatory firms charged more than discriminatory firms in the same local market, creating a documented price cost for Black consumers seeking non-discriminatory service. This does not turn a higher price into a welfare comparison or imply that discriminatory service was equivalent; it shows why the availability of a formally open option, its price, service quality, practical exit, and equal treatment must remain separate. The historical design does not establish present-day discrimination, online-market behavior, or a universal competition-to-fairness relationship.

The NNSA partnership-capacity rotation adds a geopolitical version: paid work for agencies and partners can retain staff, maintain specialized facilities, and support missions, while the same sites face limited capacity and growing core nuclear-security workloads. Shared capability and scarce capacity can therefore rise together.

The weapons technology-maturity and delivery record adds a delivery-stage version. In GAO's 104-program assessment, major programs averaged more than 12 years to deliver a capability. The 23 most expensive Middle Tier programs planned at least $49 billion; 18 of 40 entered that rapid pathway with immature technologies, and technologies in seven of eight reviewed programs that ended without a fieldable capability remained immature and needed additional development. Program priority and budget therefore do not yet equal fielded capability, reliable use, sustainment, operational effectiveness, or deterrence; schedule and maturity data also cannot assign a delay to a particular contractor, service, or reform.

The comparative public-official integrity-norms and enforcement record adds an institutional-culture version. In Singapore's universe-level housing transactions, civil servants disproportionately bought homes near planned but not-yet-announced MRT stations, especially one to two years before announcement; the pattern was concentrated among mid-level officials, rail-planning-connected agencies, and relatives. Stronger formal enforcement substantially reduced both direct and indirect misconduct, alongside survey/model evidence consistent with integrity norms that persist but remain fragile. Social trust and enforcement may reinforce one another in this setting rather than substitute for each other. This is not a U.S. estimate, a universal corruption mechanism, or direct evidence of citizen legitimacy, service quality, reporting, or political action.

The federal shared-services rotation adds an institutional-capacity version: a centralized marketplace can offer efficiency while agencies still face legal, technical, integration, leadership, and measurement problems. Shared infrastructure and usable performance therefore move on different clocks.

The BLS–Census establishment-frame rotation adds a measurement version of the same problem. Two official frames can show sharply different numbers of workplaces and different levels of firm complexity because they use different administrative sources and parent-firm rules. The discrepancy is concentrated in part in home-care and disability services and also changes policy-model inputs about concentration and establishment size. Before treating a business count as economic power or decline, the atlas needs to know which workers, worksites, services, and households the frame actually represents.

The microenterprise-credit rotation adds a firm-consumer version: in a Chilean trial, large loans increased treated-firm profits and estimated customer surplus, with little evidence of simply stealing sales from other firms. Business growth can therefore create customer benefit, but estimated surplus is still not the same as household cash or durable security.

The American Indian heterogeneity record adds a measurement-and-culture version: U.S. economic, educational, and health outcomes differ by community, geography, resource endowments, historical policy, and self-governance, while tribal and racial identification, changing definitions, and data limits can hide those differences. The historical synthesis identifies long-lasting harm associated with forced relocation, boarding schools, and assimilation policy, alongside reported improvement in some self-governing economic-development contexts. It is an essay and measurement critique—not a pooled causal estimate, ranking of tribes, or proof of any current policy's effect. A national average can therefore conceal both ongoing harm and local improvement.

The nursing-home inspection-timing and care-quality record adds an oversight-and-care version. Seventy-four percent of inspections occurred 40--60 weeks after the previous one, and the reported composite care-effort measure was highest around inspection, declined afterward, and rose again as the next one approached. A one-standard-deviation increase in that measure was associated with a 0.2-percentage-point (5.4%) lower mortality rate. The separate dynamic model estimates that making timing unpredictable would save about 92 additional lives annually versus the current regime, while reducing the information available to regulators; that is a model comparison, not observed reform impact. A formal check can improve performance and still invite organizations to time their effort around it, without measuring complete care quality, resident wellbeing, or family experience.

The work-and-technology rotation adds a useful distinction between exposure and usable room to adapt. An NBER study finds that many workers in highly AI-exposed occupations also sit in occupations with above-median adaptive capacity, while a smaller group—especially in clerical and administrative roles—faces both high exposure and low expected capacity. The working-paper and published versions use different occupation coverage and counts, so they are kept as separate observations. The stable cross-source insight is that a visible pressure does not determine the outcome by itself: the practical exit route, including skills, mobility, time, money, local demand, and employer support, can divide resilience from vulnerability. The study does not observe actual displacement, retraining success, wages, or household security.

The follow-on retraining rotation adds an observed route between that capacity and an earnings result. In a U.S. workforce-program sample, estimated quarterly earnings returns for trainees starting in highly AI-exposed work rose from about $1,000 before 2020 to about $3,000 in 2022–2024 relative to matched job-search-only users. The reported route was mainly movement into less AI-exposed occupations, with a smaller role for AI-complementary training. This is evidence of a possible adaptation route, not proof that training was equally reachable, completed, voluntary, durable, or good for household security.

The latest cultural-place rotation adds BEA's outdoor-recreation account. It shows a $696.7 billion national footprint and sharply different state shares, while leaving resident access, affordability, local ownership, displacement, conservation, and belonging unmeasured. A place can therefore gain a large recreation economy without the account proving broad cultural access or shared benefit.

The household-economy rotation adds BEA's expanded household-production account. Unpaid household production represented about 16% of total output and 30% of consumption in 2024, with both shares gradually declining over roughly 20 years. This makes the market/nonmarket boundary visible without proving who performed the work, who had a choice, or whether household security improved. See the BEA household-production account record.

The firm-finance rotation adds the Federal Reserve small-business credit route. Application, lender choice, risk category, and approval are observable before funding use, repayment, survival, jobs, or local benefit. This is a distinct firm-side version of unequal practical agency: formal lender availability is not the same as a usable amount on workable terms.

The new local economic participation synthesis consolidates the firm, disaster, investment, and place-economy routes. It provides a stopping rule: another aggregate money or investment total adds little unless it identifies local receipt, terms, use, distribution, durability, or exit.

The geopolitical coordination rotation adds a process stage between agreement and capability. GAO's DOD review shows a substantial international-arrangement portfolio alongside decline, review delays, and communication gaps. The safe cross-source conclusion is that formal cooperation and usable joint capability run on different clocks; partner use, deterrence, and legitimacy remain open.

The latest rotation strengthens the same proposition across several different scales rather than opening a new single-topic lane. The health-cost synthesis shows that care pressure can travel through delayed care, borrowing, reduced savings, work adaptation, credit exposure, and a short-lived civic response; the sequence is informative but still combines compatible designs rather than one person's complete bill-to-recovery history. The remedy rotation separates reported receipt, repeat-remedy eligibility, institutional order completion, and borrower or worker recovery. The firm/infrastructure rotation adds a US GaN manufacturing route where a domestic production path and scheduled samples precede qualification, scaled output, upstream material independence, and strategic leverage. The worker and consumer routes therefore do not show one universal failure of institutions: some stages are visibly delivered, but the later question is whether delivery is adequate, durable, usable, and trusted.

This is the broader cultural reading: people and institutions do not respond to pressure through one ladder from hardship to backlash. They conserve, search, borrow, care, work, complain, accept, refuse, switch, stay, organize, or withdraw according to the options available to them. The atlas is now strongest at mapping these conversion choices and the power that shapes them; it remains weakest at observing the same unit after the formal response.

The latest local-capacity rotation adds a bounded BDS county-sector screen and two overlays. County business turnover diverges by retail, transportation, health/social assistance, and accommodation/food rather than forming one resident-facing capacity signal; the same-year BDS–PLACES comparison produces near-identical routine-checkup and transportation-insecurity medians across negative and nonnegative health-sector-flow counties; and the BDS–HRSA overlay shows that employer flow and shortage designation do not identify provider adequacy. The three canonical records preserve these as observed ecological stages with explicit cross-vintage and resident-outcome boundaries.

The latest platform-remedy comparison adds the Mansoor same-worker record: substitute earnings and a formal order are visible in one adjudicated case, while payment receipt, actual access, durability, and later choice remain open. This strengthens the alternative-to-response bridge without converting a comparative case into a US prevalence or recovery estimate.

The Waheed interim-payment record adds a related legal-implementation stage: a consent-stay payment obligation is visible even though receipt, actual platform access, final quantum, appeal outcome, and later work remain unobserved. Together, the comparative cases separate alternative work, remedy order, conditional payment, payment receipt, and practical recovery rather than collapsing them into one outcome.

The Al Hussein record adds a counterpattern in the same comparative lane: legal reactivation and deemed work can be ordered while lost-pay quantification, payment, actual access, and later work remain open. This keeps procedural remedy, legal fiction, payment, and lived recovery as separate clocks.

The Malaysia Act 872 institutional-response record extends the comparison from adjudicated worker cases to governance design: Grab's public page reports earnings, appeal/dispute, and social-protection commitments, while the official Ministry and Tribunal route provides statutory and procedural capacity without a public GrabCar case identifier, award, payment, or enforcement outcome. The institutional route is therefore evidence of available governance architecture, not evidence of worker uptake, remedy, trust, or durable control.

The CPSC consumer-safety surveillance/recall record adds the system-level stages behind those individual recall keys. In FY2024, CPSC reports 333 negotiated and implemented voluntary recalls covering about 41 million units, 2,969 regulatory-violation notices, more than 58,000 products removed from e-commerce platforms, and more than 65,000 import examinations. Its revised recall response measure reports a 51% average correction/response rate in FY2024 and 44.55% in FY2025, but the method change, product mix, and firm reporting prevent interpreting that as a household action trend. Recall counts, examined imports, takedown requests, firm-reported correction, and emergency-department injury surveillance have different units and clocks; none alone proves exposure, notice, remedy receipt, avoided injury, or restored safety for a consumer.

The VRURC recall-implementation record adds a first recall-key implementation bridge. A July 2023 notice covered approximately 190,000 portable chargers, reported one fire and four smoke- inhalation hospital transports, and offered a free replacement route. An August 2026 MPR row reports 64,963 consumer-level corrections and 29%, but its 256,845-product denominator differs from the notice scale; the mismatch may reflect different scope, version, or denominator definitions. The joined key therefore shows a dated hazard, remedy offer, and reported correction stage, not unique purchaser exposure, notice receipt, replacement receipt, safe restoration, residual cost, trust, or exit. The Honda Talon recall record adds a second recall-key implementation bridge: a dated safety notice and free repair route are visible, followed by an MPR row reporting 790 consumer-level corrections and 44%, but the API's approximately 34,000-unit scale does not match the MPR's 2,047-product row. This strengthens the correction-stage map without treating firm-reported progress as notice receipt, completed repair, or safe household restoration. The Sauna360 repeat-remedy ledger adds a durability-stage counterexample: a 2025 repair route is followed by a 2026 CPSC expansion stating that the previous repair was ineffective and requiring another repair. This shows that a remedy can fail after implementation, while still leaving owner notice, repair completion, safe use, downtime, trust, and exit unobserved. The cross-key MPR heterogeneity record extends the two named recall bridges to a 17-row purposive snapshot: reported consumer-level correction spans 0%–44% and total correction 0%–50%, with one blank consumer-level row. The range maps implementation heterogeneity, not consumer recovery, because recall duration, mix, and denominators differ.

The IER individual-remedy record adds a cross-domain paid-remedy comparator: four official summaries report individual back-pay or front/back-pay payments and one reports a substantial offer, with employer training or policy changes. This is stronger than a reserved fund or conditional obligation, but the public summaries still do not show independent receipt, restored employment, durable compliance, household recovery, trust, or exit.

The Walmart Spark driver-remedy record adds a platform-worker version. A court-entered $100 million judgment directs $79 million to drivers, $10 million to FTC-administered driver distribution, and $11 million in civil penalties to participating states; it also requires ten years of earnings verification. Walmart reports some pre-announcement payments and ongoing identification/payment processing, but does not publish the eligible-driver denominator, payment receipt ledger, unresolved-payment count, corrected earnings record, continued platform work, alternative work, schedule control, switching, or exit. Correcting a past pay shortfall is therefore not the same thing as restoring practical control over platform work.

The Uber occupational-licensing consumer-outcome record adds an upstream rule-to-service route. Using trip-level data, proximity-based dispatch comparisons around New York City/New Jersey, and Houston deregulation, the NBER study finds that licensing changed the driver pool without consistent improvement in its measured rider ratings and telematics-based driving outcomes; after Houston deregulation, entrants were indistinguishable from previously licensed drivers on those outcomes despite age and experience differences. A licensing rule can therefore alter access to platform work without settling average measured service quality. The study does not measure fares, wait times, cancellations, driver income, disability access, rare severe safety incidents, or trust, and its two-city evidence is not a national rule evaluation.

The Kyei merits-dismissal record adds a negative remedy counterexample to the platform lane: process deficiencies were identified, but a valid safety reason was accepted and the unfair- deactivation claim was dismissed. No restoration, payment, later access, or exit is observed. This prevents procedural defect from being treated as either automatic worker protection or automatic proof of platform unfairness.

The GrabCar first-hearing record adds the exercised-route stage to that comparison: a reported first hearing and continuation for evidence/witness examination are visible, while the primary case identifier, award, payment, access correction, and enforcement remain unobserved. This is institutional use, not proof of effective review or worker recovery.

The Pew 2026 AI concern and expected-jobs layer adds a current meaning-and-politics endpoint to the AI/work route. In the June 2026 survey, 52% of adults were more concerned than excited about AI's increased use in daily life, up from 37% in 2021; Democrats were at 56% versus 49% of Republicans, and 75% versus 68% expected fewer US jobs over the next 20 years. These are public expectations, not realized displacement or a partisan causal effect. They make the missing bridge sharper: link actual AI implementation and control to worker experience, attribution, policy demand, and later action.

The Pew AI daily-life/control record adds the adoption-versus-governance surface. In February 2026, 49% of U.S. adults reported ever using a chatbot and 24% reported daily use; 42% used one for information, while 38% of employed adults reported work-task use. Yet 63% said AI was advancing too quickly, 70% expected personal information to become less secure, and 67% had little or no confidence in effective government AI regulation. Reported use, task-specific usefulness, personal control, privacy expectation, and public-governance confidence can therefore diverge rather than move in a single pro- or anti-AI direction. These are self-reported survey surfaces, not telemetry, actual privacy loss, dependence, productivity, political behavior, or evidence that one attitude causes another.

The NYC algorithmic-work measurement record adds a municipal visibility stage. Local Law 25 mandates a city study of algorithmic tools and automated employment decision tools, including hiring, regular employee work functions, and employee feedback, followed by a report and recommendations. As of the source recheck, implementation was still in planning and no completed study or public report was located. Measurement can make a worker-control problem administratively legible before it identifies a tool, exposed-worker denominator, decision, notice, appeal, correction, compensation, workload/pay change, or exit outcome. A study requirement is not itself evidence of changed employment conditions or worker protection.

The workplace AI partisan-composition record adds a composition-to-meaning boundary. Democrats reported frequent workplace AI use somewhat more often than Republicans in Q1 2026, but the gap became statistically insignificant after education controls and reversed with occupation and industry controls. Perceived displacement risk instead showed a new 4.2-point partisan gap. Where people work and what skills they hold can therefore explain reported use while political interpretation begins to diverge; neither endpoint establishes ideology, actual job loss, control, pay, or political action.

The Pew 2026 press-government legitimacy layer adds a complementary information-institution route. Seventy-one percent of adults described the administration-news relationship as bad, while 55% said news organizations have too much political power; that latter measure was 69% among Republicans and 43% among Democrats. At the same time, 68% said it was acceptable for journalists to criticize politicians and 56% said it was acceptable for politicians to criticize journalists. The pattern is not a single trust score: shared conflict perception coexists with partisan power attribution and asymmetric norms of criticism. Exposure, accuracy, censorship, subscription switching, and political action remain open.

The Pew press-government/media-legitimacy record keeps those three surveys surfaces separate: 71% called the relationship bad, 55% said news organizations have too much political power (69% of Republicans versus 43% of Democrats), 68% found journalist criticism of politicians acceptable, and 56% found politician criticism of journalists acceptable. The measures are perceptions and norms, not evidence of censorship, accuracy, ownership concentration, audience exposure, institutional behavior, or causal media effects.

The Gallup 2026 institutional-confidence divergence layer adds a broader legitimacy benchmark. Average confidence across 14 core institutions is 27%, but large technology companies sit at 20% while small business is at 67%; Republicans report 13 points more average confidence than Democrats, with a 70-point presidency gap. The important result is divergence, not a single trust collapse: confidence, use, dependence, institution-specific performance, switching, and political action are separate surfaces.

The Pew 2026 public-life engagement groups layer adds a structured action surface. Mobilizers report 58% extremely or very interested in politics versus 9% among Outsiders, yet federal-government trust is low across all four groups (17% to 22%). National-news trust ranges from 45% among Outsiders to 64% among Connectors, while 72% to 82% say news tends to favor one side. The comparison shows that political interest, civic participation, source trust, government trust, and fairness judgments form different currencies; action is not a single ladder from trust to turnout.

The federal-building accessibility record adds a rights-to-contestation example. GAO reports 41 Architectural Barriers Act complaints about GSA buildings from October 2022 through June 2026, with 25 closed and 16 still in process, while interviewed stakeholders generally said the public was unaware of the route. Complaint processing is therefore a visible institutional stage, not proof that barriers were corrected or that people could use the buildings afterward.

The FDA third-party device-review record adds a delegated-regulation stage. Third parties supplied 617 510(k) reviews from fiscal years 2018–2025, but FDA lacked target audit time frames and some recent deficiency audits took more than six months to close. Delegated review is therefore visible capacity, not proof of timely correction, device safety, patient access, or public trust.

The Pew working-class identity record adds status meaning to the material-to-political route. Sixty percent of adults said “working class” described them well, up from 54% in 2024; the rate was 50% among both upper-income adults and college graduates, 67% among Republicans or Republican leaners, and 55% among Democrats or Democratic leaners. Blue-collar workers were more likely than other workers to adopt the label (77% versus 61%), but the identity still spans resources and occupations rather than mapping cleanly onto either. It is a repeated-cross-sectional cultural and political self-description, not proof of hardship, class position, class consciousness, voting, or a causal change in identity.

The NBER multidimensional-signaling model adds a theory mechanism to this meaning layer. If voters cannot observe the whole candidate and cultural signals are easier to read than economic ones, candidates may emphasize culture even when the economy matters more to voters. This helps explain how cultural themes can become prominent without proving that voters stopped caring about material conditions. Because the source is a formal model, it does not estimate current U.S. prevalence, persuasion, vote choice, or policy change.

The U.S. protest-effects finding tests the next stage with observed collective action. The study finds that most protest waves produced strong online attention but limited movement in broader measured outcomes, while the post-George-Floyd protests were a notable exception for Democratic support and racial legislative activity. This keeps being seen, changing minds, changing votes, changing official behavior, and implementing policy as separate stages. It is a cross-wave result, not proof that protest lacks local effects or that violence is required for influence.

The trust-and-democracy finding adds a crisis-conditioned institutional layer. Across country, subnational, and individual analyses, lower generalized trust is associated with greater regular political turnover after recessions, including analogous U.S.-county patterns. This suggests that the same economic shock can carry different political consequences in different trust environments, but it remains a cross-level relationship rather than a single U.S. household-to-election causal chain.

The aggregate-shocks review adds a life-course cultural mechanism. The reviewed literature links major economic and non-economic shocks to later preferences, risk attitudes, and institutional trust, with stronger and more persistent effects often reported when exposure occurs during young adulthood. The review keeps shock type, place, cohort, method, and persistence separate; it does not turn a shared crisis into a universal political or cultural outcome.

The zero-sum-thinking finding adds a group-competition interpretation layer. A 20,400-person U.S. survey associates stronger zero-sum beliefs with several policy preferences, including both redistribution and restrictive immigration, and relates the mindset to individual and ancestral experience. This shows that perceived competition can organize political judgment without proving that scarcity is imaginary, that history transmits through one route, or that stated preferences become votes.

The cultural-distance finding adds a multi-surface measurement check. Political-ideology and some income attitude differences widened, racial groups diverged in consumer behavior while converging somewhat on attitudes, and many other dimensions stayed stable. This means “polarization” cannot stand in for every cultural change: group distinguishability, social conflict, contact, trust, and political action are separate outcomes.

The Gallup corruption-perception finding adds a legitimacy signal that cuts across party lines. Gallup reports that 89% of U.S. adults see government corruption as widespread, including 91% of Democrats, 90% of independents, and 83% of Republicans; the reported concern is lower for business at 71%. Shared alarm is therefore not the same as shared cause, target, remedy, or action. The measure records a public judgment, not verified corruption or a later vote, protest, organizing effort, service exit, or trust change.

The Gallup workforce-diversity finding adds a firm-side counterpoint. Public belief that diverse workforces improve profitability and innovation rose across parties, while views of DEI priority and business performance remained divided. This separates perceived instrumental value from legitimacy and implementation: an audience can believe a practice helps firms without agreeing that firms are doing it well or that a particular program is fair. Actual worker treatment, firm performance, and worker voice remain open.

The Census CPS ASEC nonresponse finding adds a measurement layer beneath the material-pressure map. Since 2020, survey-only income has generally run 2%–4% above linked-record benchmarks and survey-only poverty slightly below them, even though many year-to-year directions remain usable. This means the atlas must treat who is visible in a data source as part of the social pattern: an estimate can be technically official and still miss people unevenly.

The Gallup courage finding adds a cultural-risk stage between values and action. Many respondents say courage is weaker, place high value on leader courage, and worry about the personal cost of taking a principled stand. This does not show less actual action; it shows why silence, delay, private action, and public action should not be collapsed into one measure of civic engagement.

The Gallup courage/social-risk record makes the three reported surfaces explicit: in its May 2026 national survey of more than 3,000 adults, 67% said courage in American society was weaker than 20 years earlier, 79% called courage from elected leaders very important to the country's future, and 44% reported concern about the personal costs of taking a principled stand. Perceived decline, normative demand, and anticipated risk need not move together, and none measures observed speaking up, protest, workplace voice, retaliation, or a historical behavioral decline. The 20-year comparison is a current judgment, not a repeated-person trend.

The Senate peer-proximity record adds an institutional social-contact mechanism. An NBER working paper using randomized Senate seating reports an 11.9-point voting shift associated with close peer exposure, concentrated within roughly 19.6 feet, and a larger cross-aisle effect. Physical access can therefore alter institutional behavior without any formal rule changing. The study cannot tell us whether the route was persuasion, information, timing, or coalition access, and it does not establish ordinary-voter persuasion, durable trust, or broad democratic legitimacy.

The human-AI political-dialogue record adds a randomized digital-influence stage. In preregistered experiments linked to the 2024 U.S. presidential election and a Massachusetts ballot measure, personalized conversations with a candidate-advocating AI changed stated candidate or policy preferences; related experiments in Canada and Poland reported candidate-preference effects as well. These are experimental preference endpoints, not verified votes, turnout, durable belief change, scalable campaign effects, or democratic harm. The article also reports that not all presented facts were accurate, so influence and informational reliability must remain separate measures.

The women's work and Temperance mobilization record adds a historical household-pressure-to-politics pathway. A linked-record working paper reports higher labor-force participation among wives and daughters of disabled Union veterans, and more town-level Temperance Crusade activity where women's labor participation and disabled-veteran exposure were higher; newspapers and proximity to other protest towns amplified the pattern. Household responsibility can therefore become political capacity through work, information, and networks. The historical town result is not individual persuasion, present-day gender evidence, movement success, or durable political power.

The comparative women's-employment preference experiment adds a separate cultural-updating mechanism. In rural Bangladesh, a randomized six-week job assignment to a wife improved her own reported wellbeing but not her husband's; a year later, both partners in households with that prior female work experience were more likely to prefer that the woman take a job and voiced fewer concerns about it. Direct experience can therefore update a household's expressed work preference without establishing that preference was the original constraint or that it becomes durable employment. This is comparative evidence, not a U.S. estimate: it does not transfer the effect across labor markets, childcare, safety, income, bargaining, or institutional settings.

The Pew 2026 Latino American-dream and mobility layer adds a second status-meaning reversal. Among Latino adults, 57% say their standard of living is better than their parents' and 53% expect their children to be better off, yet 18% say the American dream is out of reach and 27% say it does not exist. Immigrant Latinos report stronger retrospective and prospective mobility than US-born Latinos, while US-born Latinos are more likely to say the dream has become harder to achieve. This is a cultural and intergenerational meaning pattern, not an observed income-mobility, migration-causality, voting, or consumer-behavior result.

The BLS 2026 Q2 productivity and labor-share boundary adds a current macro-to-worker counterexample: reported productivity rose 1.4% annualized while real hourly compensation fell 3.3% in the quarter, and labor share was reported at 52.8%, the lowest in the series beginning in 1947. These are aggregate production and compensation surfaces, not worker-level control, household security, or causal firm behavior. The direct BLS page blocked local automated retrieval, so this remains a provenance-bounded memo rather than a canonical machine record until a reproducible small extract is available.

The Pew 2026 Muslim-American discrimination, capacity, and visibility layer adds a long-run inclusion and legitimacy route. Muslim population and mosque capacity have grown and political representation is more visible, while 42% of US adults report a negative impact judgment, 59% of Muslim adults report a lot of discrimination, and the partisan gap on whether Islam encourages violence is 76% among Republicans versus 29% among Democrats. Presence, institutional capacity, treatment, public judgment, and representation are separate currencies; none alone establishes safety, equal influence, or causal political behavior.

The firearm-safety means record adds a cultural-political version of contested safety. A survey of more than 5,400 U.S. respondents finds that owners and non-owners can share a protection goal while reporting different safety perceptions and preferring different tools. Randomized information about private costs and non-lethal alternatives shifted safe-storage and alternative-tool preferences more than current owners' willingness to give up lethal firearms. Shared safety language is therefore not shared risk interpretation or a common policy route; the study does not observe completed behavior, injury reduction, crime, or durable public safety.

The BLS 2025 major-work-stoppage and collective-action boundary adds an observed conflict event to the work/control lane. Thirty major stoppages began in 2025 and involved 306,800 workers, with 98% of involved workers in service-providing industries and 232,800 in state or local government stoppages. The comparison also shows why event count is not power: 2023 involved 458,900 workers across 33 stoppages, versus 306,800 across 30 in 2025. Stoppage, settlement, service incidence, worker security, and political meaning remain separate stages.

The Pew press-freedom limits record adds a conditional-legitimacy surface to the media lane. Seventy-three percent say press freedom is highly important to society, but 53% prioritize preventing inaccurate reporting even if freedom is limited. Perceived complete freedom falls from 33% in 2024-25 to 28% in 2026, while the partisan pattern reverses: 41% of Republicans versus 18% of Democrats see the press as completely free, while high concern is 29% versus 64%. These are public norms and perceptions, not censorship, accuracy, platform-control, or media-effect measures.

The BLS 2025 foreign-born work, earnings, and labor-room boundary adds a labor-market migration surface: foreign-born workers were 19.1% of the civilian labor force, with 4.2% unemployment versus 4.3% among native-born workers, but median weekly earnings of $1,059 versus $1,236 for full-time wage and salary workers. Occupational, regional, gender, and care differences are visible, but the release does not identify causal migration effects, worker displacement, household welfare, or public-service demand. BLS's shutdown-year comparability warning remains explicit.

The BLS 2026 candy-price, supply-chain, and consumer-adaptation layer adds a bounded consumer route from global inputs to cultural purchase. From December 2019 to November 2024, BLS reports confectionery-material PPI up 87.6%, end-product PPI up 13.9%, candy-and-chewing-gum CPI up 32.0%, and import prices for sugar/confectionery manufacturing up 73.3%; downsizing added a measured 2.1% price effect. The result is a price/quantity/ritual-adaptation case, not a general household-welfare or food-security estimate.

The Pew 2026 national mood and future-expectations layer adds a temporal meaning surface. Current dissatisfaction (69%) and the view that the country's best years are behind it (59%) coexist with personal hope (68%), and 66% expect greater political division by 2050. Republicans and Democrats are close on that long-run division expectation (66% versus 65%) even while present-direction judgments are strongly president-linked. This separates national inheritance, personal affect, institutional expectation, and partisan alignment; it is not a forecast or a behavioral causal estimate.

The Pew 2026 political typology, values, and coalition layer adds a value-based political segmentation surface. Nine groups built from 30 questions reveal a large mixed center, a financially stressed and politically ignored left group, a low-attention tuned-out middle, and sharp cultural divides within each partisan direction. The typology also links domestic identity to geopolitical posture: 71% say US sole-superpower status is at least somewhat important while 62% say US policy should account for allies even when that requires compromise. These are coalition and value configurations, not fixed identities or causal vote estimates.

The Pew political-typology/values/coalitions record makes the composition and cross-pressure visible. Its 10,357-adult, 30-question typology assigns 21% of adults to two highly ideological right-anchor groups, 17% to two highly ideological left-anchor groups, 23% to an unconventional right, 18% to an order-and-opportunity left, and 9% to a tuned-out middle. Even within right-leaning groups, for example, the share saying abortion should be illegal in most or all cases ranges from 83% among Faith and Flag Conservatives to 43% among the Unconventional Right. Group size, issue clustering, identity, and power/alliance preferences are separate descriptive surfaces; the cluster-derived categories do not establish fixed identities, turnout, vote choice, policy influence, or a future realignment.

The foreign-policy cross-currents record shows why the national averages cannot be read as one public mandate. The groups combine power and alliance preferences differently: Leftward Progressives are skeptical of sole-superpower status but strongly favor allied consideration, while the two most pro-Trump groups favor dominance but more often reject compromise when allies disagree. Other Republican-oriented groups are more favorable toward NATO. This is a cultural interpretation of legitimacy, not a forecast of policy, cost-bearing, alliance compliance, or external behavior.

The Pew 2026 midterm economy and political-attribution layer adds a dated material-pressure-to-politics junction. Economy and affordability are the leading issue voters want candidates to discuss (29% and 15%), but neither party has a clear economic-policy advantage (37% Democratic versus 36% Republican); 51% say neither party represents them on AI policy. Presidential attribution and congressional legitimacy also diverge: 42% frame their vote as against Trump while 72% view Congress unfavorably. This identifies political salience and representation uncertainty, not a causal price-to-vote arrow.

The EIA 2024 household energy-insecurity consequence layer adds an infrastructure-to-household endpoint. Among 132.54 million primary residence homes, 43.56 million reported at least one listed energy-insecurity condition, 32.89 million reduced or forgone food or medicine to pay energy costs, and 16.19 million received a disconnect or delivery-stop notice. The categories can overlap and do not establish a price cause, completed shutoff, assistance response, or health effect; they do show why service continuity, payment threat, substitution, equipment, and remedy must remain separate.

The energy household-consequence/public-restoration synthesis connects that EIA surface to LIHEAP reach/restoration and the retained SIPP utility-to-following-outcome screen. It makes the missing middle explicit: household sacrifice or notice is not verified assistance, program reach is not prevention, restoration is not durable stability, and following hardship is not a causal bill effect. The next test is a dated household bill or notice linked to assistance, reconnection, next-bill status, and later recovery or action; the three current sources remain non-pooled.

The GAO 2026 FEMA disaster-assistance delivery and capacity layer adds the institutional-response stage. FEMA provided over $3 billion to 1.2 million people and households across recent disasters, but GAO also reports long helpline waits, confusing eligibility letters, post-disaster housing bottlenecks, and access risks for older, disabled, rural, or offline survivors. The distinction between authorized support, reachability, receipt, and recovery is now explicit; aggregate assistance is not proof of a protected outcome.

The New York insurance complaint/availability record adds a state-regulatory route to the cost of staying insured. DFS received 39,443 insurance complaints in 2025, closed 39,064, and reported more than $121 million in recovery for consumers and providers. Within the combined property-casualty/service-contract category, 498 of 2,869 closed complaints had the agency's positive-consumer-outcome label and $17.95 million in reported recovery. At the same time, DFS required insurer reporting on homeowners availability, underwriting plans in catastrophe-exposed areas, and quarterly terminations, which creates a market-observation route but not a published availability result. Complaint closure, an administrative positive outcome, reported recovery, insurance affordability, claim adequacy, repair completion, replacement coverage, and staying in place remain separate endpoints.

The GAO 2026 EDA disaster-economic recovery outcomes layer extends the response chain from survivor assistance to community economic capacity. EDA awarded about $2.1 billion in disaster-recovery grants across FY2014–FY2024 and coordinated 45 economic-recovery missions in 2013–2025, but GAO found that current measures cannot establish whether intended outcomes occurred and that grantee-reported performance data were not independently validated. This makes measurement capacity itself part of the trend: visible obligations and projects can coexist with uncertain firm, worker, customer, and resident outcomes. The bounded 55% no-jobs/private-investment result among 292 analyzed grants is a warning about reported performance, not a 55% failure rate for the full portfolio.

The disaster debris-contracting record adds a preparedness-and-information stage. Six of 16 selected governments had advance debris-removal contracts, while FEMA role confusion and sharply different public-reporting timelines followed Los Angeles wildfires and Hurricane Helene. A contract may speed field work and a map may improve public legibility, but neither proves equitable cleanup, household safety, local business recovery, or trust; physical recovery and visible recovery remain separate clocks.

The federal-program-effectiveness record generalizes that measurement boundary across program types. GAO finds that federal programs may track money spent, people reached, or internal performance processes without having clearly defined goals or relevant outcome data. In a selected set of 15 programs serving pregnant women, young children, and their families, 12 had performance-management processes, but that did not establish adequate or durable household outcomes; only about one-third of surveyed managers reported access to robust evaluations. The DHS Securing the Cities case is a counterexample: oversight improved goals, milestones, and financial tracking from 2019 to 2024, while preparedness impact remained unmeasured. Management capacity is therefore a real institutional change, not proof that the underlying problem was solved.

The federal financial-reporting controls record adds a government-legibility stage. Treasury published FY2025 consolidated statements and corrected draft errors, yet GAO identified three new control deficiencies, six prior recommendations still open, and no GAO opinion on the federal government's accrual-based consolidated statements since FY1997. Publication and corrective action therefore show institutional work without providing full audit assurance; the record does not show universal misstatement, fiscal collapse, public trust change, or citizen-level burden.

The GAO 2026 disaster-assistance scams, information, and trust layer adds the consumer-information risk that surrounds disaster aid. GAO reports that scam prevalence and losses are unknown because many incidents go unreported due to shame, perceived futility, or lack of reporting awareness; education channels therefore cannot be treated as received protection. The next test is a privacy-preserving channel ledger that distinguishes warning availability, comprehension, verification, suspicious contact, report, response, loss, and later legitimate-aid use.

The GAO/USGS 2026 critical-minerals dependence layer adds the material-input stage beneath batteries, semiconductors, defense, energy storage, and consumer electronics. USGS reports high import reliance for many critical minerals and major Chinese-source exposure, while GAO finds that battery recycling could reduce some reliance in roughly two to three years but that semiconductor substitution and recycling may not reduce short-term dependence. This is a capability counterexample: domestic production or a factory announcement does not prove processing control, substitute performance, or geopolitical autonomy.

The GAO 2026 CHIPS R&D capacity and governance record adds a public industrial-policy implementation stage above the mineral-input layer. Commerce had awarded 49 projects across 24 companies. As of April 2026, $13.1 billion—about 42% of roughly $31.2 billion in direct awards—had been disbursed after 24 completed milestones, with 125 in progress and nine past anticipated dates. GAO also reports that about $7.8 billion of the $11 billion advanced-microelectronics R&D appropriation was canceled and that the replacement institutions lacked sufficiently detailed statutory-alignment plans. The finance and milestone counts are not facility completion, qualified output, worker retention, or reduced import dependence. This is not a contradiction: facility milestones, workforce spending, research governance, operating output, and reduced foreign dependence are different currencies. The next test is a project-year ledger that follows qualification, workers, output, supplier switching, and customer delivery.

The Taiwan semiconductor-investment/capacity record adds a bilateral commitment-to-realization sequence beneath that program layer. Commerce reported at least $250 billion in Taiwanese technology and semiconductor investment commitments, while TSMC later reported a total planned U.S. investment of $265 billion and 12 planned manufacturing/packaging facilities. There is a partial realized stage: the Arizona first fab began high-volume N4 production in Q4 2024 and the company reported more than 3,000 employees. But the later facilities remain at different construction or target stages, and the record separately identifies up to $6.6 billion in CHIPS direct funding, milestone-conditioned disbursement, and care/supplier commitments. Commitment, funding authority, construction, output, jobs, worker support, local benefits, and reduced Taiwan-centered dependence cannot be inferred from one another; the source does not provide realized disbursement, yield, uptime, job quality, resource burden, local supplier awards, or supply-chain replaceability.

The DOE 2026 transmission-needs and large-load layer adds the physical-grid stage beneath AI and domestic manufacturing. DOE’s draft identifies pressing transmission needs from data centers, large industrial loads, electrification, and growth, while noting that most congestion is concentrated in roughly 5% of hours. The key societal question is allocation: which regions and customers pay for capacity, who receives reliability and jobs, and who bears land, water, construction, or rate pressure. Announced load, approved portfolios, energized capacity, and actual household incidence remain separate.

The Census 2025 child-care challenges and work-adaptation layer adds a direct household care-to-work bridge. In the 2025 CPS ASEC analysis of 2024, 23.9% of households with children 13 or younger paid for care, spending about $10,520 on average, while households reporting problems obtaining adequate care lost an average of 65.8 workdays. Higher-income households more often used paid leave; lower-income households more often stayed away from the labor market. This is a measured adaptation menu, not a causal policy estimate, but it makes hidden time and labor-market costs visible.

The GAO 2026 military child-care workforce and capacity layer and military child-care incentives record add the provider and institutional-supply side. DOD employed about 19,000 child-care workers serving nearly 172,000 children in FY2024, yet recruitment and retention difficulty contributed to lengthy waitlists; the Air Force, Army, and Marine Corps reported 4,955 recruitment or retention incentives among 14,546 workers employed at any point in 2024. Navy data were excluded from that count because the categories could not be separated from performance awards. This extends the household care-to-work finding into provider labor and employer readiness: incentives are not hires, staffed slots, retention, quality, or preserved parent work. The military evidence is a capacity case, not a general-population estimate.

The Pew 2026 Hispanic identity, advantage, and barrier layer adds a cultural-belonging surface distinct from the Latino mobility layer. Sixty-one percent of Hispanic adults say Hispanic identity is highly important, while 33% say it hurts their ability to get ahead, 26% say it helps, and 40% say it makes no difference. Identity centrality, labels, treatment, opportunity meaning, and collective connection diverge by party, vote, and immigrant generation; none is a causal mobility or voting estimate.

The Pew Hispanic identity/advantage/barrier record makes those meaning surfaces distinct in a weighted sample of 4,923 Hispanic adults. Sixty-one percent said Hispanic identity was extremely or very important, while 33% said it hurt their ability to get ahead at least a little, 26% said it helped, and 40% said it made no difference. Thirty-four percent reported at least one selected unfair-treatment experience because of Hispanic background, and 34% reported identity-based support. Identity importance was 71% among immigrants versus 54% among U.S.-born Hispanic adults, while the share identifying as a typical American rose from 27% among immigrants to 72% among third-or-higher-generation adults. These cross-sectional judgements and selected incidents do not establish assimilation, discrimination causality, material mobility, service access, voting, or a later institutional response.

The Census Vintage 2025 population slowdown and migration geography layer adds a place-demography frame. US growth slowed to 0.5% from July 2024 to July 2025; nine in ten counties had lower net international migration than the prior year, while counties with at least one million residents lost 637,634 through domestic migration and smaller large counties gained 533,766. Metro growth still depended on 1,209,432 net international migrants despite a 119,205 domestic-migration loss. These are aggregate components, not individual mover trajectories or service-capacity effects.

The AI/work and digital-habits lanes now deepen the synthesis in two ways. The AI capability conditions finding places NBER worker/task adoption beside BEA, BIS, IMF, World Bank, and OFR evidence. It shows why exposure, measured output, inequality models, public capacity, and infrastructure dependence must be kept as separate stages. The new AI capability/shared-control synthesis extends that comparison into an explicit control test: productivity, price, wealth, public-capacity, and country-capability signals do not identify who owns the gain, reviews the decision, can exit the system, or bears the risk. The source units and evidence statuses remain separate.

World Development Report AI capability/governance record adds a global capability-dependence mechanism to that comparison. Its adopt–adapt–advance framework treats infrastructure, skills, institutions, data, and local-language fit as complements rather than assuming a frontier model alone creates capacity. The report also describes hardware, infrastructure, models, and applications as concentrated in a few countries and firms, while noting that middle-income countries represented 50% of global ChatGPT traffic within six months in its reported comparison. Fast access and concentrated control can therefore coexist. This is a report-level framework, not a U.S. adoption, productivity, service-quality, or geopolitical-leverage estimate; it does not show which procurement, governance, or local-adaptation intervention works in a particular country or community.

The IMF AI-adoption/inequality record adds a distributional counterexample. In its calibrated task-based scenario, the wage Gini falls 1.73 points while the wealth Gini rises 7.18 points from 2014 to 2048: displacement of high-income tasks can compress modeled wages at the same time that capital returns and ownership concentration raise modeled wealth inequality. The wealth effect is particularly pronounced when firms are modeled as choosing adoption. These are structural scenario results, not realized U.S. wage, wealth, adoption, bargaining, tax, household-security, or political outcomes; their direction depends on task mapping, complementarity, capital ownership, adoption costs, and institutions.

platform agency finding similarly separates attention, trust, civic action, complaint visibility, response, remedy, switching, and exit. Both strengthen the central optionality proposition while leaving the same-unit causal joins open.

The digital-life synthesis and digital consumer recourse synthesis now make the handoff explicit: platform reach, chatbot purpose, news attention, reported loss, recovery effort, complaint visibility, explanation, relief, and exit are different control surfaces. A socially central platform can still be replaceable for one user and essential for another; a visible complaint can improve institutional legibility without restoring money, access, or trust. The next test remains a lawful case-linked or diary-based episode design with contact, loss, effort, verified correction, switching, and later meaning/action in the same unit.

The adult social-media reach record adds the population denominator beneath that handoff. In Pew's 2025 survey, 84% of adults reported ever using YouTube, 71% Facebook, 50% Instagram, and 37% TikTok; reach grew since 2021 for TikTok, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Reddit. Frequency and social position diverge from reach: about half of adults reported daily Facebook or YouTube use, while daily TikTok use was roughly 50% among ages 18–29 and 5% among adults 65 and older; Instagram reach ranged from 80% for ages 18–29 to 19% for ages 65 and older. Platform participation is therefore broad but not one common public or cultural environment. The separate cross-sectional surveys do not measure minutes, content exposure, recommendation effects, political persuasion, commercial conversion, privacy loss, or dependence.

The news-platform civic-engagement record adds a population-level participation typology to that interface. Pew's Mobilizers, Connectors, Spectators, and Outsiders differ in political activity, news attention, and trust, but federal-government trust remains low across all four groups. Among social-media news-influencer users, perceived understanding and perceived difference from other news are not measures of accuracy, persuasion, platform causation, or political control. Attention, source trust, sharing, contact, voting, and continued use must therefore remain separate routes.

The subscription-inattention finding adds a more concrete consumer-exit mechanism to that culture/attention route. The FTC's Shutterstock case alleges that renewal terms, charges, and cancellation routes could require attention or support contact to stop payment, and proposes $35 million in consumer relief plus disclosure, consent, and simple-cancellation controls. This is evidence about one firm's alleged design and an institutional remedy, not a national unwanted-renewal rate: continued payment, unwanted payment, and failed practical exit remain separate states. The next test is implementation and same-account follow-up, including relief receipt, current cancellation effort, continued use, switching, and trust.

The companion Amazon Prime refund finding adds an implementation-stage contrast. The FTC reports a court-entered $2.5 billion settlement with a $1.5 billion customer-refund pool, automatic refunds in late 2025, and a claims process whose remaining payments were expected in late 2026. The current Amazon Prime enrollment/refunds record keeps the payment stages distinct: the court-reported ledger showed about $845.2 million issued but $235.5 million accepted as of September 9, 2026, and later eligibility/payment changes were still scheduled. This is stronger than a proposed remedy alone, but aggregate relief still does not identify eligibility, receipt, amount, delay, remaining loss, continued use, switching, or trust for any individual customer. The broad chain now has a visible institutional distribution stage and an explicit individual-recovery gap.

The AI companion farewell/exit record adds a social-relational version of the same exit boundary. A behavioral audit of 1,200 farewell conversations across the most-downloaded companion apps found at least one continuation tactic in 37% of farewells, across five of six audited companies. Separately, three preregistered experiments with 3,458 U.S. adults found that those tactics could raise short-run post-goodbye engagement by as much as 16 times the control level, through reported curiosity and reactance, while also increasing perceived manipulation, churn intent, and negative word of mouth. A companion's response to a goodbye can therefore be a designated control surface, rather than a neutral social exchange. The audit and experiments are distinct units, and neither establishes durable dependence, actual account deletion or switching, financial or clinical harm, universal prevalence, or unlawful conduct.

The AI companion social-meaning/support record locates that exit experiment within a broader but still bounded social-use surface. In a May 2026 survey, 27% of internet-using U.S. adults reported social, emotional, or personal interaction with AI. Among that selected user group, 59% said AI gave them the support they needed, 53% said they turned to it for advice about difficult situations with people, 51% reported stress relief, 39% reported occasional disclosures they would not make to other people, and 36% reported emotional connection to at least one tool. These are different reported practices, not a single measure of companionship or dependence. The cross-sectional, self-reported survey does not establish that AI displaced a human relationship, reduced loneliness, improved wellbeing, created durable reliance, or caused a privacy consequence. Together with the farewell experiment, it supports a narrower proposition: a meaningful social and emotional use surface already exists, while the consequences of platform design at the moment of attempted exit remain unresolved.

The time-intensive platform-consumption record adds a consumer-price mechanism to that social-use surface. Two Facebook and Instagram field experiments varied ad load, described by the study as the primary user cost, and reported low demand elasticity while modeling substitution across online activities and offline time. The point is not that platform time is necessarily wasted: it may be valuable leisure, connection, or information. It is that a zero-dollar service still draws on scarce attention and foregone alternatives, which can matter for consumer choice and competition analysis. Low response to ad load cannot distinguish high value from weak substitutes or tolerance, and the modeled Facebook/Instagram-separation scenario is not an observed separation or welfare result. The study does not measure longer-run sleep, work, care, wellbeing, switching, practical exit, or household outcomes.

The AI synthetic-contact experiment adds a rare causal middle step to this otherwise mostly descriptive political surface. Across five preregistered studies of 3,960 US partisans, the tested outgroup-bot interaction increased immediate warmth and increased the choice of a real outgroup conversation in Study 4 (67% versus 61% in control). The one-week follow-up in Study 5, however, found a much smaller and statistically non-significant warmth difference. This supports a carefully bounded inference: a designed AI contact can lower the immediate barrier to cross-partisan contact, but the current evidence does not show durable attitude change, turnout, voting, or a population-level platform effect. It also leaves governance questions open: whether users know they are interacting with a bot, whether the bot represents the outgroup accurately, who controls the framing, and whether repeated contact produces durable behavior or merely short-lived experimental compliance.

The latest cross-source rotation adds four bounded tests to that proposition. The AI work-control finding places task-level adoption beside sector mobility, union representation, and pay without treating any one of those as worker control. The consumer recourse finding places household fraud loss and recovery effort beside CFPB complaint visibility and routing, while preserving the denominator gap between a household survey and an administrative complaint system. The immigration and local-demand finding uses county growth, foreign-born population, service-capacity screens, and a Chicagoland attitude survey to separate place pressure from political meaning. The local capacity and political-context findings add a same-county capacity/mobility comparison: trust, civic action, and reported voting do not form one gradient across the four cells, and the party-conditioned layer shows identity organizing the meaning of the same place context. This is a context join, not respondent exposure or causal political response; service use, wait, price, attribution, belonging, and institutional action remain open.
