The FTC Consumer Sentinel 2025 record adds the later administrative-loss surface. FTC testimony reports approximately three million fraud reports and $15.9 billion in reported losses in 2025, including more than $7.9 billion in investment-scam losses and more than $3.5 billion in imposter-scam losses. Imposter reported losses were about three times their 2020 level, while imposter reports represented roughly one in three 2025 fraud reports. These are reported administrative totals, not a population incidence or verified-loss census: reporting access, category salience, high-value cases, coverage, and nonreporting can all shape the aggregate. The source does not link a victim to recovery effort, payment reversal, remedy, residual loss, trust, switching, or exit.

The new comparative worker-control finding sharpens the AI/work arrow. JRC worker survey evidence associates algorithmic management with autonomy, break, stress, and intensity differences in Europe; ILO cases show that collective voice sometimes changes consent, pay, data limits, human oversight, or workflow discretion, while other challenges remain partial or unresolved. Read alongside the US NBER/OECD/BLS layer, this supports a conversion hypothesis rather than a US causal claim: information and voice become control only when they alter a rule or produce enforceable remedy. The housing and insurance finding tests California ZIP-level income and wildfire-risk combinations and shows that the apparent low-income/high-risk gradient is sensitive to the income cutoff. Together these are not one causal chain; they are a current stress test showing that unequal room, institutional routing, and interpretation can be aligned only when units, denominators, and counterexamples remain visible.

The tax-rulemaking public-engagement record adds a formal-voice version of the same boundary. GAO found notice-and-comment procedures in all 10 sampled proposed tax regulations, with a median 61.5-day comment period, but hearing access and documentation were uneven; selected economic analyses used alternatives analysis more consistently than specific cost, benefit, revenue, or summary accounting estimates. Treasury and IRS also had not developed a policy for mass or AI-assisted comments. A comment route is therefore a real participation channel, not proof of representative access, agency learning, influence on the final rule, or greater taxpayer legitimacy.

The latest continuation pass extends the same discipline across several scales. The SNAP transition-reason finding separates job-loss and wage-reduction reports from other entry and exit reasons instead of treating every transition as the same hardship event. The SIPP race/tenure comparison and SIPP disability/resource comparison show why subgroup intersections need explicit universes and replicate-weight checks. The fraud recovery finding adds age, income, and payment-route conditioning while keeping complaint visibility separate from household loss. The party-conditioned worry/vote finding keeps political meaning distinct from material exposure. The payment-rewards finding keeps modeled incidence distinct from observed household welfare. Finally, the infrastructure-control finding keeps project completion and ownership change distinct from sovereignty or geopolitical leverage. These additions expand the atlas; they do not close its same-unit causal arrows.

The newest continuation pass adds four further bounded results. The FTC reporting-to-recovery finding places 2025 administrative reported-loss scale beside Federal Reserve household recovery burden and CFPB response routes; it does not create a same-case remedy or trust measure. The card-offer surface finding shows why a larger public credit-card offer surface and lower product-level median APR do not prove cheaper realized credit or practical access. The regional price-and-firm-capacity finding keeps Second District household price exposure, gasoline adjustment, and small- firm employment expectations as distinct place indicators. The 2026 JOLTS finding extends the labor context through July while preserving the establishment-versus-worker boundary and preliminary status of the latest month.

The 2026 CES earnings finding adds January–August establishment pay context for four sectors. It shows why partial-year pay movement and labor mobility must remain separate surfaces: CES averages do not identify worker control, and JOLTS rates do not identify individual outside options or household security.

The gig-work outside-options record adds a firm-competition-to-worker-leverage stage. Randomized pay experiments and a natural experiment among Uber drivers find that access to one competing platform nearly doubled drivers' responsiveness to Uber, with the implied firm markdown falling from about 68% to about 50%. This is evidence that outside options can change a platform's labor-supply constraint, not proof of higher net earnings, stable hours, benefits, safety, household security, or durable worker control. Formal competitor access may still be unusable when demand, account rules, location, vehicle costs, or scheduling limit switching.

The August 2026 Employment Situation record adds a current CPS/CES layer: steady unemployment and participation alongside positive payroll growth, nominal private-sector pay and hours, long-term unemployment, and uneven industry changes. The detailed finding shows why household labor-force status, establishment payroll jobs, JOLTS turnover, and sector earnings are conditioning surfaces rather than a common worker panel or an AI/work-control estimate.

The follow-up labor-to-household-room finding connects the BLS labor surface to SIPP same-person resource/job cross-lags, Federal Reserve liquidity and repayment measures, and New York Fed aggregate credit exposure. The combined evidence supports household room as a likely conditioning variable for practical worker exit and voice, but the sources do not share a person or workplace key and therefore do not establish that arrow.

The new firm AI expectations finding adds the employer-side clock from NBER W34836: broad current use, limited retrospective own-firm effects, and larger forward expectations for productivity, output, and employment. Its employer/employee expectation gap is useful for the institutional meaning layer, but it is not realized displacement, worker control, household security, or political consequence. The worker/workplace event ledger remains the required bridge from firm expectation to implementation, appropriation, voice, and household response.

The SIPP utility-to-work following-month finding adds a same-person timing surface: utility-payment difficulty or energy- assistance status at month t sits beside earnings and hours change at month t+1. Earnings movement is common across all groups, while the utility- difficulty hours estimate is imprecise and the assistance comparison is selected. This narrows the material-to-work arrow without turning a monthly utility screen into a dated bill shock, work-loss effect, or recovery result. The 2026-09-16 reproduction recheck updates the local input provenance to the current full-v18 slice while leaving the estimates unchanged.

The BEA July 2026 income-and-outlays record adds a current aggregate benchmark for income, disposable income, consumption, services-versus-goods movement, outlays, and saving. The household-pressure finding uses it to anchor the macro environment without imputing equal household room, real purchasing power, consumer choice, or political meaning.

The Census 2025 income, poverty, and insurance vintage layer adds a newer national household-security checkpoint without replacing the household-level evidence. Real median household income reached $87,460 and official poverty was 10.2%, while the Supplemental Poverty Measure (13.1%) and full-year uninsured rate (7.9%) were not statistically different from 2024 in the release summary. These are different universes and clocks: the median is not liquid room, official poverty is not post-tax or medical-cost-adjusted security, and insurance coverage is not affordable or continuous care. The result strengthens the atlas proposition that aggregate improvement can coexist with unresolved distributional, health-access, and political-action questions.

The SIPP episodic-poverty record adds a duration layer beneath that annual checkpoint. In 2024, the monthly poverty rate stayed near 11.9% while 15.1% experienced poverty for at least two consecutive months; 59.2% of those with episodic poverty were poor all year. Children had an 18.9% episodic rate, and older adults experiencing episodic poverty averaged about 11 months, with 79.4% poor all year. The source makes spell length and subgroup concentration visible, but it does not link the spell to its cause, benefits, hardship, housing, health, trust, or later recovery in the same person.

The Census August 2026 retail-sales and consumer-activity layer adds the adjacent behavior surface: national retail and food-services sales were $773.9 billion, up 1.2% from July and 6.0% from August 2025 in current dollars. Because the release is not price-adjusted, this does not establish more units purchased, greater household room, consumer confidence, or firm profit. It does, however, make the missing middle explicit between price and household experience: channel, category, quantity, payment, debt, substitution, and resource-group incidence remain the next tests.

The BEA Q2 2026 growth/profits record adds a separate macro-firm surface for real GDP, private domestic demand, prices, and corporate profits. The work-control finding uses it to distinguish output and profit movement from worker authority, household benefit, and firm-level AI effects.

The IMF 2026 US Article IV finding adds country-surveillance context: recent aggregate resilience and productivity coexist with fiscal debt, current-account, tariff, labor, and financial-stability risks. IMF projections are conditional macro scenarios, not household or worker outcomes; the next bridge must connect any adjustment event to distributional, institutional, and political-response evidence.

The Federal Reserve financial-stability and monetary-policy finding adds the institutional-financial layer: resilient banks and moderate aggregate debt vulnerability coexist with selected household delinquency, tight credit for some borrowers, elevated inflation, high valuations, and funding-risk exposure. The Fed's system aggregates do not identify household incidence or political meaning; the next bridge must join a dated rate, energy, tariff, credit, or funding event to borrower type, firm size, repayment/spending response, and later institutional or political action.

The public financial-capacity and household-room bridge now places BEA aggregate output/profits/income, Federal Reserve financial and household surfaces, OFR public monitoring capacity, IMF fiscal scenarios, and New York Fed aggregate credit in one deliberately non-pooled architecture. It sharpens the end-to-end gap: macro resilience, public data visibility, aggregate debt/delinquency, and household liquidity can move differently; the missing test is still a dated event joined to compatible exposure, attribution, action, and recovery or remedy. The follow-up OFR institutional-finance finding turns that architecture into a longitudinal institutional sequence: 2022 repo and data-visibility pilots, 2023 elevated-risk monitoring, 2024 persistent data gaps and differentiated borrower risk, and 2025 expanded repo visibility and AI workflow reporting alongside lower staffing and budget. The sequence supports public-capacity analysis, not a claim that visibility became protection. The next empirical pass is to align those milestones with the IMF/Findex provider- demand layers and CFPB/SHED household-response layers, retaining market, institution, firm, account, household, and respondent units separately.

The financial-access route synthesis now supplies that provider/demand comparison in reader-facing form. Global Findex shows broad US adult account and device ownership and selected financial behaviors; IMF FAS shows provider-side counts, branch density, and balance ratios; SHED shows household loss, recovery time, buffers, and adaptation; and CFPB/FTC/OFR show institutional visibility, routing, and public-capacity surfaces. These layers establish reach and infrastructure as different stages, not a single inclusion score. They still do not identify favorable terms, failed-account episodes, verified correction, switching, or later trust for the same person.

The new county capacity/outcome diagnostic adds CDC PLACES modeled social-need outcomes to the existing CBP/HRSA/NHTS place architecture. Low visible health-establishment capacity aligns with higher modeled transportation, food, housing, utility, mental-distress, and uninsured medians, but routine-checkup medians are nearly unchanged. The result advances the place outcome surface while preserving the ecological and cross-vintage boundary: it does not identify patient access, provider quality, travel, price, causal effect, trust, or political response. The follow-up PLACES vintage comparison uses 2,885 common county FIPS across the 2024 and 2025 releases. Routine-care, insurance, food, transportation, housing, utility, and mental-distress medians do not move as one local-health trend, and the social-needs measure universe is not identical across releases. This strengthens the program's temporal quality control while preserving CDC's modeled small-area and non-intervention boundary. The HPSA component diagnostic then decomposes the shortage label itself. Geographic, population, facility, tract, low-income, and migrant/seasonal categories produce different overlapping county medians, which blocks a single “HPSA county” interpretation. This adds classification specificity but still does not observe component-level reach, patient use, quality, price, household time, trust, or political response. The follow-up HPSA operational-field audit finds that FTE, shortage, and estimated underserved-population fields are not uniformly populated by designation type; facility/site rows in particular have very sparse FTE and no estimated underserved-population values in the current extract. This is an institutional measurement boundary, not evidence of zero capacity or a resident-level care result.

The July 2026 Census HTOPS/HPS finding adds a current same-round household surface: expense and price perception, energy trade-offs, food and assistance routes, anxiety/loneliness, and trust in federal statistics and Congress. It strengthens alignment of material and institutional endpoints without turning a cross-sectional co-occurrence into a price-to-trust mechanism or political-action result.

The follow-up Census cross-wave finding uses the official successive-difference replicate weights across corrected March, May, and July 2026 releases. It shows broad expense difficulty nearly flat from May to July while food, energy, and trust measures move differently; the 2026 files are repeated snapshots after a documented design break, not a same-person recovery panel.

The follow-up July expense-to-confidence cross-tab tests one missing comparison within that same release. High confidence in federal statistical agencies was 43.9% among respondents reporting no usual- expense difficulty and 28.8% among those reporting at least a little difficulty; high confidence in Congress was 20.8% versus 13.8%. The replicate-weighted contrast is useful evidence that material pressure and institution-specific confidence can be related in the same population snapshot, but it still cannot identify timing, blame, prior identity, political action, or recovery. The larger statistical-agency gap also argues against collapsing all institutional confidence into a single trust score.

The April–June 2025 linked HTOPS finding adds a same-respondent transition surface for 6,564 linked IDs. Persistence, entry, and exit can now be observed for selected material, work, and institutional measures, but the retained sample lacks a documented attrition-adjusted longitudinal weight and does not identify a causal trigger. The HTOPS expense-difficulty cross-lagged record shows baseline expense difficulty alongside materially higher later food insufficiency (12.3% versus 1.1%), energy nonpayment (21.4% versus 2.2%), and job loss (11.7% versus 2.9%), while later high Congress confidence is nearly similar (17.2% versus 16.9%). The outcome-specific linked samples, April weights, and separate item universes do not support a national transition or causal interpretation. This is an associative counterexample to a single material-pressure-to-trust pathway.

The World Bank Enterprise Surveys access recheck also strengthens the acquisition map: the US AI follow-up is confirmed as an available survey, but firm microdata remain behind the authenticated portal. That is an access result, not a firm adoption estimate; the next AI firm test still requires the file, questionnaire, weights, and variance documentation.

The latest rotation adds two bounded bridges. The household adaptation and recovery finding places SHED financial-condition persistence beside health, unpaid-care, food-pressure, and fraud-recovery measures. It strengthens the recurring optionalities proposition: current stabilization can consume savings, time, health, care capacity, or attention, and broad financial improvement is not the same as restored future room. The consumer visibility and exit finding then places CFPB complaint labels beside SHED fraud burden, Pew platform/AI use and privacy concern, and the FTC information-gathering inquiry. It keeps visibility, explanation, verified remedy, attention cost, dependence, trust, and exit as separate stages; neither complaint routing nor regulatory inquiry closes the consumer-power chain.

The recurring-source watch also refreshes the AI/work mobility context through January–July 2026. The partial-year JOLTS mean remains cool (4.3714% openings and 1.9571% quits, with July preliminary), but it is an establishment-rate context rather than an annual worker trend or an AI effect.

The current macro-to-household finding adds the latest BEA July income/outlays, August CPI and PPI, August CPS/CES, JOLTS partial-year, and SHED hardship vintages. It reinforces a central denominator rule: aggregate income and payroll growth can coexist with energy/upstream price pressure and income-graded household food or bill hardship. The release set identifies adjacent currencies, not a same-household price-to-politics or recovery chain.

The safety-net transition/work-room finding adds a same-person SIPP sequence around SNAP entry. Following resource-ratio, earnings, hours, job-count, and hardship surfaces do not move as one outcome: resource position often falls while job count and hours remain stable in their selected universes. This keeps benefit receipt, work continuity, household room, administrative adequacy, and recovery separate. The next test is a same-episode notice-to-remedy record with amount, gap days, alternatives, care/work response, and later recovery or action.

The US firm-capacity baseline adds the public World Bank Enterprise Survey profile as a distinct firm-level context layer: size strata differ in reported employment growth, formal training, outage exposure, bank-financed investment, and manager-selected obstacles. This improves the AI/work bridge by making implementation capacity and infrastructure exposure visible before the gated AI follow-up is used. It does not estimate AI adoption, productivity causality, worker control, or household incidence; the next test remains the documented firm file with its AI questions, weights, missingness, and variance guidance.

The firm-to-worker comparison then places that size-conditioned baseline beside NBER task adoption, BLS representation, and JOLTS mobility. The comparison makes four gates explicit: firm complements, actual worker use, institutional voice, and practical exit are not interchangeable. It strengthens the worker-control boundary without turning size, adoption, union coverage, or quits into a composite index.

The latest household-room pass adds a FRED timing screen. From January 2024 to July 2026, the University of Michigan consumer-sentiment index fell 23.8 points while the CPI index rose 7.5% and unemployment remained close to 4%. This does not identify an inflation effect: the series have different constructions and do not share a household denominator. It does establish a useful divergence that the household-level work must explain: a comparatively strong aggregate labor signal can coexist with weak public economic confidence.

The FRED finding therefore strengthens the distinction between national conditions and practical household room. SHED, SIPP, MEPS, BEA, BLS, and Federal Reserve credit records are needed to test which households faced shelter, food, energy, insurance, debt, care, or work constraints, and what they did next. The FRED series alone cannot supply that exposure, adaptation, political attribution, or recovery step.

The Gallup institutional-confidence finding adds a parallel meaning layer: average confidence in long-tracked institutions was low, but confidence differed sharply by institution, party, and racial group. The Chatham House data-trust memo extends the route to public measurement itself, treating confidence in economic statistics as a possible condition of domestic coordination and international credibility. These are not proof of a material-to-trust or domestic-to- geopolitical causal chain. They make the missing links more precise: measure the statistic a person encountered, their own material exposure, who they believed, whether an institution acted, and whether confidence changed after a verifiable correction or remedy.

The UNDP human-development finding adds a comparative capability frame to the AI and household-room lanes. The United States has a high average HDI and a strong international rank, but that average does not show who can exercise a choice, access training, refuse an automated decision, or absorb a work or health shock. UNDP therefore helps keep the program’s question focused on human capability rather than technology or income alone. It remains a country-level context measure; subgroup incidence, distribution, agency, and worker control still require US household, worker, firm, and institutional evidence.

The UNDP AI use, control, and confidence record adds the missing perception layer for selected countries. In the US tabulation, weekly-or-more AI use (32.6%), confidence in controlling AI interactions (33.9%), confidence in government AI use (29.1%), and confidence that AI is designed in people’s interests (37.5%) are separate measures. Selected-country comparisons show why they should not be collapsed: more frequent use can coexist with lower personal control, and high public confidence does not verify service quality or actual agency. The survey is cross-sectional and internationally comparative; the next test remains a US subgroup and same-episode join to work, household, public-service, remedy, and political-action outcomes. The same survey’s domain layer adds another boundary: reported use was highest for entertainment, while likely future use was highest for entertainment and education, with work, health, and finance carrying different stakes. The next analysis must therefore follow the system into its domain of use rather than treating AI adoption as one cultural or economic event. Its work-expectation layer adds a further split: expected productivity, new job creation, and current job change or replacement can coexist, and expected productivity is much higher among people already likely to use AI for work tasks. This is an expectation bridge, not realized productivity, displacement, or bargaining power.

The newest bounded findings add four important controls to the cross-source story. The SHED household-room finding shows that income timing, outside help, assistance receipt, budget margin, and price adaptation are related but distinct household surfaces. They should not be summarized as one measure of financial stress or treated as proof of a single coping sequence. The RECS energy-room finding adds energy spending, energy burden, assistance, disconnection, and inability to repair or replace equipment as separate routes. Its burden result is a transparent spending-to-income proxy, not a complete welfare measure, and the public-use survey year limits claims about the present.

The BFS/BDS firm-and-place finding adds a firm-stage boundary: applications, establishments, openings, and net job creation are different events. A place can show entrepreneurial entry without a corresponding positive net-job result; sector composition is part of the explanation. This keeps local business formation from being used as a shortcut for local prosperity, worker bargaining power, or community recovery.

The business-application expectations/realization record adds an expectation-stage control. Linking 17 million U.S. business applications to outcomes, the Census study finds that applicants overestimate employment on average chiefly because many expect entry but never enter; among applicants who both expect and achieve entry, expected employment is typically below realized first-year employment. Expectations predict entry and employment but conditional realized employment rises less than one-for-one with them. Application volume, anticipated hiring, realized entry, first-year employment, survival, job quality, and community benefit are therefore different stages. The working paper does not identify why expectations miss, establish a psychological mechanism, or show durable firm or household outcomes.

The third-place and neighborhood-startup record adds a social-space-to-firm-formation version. An NBER comparison reports a 9.1–22.5% increase in annual startup counts over seven years after a first Starbucks entered tracts without existing cafés, with larger effects in an under-resourced partnership and no significant effect where cafés already existed. Missing gathering space may therefore matter for local networks, but the study does not establish a single mechanism, firm survival, job quality, resident welfare, displacement, or household benefit.

The Black-neighborhood startup record adds a racialized place-conversion pattern. Across 38 states, a long-standing Black-neighborhood startup deficit reversed sharply in 2020, especially in neighborhoods with larger prior deficits, and relative entrepreneurship stayed elevated through 2024, including neighborhood-oriented activity. Registration growth is not yet firm survival, ownership, financing, jobs, wages, customer welfare, household income, or reduced displacement; the change could also reflect policy, demand, migration, credit, selection, or registration behavior. The Opportunity Zones record adds a public-incentive-to-place version. GAO reports more than $108 billion in Qualified Opportunity Fund assets and nearly 9,000 designated zones, but states and selected funds generally did not track incentive-specific jobs, housing, or other community outcomes. Investment was more likely in urban places with infrastructure, ongoing development, and community support. Capital and project completion can therefore be visible while resident benefit, affordability, displacement, and durable community security remain unresolved; the record does not establish a national causal effect. Finally, the World Bank poverty, climate, and data-coverage finding adds comparative context rather than a US outcome: global poverty remains highly concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa and fragile or conflict-affected settings; climate exposure and missing household surveys constrain what can be known. Those facts matter for the geopolitical context and for interpreting international capability, but they do not establish a US household, conflict, or geopolitical-behavior effect.

The latest transmission-realization rotation adds a physical public-capacity stage. DOE's Transmission Facilitation Program makes federal support and planned capacity visible, while the current project page records termination or withdrawal notices for several selected projects. Selection and financing support therefore do not yet prove construction, energization, transmission service, cost recovery, reliability, or community benefit. The DOE record keeps the project-status evidence separate from those open outcomes.

The Champlain Hudson Power Express finding adds the named-operation counterexample to that incomplete-transmission stage. New York reports that the 339-mile Quebec-to-New York project reached commercial operation and is expected to deliver 10.4 terawatt-hours per year into New York City. Operation and a cross-border delivery route are therefore visible, but customer bills, reliability, rate allocation, host-community acceptance, and durable supply dependence are not. This sharpens the broader rule: a physical system can be functioning while the distribution of benefit, burden, and control remains unmeasured.

The Seattle SMART curb record adds a named digital-infrastructure implementation stage. Seattle's $1.996 million project completed a digital commercial-curb inventory, installed operational vehicle-to-curb infrastructure, and implemented a commercial vehicle permit system after procurement and reporting delays. The project reached operation, but its report does not establish delivery reliability, curb-user time, enforcement, price, safety, equity, user acceptance, or durable continuation.

The Technology Modernization Fund finding adds a federal IT realization comparator. GAO reports about $1.03 billion invested across 68 projects, $13.5 million in reported savings from 11 projects, and $1.06 billion in projected savings from 24 projects. The scale difference keeps investment, realized savings, and projected savings separate. It adds a measured implementation endpoint without proving agency productivity, better service, user time saved, equitable access, or household benefit.

The USPS service-performance finding adds a public-network cost-to-access counterpoint. GAO reports longer expected delivery times for some First-Class Mail, the removal of afternoon collection at more than 24,000 distant post offices, and most lowered service targets not being met since FY2021; oversight entities and stakeholders reported disproportionate rural effects. This makes the hidden trade concrete: financial sustainability efforts can move waiting and collection burden toward users. The review does not establish a household-level delay, substitution, total savings, complaint outcome, trust change, or political response.

The DROP rotation adds an administrative digital-control stage. California's system gives a resident one request, an eight-digit ID, broker-level statuses, and recurring processing duties. This makes privacy action more visible and contestable, but “deleted,” “not found,” “opted out,” “exempted,” and “pending” do not form a public aggregate completion rate or prove downstream deletion, reappearance control, safety, trust, or durable exit. The DROP record keeps those stages separate.

The TAKE IT DOWN Act record adds a mandated digital-remedy version. Covered platforms must provide a clear removal route for nonconsensual intimate images, act within 48 hours on a valid request, address known identical copies, and face an FTC escalation route. The law makes contestability more visible, but the public materials do not show a valid request, completed removal, recurrence prevention, survivor safety, wellbeing, trust, or platform exit.

The Census civic-capacity rotation adds a material-place layer to culture and politics. A large CPS-based working-paper analysis links local disadvantage and inequality to lower volunteering and reports a recession-related weakening of participation, including the disappearance of an earlier rural advantage. This does not measure community collapse: informal help, belonging, political action, and trust can move on different clocks. The Census record keeps the place association separate from those open outcomes.

The Census–AmeriCorps civic-time record adds a time-intensity boundary. Formal volunteering rose from 23.2% in 2021 to 28.3% in 2023 and informal neighbor help reached 54.2%, while mean volunteer hours fell from 96.5 in 2017 to 70 in 2023 and median hours from 40 to 24. Participation reach, time intensity, informal help, service adequacy, trust, belonging, and political influence are therefore separate currencies; the repeated cross-sections do not follow the same person or show why hours changed.

The BLS cultural-and-civic-time record adds an everyday time-use denominator. On an average 2025 day, 30.4% of people age 15+ socialized or communicated (0.58 hours per person), 9.4% engaged in religious or spiritual activities (0.13 hours), 5.3% volunteered (0.12 hours), and 13.6% did an organizational, civic, or religious activity. Socializing and religious time were higher on weekends/holidays than weekdays, while published volunteering time was 0.12 hours on both. These primary-activity averages do not show relationship quality, informal help, digital contact, belonging, organizational capacity, or political action, and they do not follow the same person across years.

The NEA arts participation/connection record adds a cultural-infrastructure route. Across four 2024 Household Pulse Survey cycles, 25.2% of adults attended a live performance or art exhibit in the prior month, but attendance ranged from 16.2% below $25,000 annual income to 55.2% at $200,000 or more. Attendees also reported more often always or usually receiving needed social/emotional support than non-attendees. Cultural participation can thus be a socially patterned resource and support-associated surface, not merely leisure consumption. The repeated cross-sectional evidence does not show that arts attendance caused support, belonging, health, or civic action; money, time, health, transport, education, place, and prior ties can produce both participation and reported connection.

The Census child cultural-participation record adds a distinct child and family layer. In 2023, among children ages 6--17, 38.4% participated in sports, 26.8% took lessons, 21.9% joined clubs, and 6.8% did all three; the all-three rate was 1.2% in families below poverty and 8.8% in families at 200% of poverty or higher. At the same time, family-routine measures need not move with organized opportunity: 67.4% of children under six were read to at least five days a week and 85.8% of children under 18 ate dinner with a reference parent at least five nights a week. These age-specific, descriptive SIPP measures do not show whether fees, time, transport, safety, program supply, preference, or school resources generated the activity gradient, nor do they establish belonging, activity quality, educational attainment, or later adult outcomes.

The American Neighbor Survey social-infrastructure record adds a neighborhood-scale view of the same distinction. In a weighted 2025 survey of 5,357 adults, 40% reported talking with neighbors at least a few times a week and 40% reported having worked with neighbors in the prior year to solve a problem or improve the community; 72% reported a great or fair amount of neighborhood trust. Access was uneven: 10% reported none of the listed neighborhood amenities within a 20-minute walk while 44% reported six or more; weekly neighbor conversation was 27% in the first group and 43% in the latter. Among parents, 56% with a college degree versus 39% without one said they would feel comfortable asking a neighbor for emergency child care. These are separate surfaces of contact, collective action, trust, accessible places, and stated mutual-aid comfort. They do not show that amenities caused connection, that a neighbor actually supplied care or money, or that social infrastructure offsets formal-service gaps, since residence, safety, resources, life stage, and selection into place can shape all of them.

The Pew Latter-day Saint communal-trust record adds an institutional-belonging counterexample. Current Latter-day Saint adults reported more volunteering and generalized trust than U.S. adults overall, but volunteering was much higher among members with a bachelor's degree and in the Mountain region, and trust also varied by education. A strong community institution can therefore generate real social capacity without distributing access, time, or role opportunity evenly. Affiliation, service, trust, belonging, political influence, and burden remain separate outcomes; the cross-sectional survey does not show that membership caused the differences.

The USMCA labor-remedy rotation adds an attributed external-response stage. A worker petition at a Mexican facility led, according to USTR, to a U.S. review request, Mexican investigation, reported reinstatement and backpay, union access, facility rules, monitoring, and resumed tariff liquidation. This is a stronger operation-to-response bridge than a policy announcement, but worker receipt, non-retaliation, durable bargaining power, and wider compliance remain open. The USMCA record keeps the institutional response separate from those outcomes.

The OFAC firm-correction rotation adds a financial-infrastructure stage to geopolitical power. A foreign firm's reported apparent sanctions violations passed through U.S.-dollar payment channels and produced a $275 million settlement plus a five-year compliance commitment. Enforcement reach and future correction are visible; later screening, recurrence, deterrence, distributional cost, and state response remain open. The OFAC record keeps the named-firm evidence separate from those outcomes.

Current evidence map by arrow

Arrow Current status Best next test
Material pressure → adaptation Compared across BLS prices, USDA, SHED food/financial layers, SIPP, household-room measures, and RECS energy layers; same-respondent evidence exists for selected SHED paths, while energy spending, assistance, disconnection, repair risk, and price adaptation remain distinct surfaces. Add dated trigger, alternatives, schedule control, care/time intensity, and a validated same-household energy episode.
Adaptation/time → wellbeing and security Health/care and ATUS layers show divergent paths and population intensity; the 2024 ATUS microdata record adds weighted work, care, travel, household-labor, socializing, and eldercare measures, while the roster and progressively standardized provider-time comparisons show care can cross household boundaries and co-occur with a partially persistent but annual-varying time profile. PSID or a valid same-unit event/panel comparison with work, care, health, household composition, and later wellbeing.
Exposure → institutional response CFPB and SNAP records measure institutional endpoints and transitions. Same-case event ledger from notice/contact through effort, decision, remedy, repeat effort, and exit.
Institutional route → meaning/action CPS, ANES, CCES, and Pew provide separate population measures. Repeated respondent or event-based design with attribution, trust, civic action, turnout, and vote.
Infrastructure → local burden/capability LBNL and international case records establish demand, commitments, and milestones; RECS adds household energy-spending, assistance, disconnection, and equipment-risk surfaces. Place-utility case comparison with approved/actual load, rates, local benefits, ownership, portability, public response, and household service continuity.
Local capacity → practical reach CBP/BFS/BDS place layers and NHTS vehicle/mode comparison establish separate provision and mobility-option surfaces; BFS/BDS now explicitly separates applications, establishments, openings, and net job creation. A common-place household/service-use design with fares, travel time, destination access, quality, firm survival/openings, and missed work/care.
Domestic capability/dependence → geopolitical leverage Case controls and state-leverage ledger define the required fields; World Bank comparative poverty, fragility, climate-exposure, and survey-coverage data provide context, not a US leverage finding. Observe a negotiation, refusal, switch, regulatory action, or external behavior change, while linking capability measures to the actors and stakes in that episode.

What is genuinely end-to-end today

The program currently has partial end-to-end coverage in bounded segments:

  1. Same-respondent persistence: SHED 2024→2025 financial-condition, adaptation, health, and selected care transitions.
  2. Time and care scale: ATUS published prevalence, care-day intensity, employment, age, and household/nonhousehold distinctions.
  3. Time-ordered public-system condition: SIPP SNAP transitions followed by rent/mortgage and utility hardship with Fay–BRR uncertainty, alongside USDA food-security severity and assistance participation. The buffer-and-credit bridge adds adjacent Federal Reserve coping measures, but does not claim a same-person route-to-credit or route-to-politics result.
  4. Pressure-to-adaptation comparison: BLS food-at-home prices, SHED income-conditioned food insufficiency and price responses, and USDA food security, with different reference periods and units kept explicit.
  5. Institutional visibility: CFPB published complaint route and endpoint trends, with product and time conditioning. The 2025 product comparison and household fraud layer now make the split between response labels, residual loss, recovery effort, and exit capacity explicit; a verified same-case remedy remains open.
  6. Political participation surface: CPS voting/registration and distinct nonvoter barriers, beside separate trust and judgment layers.
  7. Infrastructure/state-capacity boundary: national load scenarios and two international project milestones, with ownership and replaceability still open. IMF WEO adds a conditional macro-fiscal stage for defense mobilization; financing and social-spending incidence remain unlinked to US households or observed leverage.
  8. AI and platform agency boundary: task-level adoption, industry and firm outcomes, modeled distribution, public analytical capacity, attention, complaint visibility, and institutional scrutiny are now linked as bounded stages; worker/household incidence, remedy, exit, and geopolitical leverage remain unjoined.

The program does not yet have one valid record that carries a dated material or institutional trigger through adaptation, time/care, wellbeing, meaning, political action, institutional response, and later recovery. That is the central acquisition target—not a reason to erase the partial evidence or pretend that cross-source alignment is a respondent-level join.

Next rotating program cycle

The next cycle should advance all three scales together:

  • Micro/same-unit: run the PSID structural gate when authenticated files arrive; pursue SHED/ATUS/SIPP event-compatible comparisons where valid.
  • Institutional/episode: implement the same-case public-system and consumer recourse event ledger with notice, effort, remedy, and follow-up.
  • Place/state: retrieve utility, ownership, local-benefit, portability, and observed-response records for data-center and public-cloud cases.

Every new record should enter the trend-observation registry, carry its own denominator and boundary, and add either a new time period, subgroup/place conditioning, uncertainty, reversal, or same-unit link before a provisional trend is strengthened.

The Pew 2026 electorate racial and ethnic composition layer adds the demographic base beneath the political-action lane. Pew projects the 2026 eligible electorate at about 249.75 million: 61% White, 16% Hispanic, 12% Black, and 5% Asian, with Hispanic and Asian shares nearly doubled since 2006. Citizenship and age matter: only 52% of Hispanic adults and 60% of Asian adults were eligible voters in 2024, compared with 81% of White adults. These are composition estimates, not turnout or coalition forecasts; the next test follows population through eligibility, registration, participation, meaning, and representation.

The global-aging foreign-policy record adds a long-horizon demographic layer beneath geopolitical state capacity. GAO reports a projected increase in the worldwide population age 60 and over from about 1 billion in 2020 to 2.1 billion in 2050, with possible implications for partner health spending, defense resources, labor pools, migration, and global health assistance. These are plausible channels identified through literature and expert review, not evidence of a particular ally's policy change, altered burden sharing, or U.S. leverage.

The Pew 2025 religious affiliation, switching, and cultural identity layer adds family transmission, spirituality, practice, and institutional belonging to the cultural lane. Pew’s nationally representative 2023–24 RLS finds 62% of adults identify as Christian, 29% as religiously unaffiliated, and 35% have switched religious identity since childhood; 53% describe themselves as both spiritual and religious. The long-run change has slowed recently, and cultural attachment is not identical to affiliation. The next test follows identity, practice, community, family, and political meaning in repeated units.

The Pew 2026 U.S. global-role, domestic-partisan, and international-reception layer adds legitimacy and external reception to the material-capability lane. Across 36 non-U.S. countries, a median 35% said the U.S. contributes to peace and stability, versus 57% of Americans; inside the U.S., Republicans were at 82% and Democrats at 35%. The same source finds 83% of Americans see U.S. interference in other countries, with majorities in both parties. These are perception measures, not capability or behavioral outcomes; the next test is an event-country-party ledger linking policy events to reputation, cooperation, market/cultural signals, and political response.

The GAO 2026 kinship families and intergenerational care-support layer adds family composition as an operating care institution. About 2.4 million children lived in kinship families in 2023; these families were more likely to be in poverty, and children in grandparent households more often had health or special-education needs. For every child in foster care, about 18 kinship children were not, while formal supports varied by legal status and community. The next test follows caregiver capacity, benefits, housing, work, and child stability in the same family episode.

The canonical kinship-family record preserves the national descriptive frame, foster/non-foster distinction, and selected qualitative community evidence without pooling their denominators or turning family substitution into a welfare outcome.

The GAO 2026 assisted-living spending and Medicaid-coverage layer adds a care-and-housing financing bridge. Medicaid and traditional Medicare spending for assisted-living services totaled at least $12 billion in 2024, but GAO says the floor is likely an undercount because the setting is not uniformly identified; 44 state Medicaid programs covered assisted-living services as of March 2025, including 29 through HCBS waivers. Coverage, slot availability, room/board affordability, quality, family substitution, and resident outcomes remain separate. The next test is a state-year episode ledger.

The canonical assisted-living financing record preserves the federal spending floor, state-policy coverage, waiver limits, and mixed-payer care-bundle stages without treating coverage or spending as usable resident access.

The GAO 2026 telework, travel, real-estate, and planning layer adds a collective-geography consequence to changing work arrangements. Average telework remained about twice 2019 levels; MPOs reported lower transit ridership/fare revenue, changed driving geography, and shifts in commercial real-estate and housing demand. Only one of the 26 largest transit cities had 2024 ridership above 2019, while over 90% of MPOs wanted more DOT guidance. These are not causal household or city welfare estimates; the next test is a place-month-mode ledger linking telework, trips, service, property, investment, distribution, and public response.

The canonical telework/travel/planning record preserves the community-survey, selected-city, and federal-execution stages without treating telework context or MPO action as a causal welfare estimate.

The GAO 2026 airport transit availability and adoption layer adds a place and mobility conversion test. Nearly all of 51 reviewed airports had some transit service, yet passenger use ranged from 4% to 19% at the 12 airports with usable reports and only about 4% of airport and airline employees nationwide used transit to commute. Travel time, accessibility, familiarity, parking, benefits, and shift timing separate route presence from practical use; the next test is a route-day-shift ledger linking service design to completed trips, work access, cost, congestion, and intervention response.

The canonical airport transit record adds the official service and usage stages without pooling passenger reports, airport employee surveys, and national Census commute estimates.

The GAO 2026 disability workforce-program access layer extends the accessibility thesis into labor-market entry. Seven percent of participants in selected DOL workforce programs reported disabilities, 43% of those reporters did not provide a disability type, and GAO found local challenges with interpreters, outside training accessibility, monitoring aggregation, and guidance awareness. The participant and job-center samples do not identify causal barriers or employment effects. The next test links voluntary accommodation need to service completion, placement, retention, and local corrective action.

The canonical disability workforce-program record preserves participant, local implementation, oversight, and recommendation stages separately, including voluntary non-disclosure as a substantive data boundary.

The GAO 2026 working adults, Medicaid/SNAP, and employer reliance layer adds a labor–safety-net bridge. About 13.8 million Medicaid-enrolled adults and 10.6 million adults in SNAP-receiving households worked at some point in 2024; about two-thirds of each group worked at least 35 hours per week, and 88% were in the private sector. Selected-state employer data show repeated large- employer concentration, but do not prove wage inadequacy, benefit shifting, employer intent, or causal employment effects. The next test is a lawful state-year worker–household–employer ledger with hours, weeks, wages, benefits, eligibility transitions, household need, and later security.

The GAO 2026 disability health-care accessibility and oversight layer adds the usability stage after nominal coverage, facility capacity, or an appointment offer. GAO identifies physical, sensory, communication, digital, and bias barriers, while finding that none of 12 HHS population-health surveys collect national-level data on most accessibility barriers. This strengthens the interface thesis but does not estimate barrier prevalence or prove effects on diagnosis, health, work, or provider exit. The next test is an encounter- care, family/time burden, complaint, correction, and oversight response.

The canonical disability accessibility record preserves the barrier, measurement, oversight, and recommendation stages as separate observations rather than treating formal coverage as usable care.

The family-care public-capacity synthesis adds a cross-generational version of the same mechanism. Kinship families, childcare arrangements, unpaid adult care, ATUS time allocation, and assisted-living financing show that families often supply the missing care capacity between need and formal service. The protective outcome—continuity, belonging, or care received—and the sacrificed outcome—work, money, housing, transport, health, or social time—remain separate. The next test is a same-family care episode with alternatives, support receipt, schedule control, and later stability; the comparison is not a pooled family-burden estimate.

The domestic capacity/autonomy realization synthesis adds the material-input layer below infrastructure and procurement. Critical minerals, CHIPS awards and milestones, data-center/grid records, and JASSM/LRASM orders show separate commitment, capacity, operating, replaceability, and leverage clocks. Domestic production or public spending can advance while foreign processing, qualified output, delivery, ownership, or supplier switching remain unresolved. The next test is one identifier-bearing mineral/application or procurement event followed through output, local incidence, substitute qualification, and an observed switch or external response; no autonomy or leverage score is inferred.

The three-audience legitimacy synthesis adds the interpretation layer above material capability. Pew separates foreign public reception, Americans' national judgment, and domestic partisan meaning: foreign publics were less likely than Americans to say the US contributes to peace and stability, while Republicans and Democrats differed sharply inside the US. The shared judgment that the US interferes abroad shows that common descriptive perception can coexist with divergent legitimacy evaluations. The next test is an event-country-party-year ledger linking a dated policy event to cooperation, refusal, market/cultural response, or institutional action; polling alone is not geopolitical leverage. The measurement-quality rotation adds a necessary counterexample. A study that applied the same occupational-exposure rubric to three language models found a 3.6-fold difference in mean exposure estimates and downstream results that changed materially with the annotator. The atlas should therefore treat AI exposure as a measured construct with a model, rubric, and uncertainty—not as one fixed fact. Exposure findings should be compared with observed adoption, worker reports, and realized job or earnings changes before they are pooled.

The political-culture rotation adds a second caution: a raw partisan gap in workplace AI use can mostly disappear after accounting for education, occupation, and industry, while perceived displacement risk may still begin to diverge by party. This separates political exposure from political meaning. The source does not show durable polarization, policy demand, or action, but it suggests that conflict may grow around what a technology means even when its use is largely shaped by where people work.

The cultural-identity rotation adds a parallel legitimacy pattern. Pew's Muslim-American review shows population, mosque counts, and congressional representation growing while negative public judgments, perceived discrimination, unfair media treatment, and reported anti-Islamic incidents remain separate and substantial. Institutional presence can therefore grow without proving equal safety, public legitimacy, or political power.

The infrastructure-geopolitical rotation adds the material-input layer. GAO and USGS show that domestic research, recovery, or manufacturing projects can coexist with high import reliance and application-specific substitution limits. Recycling and substitution are possible routes, not operating alternatives; the missing middle is qualified output, inventory, supplier switching, local incidence, and external response. Domestic capacity therefore does not by itself prove material independence or geopolitical leverage.

The platform-control rotation adds a measured administrative endpoint. Walmart reports access, deletion, and sale-opt-out requests separately, including completed, denied, and median-time fields. This is stronger than a policy-only route, but it still does not verify complete deletion, downstream copies, re-collection, appeal, or consumer trust. Completion is therefore evidence of processing capacity, not automatically durable practical control.

The external-response rotation adds a separate geopolitical stage. The CRS 2025 tariff timeline shows China, Canada, and the European Union answering U.S. pressure with countermeasures, negotiations, pauses, exemptions, and partial reversals. A response proves interaction, not leverage: the missing tests are firm pass-through, public incidence, coalition durability, and an attributed policy change.

The export-controls and domestic-firm-spillovers record adds a domestic-incidence stage to that trade-policy lane. The share of U.S. exports subject to controls doubled between 2010 and 2024; using the 2014 Russia restriction as a natural experiment, the Census CES study finds affected firms less likely to export controlled goods to Russia, but also reducing other products' exports and exports to other destinations, with lower average payroll. The targeted transaction and the firm-wide adjustment therefore cannot be treated as the same effect. Firm payroll is not a worker-level layoff or household-loss measure, and the study does not settle security effectiveness, diplomatic outcome, consumer incidence, later adaptation, or the national welfare balance.

The foreign-sourced telecommunications procurement record adds a geopolitical supply-chain stage. Section 889 reduced obligations to five named Chinese companies, and nearly 90% of active-contract companies publicly represented compliance, but GAO found that DOD and GSA did not broadly share affiliate information and implementation lessons with other agencies. Reduced procurement exposure is therefore not the same as verified equipment absence, avoided cyber events, operational continuity, or strategic autonomy.

The federal telecom-transition record adds a modernization-to-continuity boundary. GSA's transition of 221 agencies from legacy telecommunications contracts to Enterprise Infrastructure Solutions ran more than three years past its revised deadline, with legacy periods extended through May 2026. In six selected agencies, combined legacy Networx billing rose from $13.4 million in February 2025 to $40.9 million in March—a 206% increase—yet GSA did not know which agencies, if any, experienced service disruptions. An extension can be a continuity safeguard while also exposing agencies to cost and technology risk; neither the billing spike nor the absence of a known disruption establishes vendor causality, an outage rate, mission effect, employee effect, or whether the replacement contract improved service.

The aviation-spectrum cybersecurity record adds a threat-identification-to-monitoring boundary. In its review of eight spectrum-dependent National Airspace System systems, GAO found that FAA had identified interference, spoofing, jamming, and related risks but had not completed risk/mitigation assessments and updated security documentation, nor defined real-time monitoring for all spectrum threats. FAA fully addressed two of eight leading collaboration practices and partially addressed six; nine GAO recommendations remained open. A known technical risk and partial coordination are not evidence of a cyberattack, outage, flight delay, accident, passenger harm, or a failure of any specific flight operation.

The connected-vehicle pass makes the control problem more concrete. FTC and GM records establish access, deletion, opt-out, and location-disable routes, but vehicle technology and safety exceptions can leave residual collection or a privacy-versus-service choice. A formal control is not yet a verified privacy or mobility outcome.

The cross-platform FTC review adds the system-level counterweight. Across nine large social and video platforms, the agency reported broad collection and sharing, potentially indefinite retention, and cases where not all user data was deleted after a request. This is a platform-practice assessment, not a user-level failure rate, but it shows why administrative completion cannot by itself prove that data moving through affiliates and vendors is controllable.

The AI-assistant choice record adds a user-side version of the same control gap. In a weighted survey of 1,999 U.S. users, people reported routing different tasks to different assistants and learning trust through use, while privacy concern was much more common than paid privacy protection or knowledge of training practices. Reported multihoming and hypothetical willingness to pay are not durable switching, verified privacy, or independence from a dominant default.

The rural-housing coordination record adds a hidden social-infrastructure version. Service coordinators can help residents navigate eviction and Medicaid while HUD cannot reliably count all properties with coordinators or routinely use performance reports to judge outcomes. A housing unit plus a referral is therefore not the same as a usable service bridge, completed assistance, or durable housing stability.

The press-legitimacy rotation adds a cultural meaning layer: many Americans can agree that the government-news relationship is bad while disagreeing about how much power news organizations have and whether journalists or politicians should criticize one another. Shared diagnosis therefore does not equal shared legitimacy or trust.

The Pell/FAFSA rotation adds a higher-education version of the same interface problem: GAO found that formal Pell eligibility expanded after FAFSA simplification, including maximum-award eligibility, even as fewer students completed the application. The gains were uneven and some household configurations could lose eligibility. Eligibility is therefore a measured administrative stage, not proof of aid receipt, enrollment, persistence, or college access.

The chronic-absence rotation adds a school-participation version: Department of Education data count 13.4 million of 48.3 million students as chronically absent in 2022–23, or 27.8%, with wide state variation. Enrollment and attendance are therefore separate stages. The aggregate file does not explain the absence or show school response, learning, safety, belonging, or return.

The school-facility disruption record adds a physical-continuity stage. GAO estimates that 19% of districts canceled school for at least one day because of facility problems in 2024–25, affecting about 2 million students and 3.5 million learning days, while 47% reported a chronic facility issue in at least one school. Plumbing emergencies and extreme classroom temperatures were among leading causes. Facility disruption is a distinct route from attendance, but the survey does not measure student-level learning loss, family burden, health, repair completion, or later opportunity; closing can also protect students from unsafe conditions.

The MOEquity rotation adds an institutional-memory stage after emergency funding. GAO found that Education's real-time guidance lacked written MOEquity-specific procedures, data reliability problems limited verification of which districts were protected, and lessons learned were not reliably documented or shared. The rule and funding can therefore exist without durable organizational learning or a verified student effect.

The tribal-water rotation adds a construction-to-maintenance boundary. GAO found that property rules can exclude homes from an IHS-funded project, while multi-agency grant navigation can consume substantial staff time and Tribes remain responsible for operation and maintenance after construction. A built asset is therefore not yet reliable household service, health protection, or institutional autonomy.

The rural-water funding record adds the pre-construction bottleneck: 28 possible USDA and EPA programs do not remove incompatible deadlines, matching-fund risk, limited data, or the need for local administrative capacity and knowledge. A formal funding menu can therefore coexist with an unusable route to a safe, operating system.

The GAO broadband deployment, targeting, and sustainability record adds a targeting-to-sustainability boundary. By February 2026, all nine reviewed federal programs had begun distributing funds, but only three had completed-project data available. The $42.5 billion BEAD program is expected to run through 2030 and beyond; GAO found that provider-reported maps and public challenges shape where funds go and that its long-term financial-certification system still lacked detailed monitoring guidance. Funding, awards, and intended locations therefore remain separate from completed, affordable, reliable, and lasting digital access; missing completion data do not themselves prove project failure.

The FCC broadband availability/adoption/choice record adds the household conversion stages beneath that deployment route. At year-end 2023, 53% of households subscribed where 100/20 Mbps fixed terrestrial service was available, versus 26% where 940/500 Mbps was available. In the FCC's 2022 provider-count comparison at 100/20 Mbps, 7.9% of households had no terrestrial fixed provider, 37.4% had one, 36.6% had two, and 18.2% had three or more. Availability, conditional subscription, and advertised provider count are therefore not one access measure: none reveals price, installation, devices, reliability, actual use, meaningful substitutability, or a household's ability to switch.

The related dig-once coordination record adds the physical-governance middle: 46 of 52 state contacts reported a coordinator and 46 reported broad interagency coordination, while staff, IT, provider-participation, and outcome-visibility problems remained. Coordination can reduce the expected cost of a shared highway route without establishing construction, activation, price, reliability, or household use.

The wearable-health rotation adds a data-to-care boundary. GAO identifies potentially faster, more personalized, and more remote care, but also variable device reliability, workflow and liability problems, privacy needs, and unclear AI autonomy. Sensor output is therefore an input to care, not evidence by itself of better health or equal clinical control.

The Marketplace-broker rotation adds a consent-to-continuity boundary. GAO found that federal Marketplace registration and licensing did not reliably verify consumer authorization or notify consumers of every broker action; confirmed complaints tied to unauthorized enrollments and switches grew more than fourfold from 2023 to 2025, and GAO estimated at least 160,000 likely unauthorized application changes in the 2024 plan year. Selected state Marketplaces' one-time-passcode controls provide a counterexample, but neither route yet proves lasting coverage or care continuity. See the Marketplace broker-consent record.

The No Surprises rotation adds a legal-protection-to-market-response boundary. GAO found that in-network claim shares rose after implementation for three of four selected specialties, while emergency payment trends largely continued their pre-law directions. Provider participation, negotiated payment, patient liability, affordability, and health outcome remain separate stages. See the No Surprises network-participation record.

The No Surprises arbitration/network-pricing record adds a linked provider-market countereffect. The statute capped patient surprise bill liability and created final-offer arbitration for insurer-provider payment disputes; the NBER study reports high-volume, provider-favorable awards above the statutory benchmark. Provider-network participation declined in the most affected specialties and states, including after provider groups' first favorable awards, while evidence that more-exposed insurers raised marketplace premiums is suggestive. A patient-bill protection can thus alter provider outside options and insurance-market terms without establishing a patient's network adequacy, appointment wait, realized out-of-pocket spending, care continuity, health, or household financial recovery.

The Part D rotation adds a public-subsidy-to-household-security boundary. GAO found that the stabilization demonstration kept average standalone-plan premiums near $42-$43 and enrollment rose 2%, while Medicare took on an estimated $9.8 billion in 2025-2026 risk. The planned evaluation is still needed to separate the demonstration's effect from other benefit changes and to show medication or financial outcomes. See the Medicare Part D premium- stabilization record.

The Louisiana hepatitis-C subscription-model record adds a more complete public-purchasing path. Using differences-in-differences comparisons within Louisiana Medicaid, the study estimates that the 2019 subscription model tripled hepatitis-C treatment volume, reduced new diagnoses 23%, added $37 million in antiviral spending, and produced an estimated $266 million in five-year savings. This is a program-level treatment, diagnosis, and fiscal outcome result, not proof that every eligible person was reached, completed treatment, was cured, avoided reinfection, faced equal access, or experienced lower household cost. The estimated savings may also reflect outreach, diagnosis, provider behavior, and other implementation changes rather than the contract design alone, and do not automatically transfer to other states.

The federal eligibility-data rotation adds a measurement-to-accountability boundary. GAO found data-quality issues in all nine selected sources and cross-source inconsistencies in seven, while 2,074 identifier matches remained leads rather than proof of improper awards. Public systems can therefore be information-rich without being able to make a reliable case-level judgment.

The 2025 NHIS rotation adds a coverage-to-care boundary. Exchange-based coverage rose from 4.3% of people under 65 in 2021 to 6.3% in 2025, while 28.0 million people remained uninsured and the adult uninsured rate stayed at 11.6%. Coverage expansion and persistent unequal practical protection can therefore coexist; continuity, affordability, and care use remain open.

The AI-exposed college-graduates record adds an education-to-first-job boundary. A Census CES working paper reports that the most AI-exposed decile of college majors saw initial employment fall five percentage points and full-quarter initial earnings fall 13% after ChatGPT became available. About half of the earnings change came from lower pay within sectors and the remainder from movement toward lower-wage sectors. The result sharpens a broader pattern: education and credentials can remain available while the first conversion into paid work becomes less reliable or less valuable. The working paper does not establish permanent displacement, lifetime earnings loss, household insecurity, or a ChatGPT-only cause.

The AI coding production-stage record adds a task-to-realized-output boundary. In a matched event study covering more than 500,000 GitHub developers, autocomplete tools were associated with a 30% cumulative increase in commits, interactive agents with 180%, and autonomous agents with 240%. For autonomous agents the corresponding increase was 80% in projects and 30% in actual releases, while total usage across four software marketplaces did not increase despite more new apps. AI-assisted activity, shipped software, and software that users actually use are therefore distinct clocks. The study does not measure code quality, security, worker pay or bargaining, consumer value, firm profitability, or long-run survival; lower release growth can also reflect review, quality control, demand, or deliberate experimentation rather than a simple bottleneck.

The cross-border firm-network rotation adds a supply-chain version of the same conversion problem. A Census CES working paper reports that foreign disasters can reduce U.S. importers' purchase growth by up to 25 percentage points, while non-MNC buyers contract roughly twice as much as buyers inside global corporations; the intra-firm versus arm's-length comparison shows a similar gap. Firm structure can therefore change who absorbs a foreign shock, but the abstract does not show whether the result becomes substitution, delayed production, higher prices, worker effects, or household burden.

The export-control rotation adds a state-policy version of the same split. A Census CES working paper reports that the share of U.S. exports under controls doubled between 2010 and 2024. In the 2014 Russia restriction case, affected firms reduced targeted exports, exports of other products and destinations, and average payroll. A geopolitical restriction can therefore create observable domestic adjustment while its security or diplomatic result remains unknown. Domestic cost is not proof of policy failure, just as policy intent is not proof of strategic success.

The regional hospital-capacity record adds a public-infrastructure version. A Census CES working paper reports declining hospital counts alongside increasing hospital-industry employment and larger establishments, with rural and regional differences, particularly access challenges in rural Southern localities. System capacity and local reach can therefore move in different directions. The working paper does not show whether consolidation improved specialized care, increased travel and service gaps, or changed patient and household outcomes.

The congestion-pricing and EMS record adds a policy-to-service-time version. An NBER study of New York City's congestion-zone boundary reports an 18–21% traffic decline near the boundary and a 63–70 second, roughly 5–6% reduction in total EMS travel time after pricing began. A policy can therefore improve a measurable service route while patient survival, treatment quality, neighborhood distribution, ability to avoid the charge, and political acceptance remain open.

The rural-firm innovation rotation adds a complements version. A Census CES working paper's rural/urban decomposition, summarized by Census as emphasizing digital infrastructure, R&D, and human-capital deficits, challenges the idea that rural location alone explains lower innovation activity. Place differences may therefore be bundles of missing supports. The decomposition does not show that adding one support would cause innovation, firm survival, jobs, or regional convergence.

The bankruptcy-venue record adds a legal-institution-to-firm-survival pathway. A distance-based instrumental variable design estimates that Delaware venue can reduce liquidation and closure and preserve post-bankruptcy employment for the firms affected by proximity. The result complicates a simple venue-abuse story, but it does not establish individual worker security, consumer benefit, or effects for every court and firm.

The reusable-software record adds a technology-to-firm-scope pathway. Empirical adoption patterns and a calibrated model suggest that non-rival custom software can make multi-site scope more attractive and contribute to concentration. The model does not identify the resulting prices, wages, service quality, worker control, or consumer ability to switch.

The environmental lender-liability record adds a finance-to-environmental-behavior pathway. A legal change in lender cleanup exposure was associated with a 14.7% reduction in affected firms' abatement investment and higher pollution, alongside altered loan terms. The result shows institutional incidence before the household and health middle; firm emissions are not a household exposure estimate.

The housing-wealth labor record adds a same-household time-and-care pathway. Instrumented housing wealth is associated with lower women’s labor-force participation, especially for mothers of young children and women citing child-related reasons. Participation is not the endpoint: childcare options, unpaid hours, job quality, household security, and whether the arrangement is chosen or constrained remain open.

The tariff-incidence record adds a transaction-scale layer to trade policy. Once lost quantity discounts are separated from strategic pass-through, the 2018–2019 estimate assigns about 60% of the tariff to scale-free import prices and a significant share to foreign exporter markups. That does not identify retail, household, domestic-worker, or strategic outcomes.

The status-mismatch record adds a relative-status layer to residential mobility. Household income rank and neighborhood standing are associated with different short- and long-distance move patterns, consistent with spatial assimilation and relative deprivation interpretations. The model does not identify whether movement reflects belonging, opportunity, pressure, discrimination, or displacement.

The CTC/ACTC rotation adds a benefit-measurement version. Census's linked CPS ASEC/IRS estimate reports 91% participation among eligible taxpayers but 85% dollar participation in tax year 2021. The two figures should not be treated as one take-up rate or as household relief: taxpayer participation, dollars, timing, adequacy, and later material outcomes are separate stages.

The Child Tax Credit sentiment record adds a policy-loss-to-perception stage. A study using monthly Consumer Sentiment Survey data estimates a 1.7-point sentiment decline per $1,000 of lost 2021 credit, persisting nearly two years and appearing larger among lower-income families with multiple children. Benefit receipt, benefit loss, household room, and economic judgment can therefore move together across time, but the record does not link the same households to spending, government trust, voting, political identity, housing security, or a full recovery path.

The founder-background and hiring record adds an identity-to-firm pathway. Linked Census and LinkedIn data estimate that female-founded startups have a 36.4-point higher female employee share, while the corresponding adjusted differences are 51.2 points for Black employees, 37.3 points for Hispanic employees, and 11.3 points for non-college employees. Those differences persist at least 20 years across new-firm cohorts; the wage decompositions attribute the relative pattern to labor demand and higher relative wages for workers similar to the entrepreneur. Social similarity can therefore become an organizational channel for opportunity, but the decomposition does not identify intent or separate network information, trust, skill, geography, labor supply, preference, and exclusion in every case. It also does not establish firm performance, worker wellbeing, or intergenerational mobility.

The WIC rotation adds a measurement-to-reach boundary. A Census-FNS-ERS linked data project estimates eligibility and access across states, counties, and demographic groups, while Census and USDA/FNS estimates differ in method and scope. Better visibility can locate unequal reach without explaining the route barrier or proving benefit adequacy, food security, or child health.

The public-pension/private-equity rotation adds a financial-institution-to-firm boundary. A Census CES study reports lower returns and smaller fund matching for more severely underfunded public pensions, alongside productivity decreases in financed firms. Institutional funding pressure can therefore reach firms, but the source does not show whether the final burden falls on workers, beneficiaries, taxpayers, or firms—or whether the pattern is reversible.

The minimum-wage and robot-adoption record adds a policy-to-production version. A Census CES working paper reports that a 10% increase in the minimum wage is associated with roughly an 8% increase in manufacturing robot adoption. A wage floor can therefore change the firm's technology mix before the worker result is known.
