Robot adoption is not job loss, and the public abstract does not settle pay, hours, safety, training, bargaining power, or household security.

The affirmative-action-contracting rotation adds a policy-to-market-entry version. A Census CES working paper reports that after states ended affirmative action in contracting, existing minority- and women-owned contractors gradually downsized, with larger reductions among Black-owned and larger firms, while existing firms were not more likely to shut down. New MWBEs were relatively less common. Firm survival, firm scale, and new entry therefore move on different clocks; the result does not by itself establish worker harm, community opportunity, or public-service effects.

The female-teacher rotation adds a long-run cultural-institution version. A Census CES working paper links historical rural school exposure circa 1940 to later records and reports higher educational attainment for girls exposed to female primary-school teachers, followed by delayed marriage and childbearing, better-educated husbands, higher household income, and longer life. The pattern was stronger where parents had less education or women had fewer labor-market opportunities. A local institution can therefore matter most where substitutes are scarce, but the historical setting and public abstract do not settle the mechanism or current transfer. See the female teachers/female students record.

The women's education/career/children record adds a more local causal version. A Census CES study using a school-entry birthdate cutoff reports that women induced into some college had higher employment and earnings, more professional and higher-status jobs, more socially meaningful work, and better working conditions; their children also had better early-life health and prenatal inputs. Education can therefore carry both income and job-quality effects into the household, while the design remains local to the affected schooling margin and does not identify every mechanism.

The grandparenting and mortality record adds a family-care heterogeneity version. A Census–Social Security linked working paper following adults age 50 and older reports different mortality associations for coresident grandchildren and primary-caregiving duration across White, Black, Hispanic, and Asian groups: the same family arrangement can coincide with higher, lower, or duration-specific risk. Coresidence is therefore not one cultural meaning or one burden measure; it can reflect care, reciprocity, housing need, obligation, or prior health. The working paper is associational and does not identify the mechanism or the effect of public services, income, health care, or family support.

The minimum-wage-career rotation adds an age and policy counterexample. A Census CES study merging SIPP panels into LEHD reports strong later earnings growth for minimum-wage workers, driven mostly by young workers, while older workers show a different modest dip around the minimum-wage period. State minimum-wage increases did not significantly alter the future careers of workers who were on the minimum wage when the increases occurred. Starting wage, age, firm adjustment, and policy effect therefore remain separate stages.

The local-demand-shock rotation adds a place-and-measurement version. A Census CES study harmonizes several annual commuting-zone shock measures and finds that they are weakly correlated and produce different adjustment stories: trade-related shocks show little employment or migration response, while more general Bartik-style shocks are associated with meaningful changes in both. A local shock is therefore not one common object; migration is also only one of several possible household responses.

The Census neighborhood/firm/intergenerational-mobility record adds a linked place-and-labor-market mechanism. Its linked Census and administrative employment analysis reports that the between-neighborhood intergenerational earnings relationship was about twice the within-neighborhood relationship after adjusting for parent-income measurement error; mean parent earnings captured more than 80% of modeled variation in unrestricted neighborhood effects. The authors' decomposition distinguishes children’s person effects, associated chiefly with parents' and neighbors' person effects, from establishment premiums, associated chiefly with parents' and neighbors' establishment premiums. Neighborhoods explained about 30% of the conditional Black–White child-earnings gap in the model, while higher Black-share neighborhoods had higher child adult earnings conditional on neighborhood average earnings. These are modeled associations, not proof that moving a family, racial composition, or a particular school, network, firm, or policy caused an earnings outcome; adult earnings also do not establish wellbeing, belonging, safety, or political capacity.

The immigrant-student firm-placement record adds an identity-to-firm version. A Census CES study following college students from 2000 through 2020 finds disproportionate placement at both large firms, especially multinationals, and small firms or self-employment. Degree fields predict the large-firm route, while ethnic specialization helps explain the small-firm route. Immigrant students who stay in the United States earn more than native peers in the study, but selection, visa status, opportunity, and constraint remain separate questions; the public abstract does not establish whether either placement route is chosen freely, equally accessible, secure, or beneficial for household wellbeing and belonging.

The multinational-services rotation adds a cross-border capability version. A Census CES study of the 2008–2009 crisis reports that multinationals exporting services as well as goods to the same destination had higher goods-export growth than goods-only multinationals. The difference was driven by industrial- process intellectual-property sales and accompanied by higher affiliate services sales and domestic services employment. Cross-border capability can therefore support domestic adjustment, while worker, local, consumer, and strategic effects remain open.

The HOPE VI rotation adds a place-based social-connection version. A Census CES study reports lower neighborhood poverty after revitalization but no causal earnings effect for adults in public-housing units, while children raised in revitalized units later earned more, attended college more, and were less likely to be incarcerated. Increased interaction with surrounding peers was an important reported mechanism. Neighborhood composition, adult income, child opportunity, and resident control therefore move on different clocks.

The wealth-and-income mobility rotation adds an asset version of the place story. Using the same parent-child links, Census estimates show that counties can have different mobility patterns for income, homeownership, housing wealth, and total wealth; income and wealth mobility correlations are below 0.5. The Great Recession is associated with lower later income mobility broadly, while wealth losses are concentrated more among children from poorer families. The result is a descriptive map of unequal room, not a causal explanation by schools, housing supply, segregation, debt, transfers, or local government.

The institutional rental-ownership rotation adds a firm-concentration and denominator version. Institutional investors' holdings rose in all six selected metros, but their share of all single-family homes remained 1% to 3% while their share of the single-family rental subset reached 4% to 22%. A growing actor can therefore matter at the rental interface without owning the whole housing market. Ownership is not yet tenant experience, rent burden, maintenance, eviction, homeownership access, displacement, or durable place control. See the institutional rental-ownership record.

The HUD–LEHD trajectory rotation adds a longitudinal work-and-housing middle. First-time assistance entrants moved from declining toward rising employment and earnings trends, while eventual leavers' upward trends flattened after exit relative to stayers. Because entry and exit are selected events with different need and pre-trends, the study does not identify a clean causal benefit or loss. It does show why housing assistance should be tested through work, care, transport, and later stability rather than judged by receipt or earnings alone.

The house-price/firm-credit rotation adds a financial-channel version. A Census CES study of the Great Recession reports large and persistent employment effects at small businesses, especially young firms, with entry and exit contributing to the pattern. Reliance on personal assets or home equity and local bank credit shocks were associated with sensitivity to house prices. Housing can therefore be both a household asset market and a local firm-finance channel.

The business-application rotation adds an expectations-to-capacity version. A Census CES study links 17 million applications to outcomes and finds that applicants overestimate employment overall because many expect to enter but do not. Among those who expect and achieve entry, employment is typically underestimated. Application, entry, hiring, local conditions, and learning are therefore separate stages rather than one business-formation count.

The grandparent-care rotation adds a family-care heterogeneity version. A Census-SSA study of adults 50 and older reports higher mortality for White coresident grandparents, lower mortality for Asian coresident grandparents, higher mortality for Hispanic long-term primary caregivers, and lower mortality for Black short-term primary caregivers. Coresidence, caregiving duration, family support, health, and cultural meaning therefore cannot be collapsed into one burden measure.

The trade-welfare rotation adds a geopolitical-place version. A Census CES study develops a welfare measure that includes unemployment, participation, sector switching, and where workers live, then applies it across commuting zones to China's PNTR shock. Trade welfare therefore cannot be read from wages alone; relative local effects still do not settle household meaning, political response, or the national welfare level.

The counter-China-influence audit adds a geopolitical measurement version. State and USAID can report a large project portfolio and substantial funding while missing complete project-status data and a shared assessment of what changed. Strategic spending, partner implementation, and changed external behavior must therefore remain separate stages.

The U.S.-China global-role comparison adds a comparative legitimacy stage. Across 36 countries, China is viewed more favorably than the U.S. in many publics and is more often described as reliable in several middle-income countries, while the Philippines favors the U.S. on reliability. Favorability, reliability, peace contribution, actual dependence, and government alignment are separate outcomes; public reception alone does not show a transfer of strategic influence.

The Pew democracy-evaluation record adds a domestic public-judgment counterpart. In the March 2026 survey, 68% of U.S. adults said the country used to be a good democratic example but had not been in recent years, while 24% said it was currently a good example; 69% were dissatisfied with how democracy was working and 30% satisfied. Satisfaction differed sharply by party (86% dissatisfied among Democrats and Democratic leaners versus 51% among Republicans and Republican leaners). These are current evaluations, not institutional-performance audits, evidence of a shared reform program, or proof of turnout, protest, institutional withdrawal, or a causal effect of party control, economic conditions, or any particular event.

The democracy-assistance rotation adds a civic-continuity version. When a host government becomes part of the democratic risk, U.S. support may pivot toward civil society, media, or private actors, but an unplanned pivot can interrupt momentum and coordination. Funding, recipient safety, civic voice, and later democratic change therefore remain separate stages.

The Ukraine-oversight rotation adds a wartime-learning version. State improved the format and timing of reports and used some information for oversight, while data access and delayed outcomes still prevented complete cross-project evaluation. Better reporting, delivered assistance, and strategic effect run on different clocks.

The Iran protest-response record adds a foreign-action-to-domestic-meaning version. An NBER working paper using geocoded protest events and U.S.–Israeli strike exposure reports a shift from anti-government toward pro-government and anti-U.S./Israel protest after exposure, while total protest activity changed little. External force can therefore redirect the meaning and direction of mobilization without increasing mobilization overall. Repression, state messaging, fear, selective recording, civilian effects, and later legitimacy remain unresolved, so protest direction is not by itself strategic success or failure.

The economic-place civic-capacity record adds a cultural-material version. A large CPS-based study links local disadvantage, inequality, and the Great Recession to lower or changing formal volunteering, while the earlier rural advantage disappears after the recession. Formal volunteering, informal help, belonging, and political action remain separate forms of civic life.

The jail-exposure record adds a justice-contact version. Local-jail population and admissions were lower than in 2014, yet 2024 still involved millions of admissions, a large unconvicted population, and unequal racial exposure. Lower aggregate custody, pretrial experience, conviction, and later reentry therefore run on different clocks.

The federal reentry-timing record fills in a missing administrative middle. BOP could not readily identify all eligibility dates, and in a review of 29,934 people it had not applied all earned time toward placement for 21,190; limited RRC capacity and late payments to providers added operational friction. A formal reentry option is therefore not the same as timely transfer, usable housing or work support, community reconnection, or durable inclusion. The audit does not establish the individual effect of delay on recidivism or trust.

The community-supervision record extends that route beyond the jail door. About 3.68 million adults remained under probation or parole at the end of 2024 even as comparable-agency supervision fell over the decade. Completion, incarceration, absconding, and other exits are visible administratively; work, housing, family life, safety, and the meaning of freedom afterward remain open.

The Native-housing and homelessness record adds a culturally specific legibility version. GAO identifies 30 federal housing programs, but nearly all contacted Tribes and Tribal Designated Housing Entities said funding did not keep pace with construction, rehabilitation, or maintenance needs. Doubled-up living may be common, supportive, crowded, or unstable and may not fit federal homelessness definitions. The preliminary review does not measure national prevalence, duration, safety, tribal control, application success, construction completion, or durable housing outcomes, so program reach, cultural meaning, and safe housing remain separate.

The Tribal-federal shared-decision record adds a governance version of cultural legitimacy. GAO's five selected agreement cases identify 11 design features that strengthen shared decision-making, including consensus and dispute resolution, while agency authority and staffing capacity remain uneven. Voice becomes more than consultation only when the institution supplies decision rights, resources, and a way to correct conflict; the review does not show equal power, community outcomes, or durable self-governance.

The defense-arrangements record adds an alliance-administration version. DOD established 303 acquisition-related international arrangements associated with $64 billion in FY2021–2025, but personnel shortages, review delays, and uneven communication slowed the route. Agreement count and dollar value are therefore stages before implementation, joint use, partner response, and deterrence.

The weapons-acquisition record adds a rapid-pathway-to-capability version. GAO found an average delivery time above 12 years across a selected portfolio, and 18 of 40 reviewed Middle Tier programs entered with immature technologies; some ended without a fieldable capability. A fast acquisition label, budget, or prototype is therefore not the same as reliable deployment, sustainment, warfighter use, or deterrence.

The Poland–US defense reciprocity/co-production record adds a regional defense-industrial and sovereignty-meaning layer. Official Polish announcements record a UAS/C-UAS cooperation agreement intended to expand Poland's role beyond buyer to potential seller, a Poland–US–Estonia–Latvia Barracuda-500M production and supply agreement, and a reported $4 billion Foreign Military Financing agreement. But the later ministerial response makes the implementation stage explicit: detailed production, licensing, and technology-transfer obligations depend on confirmed Polish Armed Forces demand, while working groups prepare arrangements and initial activity is described as assembly and servicing before later localization. Official statements frame domestic technological competence as resilience and sovereignty. Agreements, financing, preparation, staged localization, and political meaning are each observable, but none establishes a purchase order, licensed control rights, commissioned plant, local-content share, produced or accepted unit, fielding, supplier replaceability, bargaining leverage, or deterrence.

The Task Force X-Baltic record adds an experiment-to-alliance-capability version. NATO reports that a three-week 2025 test fielded more than 70 uncrewed air, surface, and subsurface systems, with 75% average availability for eight hours a day; eight Allies then signed a Phase II commitment to nationally owned capabilities taskable by NATO, with reported procurement and deployment following. That is a meaningful conversion from test to institutional commitment and reported real-world use. It does not independently show continuous coverage, detection quality, crisis reliability, maintenance burden, cost sharing, public consent, adversary adaptation, or deterrence.

The technology-release and foreign-disclosure record adds a permission-to-capability version. DOD estimates about 7,000 foreign technology-release cases annually, with roughly 70% continuing existing sales or precedent, while policy discovery can take days to a year. Urgent Ukraine reviews were compressed from roughly a year to weeks or hours through overtime and deprioritizing other work. The route can protect sensitive technology while still producing partner-visibility and trust problems; reform completion does not establish faster approvals, transfer, partner use, interoperability, or deterrence.

The German brigade-in-Lithuania staffing record adds a social-capacity version of alliance readiness. About 80% of reported positions were filled by volunteers, but selected mandatory measures were added because more personnel were needed before the end-2027 operational target. Staffing, maintenance, family burden, host-country acceptance, and deterrence are separate stages; a readiness target is not yet a tested capability.

The Germany/NATO hybrid-response and alliance-posture record adds a later posture, training, and legitimacy context. NATO's September 2026 statement describes a permanent German armoured brigade in Lithuania, a new eastern-flank command role for the First German-Netherlands Corps, and solidarity after a reported hybrid attack at Leipzig airport. A separate Freedom Shield 26-I report documents a brigade-level exercise in Lithuania with about 2,900 personnel, 800 tactical vehicles, eight NATO nations, movement, tactical training, and live firing. German 2025 opinion data record support for higher defense spending (64%) and more personnel (65%), but only 10% said they felt well informed about foreign missions; a 2023 Lithuanian poll reported 82% approval of permanent German brigade stationing. These different dates and units do not establish consent for a specific 2026 response, full operational capability, independent incident attribution, local burden acceptance, adversary adaptation, or deterrence.

The military-readiness and sustainment record adds a force-conversion version. GAO's cross-domain synthesis reports maintenance, personnel, training, data, housing, fatigue, and availability gaps; the Army watercraft example fell from 75% fully mission capable in 2020 to below 40% in 2024 against a 90% policy goal. Modernization and operational demand can therefore coexist with weak sustainment at the point of need. This fleet example does not establish overall force weakness, combat performance, deterrence failure, ally willingness, or an external response.

The Ukraine–JEF AURORA record adds a partner-integration version. Ukraine moved from coordination under the JEF Enhanced Partnership to reported participation by Ukrainian drone operators and specialists in Sweden's AURORA 26 exercise, with combat experience and unmanned systems identified as exchange priorities. A partnership can therefore convert into a named exercise contribution without becoming membership or a security guarantee; completed tasks, sustained access, cost, public consent, adversary adaptation, and deterrence remain open.

The NATO resilience-baseline record adds a civil-military infrastructure version. NATO's 2026 requirements place food, water, health, communications, transport, border crossing, supply chains, and private-sector dependencies inside military-readiness planning, while also requiring resource planning, Host Nation Support, whole-of-society governance, and mitigation of effects on populations. A formal resilience framework can therefore widen the alliance's scope without proving national implementation, service continuity, public consent, cost distribution, crisis performance, or deterrence.

The Denmark host-nation rehearsal record adds an observed coordination stage. NATO's Steadfast Discovery 26 account reports a deployment rehearsal in Copenhagen and Herning with Danish authorities covering logistics, transport, movement, reception, and allied sustainment. A host-nation rehearsal makes civil-military interfaces visible, but the public account does not report movement times, failed procedures, corrective action, civilian continuity, cost sharing, public consent, or crisis performance.

The KFOR local-security-integration record adds a responsibility-transfer version. NATO reported an improved Kosovo security assessment and a gradual KFOR posture adjustment; Kosovo Police personnel then began integrating into KFOR's Visoki Decani Monastery security architecture, alongside a coordination surface naming EULEX, Kosovo institutions, Serbian Orthodox Church representatives, and Serbian Armed Forces. A mission can thus operationalize local institutional integration before it establishes resident acceptance, actor agreement, incident reduction, cost distribution, durable legitimacy, or a changed external behavior.

The carbon-tariff record adds a climate-geopolitical version. A quantitative model finds that a U.S. tariff alone can lower foreign emissions while raising U.S. emissions, whereas combining it with a domestic carbon tax produces a larger modeled global reduction. Modeled GDP, household incidence, firm response, and partner acceptance must remain separate.

The geoeconomic-coercion model adds a state-power-through-firms version. A great power may pressure a foreign government, private firms, or both through trade and financial links. A firm may be easier to pressure because it does not internalize every national consequence, while a government may reach firms that the great power cannot directly control. This is a modeled mechanism, not an observed success rate: real compliance, firm losses, public cost, coalition response, and strategic effect still need episode-level evidence.

The corporate-PAC record adds a domestic legitimacy version. After fatal school shootings, firms reduced visible PAC giving to some Republican House candidates, especially where consumer exposure made reputation more salient; the reported effect was selective, did not show a shift to Democrats, and returned toward baseline within about nine months. Visible political retreat can therefore be real without proving changed lobbying, policy goals, consumer trust, or durable corporate influence.

The FEC campaign-finance record adds the disclosed-money scale to that visibility boundary. Federal committees reported about $2.13 billion in congressional-candidate receipts, $1.12 billion in party-committee receipts, and $6.30 billion in PAC receipts from January 2025 through March 2026, with independent expenditures separately reported. Committee-level money is a capacity measure, not a count of unique donors, citizen participation, communication exposure, persuasion, turnout, policy change, or legitimacy; reporting and classification boundaries remain explicit.

The EAC election-administration record adds the attempted-ballot-to-counted-ballot stage. More than 158 million ballots were counted in 2024, while 1.74 million provisional ballots were cast; 73.8% were counted and 25.1% rejected under differing state and local rules. More than 98% of jurisdictions reported paper or auditable records. This shows election administrative capacity without proving equal access, improper rejection, cure success, voter trust, persuasion, or later political action; a rejected provisional ballot is not by itself evidence of wrongful exclusion.

The employment-and-mothers political-outcomes record adds a household-side political version. Among lower-income mothers, the study's policy-induced employment variation was associated with lower turnout, registration, political knowledge, and civic engagement, alongside more conservative policy preferences. Effects were stronger for unmarried, younger, less-educated, and nonmetropolitan mothers, and the reported political shifts were concentrated among White women despite larger employment gains among non-White women. Employment gains and political change therefore do not move one-for-one. Work may add income and social contact while taking time from civic life; the working paper does not identify the full care, workplace, income, household-security, or long-term political mechanism.

Latest breadth synthesis: usable participation is the common middle

The Census nonprofit-sector study adds a labor condition beneath community institutions. Nonprofits employ roughly one in ten US workers, yet average earnings are lower than in for-profit firms and the estimated gap varies widely by industry. This does not establish weaker mission or service; it identifies a material staffing and retention layer that must be connected to capacity, client access, quality, and trust before making a social-infrastructure claim.

The Census ACS review supplies a public-data version of the same interface pattern. Selected changes to layout, messaging, internet response, and mailings raised response in particular periods, while a 2022 test was neutral and the longer-run self-response rate continued to decline. Better institutional design can therefore help without proving equal representation, accurate completion, trust, or policy feedback.

The CDC Community & Connection page supplies a social-life version of the usable-participation boundary. Most adults in the displayed 2021 indicator reported receiving needed support, but the youth indicator was lower and a separate 2024 measure found health-related difficulty participating in social activities for 12% of adults. These are not same-year or same-person results; they support a distinction between support, ability to participate, belonging, and recovery rather than a causal claim about isolation.

The household-energy rotation makes the time dimension of usable participation more concrete. SIPP's adjacent-month screen places utility difficulty and tenure before childcare-related work prevention, food insecurity, housing hardship, and resource-band movement on the following record. The renter cells with utility difficulty and work-prevention care constraints show a particularly high hardship surface, but they are sparse and the fields are not a dated bill, shutoff, or newly occurring care episode. HHS and EIA evidence adds the institutional counterpart: LIHEAP can reach households and restore service, while public counts do not show whether the next bill, food, medicine, work, or safe-temperature trade-off was avoided. The combined lesson is not that assistance failed; it is that a payment can buy time without proving that the household's next usable option expanded. Timing of application, approval, payment, restoration, and the next bill should therefore be treated as separate stages rather than collapsed into "served" or "restored."

The historical US selection record adds a domestic political-access layer. Across Members of Congress born from 1830 to 1950, future officeholders came from economically advantaged families, and the family-background gap held or widened across cohorts. Four tested Progressive-Era reforms did not detectably change who reached Congress. This does not prove present-day exclusion or bad policy; it identifies a separate pre-vote stage where family resources, education, networks, money, and time may shape political entry.

The Vietnam draft-lottery study adds an institution-and-identity counterexample. Veteran status was positively associated with immigrant integration, but random draft risk did not produce a comparable positive effect on naturalization, language, residential integration, or cross-national marriage. Military service did produce a college-completion benefit, especially for non-Western immigrants. The broader lesson is that an institution can provide a concrete resource while its symbolic promise of shared belonging remains unproven; selection into the institution matters.

The newest cultural, household, public-system, and geopolitical rotations make one recurring subtheme clearer: formal availability is not the same as usable participation.

Surface What is visible What remains open
Housing and work HUD reports about 66 affordable units per 100 extremely low-income renter households, but only 38 affordable and available, and 34 affordable, available, and adequate; BLS finds leave access for 94% of wage and salary workers while 8% needed leave and did not take it Search, acceptance, workload, income loss, care result, lease-up, and later stability
Culture and civic life ATUS separates socializing, religious activity, and volunteering; NEA finds large income differences in arts attendance; Census CES links place disadvantage and recession to lower volunteering Meaning, transport and time cost, informal help, belonging, continuity, and political action
Digital participation A Facebook deactivation experiment finds short-run wellbeing gains while a separate study finds social pressure around collective exit; FTC reports $2.1 billion in 2025 reported scam losses where social media was the contact method Durable deletion, replacement, recovery, platform responsibility, and later trust or exit
Public and geopolitical systems BJS finds 23.3 violent victimizations per 1,000 people but 11.2 reported to police; a Secure Communities study estimates reduced reporting by Hispanic victims alongside increased offending, with reported crime unchanged as those changes offset; GAO finds allied space-coordination mechanisms alongside staffing and responsibility gaps; state budgets can retain reserves while adjusting positions and programs Response quality, safety, operational coordination, service incidence, partner contribution, and legitimacy

The social-media scam-loss record refines the digital-participation row. FTC reports $2.1 billion in 2025 losses from fraud reports identifying social media as the contact method, up from $261 million in 2020; 28% of loss reports identified social media as the contact route, more than 40% of those reports began with a product/service ad, and reported investment-scam losses initiated on social media totaled $1.1 billion. These are selected public and partner reports, not a population fraud rate, verified household loss ledger, or measure of platform causation. The record does not show individual exposure, platform response, refund/chargeback, household recovery, or durable trust and exit.

The newer Amazon Prime redress-route record adds a later remedy-design stage to the same receipt boundary. An FTC September 2026 update reports $845 million in aggregate redress issued by that point, a maximum of $200 per eligible consumer under the revised order, and automatic payment channels through mailed check, PayPal, or Venmo. Automatic distribution can reduce claim-form and notice-response burden, but the source does not provide a common eligible-consumer denominator, individual receipt or acceptance, account correction, continued use or exit, trust, or household recovery; future payment stages remained scheduled. The right cross-source comparison is therefore low-friction remedy design versus verified recovery, not “money issued equals consumers made whole.”

The allied-space coordination record keeps that geopolitical example bounded. GAO found multiple cooperation mechanisms with six partner nations, alongside staffing gaps, overlapping responsibilities, difficult points of contact, and missing implementation milestones; three recommendations remained open through the review period. Formal cooperation is therefore not the same as linked mission coordination, readiness, partner consent, or strategic effect. The review also does not show alliance collapse or a named operational failure: an emerging cooperation system can be incomplete while still functioning.

Lithuania's September 2026 air-policing record supplies a distinct later stage: the official Lithuanian account reports Italian NATO fighters scrambling to identify, intercept, and destroy a drone that entered Lithuanian airspace. Lithuanian and Italian defense ministers then framed the response as alliance unity and called for stronger European air defense, critical-infrastructure protection, and detection/neutralization capability. This supports a narrow geopolitical pattern: standing allied posture can become a reported protective action and an official legitimacy claim before strategic consequence is known.

Evidence unit Directly observed or reported What the atlas can safely connect Still open
Lithuanian Ministry of National Defence incident account and follow-up Named reported drone incursion; scramble, identification, interception, destruction; host-government alliance-unity framing and stated capability priorities airspace incursion → reported multinational operational response → official political interpretation/capability priority independent attribution/intent, full response sequence, cost, readiness depletion, civilian-risk reduction, public consent, procurement/delivery, deterrence, or adversary adaptation

The source is a host-government operational account, not independent incident verification or a measure of recurring mission effectiveness. A successful interception does not establish the affordability, sustainability, escalation, or legitimacy of repeated air-policing responses. See the Lithuania drone interception record.

Detailed cross-cutting map: from formal provision to lived agency, meaning, and power

The current corpus is now broad enough to support a more explicit social, cultural, institutional, consumer, technological, and geopolitical map. The sources should still not be pooled: they use different populations, units, periods, designs, and outcome definitions. What can be compared is the recurring conversion problem—how a formal resource, right, service, platform, institution, or strategic capability becomes (or fails to become) a usable option for an actor, and how that experience can acquire meaning and alter subsequent action.

The most defensible common sequence is:

material or institutional condition
  -> formal offer, capacity, or exposure
  -> usable route, attempted use, non-use, or exit
  -> receipt, burden, correction, remedy, or unresolved loss
  -> interpretation through fairness, trust, belonging, dependence, or control
  -> individual, household, organizational, civic, or geopolitical action
  -> later adaptation, legitimacy, substitution, resilience, or power shift

This is an organizing hypothesis and measurement discipline, not a claim that every source observes every arrow. The atlas is strongest on the first two or three stages, has partial evidence on receipt and correction, and is much more fragmented on attribution, meaning, and durable downstream action.

1. The main cross-cutting themes and their subthemes

Cross-cutting theme Recurrent subthemes What the current sources show What remains unobserved or weakly linked
Usable access rather than nominal access eligibility versus reachability; availability versus adequacy; application and timing friction; accessibility and information; attempted versus completed use Housing, leave, utility, health, election, ACS-response, and public-benefit records repeatedly separate a stated route from a route that can actually be used. Medicare Advantage prior-authorization records show denial, appeal, and reversal as distinct stages; provisional-ballot records similarly distinguish casting from counting. Whether the affected actor understood the route, whether a substitute existed, how much time or money was spent, and whether the final result protected the underlying need.
Receipt, remedy, and recovery are separate stages payment versus usable relief; replacement authorization versus replacement received; refund issued versus refund accepted; correction versus restored status; service restoration versus durable security SNAP EBT theft records, Amazon refund records, consumer-loss sources, Medicaid eligibility correction, and housing-exit evidence show why an approved remedy is not the same as recovered food, money, coverage, housing, or safety. A linked household-level recovery ledger, adequacy of the remedy, later arrears or hardship, and whether the person returns to or exits the institution.
Unequal optionality and replaceability cost of refusal; switching friction; lock-in; local scarcity; income and care constraints; strategic dependence Mortgage lock-in, platform choice and non-use, job mobility, AI-assistant choice, large-load infrastructure, arms-transfer concentration, and social-media exit evidence all show that formal choice varies with resources and alternatives. The counterfactual route actually available to each actor, the cost paid to switch, and whether a new option changes behavior beyond a short experiment or stated preference.
Material pressure is mediated by time and care work-care conflict; eldercare and childcare; health limitation; disaster disruption; household adaptation; labor-market meaning SIPP, ATUS, wildfire, SHED, NHIS, and employment-and-mothers records show that money, work, health, and care interact. A resource gain can coexist with time loss, unfilled care, or reduced civic participation. Complete household production, intra-household bargaining, care quality, longer-run wellbeing, and the mechanism connecting time pressure to trust, identity, or political action.
Institutional capacity is carried by people and infrastructure staffing and pay; maintenance; data governance; administrative learning; local implementation; interoperability; reliability Nonprofit earnings, FEMA and county capacity, USPS performance, GAO modernization and cybersecurity, SNAP data governance, allied-space coordination, and infrastructure records show that formal responsibility does not guarantee operational reach. Whether capacity gaps are visible to users, how responsibility is attributed, and whether learning or investment changes later service quality and legitimacy.
Participation, belonging, and meaning are not interchangeable support versus participation; membership versus service; identity versus action; social connection; collective exit CDC support/participation measures, Pew religious-institution and Latter-day Saint records, CIRCLE/civic-time evidence, Pew working-class and Latino-American-Dream records, and platform-exit studies distinguish belonging, perceived value, use, identity, and action. Person-level pathways from received support or identity to durable participation, collective organization, trust, or political behavior.
Information changes interpretation, but not automatically outcomes attribution; comparative information; prediction and advice; privacy knowledge; learning by trying; media exposure AI political-advice theory, working-class and American-Dream identity, news-platform civic engagement, privacy/deletion records, search experiments, and health-influencer evidence show that information can change beliefs, perceived agency, or contestation. Whether information is accurate, retained, acted upon, socially reinforced, and translated into material protection or institutional change.
Public and private systems distribute responsibility state versus firm accountability; platform governance; fraud and recourse; administrative correction; contractor and partner dependence Consumer remedies, AI companion inquiry, California broker deletion, FTC scam-loss reporting, Medicaid correction, and USPS/GAO records show that responsibility is often distributed across firms, agencies, contractors, interfaces, and users. Which actor can actually correct the harm, whether responsibility is accepted, and whether correction changes future design or behavior.
Geopolitical capacity becomes power only through use and response capability versus readiness; coordination versus operation; protection versus deterrence; supplier concentration; bargaining and coercion SIPRI, allied-space coordination, NATO ISR/KFOR, large-load and energy-infrastructure, AI-compute, arms-transfer, and Lithuania air-policing records show capacity, dependence, coordination, and some visible response. Partner consent, civilian burden, sustainment, adversary adaptation, deterrence, strategic substitution, and durable changes in counterpart behavior.

2. The strongest recurring trend propositions

The corpus supports the following bounded propositions. “Trend” here means a recurrent pattern across source families or a change documented within a source; it does not mean that every proposition is a time-series trend or a causal effect.

Trend A — Formal provision is increasingly being tested at the interface. Across benefits, health coverage, elections, public data collection, digital privacy, and strategic cooperation, the important question is moving from “does a route exist?” to “can the relevant actor discover, afford, complete, and rely on it?” The newest correction and remedy records make the middle stages visible: denial, appeal, reversal; theft, replacement authorization, receipt; request, deletion status, verified deletion; and formal cooperation, staffing, contact, and milestone gaps. This is a measurement trend in the atlas, not proof that institutions are universally deteriorating.

Trend B — Recovery is a bottleneck and a distributional divider. A visible payment, refund, replacement, or correction can stop short of restoring the thing that mattered: food, coverage, cash flow, housing stability, service quality, privacy, or safety. The gap is likely to be largest where the actor has little slack, few substitutes, or high costs of delay. The records support this as a recurring process distinction; they do not yet estimate a common recovery rate or show a universal decline.

Trend C — Agency is conditional on replaceability. Digital choice, employment mobility, mortgage decisions, care routes, consumer remedies, and state or alliance dependence all show that nominal choice can coexist with high costs of refusal. A user may be able to deactivate, a worker may be able to search, or a government may be able to diversify, while the practical cost of doing so remains high. The key subtheme is not choice versus no choice but unequal replaceability.

Trend D — Material conditions reach culture and politics through time, attribution, and social position. The corpus does not support a simple material-to-political-action law. Cash-transfer, employment, care, housing, working-class identity, Latino mobility, news-platform, and religious-life records show several possible pathways: more security, less available civic time, changed identity, changed attribution, more or less belonging, or no detected political shift. The same material change can therefore carry different cultural meaning across subgroup, tenure, race, family status, or institutional context.

Trend E — Institutional legitimacy is produced in encounters, not only in coverage or stated values. Religious organizations may be viewed as community-building while membership and participation are lower; a public agency may offer a correction while leaving restored status open; an alliance may frame an interception as unity while readiness and independent verification remain open. Legitimacy is therefore best treated as an outcome of visible competence, fairness, explanation, response, and alternatives—not inferred from provision alone.

Trend F — Capacity is becoming more networked, but accountability can become more diffuse. AI infrastructure, energy load, data brokers, fraud pathways, public-benefit administration, nonprofit delivery, and allied operations all depend on chains of firms, agencies, platforms, contractors, local systems, and partners. Networks can add resilience and capability, but they can also make failure attribution and remedy harder. The records establish distributed capacity and responsibility; they do not prove that networked systems are inherently less accountable.

3. Cross-lane mechanisms and counterexamples

The same apparent pattern should be tested against the following counterexamples before being promoted as a general theory:

  1. Assistance can coexist with pressure, but can also be protective in a narrower subgroup. The SIPP housing screen reverses direction by renter resource band; pooled assistance contrasts therefore cannot be read as one effect.
  2. A remedy can be real without being complete. Amazon refunds, EBT replacement authority, Medicaid correction, and prior-authorization reversal each show an institutional response, but not the same degree of receipt, adequacy, or recovery.
  3. Exit can improve wellbeing while collective exit remains costly. The Facebook deactivation experiment, social-media non-use comparisons, and platform-choice records distinguish individual short-run relief from durable substitution, social pressure, and collective bargaining power.
  4. Capacity can produce a visible success without proving durable power. The Lithuania interception and allied-space records show response and coordination claims, but not deterrence, sustainment, consent, or changed adversary behavior.
  5. Belonging can be institutionally meaningful without becoming formal participation. Pew religious-community measures and civic-time records show that perceived social value, membership, attendance, volunteering, and political action are different outcomes.
  6. Material improvement can coincide with reduced civic capacity. The employment-and-mothers record and care/work studies show why increased work or income cannot automatically be interpreted as increased agency or political participation.

These counterexamples are not exceptions to be discarded. They are the reason the atlas keeps source-specific units, clocks, subgroup boundaries, and missing arrows visible.

4. The current end-to-end status of the atlas

The atlas now has several strong partial chains, but not one fully observed social-cultural-geopolitical chain:

Chain stage Current evidence strength Representative examples
Material condition or exposure Strong in many bounded sources household finances, work/care, housing, infrastructure, platform exposure, capacity, military expenditure
Formal offer or institutional capacity Strong eligibility, coverage, public programs, platform controls, alliance mechanisms, infrastructure plans
Attempt, use, non-use, or exit Moderate and uneven leave not taken, provisional ballots, platform deactivation/non-use, care-seeking, privacy deletion request, participation time
Receipt, correction, remedy, or operational response Growing but fragmented appeal reversal, EBT replacement, refund/reissue, Medicaid correction, USPS performance, air-policing response
Adequacy, recovery, and protected outcome Weakly linked some housing, earnings, health, hardship, and exit-type outcomes; few complete remedy-to-recovery episodes
Attribution, meaning, trust, and belonging Observed in separate surveys/experiments institutional trust, identity, religious-community value, platform beliefs, perceived fairness, civic connection
Durable political, organizational, or geopolitical action Partial turnout and civic engagement measures, policy contestation, firm/platform response, alliance claims; causal persistence remains open

The central research gap is therefore not a lack of facts. It is a lack of linked episodes that preserve the actor, timing, alternatives, response, interpretation, and later consequence in one record. The next high-value work should prioritize such episodes over adding another unconnected percentage.

5. Priority next-pass questions

  1. Which public or private routes convert a formal remedy into verified recovery for the same person or household?
  2. When do people attribute a failed route to policy, institution, firm, frontline capacity, bad luck, or their own constrained options?
  3. Which combinations of money, time, social support, information, and alternatives convert material relief into durable agency rather than merely temporary stabilization?
  4. When does non-use indicate preference, protection, cost, fear, distrust, exclusion, or the absence of a substitute?
  5. Which institutional investments—staffing, maintenance, interoperability, data governance, or local implementation—produce observable improvements in receipt, correction, trust, and repeat use?
  6. In geopolitical networks, when does coordination become partner acceptance, sustainable readiness, deterrence, or bargaining power rather than only a formal agreement or one successful response?

This section is a comparative synthesis of bounded records. It should be updated when a new source fills an arrow, supplies a counterexample, or changes the unit of analysis; it should not be used to manufacture a pooled index of social health, cultural cohesion, institutional legitimacy, or geopolitical power.

New cross-cutting bridge: distribution becomes meaning through attribution

Across the corpus, material and operational outputs acquire cultural or geopolitical meaning through a further sequence that should not be assumed:

offered protection, service, capacity, or coordination
  -> uneven receipt, burden, delay, visibility, and practical usability
  -> attribution: who is seen as responsible, capable, indifferent, or coercive
  -> interpretation as fairness, abandonment, dependence, solidarity, or control
  -> non-use, complaint, support, organizing, exit, partner acceptance, or resistance
  -> later legitimacy, trust, adaptation, or changed counterpart behavior

This bridge joins the cultural and geopolitical lanes without claiming they are the same phenomenon. On the household and civic side, SIPP assistance and housing-pressure records show that an offered benefit can coexist with different next-month hardship paths; CIRCLE, CDC, and civic-time records show that support, belonging, and participation have different distributions and time requirements. The person may therefore interpret a public system through whether it was reachable and adequate, not merely through the formal promise. Those records do not identify the person's attribution or later political judgment.

On the institutional side, nonprofit pay and staffing evidence, ACS response experiments, and public-system records show that the organizations carrying care, culture, representation, and administrative access have their own capacity constraints. A visible service gap may be read as institutional indifference even when the immediate cause is staffing, funding, timing, or interface design. Conversely, a successful receipt can support confidence without proving durable legitimacy. The source units do not permit a general theory of public trust from output or coverage alone.

The geopolitical analogue is similarly staged. GAO's allied-space review shows formal cooperation with staffing, responsibility, contact, and milestone gaps; the NATO ISR and KFOR records show movement into operation and local coordination; the Lithuania incident account reports a concrete allied response and an official unity interpretation. Together they support a capability-to-meaning pathway—coordination can become a visible protective signal—but they do not establish partner consent, civilian burden, deterrence, or changed adversary behavior. Official framing is evidence of a claimed interpretation, not proof that all audiences shared it.

The same distinction applies to private and digital systems. FTC social-media scam-loss reporting makes exposure and loss visible at an aggregate contact route, while the platform records leave recovery, responsibility, and exit open. A user may interpret the same platform as useful, risky, unavoidable, or unaccountable depending on loss, remedy, alternatives, and information about who could have prevented it. The source does not observe that interpretation for each affected person.

Cross-cutting finding: distribution is not yet meaning. Meaning is formed through the interaction of incidence, visibility, attribution, alternatives, and response. This is the strongest current bridge between household security, civic culture, institutional legitimacy, and geopolitical power, but the corpus mostly observes these stages in separate source units.

Next decisive test: link a dated intervention or incident to the affected person, place, organization, or partner; record who received what, who bore the cost, what alternatives existed, what explanation or attribution was available, and whether the response was used, contested, supported, or avoided. Then follow later trust, belonging, political action, recovery, partner acceptance, or counterpart adaptation. Without that linkage, the atlas should label cultural and geopolitical meaning as an observed interpretation or open mechanism—not as the automatic consequence of unequal distribution.

These sources are not a pooled dataset and do not describe the same people or episodes. Their value is comparative. Across housing, leave, arts, volunteering, digital life, public safety, state budgeting, and allied operations, the important missing middle is the interface where a person, community, worker, or partner must actually use the offered route. That interface carries money, time, fear, social cost, information, staffing, and dependence.

This sharpens the program's cultural-geopolitical interpretation. Civic capacity and alliance capacity are not only matters of stated values or formal commitment; both depend on mundane organizational pathways being reachable, understandable, staffed, and safe enough to use. Conversely, non-use is not one meaning: it can reflect preference, protection, cost, fear, missing trust, or the absence of a workable substitute.

The next decisive comparison is therefore not another availability count. It is a repeated person-, household-, place-, or operation-linked record that follows an offered route through attempt, alternative or non-use, response, protected or sacrificed outcome, and later belonging, trust, action, recovery, or exit. Until that exists, the atlas should describe this as a recurring interface pattern, not a single causal social theory.

Latest breadth rotation: time, consumer recourse, and geopolitical capacity

Three new primary records widen the active map without pretending to close the same-unit gap. The 2025 ATUS release shows that household work and care remain unevenly allocated by gender and employment status, while average socializing and communication time is lower than in 2015 and games/computer leisure time is higher. This is a time-allocation and cultural-participation signal, not proof of social withdrawal or a causal digital substitution.

The 2026 GAO review of countering-Chinese-influence programs adds a state-capacity and geopolitical evidence pattern: State and USAID reported an estimated 470 projects and $1.2 billion in allocations, but missing project metadata and the absence of a portfolio-wide results-assessment process make strategic effect harder to observe. Spending and proposal machinery therefore outpace evidence of influence, partner response, or durable geopolitical leverage.

The September 2026 FTC/Amazon Prime redress revision adds a consumer-power implementation shift: more than $845 million had been issued, eligibility was expanded, and new payments were to become automatic rather than claim-based. That reduces paperwork and may widen reach, but aggregate issuance still does not show individual receipt, adequacy, continued use, switching, or trust repair.

Rotation finding: across care, geopolitics, and consumer recourse, formal capacity is becoming more visible and sometimes more automated, while the distribution of usable time, strategic effect, and lived recovery remains the decisive unmeasured middle. These records strengthen the broad trend atlas; they are separate units and must not be pooled into one causal story.

The next platform-and-AI rotation adds a sharper cultural and geopolitical version of the same tension. The FTC's TAKE IT DOWN enforcement regime turns platform safety into a request process with a 48-hour removal window and a regulator complaint route, but the public record does not yet show completed removal or non-recurrence for affected people. Pew's 2026 U.S. survey finds chatbot use rising to 49% from 33% in 2024 while 67% report little or no confidence that the U.S. government can regulate AI effectively. A separate Pew cross-national survey finds median trust in China to regulate AI at 43%, versus 35% for the U.S. and 34% for the EU. Adoption, domestic legitimacy, and geopolitical regulatory trust are therefore moving on different clocks.

These are not evidence that one governance model is superior. They show that platform rules, everyday use, perceived institutional control, and international legitimacy are distinct trend surfaces that can diverge even as AI becomes more embedded in daily life.

Latest breadth rotation: civic participation, firm diffusion, and incidence

Four additional records extend the map across social participation, business technology, household consumption, and trade. They point to a common mechanism without implying a common population or effect.

Pew's 2025 engagement study separates adults into Mobilizers (9%), Connectors (28%), Spectators (31%), and Outsiders (31%) using political, civic, religious, and news behaviors. Voting and contacting officials vary sharply across the groups, but the groups are politically mixed. This is evidence that civic participation is multidimensional, not a single enthusiasm scale; it does not show why a person enters a group or whether the classification persists.

Census BTOS data add a firm-side asymmetry to the AI story. Current AI use was reported by roughly 20% of employer businesses overall in May 2026, compared with 37% of firms with at least 250 employees, 32% of firms with 100–249 employees, and 39.7% in information. Fewer than 20% of firms with four or fewer employees reported use. Adoption therefore appears to diffuse through firm size and sector capacity rather than evenly across workplaces. The record does not establish productivity, worker displacement, or redistribution of control.

The consumption channel is also organizational. An NBER working paper using consumer-panel data finds that working from home shifts shopping online and toward weekdays, increases trips while reducing shopping minutes, and can raise prices paid partly through fewer deals and a redistribution of shopping responsibility. The estimated grocery-price effect is about 1%, but the source does not measure welfare or food hardship. The relevant trend is that work arrangement changes household market behavior and the hidden price of convenience.

Finally, the NBER tariff study traces geopolitical policy into domestic incidence: about 26% of the tariff increase passed through to consumer prices, with 64% of that consumer-price effect attributed to direct foreign-variety effects and 36% to imported inputs and domestic markups. The indirect channel arrived over roughly nine to twelve months. This makes attribution and timing central: a policy can be formally imposed at the border while its costs are distributed later through firms, products, and household purchasing decisions.

Rotation finding: civic capacity, workplace technology, household consumption, and geopolitical trade policy are all stratified by the practical capacity of the unit receiving or transmitting the change. Participation is organized into different civic modes; AI adoption is concentrated in larger and information-intensive firms; remote work reallocates shopping labor and price exposure; and tariff incidence travels through supply-chain layers. Together these records strengthen the atlas's broader claim that nominal availability is not the same as usable capacity or equal incidence. They remain separate source units: none supplies the missing link from exposure through individual interpretation, recovery, or durable political action.

New institutional-structure signal: public capacity is organized through many units

The machine-readable record us-census-government-organization-units-1942-2026 and the Census Bureau's 2026 Government Organization tables add a structural public-sector signal to the source rotation. The United States contains 91,780 federal, state, and local government units in the 2026 table. The comparable series was 155,116 in 1942, reached a low of 78,269 in 1972, and then rose to 91,780 by 2026. State totals also vary substantially, from 182 units in Alaska to 4,547 in California (with the District of Columbia counted separately).

This is not evidence that fragmentation is good or bad. It shows that public capacity is delivered through an historically changing and geographically uneven organizational structure. That structure can support local tailoring, but it can also create coordination, attribution, and route-discovery costs. The counts do not measure budgets, staffing, service quality, resident trust, or whether a person can successfully use any particular government route.

Rotation finding: the atlas now has a cleaner institutional bridge between formal public capacity and lived access. Government-unit counts describe the organizational layer; the household, civic, consumer, and remedy records describe the encounter layer. The trend question is therefore not simply how much government exists, but how organizational structure changes the visibility, coordination, and contestability of the routes people and firms actually use.

New mobility signal: emerging automation is already ordinary infrastructure

The machine-readable record us-census-htops-autonomous-features-2026 adds an everyday technology signal from the Census HTOPS transportation tables. In the July 15–August 3, 2026 topical release, 129.4 million represented adults reported driving a vehicle with autonomous features in the prior week—about 49.5% of the represented adult population. The table defines the features broadly, including speed adjustment, lane steering, and braking; reported use was about 42.0% among ages 35–49 and 56.5% among adults 65 and older.

This is not a finding that half of adults use fully autonomous vehicles. It is an exposure-and-use measure for driver-assistance functions, and Census labels the estimates experimental. It does, however, widen the technology trend from firm adoption and platform use into ordinary mobility: automation can become embedded in daily routines before public debate settles questions of safety, trust, liability, access, or human control.

Rotation finding: technology diffusion is not only an enterprise or policy event. It can become mundane household infrastructure, with the important social and political questions moving to who gets access, who remains in control, who bears failure, and how people interpret a system they use without necessarily choosing it as a political or cultural identity.

New comparative signal: global-order preferences are locally routed

The record comparative-pew-india-pakistan-global-order-2026 adds a distinct public-geopolitics mechanism: rival populations can assign threat and alliance roles differently even while viewing each other as the central danger. Pew's 2026 survey finds that 54% of Indians name Pakistan as India's greatest threat, while 43% of Pakistanis name India. Pakistanis most often name China as their most important ally (75%); Indians most often name Russia (36%), followed by the U.S. (16%).

The divergence is also internally structured. Indian Muslims are less likely than Hindus to name Pakistan as India's greatest threat and more likely to view Pakistan favorably. These are public judgments, not direct measures of capability or alliance reliability, but they show that the global order is not received as a single strategic map. National conflict, domestic identity, religious position, and perceived economic or security partners route the same external powers into different political meanings.

Rotation finding: geopolitical influence should be tracked through at least three separate surfaces—material capability, elite alignment, and public interpretation. A state can be formally partnered with one actor while its public sees another as the key ally, threat, or economic reference point. The gap is a potential source of legitimacy, bargaining, and policy constraint, not proof of future realignment.

New geopolitical meaning signal: the same conflict is attributed through different routes

The record comparative-pew-israel-palestinian-coexistence-meaning-2026 adds an attribution layer that operational and opinion-only records cannot provide. In Pew's spring 2026 survey, only 17% of Israelis and 21% of Palestinians in the West Bank and East Jerusalem said Israel and an independent Palestinian state could coexist peacefully; 56% of Israelis and 68% of Palestinians in the West Bank and East Jerusalem said this was not possible. Respondents were then asked to explain their answers in their own words.

The explanations overlap around land, violence, and distrust, but the attributed obstacle differs: Israeli respondents more often described an independent Palestinian state as a security or existential threat, while Palestinian respondents more often described occupation, control, checkpoints, and political rights as barriers. That is not just a difference in sentiment; it is a difference in the causal story each population uses to interpret the same geopolitical arrangement.

The study was fielded during the Iran war, did not include Gaza, and observes stated explanations rather than later action or reconciliation. Its value for the atlas is narrower and stronger: geopolitical meaning is not produced by capacity or violence alone. It is produced through attribution—who is seen as responsible, what risk is visible, what remedy is credible, and whose security or sovereignty is treated as the relevant unit.

Rotation finding: cross-source geopolitical analysis should preserve both the shared condition and the competing causal narratives. A common event can generate incompatible interpretations of protection, threat, occupation, security, or inevitability; those interpretations are potential mechanisms of future support, resistance, non-use, or bargaining, not interchangeable survey opinions.

New U.S. perception signal: sentiment can warm without strategic convergence

The record us-pew-china-feeling-thermometer-2016-2026 adds a U.S.-specific time trend to the geopolitical perception layer. Americans' average feeling- thermometer rating of China rose from 28 in 2021 to 37 in 2026. Warm ratings rose from 11% to 19%, neutral ratings from 20% to 27%, and cold ratings fell from 68% to 54%; views remain more negative than positive overall.

The result should not be read as a simple normalization of China. Younger adults and Democrats report warmer views than older adults and Republicans, and a warmer feeling thermometer does not measure support for Chinese policy, reduced security concern, or willingness to deepen economic dependence.

Rotation finding: geopolitical sentiment has its own clock. Public warmth can increase while strategic competition, regulatory distrust, or policy disagreement remain. The atlas should therefore keep affect, threat judgment, material dependence, elite policy, and observed counterpart behavior as separate trend surfaces rather than treating any one as a proxy for the others.

New AI meaning signal: perceived economic risk is stratified by exposure and awareness

The record comparative-pew-global-ai-job-inequality-expectations-2026 adds a comparative perception layer to the firm-adoption and U.S. AI records. In 34 of 37 countries, more people expect AI to reduce jobs than to create them. The median is 55% in high-income countries versus 36% in middle-income countries; middle-income publics are more likely to say they are unsure. Similarly, the median share expecting AI to increase inequality is 35% in high-income countries versus 22% in middle-income countries, while the U.S. share is 46%.

The pattern is not simply optimism versus pessimism. It may reflect differences in exposure to automation, awareness, labor-market structure, or the ability to imagine the technology's consequences. In the U.S., adults ages 18–34 who are more concerned than excited rose from 40% in 2024 to 55% in 2026. These are expectations, not observed job losses or productivity effects.

Rotation finding: technology becomes politically meaningful before its outcomes are settled. Firm adoption, public awareness, perceived job risk, and inequality expectations can move on different clocks; the gap between them is part of the social trend rather than noise to be averaged away.

New Brazil signal: democratic satisfaction and external-partner meaning diverge

The record comparative-pew-brazil-democracy-trading-partners-2026 adds a pre-election public-meaning surface outside the U.S. In spring 2026, 37% of Brazilian adults said they were satisfied with how democracy was working and 59% were not satisfied. Confidence was not uniformly low: 73% expressed at least some confidence in college and university professors and 70% in scientists, while 68% had little or no confidence in elected officials and 57% in business leaders.

Brazilian views of its two major trading partners were nearly balanced in 2026: 47% favorable toward the U.S. and 46% toward China. But the balance had moved over time—U.S. favorability fell from 64% in 2024, while China rose from 39% in 2023—and ideology routed the meanings differently. Left-leaning adults were more favorable toward China; right-leaning adults were more favorable toward the U.S.

Rotation finding: political legitimacy, institutional trust, and external partner preference need not travel together. A public can be dissatisfied with domestic democracy, trust scientific or professional authorities, and still hold roughly balanced views of competing international partners. That is a political-cultural configuration, not a single trust score or a forecast of electoral alignment.

New infrastructure legitimacy signal: AI capacity can become local burden before benefit

The record us-pew-data-center-local-legitimacy-2026 adds a place-based legitimacy layer to the AI infrastructure and firm-adoption surfaces. In the Pew January-August 2026 comparison, the share of U.S. adults saying data centers have a mostly bad impact rose from 39% to 54% for the environment, 38% to 50% for home energy costs, and 30% to 49% for nearby quality of life. Perceived benefits also rose, but more modestly: local jobs went from 15% to 24% mostly bad and local tax revenue from 12% to 21% mostly bad. By August, 60% were not too or not at all comfortable with a new data center in their area, while awareness of data centers had become nearly universal.

This is not evidence that communities reject AI capacity in the abstract. It shows that the infrastructure can acquire a local burden meaning before its benefits are trusted or evenly distributed. Rural environmental concern and Republican concern about nearby quality of life both increased, so the issue cannot be reduced to one partisan or urban political route.

Rotation finding: AI build-out has a siting-legitimacy pathway distinct from adoption, jobs, or national competitiveness. The atlas should track capacity expansion, local resource pressure, perceived benefit, awareness, and comfort with siting as separate surfaces; otherwise public resistance or acceptance will be misread as a generic attitude toward technology.

New democracy signal: national frustration can coexist with local legitimacy

The record us-gallup-local-national-democracy-gap-2026 adds a local-versus- national legitimacy surface to the political and trust lanes. In the 2026 Gallup-Kettering survey, 56% of U.S. adults said national democracy was doing very or moderately poorly and only 19% said it was doing well. Their city or town received a less negative assessment: 34% said local democracy was doing well and 21% said it was doing poorly. At the same time, 60% said democracy was stronger 50 years ago, and 45% expected it to become weaker over the next 50 years rather than stronger (31%).

The gap is not simple optimism about proximity. Only 28% trusted that political leaders would be held accountable to the nation's laws and Constitution; 59% said the executive branch had too much power; and 60% rated equal treatment under the law poorly. The source also reports that trust in local leaders and neighbors is associated with more positive views of democracy, but this is not a causal estimate.

Rotation finding: democratic legitimacy is geographically layered. People can distrust national accountability while retaining more favorable local judgments, suggesting that proximity, observability, and social relationships are mechanisms to track separately from national institutional confidence.

New cultural-consumption signal: local opportunity and cultural use do not align automatically

The record us-census-htops-arts-cultural-participation-2026 adds a recent cultural-practice layer using the Census HTOPS arts tables. During the four weeks before the July 15-August 3, 2026 survey, an estimated 20.5% of adults attended live music, dance, or theater, 9.5% attended an art exhibit, 22.6% went to the movies, and 17.9% created, practiced, or performed personal art. About 62.9% agreed that their neighborhood or community had plentiful arts and cultural opportunities.

The age pattern is not a simple scarcity gradient. Personal art creation was reported by 26.2% of adults ages 18-34 versus 13.8% of adults 65 and older, while agreement that local opportunities were plentiful was higher among older adults (71.5% versus 52.3%). Perceived local supply and recent cultural use therefore need to remain separate surfaces; one does not establish the other.

Rotation finding: cultural participation is organized through both opportunity and practice, with different age groups occupying different parts of that route. The atlas should track local supply, recent attendance, personal creation, cost, time, and social invitation separately rather than treating cultural vitality as a single participation rate.

New public-capacity signal: infrastructure access is shaped by rules and maintenance, not construction alone

The record us-gao-tribal-water-infrastructure-access-maintenance-2026 adds a public-service lifecycle layer to the infrastructure and unequal-exposure themes. GAO reports that IHS estimated at least $6 billion was still needed as of November 2025 for safe tribal drinking water and wastewater disposal, even after major federal appropriations. The report identifies two distinct access frictions: eligibility rules can exclude homes and community properties inside tribal communities, and fragmented IHS, EPA, and USDA processes can turn a small capital need into a large administrative route. In one example, IHS officials reported spending more than 80 hours helping a Tribe obtain an $8,000 grant.

The lifecycle does not end at construction. GAO reports that IHS generally does not fund routine long-term operations and maintenance such as water operator salaries and energy costs; one area office's four tribal utility consultants were expected to support 104 Tribes. Eligible costs in the sanitation-deficiency database rose from $4.7 billion in FY2023 to $5.9 billion in FY2024, partly because of aging infrastructure and inadequate maintenance.

Rotation finding: public capacity should be modeled as eligibility, application, construction, operating labor, energy, maintenance, and repair stages. A completed project is not the same as reliable service, and a formal funding program is not the same as reachable assistance for the people and properties within a community.

New health-AI signal: convenience can drive use while transparency and control lag

The record us-pew-ai-health-information-control-transparency-2026 adds a practical decision-making layer to the AI, health, and trust surfaces. In the June 2026 Pew survey, 34% of U.S. adults had used an AI chatbot for at least one health or medical reason. Speed was the most common stated motivation (28%), followed by figuring out symptoms (25%), low or no cost (22%), understanding a doctor's diagnosis (22%), and lab results (20%). Among these users, 95% said the information was at least somewhat helpful.

The use signal is not the same as institutional acceptance. Seventy-two percent said it was highly important for a provider to disclose AI use, 53% said they had little or no say over whether a provider uses AI, and 63% wanted more input compared with 21% who were comfortable with their current input. Nearly half (46%) were unsure whether a provider had used AI, and among those who said a provider had used it, only 22% understood very or extremely well how it was used.

Rotation finding: AI can enter consequential decisions through a convenience-and-cost route before visibility, consent, and control are settled. The atlas should therefore track personal use, perceived usefulness, provider disclosure, data comfort, and decision authority as separate stages rather than using adoption as a proxy for legitimacy.

New firm-side signal: input-price pressure is running ahead of the business outlook
