The record us-census-btos-business-price-pressure-outlook-2026 adds a high-frequency firm-side layer to the household cost and business-capacity surfaces. In Census BTOS data as of September 6, 2026, the current input-price index was 70.1, while current revenue, employees, and hours indexes were 42.9, 48.1, and 46.6. The six-month outlook was also more price-heavy: future input prices were 76.3, compared with 52.3 for future demand and 51.0 for future employees.

This is not a direct consumer-price or employment estimate. It is a useful mechanism signal because firms can translate input pressure through prices, hours, staffing, quality, margins, or substitution, and different sectors may choose different routes. The future indexes represent expectations, not realized outcomes.

Rotation finding: household cost pressure and firm cost pressure should be linked as a chain with an open transmission stage. The atlas should track input prices, firm responses, consumer incidence, employment, and expectations separately rather than treating a business outlook index as a realized household trend.

New household-material signal: improving headline indicators do not collapse the security surface

The record us-census-2025-income-poverty-insurance-divergence adds realized household outcomes to the firm-price and cost-pressure lanes. Census reports that real median household income reached $87,460 in 2025, up 2.6%, while the official poverty rate fell to 10.2% and child poverty reached a historic low of 13.4%. But the Supplemental Poverty Measure remained 13.1%, not statistically different from 2024, and 7.9% of people were uninsured for the entire year, also unchanged statistically.

The route composition matters. Public coverage for adults ages 19-64 fell to 17.3%, driven by a Medicaid decline, while employment-based coverage remained the largest route. Income at the 90th percentile increased 1.7% while the 10th-percentile estimate did not change significantly. These are not contradictory statistics: they measure different resource definitions, expenses, transfer systems, and coverage pathways.

Rotation finding: household security is a bundle, not a single prosperity score. The atlas should keep pretax income, official poverty, after-tax and transfer resources, medical and housing expenses, insurance route, and lower- tail movement separate; a favorable headline can coexist with persistent exposure in the channels households actually use.

New multilateral signal: support for an institution can exceed confidence in its performance

The record us-gallup-un-global-support-performance-gap-2025-2026 adds a global-institution layer to the geopolitical and public-systems surfaces. Across 137 countries in Gallup's 2025 World Poll, the median share approving of the UN's job was 50%, versus 26% disapproving, with majorities approving in 67 countries. But the pattern was geographically uneven: net approval was strongly positive in Southeast Asia and sub-Saharan Africa and negative in the Middle East and North Africa; among Security Council members with data, approval ranged from 79% in Denmark to 15% in Russia.

The U.S. role-specific evaluation is more critical. In September 2026, 45% said the UN was doing a good job providing humanitarian assistance, while 73% said it was doing a poor job maintaining international peace and security and about seven in ten rated it poorly on human rights and international law. The humanitarian rating was the strongest of the five roles tested, and party groups differed in their positive assessments of peacekeeping (32% of Democrats, 23% of independents, and 19% of Republicans).

Rotation finding: institutional legitimacy has at least two clocks: whether an institution is wanted in principle and whether it is credited with delivering in a specific role. The atlas should preserve role, place, crisis, familiarity, and performance attribution rather than collapse them into one global approval score.

New platform-consumption signal: speculative attention is expanding through sports, not just politics

The record us-pew-prediction-markets-sports-attention-2026 adds a platform-mediated consumer and attention layer. Pew's analysis of Kalshi and Polymarket data finds combined monthly global notional trading volume rising from $25.7 billion in May 2026 to $53.0 billion in July. The increase was largely sports-driven: in July, sports volume was $31.4 billion on Kalshi and $10.6 billion on Polymarket, while politics volume was only $169 million and $727 million respectively.

This is a different participation mechanism from polling or political action. Users buy and sell binary event contracts, so repeated trading, platform liquidity, seasonal events, and speculative attention can generate large volume without showing broad user adoption or civic persuasion. Polymarket US also rose from 4% to 39% of Polymarket's volume between January and July, adding a jurisdiction and platform-design shift alongside the sports surge.

Rotation finding: public attention can be monetized through prediction, entertainment, and repeated micro-trades before it becomes political participation. The atlas should track topic, platform, contract turnover, user reach, money exposure, and civic meaning separately rather than treating trading volume as a proxy for public belief or democratic engagement.

New cultural-identity signal: institutional continuity can coexist with retention loss and internal change

The record us-pew-latter-day-saints-retention-demographic-change-2007-2024 adds a within-community cultural-demographic layer. Among adults raised as Latter-day Saints, current identification fell from 70% in 2007 to 54% in 2023-24, while religious unaffiliation rose from 14% to 28%. The remaining community also became more racially diverse: the White share fell from 85% to 72%, while Hispanic and Black shares rose from 6% to 12% and 2% to 6%.

The change is not a simple secularization or partisan-realignment story. About three-quarters of members still identify as Republican or lean Republican, but religion-importance and daily-prayer measures declined, while acceptance of homosexuality and support for more women in the workforce increased. Existing communal-trust and volunteering records therefore need to be read alongside retention and composition: strong ties among current members can coexist with long-run membership loss and changing internal meanings.

Rotation finding: institutions can preserve an outward political profile while changing through retention, conversion, demographic composition, and issue reinterpretation. The atlas should track who remains, who leaves, who joins, what practices persist, and which meanings shift instead of using membership size or partisan identity as a proxy for institutional continuity.

New cultural-memory signal: collective memory outlasts personal behavior change

The record us-gallup-911-memory-lifestyle-security-confidence-2000-2026 adds a long-horizon memory and security-perception layer. Gallup's latest anniversary poll finds that 64% say Americans permanently changed how they live because of 9/11, but only 28% say they personally did so. Terrorism worry has also eased to 37%, compared with 58% immediately after 9/11 and 24% in 2000. The gap indicates that a public event can remain culturally consequential without producing an equally large reported change in everyday life.

Confidence in government protection is a separate route. It is 55% overall, well below the 88% recorded immediately after 9/11, and its current partisan pattern has reversed: 78% among Republicans, 59% among independents, and 29% among Democrats, compared with 41%, 53%, and 80% respectively in 2021. The source also reports higher personal-change shares among Hispanic and Black adults than White adults, and among weekly religious attenders than those who seldom or never attend; these are subgroup contrasts, not causal explanations.

Rotation finding: collective memory, personal adaptation, perceived risk, and confidence in state protection run on different clocks. The atlas should track narrative persistence, observed or reported behavior change, risk salience, institutional attribution, and subgroup exposure separately rather than treating remembrance as evidence of behavioral transformation or trust in government capability.

New place-based shock signal: public-sector contraction can weaken job confidence before regional life visibly unravels

The record us-gallup-dmv-federal-cuts-local-labor-housing-pressure-2023-2026 adds a place-specific public-sector shock layer. In the Greater Washington region, 55% of residents say they or someone in their household has been negatively affected by federal job cuts, while the share rating local job availability excellent or good fell from 65% in 2023 to 51% in 2026. The source allows “impact” to include lost employment, lost clients or business, reduced access to federal programs or amenities, and other effects, so this is an exposure and attribution measure rather than a verified layoff count.

The regional picture is uneven rather than uniformly deteriorating. Grocery availability, healthcare, restaurants, transportation, and the quality of the region as a place to raise children retain majority-positive ratings, while affordable housing is rated positively by only 11%. One-third report being very or somewhat worried about rent or mortgage payments, rising to 48% among renters; among residents planning to leave, 58% cite rising housing costs and 59% the broader cost of living as major reasons.

Rotation finding: a concentrated public-sector shock can appear first as weaker labor-market confidence and household exposure, while amenity systems remain comparatively resilient and housing acts as the mobility constraint. The atlas should track shock attribution, direct and indirect employment routes, local demand, housing payment pressure, tenure, planned mobility, and actual moves separately rather than treating a regional sentiment decline as either a verified job-loss count or generalized place collapse.

New infrastructure-governance signal: authorization, obligation, disbursement, and usable delivery are separate clocks

The record us-gao-iija-ira-funding-obligation-disbursement-review-2022-2026 adds a federal implementation layer to the infrastructure and state-capacity surfaces. In GAO's review of EPA, Interior, NTIA, and DOT, the selected agencies had $574.7 billion in IIJA authority for fiscal years 2022-25, of which $434.2 billion was obligated and $235.6 billion disbursed. That is 76% of authority obligated, but only 54% of obligations and 41% of authority disbursed. IRA execution was similarly staged: 72% of selected authority was obligated and 60% of those obligations disbursed.

The gap is not only administrative delay. NTIA had obligated $45.1 billion of $47.7 billion in IIJA authority but disbursed $1.1 billion, in part because many BEAD awards had not reached implementation. Conversely, GAO notes that reported EPA disbursements of nearly $20 billion connected to two Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund programs were held at a private financial agent and subject to litigation, so a disbursement record did not necessarily mean recipient usability. Review politics added another layer: agencies reported about 9,500 approved awards, roughly 800 canceled awards, and 2,528 awards totaling about $33.6 billion still pending as of different dates.

Rotation finding: infrastructure capacity is produced through a sequence of authority, obligation, review, disbursement, recipient usability, project implementation, and public service—not by an appropriation headline. The atlas should preserve each stage, agency, program, legal constraint, review date, recipient route, and eventual service endpoint rather than treating federal spending as completed infrastructure or public benefit.

New judicial-legitimacy signal: approval, favorability, perceived ideology, and accepted power are different surfaces

The record us-cross-source-supreme-court-legitimacy-approval-favorability-2000-2026 adds a cross-source institutional-meaning layer. Gallup reports Supreme Court job approval at 33% after the 2025-26 term, the lowest reading in its 26-year trend, with 61% disapproving. Republican approval fell from 79% in September 2025 to 58%, while Democratic approval was 12% and independent approval 35%. Pew's contemporaneous but different measure finds 45% favorable and 53% unfavorable, with favorability at 69% among Republicans and 25% among Democrats.

The measurement split is analytically useful. Pew finds 43% calling the court conservative, 44% middle of the road, and 9% liberal; it also finds 56% saying the court has the right amount of power, versus 32% saying too much. Thus a person can judge the court's job poorly, view its ideology as conservative, and still accept its formal power—or reject its performance without rejecting its authority. The two sources should not be pooled: Gallup measures job approval with an undisclosed article-page sample, while Pew surveyed 3,554 American Trend Panel members and asked different questions.

Rotation finding: institutional legitimacy is multidimensional: performance approval, general favorability, ideological placement, and power acceptance can move together or apart. The atlas should preserve question wording, source, field period, party route, demographic exposure, and later institutional action rather than turn one approval score into a claim about judicial authority or democratic stability.

New institutional-capacity signal: public mission depends on physical support space and management information

The record us-gao-federal-judiciary-administrative-space-utilization-2021-2025 adds a physical-capacity layer behind judicial legitimacy. In fiscal year 2025, the federal judiciary occupied 12.2 million usable square feet of administrative space across 716 of 772 facilities; administrative space represented 40% of the judiciary's total space and 39%-40% of annual rent from 2021 through 2025. The judiciary paid more than $1 billion in rent, and 234 of the 272 facilities whose only space was administrative were commercially owned. Most of those commercial facilities served federal public defender organizations and probation offices.

The key gap is informational, not merely physical. GAO found that the judiciary tracks space and rent but does not collect or review occupancy data, so it cannot calculate utilization or establish benchmarks. The recommended control—regular occupancy measurement incorporated into space decisions—remains open. This does not prove waste: specialized, secure, geographically distributed, or surge capacity can be necessary even when average occupancy is low.

Rotation finding: institutional capability has a material substrate and a measurement substrate. The atlas should track mission space, cost, ownership, occupancy, security and specialization, data quality, management action, and downstream service endpoints separately rather than treating rent as waste or physical capacity as realized public access.

New comparative state-capacity signal: external shocks become household and service risk through fiscally fragile public enterprises

The record comparative-world-bank-malawi-macro-shocks-soe-service-delivery-2026 adds a comparative macro-to-service route. The World Bank's Malawi Economic Monitor describes a country facing commodity shocks, inflation, foreign-exchange distortions, import shortages, unreliable electricity, and weak supply chains. Growth is projected at 2.8% in 2027, the fiscal deficit was 8.8% of GDP in 2025/26, and reserves remained below one month of import cover. The report also describes increased food poverty, wider inequality, fragile food security, and heavy reliance on casual labor, especially among young people.

The state-owned-enterprise channel makes the transmission institutional rather than purely macroeconomic. SOEs provide energy, water, agricultural services, and other essential goods, but many rely on transfers, subsidies, and guarantees while facing losses, weak cash flow, arrears, and poor debt service. Political interference, fragmented oversight, and limited transparency are part of the report's diagnosis of recurring bailouts and declining service quality. The recommended route—independent boards, transparency, revenue collection, cost-reflective tariffs, and debt management—also creates a distributional tradeoff: stronger enterprise finances can raise user burdens unless social protection and service access are tracked alongside reform.

Rotation finding: external shocks reach households through fiscal room, public enterprises, infrastructure reliability, tariffs, and labor-market options. The atlas should preserve shock, financing, governance, service, price, household-exposure, and reform-implementation stages separately rather than turning a macro outlook or an SOE diagnosis into a claim about individual welfare or successful state reform.

New subnational-finance signal: infrastructure reach depends on an intermediary and project-preparation route before local service delivery

The record comparative-world-bank-ecuador-subnational-infrastructure-finance-2026 adds a subnational financing architecture to the comparative state-capacity surface. The World Bank approved an $800 million, three-phase program over ten years for Ecuador, with $200 million in first-phase World Bank financing and $50 million in parallel AECID co-financing. Banco de Desarrollo del Ecuador will implement the program for municipalities, provincial governments, and public service providers, while the first phase also funds project preparation and technical and institutional capacity.

The announcement expects more than 3 million people to benefit and up to $750 million in private capital to be mobilized across energy, transport, urban development, disaster-risk management, and affordable housing. These are forward-looking targets, not realized reach or investment. The intermediary route is itself a mechanism: it may improve coordination and local project quality, but can also concentrate gatekeeping, create debt or fiscal exposure, or leave lower-capacity local governments behind.

Rotation finding: subnational infrastructure is not only a capital stock; it is a financing, intermediary, preparation, eligibility, procurement, and maintenance chain. The atlas should track who receives finance, who prepares projects, what gets built, how private capital is counted, how benefits are distributed, and whether services become affordable and reliable rather than treating an approved envelope or beneficiary target as completed public value.

New trade-livelihood signal: logistics infrastructure and coastal resource upgrading join market access to climate and gender exposure

The record comparative-world-bank-vietnam-trade-connectivity-coastal-livelihoods-2026 adds a trade-corridor and coastal-livelihood route. The World Bank approved three Vietnam projects totaling $666.74 million: Hai Phong resilience and urban connectivity, Mekong Delta highway rehabilitation, and sustainable fisheries development. The plans include 251 kilometers of highway work, a new Ring Road 3 section, wastewater and flood protection, and modernization of nine fishing ports. Construction employment is projected at about 10,700 casual and 2,300 professional jobs in Hai Phong and 10,900 jobs annually for the Mekong connectivity project.

The fisheries project expects more than 525,000 fishers, aquaculture farmers, and coastal residents to benefit, with women targeted to represent at least half of direct beneficiaries. These are program targets rather than observed income or access outcomes. The chain can improve market reliability and reduce post-harvest losses, but port modernization can also favor larger operators, change access rules, raise costs, or shift environmental pressure. A gender target does not by itself establish control over income, assets, or decisions.

Rotation finding: trade infrastructure changes the social distribution of time, logistics cost, climate exposure, work, and resource access. The atlas should preserve corridor, port, worker, producer, gender, climate, procurement, and realized-benefit stages separately rather than treating a loan, job projection, or beneficiary target as completed livelihood improvement.

New resource-security signal: water scarcity becomes a growth, labor, service, and household-protection problem through governance

The record comparative-world-bank-tunisia-water-scarcity-growth-jobs-2026 adds a resource-security route. Tunisia has about 380 cubic meters of renewable freshwater per person annually, below the international threshold for absolute water scarcity. The World Bank estimates that water scarcity could reduce GDP by 6.4% by 2050 and, without action, eliminate at least 30% of agricultural jobs by mid-century; agriculture employs 14% of the national workforce and up to half of rural workers. The risk spills into tourism, agro-processing, industry, and other water-dependent sectors.

The proposed response is institutional as well as physical. Plan Eau 2050 envisions roughly $900 million a year in investment through mid-century, while the RESEau program is expected to generate about 4,000 permanent and 13,400 temporary jobs in its first phase. But the monitor says infrastructure must be paired with water governance, provider financial sustainability, cost recovery, network-loss reduction, wastewater reuse, digitalization, and irrigation management—with vulnerable households protected. That creates a clear distributional hinge: stronger providers and cost recovery can improve reliability while increasing burdens for users if protection is weak.

Rotation finding: environmental scarcity becomes social risk through labor dependence, prices, service-provider finance, infrastructure maintenance, and the reach of household protections. The atlas should track resource condition, modeled exposure, sector and worker dependence, provider performance, tariff and affordability changes, adaptation, and realized service separately rather than treating a water plan or modeled GDP loss as an observed household outcome.

New public-risk signal: politics enters personal safety perception as a cross-partisan social risk

The record us-cross-source-gallup-world-risk-politics-safety-2021-2026 adds a public-risk and political-meaning route. Gallup's 2025 World Risk Poll, covering 140 countries, reports that 10% of U.S. adults named politics as the greatest personal safety risk, up from 6% in both 2021 and 2023 and roughly ten times the 1% global average. The U.S. tied Hungary for the highest country estimate. The poll reports no statistically significant U.S. differences by gender, age, education, or party, so this signal should not be reduced to one partisan subgroup.

The surrounding U.S. context is also institutionally meaningful: 33% named politics or government the country's most important problem in 2025, while 58% said the government does not care at all about people like them, 11 points higher than in 2021. Politics was below roads (34%) and crime or violence (19%) but above personal health (5%) as a named personal safety risk; the comparison is a perception measure, not an observed violence or safety event.

Rotation finding: political conditions can enter everyday risk perception and institutional meaning before the atlas can claim a change in physical safety, disorder, participation, polarization, or institutional withdrawal. The next tests should preserve the distinction between perceived risk, reported concern, actual exposure, public behavior, and institutional response, while checking whether this meaning signal connects to trust, mobility, consumption, or civic action through separately measured endpoints.

New civic-architecture signal: public life splits into action, community, attention, and lower-participation routes

The record us-pew-public-life-engagement-types-2025-2026 adds a cross-domain participation route from Pew's 2025 Cross-Sectional Engagement Survey. Rather than placing Americans on one engaged-to-disengaged ladder, Pew classifies them into Mobilizers (9%), Connectors (28%), Spectators (31%), and Outsiders (31%) using 19 measures spanning political activity, civic involvement, religious attendance, and news attention. The classification is a source-defined cluster, not a durable identity or a time series.

The endpoints separate in consequential ways. Mobilizers and Connectors both report voting at 87%, but Mobilizers are much more likely to have contacted an elected official (65% versus 13%) and volunteered (77% versus 42%), while Connectors report more nonpolitical donations (90% versus 83%). Spectators follow national news at 84% while reporting much less volunteering (17%) and official contact (7%). Outsiders report lower levels across the measured activities, but 41% say they voted in 2024 and 24% attend religious services monthly. These are not interchangeable forms of participation.

Rotation finding: civic and political life is better modeled as a set of routes—public action, community connection, mediated attention, religious practice, charitable behavior, and voting—than as one participation score. The atlas should test which routes are enabled by time, money, institutions, identity, or information environments, while keeping cross-sectional group membership separate from causality, durable engagement, efficacy, and social capital.

New cultural-access signal: recent arts participation is lower than perceived local opportunity

The record us-census-htops-arts-participation-community-supply-2026 adds a current cultural-consumption and cultural-supply route from the Census Bureau's experimental July 2026 HTOPS tables. In the prior four weeks, the published weighted counts imply that about 20.5% of adults attended a live music, dance, or theater performance, 9.5% attended an art exhibit, 22.6% went to the movies, and 17.9% created, practiced, or performed personal art. These are distinct forms of cultural activity, not one arts-participation score.

The same release implies that 63.1% agreed or strongly agreed that there were plenty of opportunities to take part in arts and cultural activities in their neighborhood or community, while 25.4% disagreed or strongly disagreed. The contrast between perceived opportunity and recent participation is a useful screen for conversion: supply, affordability, time, transport, caregiving, health, preference, and the recall window can all intervene between an available cultural route and actual attendance or creation.

Rotation finding: cultural life should be tracked as a chain from perceived local supply to available venue or activity, affordability and time, travel and care constraints, participation, creation, and durable meaning. The HTOPS figures are experimental and cross-sectional; they do not establish a venue shortage, cultural disengagement, spending pattern, or causal access barrier.

New infrastructure-geopolitics signal: undersea cable redundancy is a state-power and economic-continuity dependency

The record us-uscc-transpacific-undersea-cable-gray-zone-resilience-2026 adds a physical-digital infrastructure route to the geopolitical atlas. A September 2026 research report posted by the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission examines 25 operational trans-Pacific cable systems, Chinese military-civil capabilities, a gray-zone vulnerability index, repair capacity, and modeled network consequences. It reports that U.S. operator data covers about 83.5% of trans-Pacific cable capacity, while the global repair fleet has 62 cable vessels, with up to 36 potentially unavailable at a given time. These are infrastructure and research inputs, not an observed sabotage rate.

The modeled scenarios make redundancy a distributional and firm-continuity question. Under peak-demand assumptions, disruption of the report's top five highest-risk cables leaves zero headroom relative to lit capacity; a Taiwan contingency leaves 1.76%; and disruption of two large cables produces modeled negative headroom of 69.76%. Guam is especially exposed: the report says that breaking one of its two continental-U.S. cables leaves less than 0.1% headroom even after maximum-design-capacity upgrades. The model also connects latency to financial services, cloud, AI, and internet users.

Rotation finding: geopolitical leverage can run through repair fleets, route redundancy, ownership and supplier capability, maintenance access, capacity activation, and allied monitoring before it appears as a visible consumer outage or firm loss. The atlas should keep strategic intent, modeled vulnerability, infrastructure response, realized disruption, service quality, and downstream economic effects as separate stages, particularly where a contracted report's analysis is not itself a verified incident.

New comparative-capacity signal: growth, competition, formalization, and climate adaptation are one institutional package

The record comparative-oecd-philippines-productivity-formality-climate-2026 adds an OECD country-survey route for testing how macro growth becomes—or fails to become—broad capability. The Philippines is forecast to grow 5.1% in 2026 and 5.8% in 2027, but the survey says reaching the country's 2040 income target requires roughly three-quarters of a percentage point more annual productivity growth than its pre-pandemic average. It identifies high electricity and telecommunications prices, vertical integration, limited access to critical infrastructure, administrative burden, and corruption as constraints on firms and investment.

The distributional hinge is labor-market formality and protection: only about one-third of workers are in formal-sector jobs with comprehensive protection, while roughly two-thirds work informally; mandatory social contributions are about 23% of gross wages. The survey pairs lower formalization costs with a universal basic tier and expanded non-contributory protection, while also calling for climate adaptation in high-risk areas and stronger natural-resource governance. The recommendations are not implementation or welfare outcomes.

Rotation finding: comparative growth evidence is most useful when it keeps the chain visible: competition and infrastructure access affect firm capacity; formalization affects protection and fiscal reach; climate exposure tests state adaptation; and macro growth can coexist with weak coverage. The Philippines record is a mechanism and comparison layer, not a U.S. estimate or a claim that any recommended reform has been delivered.

New control-route signal: critical-infrastructure exposure can run through ownership, boards, and organizational networks

The record us-inl-topgear-organizational-influence-critical-infrastructure-2026 adds a less visible control route to the infrastructure and geopolitical atlas. Idaho National Laboratory describes TOPGEAR as a tool that links three layers: business ties and leadership roles, physical and digital infrastructure assets, and cross-layer influence paths connecting an organization or person to a specific asset. The stated inputs include SEC filings and Energy Information Administration data, supplemented by proprietary sources when needed. INL says the project completed 76 market analyses through DOE's Energy I-Corps program and is already used by state energy offices.

The publication describes policy responses around foreign ownership near power, water, and military assets; procurement restrictions involving companies tied to countries of concern; CFIUS real-estate and agricultural oversight; and FOCI limits on sensitive U.S. companies. These are policy and implementation signals, not evidence that any particular investor or board relationship caused harm. Screening can reveal hidden influence, but it can also raise compliance costs, constrain beneficial investment, or shift ownership without improving operational resilience.

Rotation finding: infrastructure power is not only about cyber compromise, physical sabotage, or formal control. Ownership, board access, procurement, leadership networks, and asset adjacency can create a latent influence route that requires different evidence and safeguards. The atlas should separate relationship mapping, suspicious-pattern screening, verified operational control, realized disruption, and public-service consequences.

New consumer-finance signal: credit-market expansion is product-specific and risk-tier uneven

The record us-cfpb-consumer-credit-trends-february-2026 adds a current market endpoint between macro conditions and household room. In the latest available CFPB dashboard month, February 2026, seasonally adjusted originations were up year over year by 5.3% for auto loans, 13.1% for credit cards, 36.2% for mortgages, and 142.5% for student loans. The product mix matters: the dashboard also reports credit-tightness indexes below the January 2010 base of 100 for auto (81.0), cards (79.0), and mortgages (82.9), while inquiry indexes were well above that base for auto and cards. These are market indicators, not household affordability or repayment outcomes.

The risk-tier view prevents the aggregate expansion from becoming a single consumer story. February credit-card originations rose 24.9% year over year for the deep-subprime group and 13.8% for the superprime group; auto originations rose 34.3% for deep subprime while falling 1.0% for prime. A sharp tier change can reflect access, refinancing, program rules, low bases, or reporting mix, and does not by itself establish beneficial inclusion or harmful lending.

Rotation finding: consumer finance should be tracked as product, inquiry, underwriting tightness, risk tier, originations, dollar volume, repayment, delinquency, and household adaptation stages. Market expansion can coexist with unequal access and unresolved cost; the CFPB data adds the credit-route screen while leaving individual debt burden, affordability, and welfare open.

New commerce-interface signal: AI is becoming a shopping intermediary before transaction effects are observable

The record us-niq-ai-assisted-shopping-agentic-commerce-2026 adds a commercial consumer-behavior route from NielsenIQ's Agentic Commerce Tracker. NIQ reports that 51% of U.S. consumers used at least one AI-powered tool to support shopping in the past month, with AI product recommendations at 20% and personal shopping assistants at 16%. The release describes adoption as crossing the halfway mark after growth over the prior two quarters and places AI use across discovery, comparison, value evaluation, choice narrowing, and final purchase decisions.

The firm-side endpoint is also part of the trend: NIQ says brands and retailers will need stronger product content, digital discoverability, and structured product information, and that it will measure agentic commerce as a distinct channel. But the source is a vendor press release based on approximate monthly samples of about 500 consumers, with limited public methodology. Reported use is not transaction share, trust, accuracy, savings, conversion, or autonomous delegation.

Rotation finding: the path to purchase may be reorganized by an AI intermediary before the atlas can observe realized sales, price effects, or consumer welfare. The next tests should separate tool exposure, recommendation, comparison, retailer visibility, purchase, post-purchase recourse, and who controls the product information and ranking layer.

New financial-access signal: eligibility is broader than realized private-market participation

The SEC accredited-investor qualification record adds an access-and-participation route from the SEC Office of the Investor Advocate's longitudinal THRIVE research. The SEC estimates that 14.2% of the U.S. population qualified as accredited investors in January 2026, up from 12.1% in the paired 2024 wave; the net-worth criterion alone covered 12.1% in the 2026 cross-sectional estimate. Status is dynamic: 21.3% of those accredited in 2024 no longer qualified in 2026, while 5.3% of those not accredited in 2024 qualified by 2026.

The participation endpoint is much narrower. Only 5.8% of accredited investors reported owning private-market securities in 2026, while 11.5% reported plans to invest in the next 12 months. Persistent accredited investors reported higher ownership than newly qualifying investors (7.8% vs. 1.8%), and 38.0% of those accredited in both waves used a financial professional for investment decisions in both years. The paper's paired panel, weighting, thresholds, and self-reported ownership measures make this a useful institutional-access signal, not a respondent-level dataset or a causal claim about wealth inequality.

Rotation finding: financial access should be tracked as eligibility, qualification stability, intermediation, offer exposure, ownership, planned investment, realized transaction, return, and loss/exit stages. A larger eligible population can coexist with concentrated participation; the next tests should distinguish threshold expansion from actual opportunity, advice, portfolio ownership, and household outcomes.

New civic-culture signal: public-life engagement is plural, not a single ladder

The Pew public-life engagement record adds a cross-domain cultural and political participation route. Pew's cluster analysis of 19 measures identifies four groups: Mobilizers (9%), Connectors (28%), Spectators (31%), and Outsiders (31%); the displayed groups exclude adults not assigned to a group. The distinction is behavioral rather than simply partisan: Mobilizers and Connectors both report 87% voting in 2024, but Mobilizers report much more contact with elected officials (65% versus 13%) and Connectors more nonpolitical donation and group participation. Spectators follow news relatively closely while acting less publicly, and Outsiders are low across the measured channels but still include voters and religious attenders.

The political endpoint is deliberately non-binary. Pew finds that each group contains Republicans and Democrats rather than one group being owned by one party. The source is a one-time late-2025 survey window and many measures cover the prior 12 months, including the 2024 presidential election, so the record does not treat these as stable identities or a time trend.

Rotation finding: civic and political capacity should be tracked across attention, private discussion, voting, volunteering, donation, group/religious participation, direct official contact, knowledge, and institutional response. Party labels alone miss distinct routes into public life; low participation in one channel can coexist with episodic action or meaningful community activity elsewhere.

New comparative geopolitical signal: digital services growth is not translating evenly into trade participation

The UNCTAD digital-services trade record adds a cross-border production and rule-making layer. UNCTAD reports that services accounted for 71% of global intermediate inputs in 2022 and 27% of global exports in 2025; digitally deliverable services grew 7.1% annually over the past decade and now represent 56% of global services exports. The growth is therefore not just a consumer-internet story: services are embedded in manufacturing, agriculture, logistics, finance, and global value chains.

The distributional endpoint is stark. Least developed countries held 0.6% of global services exports in 2025, and digitally deliverable services were only 16% of their services exports versus 61% in developed economies. UNCTAD points to connectivity, cross-border payments, skills, computing capacity, finance, data, AI expertise, and fragmented digital-trade rules as linked capability constraints. Since 2020, 90% of developed countries, 62% of developing countries, and 66% of LDCs participated in agreements containing digital-trade provisions; participation in a rule-making venue is not the same as export access or bargaining power.

Rotation finding: global digital transformation should be tracked as inputs, infrastructure, payment friction, skills, firm entry, remote delivery, export value, domestic capture, trade-rule participation, and AI capability. Headline services growth can coexist with marginal integration for poorer countries and with unresolved questions about who captures value.

New household-cost signal: energy affordability is shaped by bills, buildings, access, and policy design

The IEA household-energy affordability record adds a global household-cost and infrastructure route. The IEA estimates that global household energy bills were still 4% higher in real terms in 2024 than in 2019 after the 2022 shock, when bills rose 16% year over year. In advanced economies, more than 120 million households spent over 10% of income on residential heating, cooling, and appliances; adding private transport pushed the poorest households' energy share above 20%. Electricity now represents about 30% of residential energy use globally and household electricity spending exceeded USD 1 trillion in 2024.

The policy endpoint is uneven targeting. The IEA tracked more than 120 new or updated demand-side affordability policies across 45 countries in 2025, but only about one-third specifically targeted households most in need. Access and upfront-cost constraints remain central: the IEA estimates that 730 million people lack electricity, around 2 billion lack clean cooking, and 40% of people without electricity in sub-Saharan Africa may not afford a basic provision. The companion IEA framework treats affordability as a policy-data feedback loop spanning drivers, impacts, population groups, indicators, and data rather than a single price metric.

Rotation finding: energy pressure should be tracked across wholesale price, retail tariff, network charge, tax/subsidy, building efficiency, appliance and transport choice, access, clean cooking, health, utility finance, and policy targeting. A lower bill or a new support policy is not by itself evidence of adequate service, fair distribution, or durable household relief.

New fiscal-policy signal: tax systems are balancing household room, firm incentives, and public-finance pressure

The OECD tax-policy reform record adds the fiscal mechanism behind several household and firm trends. Its 2026 review covers reforms introduced or announced in 2025 across 92 jurisdictions. The broad direction is mixed: governments used personal-income-tax relief and more progressive measures to address cost-of-living pressure, while social- security contributions moved toward broader bases and higher rates in several countries as demographic and social-protection financing pressures grew. Revenue-raising measures remained relatively limited even as public debt and debt-service costs stayed elevated.

The firm-side response is targeted rather than a simple tax-rate race. The average combined statutory corporate-income-tax rate across 145 jurisdictions was 21.2% in 2025, versus 28.0% in 2000, while corporate base-narrowing measures still exceeded base-broadening measures. Countries continued using incentives for R&D, AI, emerging technologies, defence, and strategic sectors; more jurisdictions also extended VAT collection to non-resident suppliers and online platforms. Health-related taxes, especially tobacco and nicotine excises, were among the common tax-increasing measures.

Rotation finding: fiscal policy should be tracked across statutory rate, effective burden, tax base, transfer/relief, contribution, platform collection, firm incentive, public revenue, service financing, consumption response, and household distribution. A reported progressive reform or strategic incentive does not by itself establish who pays, who benefits, or what behavior changes.

New global-work signal: headline employment stability is masking a jobs-quality and access deficit

The ILO global jobs-gap record adds a labour-market layer distinct from country-specific work records. The ILO projects global unemployment at 4.9% in 2026, but estimates a broader jobs gap of 408 million people who want paid work and cannot access it. Nearly 300 million workers remain in extreme working poverty and 2.1 billion remain in informal employment, often without basic rights, social protection, or income security. In low-income countries employment is projected to grow 3.1% in 2026, but weak productivity and slow formalisation mean that more jobs do not necessarily mean better jobs.

The distributional and geopolitical endpoints are also connected. Women account for about two-fifths of global employment and are 24.2% less likely than men to participate in the labour force; 20% of young people—about 260 million—are not in employment, education, or training. Around 465 million jobs are linked to foreign demand, but trade uncertainty, AI adoption, and sovereign debt could weaken the ability of trade to improve job quality. The ILO therefore points toward domestic skills, social protection, and labour-institution capacity as the next policy route.

Rotation finding: work should be tracked across labour demand, access, employment, formalisation, productivity, pay, protection, bargaining, household income, trade exposure, and technology-mediated change. Low headline unemployment is not a sufficient endpoint for decent work or social stability.

New intergenerational-risk signal: child climate exposure is a compound hazard and service-capacity problem

The UNICEF child climate-risk record adds an intergenerational and infrastructure-service layer. UNICEF estimates that 1.1 billion children face at least three overlapping climate hazards; its component exposure estimates include 1.8 billion children exposed to drought, 1.5 billion to worsening heatwaves, 662 million to tropical storms, and 2.3 billion living where air pollutants are detectable. These are modeled exposure surfaces, not counts of children already experiencing a specified injury, displacement, learning loss, or health outcome.

The important mechanism is compounding. UNICEF pairs the Global Child Hazard Database with a Children’s Climate Risk Framework covering health, WASH, nutrition, education, protection, and social protection. Drought, fire, air pollution, floods, damaged schools and hospitals, displacement, and disease can form a cascading pathway when service capacity is weak. The policy endpoint therefore includes climate-resilient facilities, food and water security, shock-responsive protection, and children’s meaningful participation in climate decisions.

Rotation finding: climate risk should be tracked across hazard exposure, compound sequence, service capacity, displacement, learning, health, food, WASH, protection, adaptation, and child voice. Counting exposure alone misses both buffering institutions and the distribution of realized harm.

New social-health signal: loneliness is a population-level connection gap, not simply an individual mental-health condition

The WHO social-connection record adds a relationship and community layer. The WHO Commission estimates that 15.8% of the global population experienced loneliness across its 2014–2023 evidence period, drawing on 23 datasets covering 153 countries and territories. Estimated prevalence was highest among adolescents (20.9%) and young adults (17.4%), and was higher in low-income countries (24.3%) than high-income countries (11%). The source distinguishes loneliness from social isolation and from clinical diagnosis, so the figures are a social-health signal rather than a respondent-level mental-health finding.

The mechanism spans health, education, work, income, marginalization, life transitions, and community institutions. WHO frames social connection as a public-health priority and points toward cross-sector action, including a 2025 World Health Assembly resolution. The policy response remains open: recognizing the problem or deploying digital/community programs does not establish durable, equitable improvement.

Rotation finding: social resilience should be tracked across contact, belonging, subjective loneliness, isolation, school/work participation, health, community institutions, digital mediation, and policy response. A connection gap can be widespread without having one cause or one universal remedy.

New digital-safety signal: platform-mediated child abuse is an exposure, trust, and reporting-system problem

The UNICEF digital child-safety record adds a safety and institutional-trust endpoint. UNICEF estimates that almost one in five surveyed internet-using children aged 12–17 across 21 countries experienced at least one form of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation or abuse in a single year. The study estimates more than 15 million exposed to unwanted sexual content, 9 million asked to engage in sexual conversations or share images against their will, and 4 million having sexual images shared without consent. Around 60% of cases occurred on mainstream social platforms and 14% in online games.

The pathway is not simply stranger danger or platform use. UNICEF reports that 57% of cases involved someone the child already knew, while 38% first encountered the perpetrator online. More than 40% of cases were never shared with anyone and fewer than 1% were reported to authorities. The report calls for safer-by-design platforms, trusted reporting and support systems, stronger regulation, and shifting protection burdens away from children. Its prevalence and mental-health findings remain bounded to internet-using children and reported associations.

Rotation finding: digital safety should be tracked across access, platform features, contact, exploitation, disclosure, reporting, service response, recourse, child trust, and institutional accountability. Platform exposure is not itself a causal explanation, and low official reporting is not proof that no informal disclosure or support occurred.

New displacement-livelihood signal: integration depends on labor absorption and shared service capacity

The World Bank Kenya refugee-host livelihoods record adds a comparative migration and local-economy route. A two-wave panel study summarized by the World Bank follows refugee and host households as aid tightens and Kenya shifts toward integrated settlements. Employment among camp-based refugees fell from 13% to 7% between waves, while urban refugee employment fell from 50% to 37%. In camp settings, 89% were inactive in the second wave and 64% of those citing no available jobs rose from 41% previously. Host employment near camps remained low, edging from 35% to 33%.

The mechanism is shared absorptive capacity, not simply refugee presence. Aid accounted for about three quarters of camp-based refugee revenue in 2024; the source reports food reduction by 64% of camp households and credit use for food by 44%. Refugees and hosts also rely on the same constrained schools, clinics, roads, water systems, and thin labor markets. These are descriptive, bounded Kenya findings—not a causal estimate of aid cuts or a verdict on the Shirika Plan—but they create a reusable cross-source test: whether integration policy is accompanied by work authorization, mobility, childcare, private investment, shock-responsive support, and enough local service capacity to prevent shared scarcity from becoming social fracture.

Rotation finding: displacement should be tracked across legal status, mobility, aid, work access, household income, food coping, shared services, host-market absorption, gendered care constraints, and social cohesion. Formal integration is not the same as economic inclusion or durable self-reliance.

New geopolitical signal: perceived risk is moving faster than perceived multilateral capacity

The UN Global Risk Report record adds a global institutional-perception layer. The 2026 exercise drew on approximately 1,300 stakeholders across 155 countries and assessed 28 risks. Large-scale war moved toward the center of the risk map, with 36% expecting it within one year; concern about AI and frontier-technology power concentration also rose. Climate-change inaction nevertheless remained the most important risk overall, and joint government action remained the response viewed as most effective.

The useful mechanism is the gap between salience and capacity. The UN frames global vulnerability as a difference between how important a risk appears and how capable multilateral institutions are perceived to be in responding. This is not an event forecast or an audit of institutional performance. It is a cross-source bridge for testing whether geopolitical attention, technology concern, climate exposure, and economic stress are matched by coordination, preparedness, implementation, and credible public or state response.

Rotation finding: geopolitical change should be tracked across risk salience, hazard realization, preparedness, coordination, institutional capacity, implementation, legitimacy, and response feedback. A risk moving to the center of attention is not the same as a changed probability or a closed governance gap.

New social-cohesion signal: insecurity and inequality are becoming trust and collective-action constraints

The UN World Social Report trust and cohesion record adds a cultural-social route that is broader than loneliness or civic participation alone. The report synthesizes evidence that more than half of the global population has little or no trust in government, fewer than 30% believe other people can be trusted, and more than a third live on between $2.15 and $6.85 per day. It also reports a decline in government trust across successive birth cohorts and growing inequality in much of the world.

The mechanism is not simply an attitudinal mood. The report defines cohesion through cooperation, fairness and inclusion, belonging, and trust, and links economic insecurity, public-service delivery, social protection, perceived inequality, and mis/disinformation to the ability to act collectively. The figures come from different surveys and country evidence and should not be collapsed into one global trust index or causal estimate. They do add a useful cross-source test: whether material security, fair institutional treatment, credible information, and local solidarity reinforce one another—or whether insecurity converts into distrust, polarization, and policy paralysis.

Rotation finding: social cohesion should be tracked across material security, inequality, service delivery, institutional legitimacy, interpersonal trust, belonging, information environments, participation, and collective action. Low generalized trust does not prove the absence of strong local or familial ties, and policy recognition is not a verified repair.

New housing-market signal: digital rental search can convert access pressure into upfront loss and identity exposure

The FTC rental-scam record adds a concrete housing-search and platform-recourse endpoint. The FTC identified nearly 65,000 likely rental-scam reports from January 2020 through June 2025, with about $65 million in reported losses and a $1,000 median reported loss. In the most recent year, about half of platform-specified reports said the scam began with a fake Facebook ad and 16% with Craigslist. The reported mechanisms include copied or fabricated listings, below-market prices, upfront deposits or fees, fake credit-check subscriptions, and early collection of identity documents.

The age gradient matters as a housing-access signal: among reports from July 2024 through June 2025, 46% of 18–29-year-old reports indicated monetary loss, compared with 23% for ages 30–39 and 13% for ages 40–49. These are normalized reporting patterns, not prevalence or causal age effects; the FTC notes that most scams are never reported. The distinct cross-source test is whether housing scarcity, urgency, platform ranking, identity verification, payment timing, and recourse combine to redistribute risk toward people with fewer alternatives.

Rotation finding: housing access should be tracked across search, listing visibility, verification, urgency, upfront payment, identity exposure, loss, reporting, recovery, landlord/platform responsibility, and ability to switch. An attractive listing or a complaint route is not the same as a safe home or restored financial room.

New creative-economy signal: digital cultural production is expanding while value capture and participation remain uneven

The UNCTAD creative-economy record adds a cultural-production and market-structure route. UNCTAD reports that the developing-country share of global creative-goods and services exports rose from 10% in 2010 to 20% in 2022. But the leading creative-services categories were software (41.3%), research and development (30%), advertising/market research/architecture (15.5%), and audiovisual services (7.9%), while cultural, recreational, and heritage services were 0.6%. This is a reminder that “creative economy” growth can mean digitally mediated business services as well as cultural production.

Digital distribution also changes the consumer and firm endpoint. Streaming accounted for 67.3% of global music revenue streams in the cited 2022 data, and the report describes AI as altering creation, distribution, and consumption, including use in newsrooms. These shares do not establish worker displacement, creator autonomy, audience welfare, or equitable cultural representation. They do create a cross-source test: whether digital scale broadens participation and market access, or shifts discovery, rights, income, and cultural visibility toward a smaller set of platforms and high-capacity firms.

Rotation finding: culture should be tracked across creation, access, distribution, platform mediation, intellectual property, worker bargaining, consumer payment, local identity, export concentration, and who captures the economic and symbolic value.

New tourism signal: travel demand has recovered, but place capacity and geopolitical resilience determine who benefits

The OECD tourism trends record adds a movement, destination, and host-community route. International arrivals to OECD countries rose 8.1% to 819.5 million in 2024, with tourism directly accounting for 4.0% of GDP and 19.3% of services exports; arrivals were estimated to grow another 3.4% in 2025. The rebound is economically important, but the OECD describes concentrated visitor flows, infrastructure and community pressures, extreme-weather risk, and the early-2026 Middle East conflict as forces reshaping safety, affordability, transport, and demand.

The U.S. profile shows the same split between scale and exposure: tourism directly represented 3.0% of U.S. GVA and 4.0% of employment in 2023, while 2025 international arrivals fell 5.5% from 2024 to 68.3 million—86% of the 2019 level—even as domestic travel reached an estimated 2.4 billion person- trips. These are sector and trip measures, not resident sentiment or individual travel motives. They add a cross-source test: whether tourism growth is matched by transport, housing, water, labor, community voice, crisis preparedness, and local value retention rather than merely higher arrival counts.

Rotation finding: mobility and place should be tracked across demand, affordability, connectivity, visitor concentration, housing and infrastructure, worker and host-community benefits, environmental pressure, safety, shocks, governance, and distribution of local value.

New firm-finance signal: SME credit is recovering unevenly while long-term investment capacity remains constrained

The OECD SME-finance record adds a firm-side liquidity and investment route. Across the 2026 Scoreboard, 34 of 39 countries had SME interest rates above pre-pandemic levels, 10 of 17 showed higher shares of SMEs requiring collateral, and the outstanding SME-loan stock was broadly stagnant. Aggregate real long-term SME-loan volumes in the selected country group fell 11% since 2021, while venture-capital growth was reported in 18 of 30 countries but concentrated in a limited number of large AI deals.

The implication is not simply “small firms cannot borrow.” New lending can recover while stock stays flat because short-term loans are repaid; firms can also use internal funds, leasing, factoring, equity, guarantees, or fintech finance. The distinct cross-source test is whether the available instrument supports working capital only or enables durable investment, digitalisation, skills, green transition, resilience, succession, and worker stability—and which firms or regions receive patient capital versus short-term survival liquidity.

Rotation finding: firm capacity should be tracked across loan access, collateral, cost, maturity, liquidity, investment, alternative finance, public guarantees, ownership, technology adoption, worker outcomes, regional concentration, and long-term survival.

New education signal: access expansion is real, but exclusion and equity-system capacity are falling behind the target clock

The UNESCO 2026 GEM education record adds a human-capital and public-system capacity route. Global primary and secondary enrollment reached 1.4 billion in 2024, up 30% or 327 million from 2000, while completion also improved. Yet 273 million children, adolescents, and youth remained out of school in 2024, the out-of-school population rose 3% since 2015, and at current expansion rates the world would reach 95% upper- secondary completion only in 2105.

The bottleneck is not only demand or school places. UNESCO reports that one in three countries does not report urban-rural disparity and one in two does not report wealth disparity; fewer than one in ten countries have a sufficiently strong intended equity-policy focus. Inclusive-education laws and financing mechanisms have expanded, but target-setting, measurement, transportation, technology, health, nutrition, and institutional follow-through determine who can convert formal access into timely completion and future capability. These are global system indicators, not classroom or individual learning outcomes.

Rotation finding: education should be tracked across access, timing, completion, learning, equity, financing, transport, digital infrastructure, health and nutrition, teacher capacity, data visibility, household demand, and later work and civic capability. Enrollment is not the same as timely, equitable, or meaningful completion.

New gendered-opportunity signal: equal laws are advancing faster than the systems that make them usable

The World Bank Women, Business and the Law record adds a legal-rights-to-practice route. Across 190 economies, women hold about 67% of men's measured legal rights; fewer than half of the supportive policies and institutions needed to make those rights effective are in place, and legal experts rate enforcement at about 53 out of 100. Only 4% of women live in economies close to full legal equality, even though 68 economies enacted 113 strengthening reforms between 2023 and 2025.

The implementation gap is the useful mechanism. The framework covers safety, mobility, work, pay, marriage, parenthood, childcare, entrepreneurship, assets, and pensions, so formal rights can be connected to time, care, household room, firm participation, and later security. The U.S. profile scores legal frameworks above supportive frameworks and enforcement perceptions and reports no reforms in the measured topics during the covered interval. These are institutional diagnostics, not individual women's outcomes or causal estimates; they create a cross-source test of whether legal recognition is translated into accessible services, safe mobility, finance, childcare, work, business growth, and retirement security.

Rotation finding: gender inequality should be tracked across law, policy support, enforcement, safety, mobility, care, pay, assets, entrepreneurship, work, household bargaining, and durable economic security. A right on paper is not the same as a usable option.

New health-access signal: coverage gains still leave care costs large enough to crowd out household consumption

The WHO/World Bank universal-health-coverage record adds a global public-system and household-affordability route. The UHC service coverage index rose from 54 in 2000 to 71 in 2023, but WHO estimates that 4.6 billion people still lacked coverage for essential health services in 2023. Financial protection also improved: the share experiencing large or impoverishing out-of-pocket health-payment hardship fell from 34% in 2000 to 26% in 2022. Even so, 2.1 billion people were estimated to face that hardship in 2022.

The important mechanism is the conversion of formal or nominal access into usable care and remaining household room. The revised financial-hardship measure explicitly treats health spending as harmful when it exceeds 40% of a household's discretionary budget, linking care access to medicines, food, housing, work, debt, and other consumption choices. These are population and system indicators, not respondent-level outcomes or individual causal effects.

Rotation finding: health-system pressure should be tracked across service coverage, primary-care capacity, medicines, timeliness, quality, public financing, out-of-pocket exposure, household consumption displacement, inequality, and crisis resilience. Coverage improvement is not the same as affordable, timely, effective care.

New social-protection signal: changing work is exposing gaps in who is covered, what protection is adequate, and who pays for resilience

The ILO universal social-protection record adds an institutional coverage-and-financing route. The ILO identifies persistent protection gaps for temporary, part-time, self-employed, domestic, agricultural, micro- and small-enterprise, and other workers in complex employment arrangements. It also separates coverage from adequacy: being formally included does not guarantee sufficient protection through unemployment, illness, disability, parenthood, old age, or job and sector transitions.

The second mechanism is resilience architecture. The paper links social-security contributions, progressive taxation, public subsidies, and—where fiscal capacity is insufficient—international solidarity to the ability of workers, enterprises, and households to absorb climate, demographic, technological, and economic shocks. This is a policy synthesis and institutional mechanism map, not respondent-level take-up data or a causal estimate of benefits on later consumption, work, health, or political behavior.

Rotation finding: social protection should be tracked across legal coverage, actual reach, benefit adequacy, portability, financing, administration, employment transitions, care, health, disability, old age, climate exposure, informality, and household security. Coverage is not the same as usable protection, and financing design determines who can sustain it.

New diaspora-consumption signal: cross-border transfers are large household infrastructure, and payment competition determines how much survives the journey

The World Bank remittance-cost record adds a cross-border household-transfer and digital-payment route. The World Bank estimates global remittance flows at $856 billion in 2024, including $653 billion to low- and middle-income countries. Average sending costs remain around 6%, and only about half of corridors record average costs below 5%. These flows can support everyday consumption, school fees, housing repair, savings, small business, and local resilience, while also making recipient communities sensitive to destination-country labour demand, migration policy, exchange rates, and payment access.

The infrastructure mechanism is distinct: World Bank-summarized research finds that a domestic fast-payment system is associated with a 0.3-to-1 percentage- point reduction in the cost of a $200 remittance, primarily through competition. That is an institutional and market-architecture signal, not proof that every recipient receives more, spends differently, or becomes more secure. Access, identity, interoperability, connectivity, consumer protection, and provider competition determine whether cheaper rails become usable transfers.

Rotation finding: migration should be tracked across mobility, labour demand, remittance volume, fees, exchange-rate spreads, payment speed, digital access, recipient consumption, savings, enterprise, housing, education, diaspora institutions, and policy shocks. A large transfer flow is not the same as low-cost, reliable, or evenly distributed household support.

New national-meaning signal: people assemble pride from culture, services, political institutions, and economic conditions

The Pew national-pride record adds a comparative cultural-legitimacy route. Pew asked 33,486 adults in 25 countries an open-ended question about what makes them proud of their country. In the United States, 22% mentioned freedom while 20% said they were not proud; in the United Kingdom, 29% said they were not proud. Sweden provides a useful institutional contrast: 53% mentioned the way the country is governed as a source of pride.

The public-system mechanism is especially useful for cross-source work. Pride mentions include democracy, freedom, welfare, health care, education, infrastructure, safety, and social programs, while criticism includes leadership, democratic backsliding, prices, wages, debt, jobs, immigration, and international affairs. Among Spaniards, 24% of those satisfied with democracy mentioned government as a source of pride versus 5% of those dissatisfied. These are coded public-attitude aggregates, not individual identity forecasts or causal evidence that services produce pride or pride produces political action.

Rotation finding: cultural legitimacy should be tracked across pride, belonging, morality, public services, material conditions, political performance, freedom, equality, immigration, international standing, age, ideology, party alignment, and reform demand. National identity is a bundle of experiences and institutions, not a single stable attitude.

New food-consumption signal: healthy diets are constrained by value-chain costs and household affordability, not simply by aggregate food supply

The FAO healthy-diet-cost record adds a food-system and everyday-consumption route. FAO estimates that 645 million people faced hunger in 2025, while about 2.7 billion people could not afford a healthy diet. The distinction matters: hunger, dietary adequacy, and the economic ability to purchase diverse nutritious foods are related but not identical conditions.

FAO reports a healthy-diet cost of $4.28 per person per day in 2021 PPP, roughly 25% higher than five years earlier. The cost is shaped after the farm through storage, processing, transport, energy, retail, cold chains, market information, and food loss, while nutrient-dense foods often cost more than cheap calorie sources. That creates a cross-source bridge between food prices, household room, infrastructure, cultural fit, health, work capacity, and agrifood market power. These are global system estimates, not individual diet histories or causal nutrition outcomes.

Rotation finding: food security should be tracked across hunger, healthy- diet affordability, incomes, non-food expenses, food preferences, cultural fit, retail prices, logistics, energy, cold chains, trade, climate, conflict, market concentration, subsidies, and later health and household adaptation. Food availability is not the same as affordable nutrition.

New geopolitical-supply signal: trade integration is both a resilience asset and a shock-transmission network

The FAO agricultural-commodity-market record adds an upstream geopolitical and market-network route. FAO reports that the value of food and agricultural trade increased fivefold between 2000 and 2024, with low- and middle-income countries more integrated into global markets. That integration can diversify supply and create adjustment options, but it also exposes domestic food systems to extreme weather, conflict, pandemics, financial crises, macroeconomic shocks, and logistics disruptions.

The key mechanism is transmission rather than a simple “globalization good or bad” judgment. FAO background analysis says shocks can spread across countries and commodities, reduce trade connectivity, and create caloric deficits where import sources are concentrated. International shocks affect domestic markets unevenly because trade openness, market structure, and policy environments shape the scale and persistence of price effects. Export restrictions, import-promotion, trade agreements, reserves, and price stabilization can dampen or amplify those effects. This is network and policy evidence, not a country-specific price forecast or household causal estimate.

Rotation finding: geopolitical exposure should be tracked across trade connectivity, import concentration, commodity substitution, logistics, fertilizer and energy inputs, price transmission, reserves, export controls, trade agreements, climate, conflict, domestic market structure, and household food security. Integration is not the same as resilience.

New displacement-governance signal: forced movement has eased from its peak while return and reintegration remain high-risk institutional processes

The UNHCR Global Trends record adds a global displacement, hosting, and return route. At the end of 2025, UNHCR counted about 117.8 million forcibly displaced people, including 41.6 million refugees, 9 million asylum-seekers, and 68.7 million people internally displaced by conflict or violence. The aggregate total declined from 2024, but the scale remains equivalent to roughly 1.4% of the world's population.

The useful mechanism is not only movement out of danger; it is the institutional path after movement. UNHCR reports 14.7 million returns in 2025, while 68% of refugees and other people needing international protection were hosted in low- and middle-income countries and 65% lived in neighboring countries. Returns can occur amid damaged homes, degraded infrastructure, weak services, limited economic opportunity, or adverse host-country policies. This creates a cross-source bridge from conflict and governance to housing, education, health, work, food, local host capacity, and political legitimacy. These are population statistics, not individual trajectory or voluntariness evidence.

Rotation finding: displacement should be tracked across origin shocks, route governance, legal status, host concentration, service capacity, duration, returns, reintegration, re-displacement, household assets, education, work, health, gender, disability, and host-community politics. A return count is not the same as a safe or durable solution.

New mobility-governance signal: international movement is limited in aggregate, but pathway design and climate adaptation redistribute risk

The IOM World Migration Report 2026 record complements the UNHCR displacement stock with a broader mobility and governance route. IOM estimates about 304 million international migrants at mid-2024 and more than 83 million people in internal displacement at the end of 2024. Most people still live in their country of birth, so the global migrant stock should not be mistaken for universal or accelerating cross-border movement.

The institutional mechanism is pathway selection. IOM describes regular routes as increasingly selective and unequally distributed across regions and groups; restrictive policies can shift mobility into riskier and more precarious journeys rather than eliminate it. Its climate-mobility analysis links sudden disasters and slow-onset degradation to migration while criticizing reactive responses detached from long-term adaptation. Local governments, communities, Indigenous peoples, diasporas, civil society, and private actors become part of the response architecture. These are population and policy findings, not individual route histories or causal estimates.

Rotation finding: mobility should be tracked across migrant stocks, routes, legal status, visa selectivity, labour demand, remittances, climate exposure, adaptation, local governance, social protection, regularization, risk transfer, internal displacement, and development outcomes. Restriction is not the same as reduced mobility; it can change who bears the risk.

New digital-dependence signal: cyber resilience is becoming an uneven public, economic, and geopolitical capability

The WEF Global Cybersecurity Outlook record adds a digital-infrastructure and cyber-inequity route. In the 2026 leader survey, 87% identified AI-related vulnerabilities as the fastest-growing cyber risk, while the share reporting security assessment of AI tools before deployment rose from 37% to 64%. Geopolitics still influenced cybersecurity strategy for 66% of organizations.

The resilience gap is the more durable mechanism. Sixty-four percent reported meeting minimum cyber-resilience requirements, but only 19% said resilience exceeded requirements; 54% identified limited knowledge and skills as an obstacle to AI-driven cybersecurity. The report links uneven resources, infrastructure, governance, organization size, and supply-chain dependence to systemic exposure. A local breach, cloud outage, or supplier weakness can cascade through retail, manufacturing, aviation, public administration, finance, and daily services. These are leader-survey and systems indicators, not incident counts or individual cyber-harm estimates.

Rotation finding: digital dependence should be tracked across AI adoption, predeployment governance, cyber skills, baseline versus excess resilience, supply-chain exposure, cloud and cable dependence, geopolitical sovereignty, fraud, public-service continuity, organization size, sector, and consumer trust. Connectivity is not the same as resilience.

New digital-social signal: the wellbeing effects of internet use depend on trust, offline activity, generation, gender, and peer saturation

The World Happiness Report Chapter 8 record adds a distinct social-connection mechanism to the existing platform-exit evidence. Using four European Social Survey rounds across 30 countries from 2016–2024 and regional internet speed as an instrument, the chapter reports a negative internet-wellbeing gradient strongest for Gen Z, moderate for Millennials, near zero for Gen X, and slightly positive for Baby Boomers. Younger Europeans—especially Gen Z and Millennial women—also experienced the largest deterioration in trust, perceived social activity, and meeting frequency. Trust, friendship interaction, perceived safety, and attachment to country or Europe are positively related to wellbeing.

The important moderation route is social environment. Internet use appears more beneficial in low-saturation peer environments and increasingly harmful as social-media use becomes widespread among peers; the chapter also reports lower wellbeing among people who post political views online. These results remain heterogeneous by platform, region, generation, gender, and social connection, and they do not establish a universal technology effect or predict an individual's mental health or political behavior.

Rotation finding: digital sociality should be tracked across exposure, platform design, peer saturation, trust, offline meetings, perceived activity, community safety, attachment, political expression, age, gender, region, income, and substitution or complementarity with real-world relationships. Connectivity is not the same as connection.

New water-security signal: infrastructure scarcity becomes a gendered time, safety, health, and governance burden
