The UN World Water Development Report 2026 record adds a global water-and-equal-opportunity route. UN-Water reports that 2.1 billion people still lack safely managed drinking water, while women and girls spend an estimated 250 million hours each day collecting water. In more than 80% of rural households without direct access, women are responsible for collection. The downstream mechanism spans health, education, livelihoods, safety, food security, and lost time for paid, civic, and social activity.

The governance side is equally important: fewer than 20% of formal water- utility workers worldwide are women, and women remain underrepresented in water governance, financing, leadership, technical roles, and infrastructure decisions. Climate change, scarcity, floods, droughts, and disasters amplify these inequalities. This is a global system and institutional signal, not individual time-use or causal health data.

Rotation finding: water security should be tracked across safely managed access, collection time, sanitation, safety, health, education, livelihoods, gender, rurality, climate exposure, infrastructure reliability, affordability, utility workforce, decision power, financing, and community governance. Availability is not the same as equal access or usable time.

New human-development AI signal: public expectations center augmentation, but access and agency decide who benefits

The UNDP Human Development Report 2025 AI record adds a broad human-development and technology-expectations route. UNDP's 21-country global survey reports that 60% expect AI to affect employment positively by creating opportunities in jobs that may not exist today, while 50% expect their current job could be automated; only 13% fear AI could lead to job losses. In lower-human-development countries, about two-thirds anticipate using AI in education, health, or work within a year, and 70% in low- and medium-HDI countries expect productivity gains.

The useful mechanism is not respondent-level prediction. It is the bridge from public expectation to development choice: AI may augment work and personalize health or education, but online access, skills, affordability, local-language fit, service capacity, and human agency determine whether that possibility becomes usable capability. This complements the government-AI governance and cyber-resilience records without claiming that optimism is adoption, job creation, or improved outcomes.

Rotation finding: AI diffusion should be tracked across augmentation, automation, productivity, connectivity, electricity, skills, language fit, health, education, work quality, institutional accountability, human agency, and unequal access. Expectations are not outcomes, and access is not agency.

New social-connection signal: thinner face-to-face contact is becoming a structural and civic-capacity concern

The OECD social-connections record adds a comparative OECD route distinct from the WHO global prevalence record and the World Happiness Report's internet-wellbeing analysis. Across 21 European OECD countries, daily in-person interaction with friends and family declined between 2006, 2015, and 2022 while daily remote contact increased. The share reporting never feeling lonely fell from 59% in 2018 to 51% in 2022, with the youngest group showing a 14-point decline.

The policy mechanism is broader than loneliness as an individual condition. OECD reports that low income and unemployment are associated with roughly twice the likelihood of loneliness, while libraries, parks, community organisations, commercial gathering places, and safe online spaces are possible social infrastructure routes. This creates a public-capacity and civic-participation question: social connection can support health, work, education, and civic engagement, but policy response remains under-evaluated and strong aggregate connection can conceal unequal relationship quality.

Rotation finding: social connection should be tracked across face-to-face contact, remote contact, loneliness, support, relationship quality, age, gender, income, unemployment, living arrangement, place, digital mediation, social infrastructure, health, work, education, and civic participation. Contact is not the same as support, and policy attention is not proof of repair.

New child-digital signal: near-universal access shifts the question from connection to design, exposure, and protection

The OECD child digital-wellbeing record adds a youth and platform-governance route. In OECD comparisons, 96% of 15-year-olds had a desktop, laptop, or tablet at home and 98% had a smartphone with internet access in 2022; at least half of 15-year-olds in most countries spent 30 or more hours per week on digital devices. About 10% of adolescents reported problematic social-media use in 2021–22, up from less than 7% in 2017–18, with higher reported rates among girls and adolescents with a migrant background.

The mechanism is not “screen time causes harm.” OECD emphasizes activity type, platform design, passive versus active engagement, social comparison, cyberbullying, family context, offline vulnerability, and child voice in policy. That makes digital childhood a consumer-protection and institutional-capacity question: when access is ordinary, safety, age assurance, accountability, rights, and usable recourse determine whether children are protected or merely connected.

Rotation finding: child digital life should be tracked across access, device time, activity type, social comparison, harmful content, problematic use, gender, migration, socio-economic status, family context, platform design, age assurance, parental and school support, child voice, safety, and offline well-being. Access is not empowerment, and exposure is not diagnosis.

New platform-governance signal: age limits exist more often than age assurance works at account creation

The OECD age-assurance record adds a service-level implementation endpoint to the child-digital map. In an OECD review of 50 services used by children, only two systematically assured age at account creation, although 26 had some age-assurance mechanism. The remaining gap is not simply a missing rule: minimum ages often arise from privacy or contract law rather than safety, vary by geography, and age-tiered safeguards can be optional or dependent on parental controls.

This makes platform protection a cross-border governance and consumer-recourse problem. A stated minimum age is not the same as knowing who is using a service; age assurance can also create privacy, bias, exclusion, and data-minimisation trade-offs. The source is a public service benchmark, not a test of individual children, enforcement accuracy, or actual harm.

Rotation finding: child online safety should be tracked across stated age rules, systematic assurance, trigger conditions, age tiers, parental controls, privacy, bias, geography, platform design, reporting, moderation, remedy, and regulatory enforceability. A rule is not implementation, and implementation is not safety.

New democratic-resilience signal: institutional quality is weakening unevenly while participation remains a separate capacity

The International IDEA democracy-and-migration record adds a global political-institution route. Across the 173 countries with 2024 data, Freedom of the Press declined in 43 countries, or 24.9% of those covered. Participation was comparatively stable, but only 11 countries had notable changes between 2019 and 2024: nine declines and two advances. Civic Engagement and Civil Society together recorded 22 declines against five advances.

The migration endpoint is institutional inclusion rather than migrant opinion. International IDEA reports that out-of-country voting can strengthen democratic resilience in home and host countries, but diaspora turnout is relatively low and policy and administrative arrangements are often inadequate. This keeps press freedom, rule of law, participation, belonging, and voting access as separate surfaces rather than one democracy score.

Rotation finding: democratic resilience should be tracked across media freedom, expression, courts, electoral integrity, civil society, civic engagement, turnout, migrant status, registration, out-of-country voting, administrative access, belonging, and institutional response. Stability in one pillar is not repair of another.

New social-consumption signal: drug-use demand and synthetic-market adaptation are outrunning equitable treatment access

The UNODC World Drug Report 2025 record adds a global social-consumption and public-health-capacity route. UNODC estimates that 316 million people aged 15–64 used a drug excluding alcohol and tobacco in 2023, about 6% of that population versus 5.2% in 2013. Cannabis accounted for 244 million users, cocaine use reached 25 million, and potential cocaine manufacture reached 3,708 tons; synthetic stimulant seizures also hit a record level.

The more consequential inequality signal is the conversion bottleneck. Of an estimated 64 million people with drug use disorders, only about 8.1% received treatment; the reported ratio was one in 18 women versus one in seven men. Service coverage also varies sharply by region and can be concentrated in urban areas or capitals. This joins market change to gender, stigma, childcare, distance, capacity, and public-health response without treating use as a disorder or seizures as consumption.

Rotation finding: drug trends should be tracked across prevalence, substance mix, synthetic production, trafficking, conflict, price, criminalization, treatment, harm reduction, gender, age, geography, stigma, childcare, service capacity, and recovery. Market growth is not diagnosis, and treatment contact is not recovery.

New macro-capacity signal: sovereign debt is becoming a public-service and everyday-development constraint

The UNCTAD debt record adds a macro-finance-to-public-capacity route. Global public debt reached $102 trillion in 2024, including $31 trillion in developing countries. Developing countries paid $921 billion in public-debt interest, and 61 allocated at least 10% of government revenue to interest payments. UNCTAD estimates that 3.4 billion people live in countries where interest payments exceed spending on either health or education.

The external-finance mechanism is also unequal: developing regions have been borrowing at average rates two to four times those of the United States since 2020; external public-debt service reached $487 billion in 2023, and developing countries paid $25 billion more to external creditors than they received in new disbursements. This does not prove that debt alone caused a household or service loss, but it makes fiscal room, public investment, health, education, infrastructure, and political legitimacy part of the same observable pressure system.

Rotation finding: debt pressure should be tracked across borrowing costs, interest, revenue, exports, aid, liquidity, restructuring, public services, health, education, infrastructure, climate investment, household exposure, and political voice. Aggregate debt is not household incidence, but fiscal space is not abstract when it governs public capacity.

New consumer-market signal: digital choice architecture is turning convenience into a route for financial, privacy, and time detriment

The OECD dark-patterns record adds a consumer-choice and firm-conduct route distinct from scam-loss records. Preliminary OECD survey findings across 20 countries report that 90% of consumers encountered online manipulative design techniques. The relevant exposure is not just advertising: defaults, false urgency, misleading social proof, forced disclosure, hidden fees, and hard-to-cancel services can steer choices, extract data, or consume time. OECD also cites earlier evidence that 50% of online consumers encountered a shopping problem in the prior year and that cumulative severe e-commerce detriment exceeded $22 billion in the cited study.

The institutional mechanism is recourse and market integrity. More information alone may not overcome choice architecture, especially for children, less educated consumers, or people facing financial and digital vulnerability. But encountering a dark pattern is not proof of loss, deception, intent, or legal liability; the next test is to connect interface exposure to payment, privacy, cancellation, switching, remedy, trust, and durable consumer behavior.

Rotation finding: consumer power should be tracked across defaults, fees, urgency, data disclosure, personalization, device, literacy, age, income, privacy, payment, cancellation, switching, enforcement, remedy, and trust. Choice is not autonomy when exit is costly.

New resource-consumption signal: rising material demand is an unequal infrastructure and provisioning problem, not just a climate statistic

The UNEP Global Resources Outlook record adds a material-consumption and planetary-capacity route. Global material extraction rose from 30 billion tonnes in 1970 to 106.6 billion tonnes in 2024, while per-capita demand rose from 8.4 to 13.2 tonnes. High-income countries consume materials at roughly six times the rate of low-income countries, and built environment, mobility, food, and energy together account for about 90% of global material demand.

The household-facing mechanism is provisioning. Under the Historical Trends scenario, extraction could reach roughly 160% of its 2020 level by 2060, with food-and-fibre biomass around 180% and net greenhouse-gas emissions above 120%. UNEP also describes a Sustainability Transition pathway in which resource pressures and inequalities fall, but that outcome depends on infrastructure, trade, finance, circularity, public services, and social acceptance—not individual restraint alone.

Rotation finding: resource pressure should be tracked across extraction, material footprints, trade, housing, mobility, food, energy, waste, pollution, income, infrastructure, affordability, local extraction, circularity, public provisioning, transition costs, and equity. Aggregate efficiency is not local justice, and consumption is not a household moral category.

New work-health signal: psychosocial risk is a work-design and public-capacity problem

The ILO psychosocial-working-environment record adds a work-organization-to-health and productivity route. The ILO's 2026 global report estimates more than 840,000 deaths and nearly 45 million DALYs annually from psychosocial risk factors at work, with an estimated annual loss equivalent to 1.37% of global GDP. These are modelled global estimates, not individual diagnoses or a claim about any particular employer.

The useful cross-source mechanism is the conversion point: job demands, workload, role clarity, autonomy, working-time arrangements, and fair or transparent processes are treated as design and governance conditions. Formal wellbeing programmes can therefore coexist with unchanged staffing, schedules, workload, or worker control. The report makes prevention and management a shared workplace, institutional, and public-health question rather than an individual resilience burden.

Rotation finding: work-health pressure should be tracked across job design, workload, autonomy, scheduling, management, fairness, worker voice, sector, employment status, care demands, health, productivity, compensation, remedy, and exit. A global burden estimate is not worker-level causality, and policy adoption is not safer work.

New adaptation signal: recognized learning is an unequal gateway through digital, green, and care transitions

The ILO lifelong-learning record adds an education-to-work-adaptation route. The report says 16% of workers received training in the past year, compared with 51% of full-time permanent workers in formal firms; access is weakest for lower-educated, insecure, and small-enterprise workers. Informal learning is widespread, but often remains unrecognized and therefore does not reliably convert into qualifications or mobility.

The transition mechanism is broader than technical skill acquisition. ILO links digitalization, AI, green work, and demographic change to rounded skill profiles, infrastructure, industrial and employment policy, and the valuation of care work. Long-term-care employment is projected to rise from 85 million workers in 2023 to 158 million by 2050. The institutional bottleneck is delivery: fragmented systems, weak coordination, financing gaps, and limited social dialogue can leave learning demand disconnected from actual opportunity.

Rotation finding: adaptation capacity should be tracked across training access, informal learning, recognition, qualifications, employer size, job security, digital and green tasks, care work, wages, infrastructure, public financing, worker voice, mobility, and exclusion. Skills demand is not skill power, and training participation is not a guaranteed return.

New state-capacity signal: development finance is becoming a geopolitical and public-service bottleneck

The UN Financing for Sustainable Development 2026 record adds a macro-finance-to-state-capacity route. The UN Inter-agency Task Force places the annual Sustainable Development Goal financing gap above $4 trillion, reports that debt-service burdens reached 20-year highs in developing countries and Small Island Developing States in 2024, and notes that more than 70 developing countries collect tax revenue below 15% of GDP. Official development assistance fell 23.1% from 2024 to 2025 in the report's comparison.

This is not just a debt-total story. The report links geopolitical fragmentation to diverted trade and investment, weaker cross-border capital flows, and greater volatility, while renewable-energy investment reached $2.2 trillion in 2024—about twice fossil-fuel investment. The conversion question is whether financial room becomes resilient public infrastructure and services, or whether financing constraints redistribute costs to governments, firms, households, and vulnerable communities. Neither the financing gap nor the investment total identifies local incidence or political legitimacy by itself.

Rotation finding: state capacity should be tracked across borrowing costs, tax room, aid, trade, investment, energy transition, debt restructuring, infrastructure, public services, resilience, ownership, dependency, multilateral cooperation, and geopolitical leverage. Fiscal pressure is a condition on public action, not proof of a particular service or household outcome.

New digital-capability signal: investment quality is part of infrastructure and state power

The OECD digital-transformation investment record adds an investment-governance route distinct from digital-government adoption. The OECD framework organizes digital investment around governance, regulation, technical and financial support, and information/facilitation, while connecting investment to competition, cross-border data flows, trade agreements, skills, and responsible business conduct.

The important mechanism is quality and control, not capital volume. The OECD uses Morocco, Uzbekistan, and Viet Nam as country examples and draws on FDI quality, regulatory-restrictiveness, tax-incentive, and investment-promotion tools. The framework makes domestic capability, data governance, local skills, and public bargaining conditions part of whether international investment creates usable digital infrastructure or deeper dependency. It does not itself measure local service quality, ownership, worker outcomes, or household access.

Rotation finding: digital transformation should be tracked across capital source, infrastructure, regulation, competition, data flows, skills, local capability, firm concentration, public procurement, ownership, portability, service quality, and geopolitical dependence. Investment attraction is not digital inclusion, and policy coherence is not realized capacity.

New digital-participation signal: connectivity is expanding while meaningful access remains stratified

The ITU connectivity-divides record adds a population-facing digital-infrastructure route. ITU estimates roughly 6 billion people online in 2025, with 2.2 billion still offline. Yet the quality and affordability gradient is substantial: 5G coverage reaches 84% of people in high-income countries versus 4% in low-income countries, and mobile-broadband service remains unaffordable in about 60% of low- and middle-income countries.

The social mechanism is meaningful participation rather than a binary access count. ITU reports internet use at 94% in high-income countries versus 23% in low-income countries, 77% for men versus 71% for women, and 85% in urban areas versus 58% in rural areas. These gaps shape who can use digital public services, education, work, markets, platforms, and political information, but they do not by themselves identify individual preference, harm, or outcome.

Rotation finding: digital participation should be tracked across coverage, quality, affordability, devices, skills, safety, age, gender, income, rurality, public-service access, platform use, work, misinformation, environmental cost, and exit or non-use. Being online is not meaningful connectivity, and meaningful connectivity is not equal power.

New innovation-power signal: breakthrough technology is concentrated in metropolitan ecosystems while investment momentum cools

The WIPO innovation-cluster record adds a firm, place, and geopolitical-capability route. WIPO's 2025 index covers 139 economies and describes AI and quantum progress advancing while innovation- investment growth slows, venture-capital activity moderates, and patenting gains remain modest. Its top 100 innovation clusters account for roughly 70% of global PCT filings and VC deal activity and about half of scientific publications; the top ten alone account for about 40% of PCT filings and 35% of VC deals.

The concentration is not just a ranking. Clusters unite universities, inventors, venture capital, and R&D firms, often across administrative borders. China has 24 top-100 clusters and the United States 22, while middle-income clusters appear across Brazil, Egypt, India, Iran, Malaysia/Singapore, Mexico, and Türkiye. This creates a route from local infrastructure, skills, housing, and firm ecosystems to national technological capacity and external leverage, but cluster presence does not establish local benefit, ownership, or reduced inequality.

Rotation finding: innovation power should be tracked across research, patents, VC, firms, universities, skills, energy, housing, local labour markets, ownership, diffusion, public procurement, supply chains, and geopolitical dependence. Innovation leadership is not broad prosperity, and cluster density is not community control.

New information-culture signal: social video and personality-led news are reshaping trust and political attention

The Reuters Institute Digital News Report record adds a cultural, platform, and political-attention route. Across 48 markets, social-video news consumption rose from 52% in 2020 to 65% in 2025, while any online video rose from 67% to 75%. Six online networks now reach more than 10% weekly for news, compared with two a decade ago. In the United States, social and video networks reached 54% weekly—above TV news at 50% and news websites or apps at 48%—and the shift is especially strong among younger adults.

The trust mechanism is unsettled rather than one-directional. Fifty-eight percent across markets are concerned about telling true from false online news, yet overall news trust remains 40%. AI chatbots are already used for news by 7% weekly overall and 15% of under-25s; audiences expect AI to make news cheaper and more current but less transparent, accurate, and trustworthy. The source also finds that people most often say they would verify suspected falsehoods through trusted news outlets or official sources, not social media alone. These are aggregate survey results, not proof of persuasion, voting, or platform causality.

Rotation finding: information power should be tracked across format, creator, platform, algorithmic distribution, age, political identity, local news, verification, moderation, AI mediation, trust, misinformation, payment, participation, and exit. Reach is not influence, exposure is not belief, and trust is not accuracy.

New demographic signal: population ageing and continued growth are splitting the policy map

The UN World Population Prospects record adds a demographic-structure route. UN DESA projects global population to rise from about 8.2 billion in 2024 to 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s before easing to roughly 10.2 billion by 2100, with an 80% probability of a peak this century. More than half of countries are already below replacement fertility, while nearly one-fifth are below 1.4 births per woman. This is a split system: 63 countries had already peaked by 2024, while 126 are projected to keep growing through 2054.

The downstream route is institutional and cultural, not merely numerical. Global life expectancy reached 73.3 years in 2024; by the late 2070s people aged 65 and older are projected to outnumber children under 18, while rapid- growth countries face youth, education, employment, and infrastructure demands. The same demographic transition therefore changes care supply, work, migration, housing, family formation, social protection, and state legitimacy in different places. Projections do not reveal desired family size, individual agency, or whether longer life is healthy, secure, or supported.

Rotation finding: demographic change should be tracked across fertility, longevity, care, work, migration, housing, education, family time, social protection, health, disability, gender, consumption, and state capacity. A population projection is not a household preference, and ageing is not dependency by definition.

New place signal: urban growth is concentrated in cities and smaller settlements, not only megacities

The UN World Urbanization Prospects record adds a settlement-structure route distinct from the population-ageing record. Using a harmonized Degree of Urbanization, UN DESA estimates that cities held 45% of the world's 8.2 billion people in 2025, towns 36%, and rural areas 19%. Two-thirds of population growth through 2050 is projected to occur in cities, with most of the remainder in towns; the rural population is expected to peak in the 2040s and then decline.

The policy mechanism is distributed urban capacity. The number of megacities rose from 8 in 1975 to 33 in 2025 and is projected to reach 37 by 2050, but 96% of the roughly 12,000 cities have fewer than one million residents and 81% have fewer than 250,000. More than half of the projected 989 million increase in city residents is concentrated in seven countries. This points to planning, land, housing, transport, digital access, care, energy, water, and local-state capacity in smaller and rapidly growing places—not just global-city power.

Rotation finding: place change should be tracked across settlement type, city size, housing, land, transport, work, care, energy, water, digital access, climate exposure, local finance, migration, service quality, and resident voice. Urbanization is not megacity concentration, and population growth is not service capacity.

New generational signal: youth opportunity is moving toward growing lower-income regions

The UN World Population Highlights 2026: Youth record adds a youth-demography and transition-capacity route distinct from the broader population and settlement projections. The UN estimates roughly 1.3 billion people aged 15-24 in 2025. Between 2025 and 2050, the youth population is projected to grow 16% in low- and lower-middle-income countries and decline 24% in high- and upper-middle-income countries; the lower-income group would contain 69% of the world's youth by 2050, up from 59% in 2025.

That shift changes where education, health, decent work, migration, rights, digital safety, and political voice become capacity bottlenecks. In higher- income countries, the publication projects roughly three people aged 65 or older for every person aged 15-24 by 2050, making youth representation and intergenerational solidarity an institutional question as well. These are population projections and policy priorities, not individual attitudes, respondent outcomes, or proof of a demographic dividend.

Rotation finding: youth change should be tracked across cohort size, education, skills, decent work, health, reproduction, migration, housing, digital life, rights, intergenerational bargaining, participation, and state investment. A growing youth population is an opportunity only when institutions convert it into usable capability and voice.

New social-capacity signal: youth mental health is shaped by linked institutions and social conditions

The UN World Youth Report mental-health record adds a social-capacity route distinct from the youth population projection. The report organizes youth mental health and well-being around six interlinked determinants: education, employment, family dynamics, poverty and deprivation, technology and the digital environment, and society and community. It treats inequality, stigma, discrimination, and unequal access to opportunity and care as connected barriers rather than isolated clinical variables.

The institutional implication is broad: supportive schools and social-emotional learning, decent and less precarious work transitions, family and community support, safer digital environments, privacy-protective data practices, prevention, early intervention, and youth-led initiatives all sit in the same policy route. The publication synthesizes evidence and mechanisms; it does not prove a single determinant caused an individual's outcome or substitute for local service evaluation.

Rotation finding: youth well-being should be tracked across exposure, stigma, school, work, family, poverty, technology, community, service access, prevention, privacy, agency, and institutional remedy. Mental-health capacity is partly a question of social conditions and usable public infrastructure.

New macro-consumer signal: geopolitical energy shocks transmit through prices, supply chains, and public capacity

The UN WESP mid-2026 record adds a macroeconomic transmission route. UN DESA projects global growth at 2.5% in 2026 and 2.8% in 2027, while global inflation is projected to reach 3.9% in 2026 after the Middle East crisis reversed the recent disinflationary trend. The report describes the shock as moving through energy, fertilizer, food, freight, insurance, transport, and import costs, with low-income households more exposed because food and energy occupy a larger budget share.

The downstream political-economic route is equally important: higher rates can contain inflation while weakening growth, while weaker growth and crisis spending constrain fiscal space. Developing economies face tighter external financing and greater food-insecurity, debt, and SDG risks. These are forecasts and transmission mechanisms, not household incidence, product-level pass-through, or proof of realized political action.

Rotation finding: geopolitical events should be tracked across energy transit, commodity prices, supply chains, household purchasing power, firm costs, labour markets, financial flows, fiscal response, food security, inequality, and international coordination. Positive aggregate growth can coexist with severe distributional pressure.

New implementation signal: public systems have delivered gains at scale, but progress is uneven and increasingly exposed to crisis

The UN Sustainable Development Goals Report 2026 record adds a public-system-results route. Since 2015, the report attributes roughly one billion additional people to safely managed drinking water and 1.2 billion to safely managed sanitation, while electricity access reaches 92% of the world's population, internet access rose from 40% to 74%, and social protection now covers more than half the global population. This is evidence that policy, investment, data, and cooperation can produce gains at scale.

The counter-signal is implementation fragility. Among 139 targets with trend data, 36% are on track or making moderate progress, 49% are advancing too slowly, and 15% have regressed below 2015 baselines. The report also highlights 273 million children and young people out of school, one in five young people not in employment, education, or training, a 23.1% fall in official development assistance in 2025, and major displacement and informal-settlement pressures. Coverage is not reliability, affordability, adequacy, or individual receipt.

Rotation finding: public progress should be tracked across policy input, infrastructure, access, quality, affordability, reach, durability, crisis resilience, financing, data, remedy, and unequal distribution. The existence of large-scale gains does not erase implementation gaps; regression does not erase the capacity to scale what works.

New civic-digital signal: online space is becoming more controlled, manipulated, and politically consequential

The Freedom on the Net 2025 record adds a civic-digital control route distinct from news consumption and basic connectivity. Freedom House reports a fifteenth consecutive year of global internet-freedom decline: conditions deteriorated in 27 of 72 assessed countries, while 17 improved. Its population-weighted control indicators report that 81% of internet users live where people were arrested or imprisoned for online expression, 69% where political, social, or religious content was blocked, 61% where social-media access was restricted, and 52% where authorities disconnected networks.

The mechanism is not only blocking. Paid commenters, imitation news sites, AI-generated misleading content, undisclosed progovernment influencers, and pressure on satellite providers create a layered environment in which access, visibility, trust, anonymity, and political action can diverge. These are expert-coded country assessments and documented control environments, not proof of individual persuasion, voting, or belief change.

Rotation finding: digital civic power should be tracked across access, content, manipulation, identity, privacy, surveillance, shutdowns, platform rules, infrastructure, circumvention, journalism, protest, trust, and remedy. Connectivity can expand participation while the same infrastructure expands control.

New material-land signal: forest loss is slowing, but land-use, ownership, and livelihood pressures remain uneven

The FAO Global Forest Resources Assessment 2025 record adds a land, livelihood, and ecological-capacity route. Forests cover roughly 4.14 billion hectares, or 32% of global land. Annual net forest loss fell from 10.7 million hectares in the 1990s to 4.12 million in 2015-2025, but that net improvement combines slower deforestation with slower forest expansion; it does not mean ecological recovery is uniform. Naturally regenerating forests make up 92% of forest area, while primary forests cover at least 1.18 billion hectares.

The governance signal is distributed ownership and use. Public ownership is 71% globally, about 20% of forests are legally protected, 55% are covered by long-term management plans, and only 5% are designated primarily for social services such as recreation, culture, and education. Formal designation is not the same as enforcement, community consent, benefit sharing, or ecological quality; forest area is not a proxy for local livelihood security.

Rotation finding: land and ecological change should be tracked across commodity demand, deforestation, regeneration, ownership, management rights, protection, carbon, biodiversity, water, food, culture, restoration, community voice, and benefit distribution. Aggregate environmental improvement can coexist with local dispossession or degraded ecological function.

New trade-technology signal: AI may expand global trade, but infrastructure gaps and regulatory fragmentation can concentrate the gains

The WTO World Trade Report 2025 record adds a trade, firm-capability, and geopolitical-technology route. WTO scenarios project that AI could increase global trade by 34-37% and global GDP by 12-13% by 2040, with digitally deliverable services trade rising 42% across scenarios. The report frames the mechanism through lower trade costs, supply-chain visibility, customs and compliance, language barriers, market intelligence, contract enforcement, and small-firm access—not simply automation.

The distributional hinge is catch-up. In one scenario, halving the digital- infrastructure gap and increasing AI adoption produces modeled income gains of 15% for low-income and 14% for middle-income economies. But AI-enabling-goods trade was already about $2.3 trillion in 2023 while quantitative restrictions on those goods rose from 130 in 2012 to nearly 500 in 2024. These are models and policy indicators, not realized firm or worker outcomes; access is not ownership, control, or bargaining power.

Rotation finding: AI globalization should be tracked across infrastructure, skills, data, firms, supply chains, trade costs, tasks, wages, ownership, standards, tariffs, restrictions, interoperability, labour policy, and local capability. Aggregate AI growth can coexist with concentrated value and uneven voice.

New digital-material signal: digital consumption is becoming an energy, water, mineral, and waste system

The UNCTAD Digital Economy Report 2024 record adds a material-footprint route distinct from digital access, civic control, and AI-trade scenarios. Smartphone shipments reached roughly 1.2 billion in 2023, IoT devices are projected to reach 39 billion by 2029, and business e-commerce sales across 43 countries reached about $27 trillion in 2022. Digital devices, data centres, and ICT networks account for an estimated 6-12% of global electricity use.

The infrastructure and supply-chain effects are uneven. Data centres used an estimated 460 TWh in 2022 and could reach 1,000 TWh in 2026; critical-mineral demand for cobalt, graphite, and lithium is projected to rise 500% by 2050. Developing countries formally collected only 7.5% of digital waste in 2022, versus 47% in developed countries, while they often bear extraction and waste costs without capturing high-value processing. These are aggregate footprint and value-chain indicators, not household device-use or local causal estimates.

Rotation finding: digital change should be tracked across devices, e-commerce, energy, water, minerals, data centres, waste, repair, recycling, ownership, value capture, local resource competition, labour, and circularity. Digital inclusion without material accountability can shift costs rather than remove them.

New legitimacy signal: institutions are redefining progress beyond GDP toward well-being, equity, sustainability, and resilience

The UN Beyond GDP record adds a measurement-and-legitimacy route. The UN High-Level Expert Group proposes a 31-indicator dashboard organized around four pillars: foundational principles, current well-being, equity and inclusion, and sustainability and resilience. The proposed domains include material conditions and work, health, education, security, subjective well-being, inequality, poverty, work inclusion, regional disparities, social cohesion, human and social capital, institutional quality, natural capital, and environmental quality.

The cultural and political shift is in what becomes visible to decision-makers. The framework argues that GDP can rise while safety, environmental quality, health, equality, peace, or social cohesion deteriorate. It recommends country-owned dashboards and recognizes cross-border spillovers, while UNCTAD is piloting implementation. This is a proposed measurement framework—not proof that governments have adopted it or that indicators have changed outcomes.

Rotation finding: legitimacy should be tracked across what institutions measure, fund, communicate, and remedy. Progress metrics can broaden public judgment, but they can also become symbolic unless data, budgets, accountability, and local voice follow.

New firm-geopolitical signal: investment is recovering but concentrating in strategic megaprojects and a narrow host-economy set

The UNCTAD World Investment Report 2026 record adds a firm, capital, and geopolitical-capacity route. Global FDI rose 6% to about $1.6 trillion in 2025, but inflows to developing economies rose only 2% to $901 billion compared with 11% growth in developed economies. More than 80% of global FDI went to the top 20 host economies, while strategic sectors made up 44% of global greenfield project value in 2025, up from 16% in 2020; AI-related digital-infrastructure megaprojects were a major driver.

The key conversion question is what capital builds. UNCTAD identifies productive capacity, jobs, skills, technology transfer, and resilient value chains as the conditions that turn investment into broader development impact. Announced projects and FDI totals do not prove completed capacity, local ownership, quality jobs, technology diffusion, or community acceptance; geopolitical fragmentation and high financing costs may further intensify concentration.

Rotation finding: firm power should be tracked across capital source, project completion, sector, host place, ownership, infrastructure, jobs, skills, technology transfer, supplier linkages, environmental burden, public leverage, and local voice. Investment recovery can coexist with narrow development reach.

New climate-education signal: climate disruption is interrupting schooling and future opportunity, not only physical safety

The UNICEF Learning Interrupted record adds an education-continuity route. UNICEF estimates that at least 171 million students experienced climate-related school disruption in 2025 across 106 countries and territories—at least one in ten students—with 75% of affected students in low- and lower-middle-income countries. Forty countries experienced multiple disruption events, making recovery between shocks a distinct concern.

UNICEF estimates that disrupted learning and widening education inequality could put at least $200 billion in lifetime earnings at risk. The important mechanism is broader than attendance: school closure interrupts learning, routines, peer relationships, protection, access to services, and pathways into work, while resilient infrastructure, early warning, flexible delivery, and recovery support can buffer the effects. These are aggregate and modeled estimates, not student- level learning or earnings data.

Rotation finding: climate impacts should be tracked across hazard exposure, school closure, duration, learning continuity, infrastructure, transport, teachers, digital access, protection, family adaptation, recovery, future work, and local voice. Education systems are also social and cultural resilience infrastructure.

New mineral-security signal: transition demand is colliding with concentrated refining and strategic trade controls

The IEA Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 record adds a material, firm, infrastructure, and geopolitical route. Global battery demand exceeded 1.5 TWh in 2025 and grew more than 35%; the energy sector drove about 75% of demand growth for key energy minerals. At the same time, the average share of the top refined supplier reached 70% in 2025, up from 68% in 2020, while export controls and conflict-related chokepoints transmitted risk into batteries, vehicles, grids, semiconductors, fertiliser inputs, and defence systems.

The Latin America section makes the conversion question visible: the region produces large shares of copper and lithium but refines only about one-fifth of its mined output of key energy minerals. IEA models substantial additional regional value if processing expands, while identifying finance, power, water, technology, skills, and local-stakeholder engagement as constraints. These are market, policy, and modeled exposure signals—not mine-level environmental incidence, completed projects, consumer losses, or proof of geopolitical leverage.

Rotation finding: transition security should be tracked across extraction, refining, ownership, trade controls, stockpiles, substitution, recycling, power and water, skills, local voice, downstream firms, prices, and external response. Clean-energy and digital expansion can increase capability while also deepening concentrated mineral dependence.

New cultural-policy signal: culture is being elevated into development infrastructure while protection and distribution lag

The UNESCO cultural-policy and creative-economy record adds a direct cultural route to the atlas. UNESCO's global policy report draws on more than 1,200 national and local reports and finds that 93% of reporting Member States recognize culture in national sustainable-development plans. Yet the more operational measure is narrower: 85% of reporting countries include cultural and creative industries in development plans, while only 56% set specific cultural objectives.

The sector is economically material—UNESCO reports cultural and creative industries generate about 3.39% of global GDP and 3.55% of jobs—but the support system is uneven. The companion 2026 creativity report records low public funding, weak reported protection of artists' economic and social rights, unequal inward artistic mobility, platform concentration, a large digital- skills gap, and modeled generative-AI revenue exposure for music and audiovisual creators. Cultural recognition therefore does not automatically become creator security, diverse production, accessible participation, or social cohesion.

Rotation finding: cultural trends should be tracked across public recognition, funding, rights, platform distribution, creator income, AI use, artistic freedom, education, mobility, local institutions, participation, and political or social meaning. Culture is both an economy and a governance infrastructure, with a measurable gap between symbolic inclusion and usable capacity.

New public-workforce signal: state capacity is a labor, management, and digital conversion problem

The World Bank Public Workforce Performance and Prosperity record adds an institutional route between public resources and usable outcomes. The report frames roughly 400 million public-sector workers as the operational layer connecting wage bills, staffing, skills, management, integrity, community engagement, and digital systems to education, health, climate, revenue, peace, fiscal sustainability, and citizen trust.

The cross-country contrast is substantial: low-income countries typically have 10–20 public workers per 1,000 people, compared with 50–140 in high-income countries. The public sector accounts for 38% of formal employment globally and 59% in fragile, conflict, or violence-affected states, while women represent 46% of the public workforce versus 33% of the private workforce. Public-sector pay, management, and digital systems therefore affect both service capacity and labor-market structure. These are aggregate and organizational findings, not individual worker or citizen respondent outcomes, and they do not prove that reform produces better services or trust.

Rotation finding: state capacity should be tracked across recruitment, staffing location, pay, management, digital use, worker voice, service delivery, fiscal capacity, integrity, community connection, citizen trust, and reform implementation. A larger budget or a new information system is not yet a usable institution.

New consumer-finance signal: digital access is becoming a protection and recourse problem, not only an inclusion problem

The OECD Consumer Finance Risk Monitor 2026 record adds a market-to-protection route across 60 jurisdictions and 107 government ministries or financial authorities. Financial scams and frauds were the leading operating-environment risk identified for consumers. The report also maps harm through mobile banking, transaction accounts, digital wallets, debit cards, push payments, cross-border transactions, insurance, credit, investment, and pension products.

The important consumer pattern is institutional routing. In the banking and payments sector, scams and fraud were the most common complaint subject across firms, alternative-dispute-resolution schemes, and supervisory authorities. Complaint volumes received by supervisory authorities rose in almost 70% of reporting jurisdictions from 2024 to 2025, but complaint growth can reflect worsening harm, better awareness, stronger confidence in redress, or improved reporting. These are authority-level assessments, not individual consumer respondent or victimization data, and they do not prove loss, remedy, recovery, switching, or trust change.

Rotation finding: consumer-finance trends should be tracked across product design, digital access, fraud exposure, loss, reporting, complaint routing, redress, recovery, switching, and trust. Digital finance can expand access and simultaneously raise the cost of safe participation when protection capacity lags product and platform expansion.

New public-institutions signal: administrative quality reaches firms through procurement prices, delays, and regulatory predictability

The World Bank Institutions and Prosperity record adds a firm and market conversion layer distinct from the public-workforce record. Its framework separates four organizational dimensions—personnel, financial resources, information systems, and management—from three governance dimensions—independence, accountability, and transparency. The key claim is that policy mandates do not become market outcomes unless an institution can implement them with those complements.

The procurement evidence makes the mechanism tangible. Better personnel, systems, management, compensation, and timely payment are associated with easier contracting and fewer delays, renegotiations, overruns, and barriers to smaller suppliers. In an Italy case, the lowest-performing procurement units paid about 55% more than the highest-performing units for similar products. A Peru telecommunications case links leadership turnover to delayed regulatory milestones and stronger transparency/accountability to lower uncertainty. These are comparative and named-case findings—not firm respondents, consumer price incidence, or universal causal estimates.

Rotation finding: firm and consumer outcomes should be tracked from mandate through agency capacity, contract design, bidder access, payment, price, delay, service quality, oversight, and political response. “Regulation” and “procurement” are not single variables; their organizational conversion layer can redistribute cost, competition, and market access.

New information-integrity signal: press freedom is public infrastructure for accountability, while platforms and AI reshape discourse control

The UNESCO World Trends in Freedom of Expression and Media Development record adds an information-as-public-good route distinct from platform-use and news- attention records. UNESCO reports a 10% global decline in its Freedom of Expression Index since 2012 and frames journalism as an institutional condition for public access to information, accountability, human rights, electoral integrity, and informed citizenship.

The report connects that decline to weakened governance, hostility toward journalists, digital repression, platform-policy abuse, algorithmic manipulation, synthetic or altered AI content, and concentration of economic and political power among technology companies. It also preserves countervailing developments—social-media access, collaborative investigative journalism, subscription models, and community media—so the direction is not simply “more technology equals less voice.” These are global index and publication findings, not individual media-use, persuasion, voting, or respondent-level outcomes.

Rotation finding: information trends should be tracked across press freedom, ownership, platform distribution, AI mediation, moderation, journalist safety, public access, local news, trust, institutional accountability, and civic action. Access to content is not the same as an independent information system.

New integrated-development signal: geopolitical fracture, digital capacity, and civic distrust are interacting rather than moving in separate lanes

The UNDP Trends Update 2026 record adds a cross-domain connector to the atlas. Its 12-theme development landscape links multilateral fracture, conflict cascades, gender, health, digital and AI capacity, uneven prosperity, migration, distrust, debt, sustainable finance, energy transition, and environmental limits. The update reports 59 active state-based conflicts, 78 countries involved in conflict beyond their borders, 2.2 billion people offline, and protest activity increasing in 88 countries.

The value of this source is the interaction map: defense and aid choices affect development room; conflict and resource competition affect energy and digital systems; identity and AI capacity affect access and governance; and grievance can shift participation toward localized or confrontational action when formal institutions cannot absorb it. These are source-specific aggregate indicators in an analytical trends update—not respondent-level data, a pooled causal model, or proof that any one fracture caused later political or social behavior.

Rotation finding: cross-domain trends should be followed across state action, resource allocation, infrastructure, identity, platforms, conflict exposure, civic voice, institutional response, and later adaptation. The important endpoint is not one trend line but whether interacting pressures narrow or widen the practical room for cooperation and development.

New geopolitical-labor signal: an external crisis can become a household shock through work hours, real income, migration, and remittances

The ILO Middle East crisis labor-transmission record adds a dated shock-to-work-to-household route. Under an illustrative scenario with oil prices about 50% above their early-2026 average, the ILO projects global hours worked to fall 0.5% in 2026 and 1.1% in 2027—equivalent to about 14 million and 38 million full-time jobs—with real labor income down 1.1% and 3.0%. The transmission runs through energy prices, transport, supply chains, tourism, investment confidence, labor demand, migration, and remittances.

Exposure is not uniform: Arab States have roughly 40% of employment in high-exposure sectors, while Asia and the Pacific have 22% of workers in such sectors. The ILO also reports disproportionate adjustment risk for migrant workers and early pressure on remittances. These are modeled and aggregate signals, not worker or household respondent data, realized losses, or a completed crisis forecast.

Rotation finding: geopolitical shocks should be tracked across conflict, energy, transport, firms, sectors, hours, wages, migration, remittances, social protection, and household adaptation. A distant crisis becomes socially meaningful when the transmission reaches work, income, and the practical room of households and origin communities.

Energy-policy implementation: shocks are widening the state response

The IEA State of Energy Policy 2026 record adds a distinct policy-response layer to the atlas. The IEA tracks more than 6,500 measures across 84 countries and shows governments responding through emergency reserves, gas buffers, demand restraint, affordability support, energy-access initiatives, regulatory changes, and policies for renewable and nuclear deployment, electrification, and supply-chain resilience. This connects geopolitical disruption to public capacity, fiscal targeting, infrastructure, firm incentives, and unequal exposure without treating policy counts as proof of implementation or household benefit.

The distributional signal is especially important: the IEA reports about USD 220 billion in household energy-affordability support during 2022–2023, while only 25% of short-term interventions since 2022 targeted vulnerable households most exposed to price shocks. At the same time, regulatory rollbacks in 2025 affected 30% of regulated energy consumption versus 17% subject to stricter rules. These are aggregate policy patterns, not respondent-level data, take-up estimates, or evidence that any specific household gained or lost protection.

Rotation finding: energy policy should be followed across shock management, budget allocation, regulation, access, technology deployment, firm response, consumer exposure, and later reliability or affordability outcomes. The key open arrow is whether broad policy activity becomes durable, targeted capacity that changes practical room for households, workers, firms, and communities.

Humanitarian capacity: displacement need is filtered through funding and access systems

The UNHCR Global Report 2025 record adds a distinct displacement-to-institutional-capacity route. UNHCR aimed to protect and assist 129.4 million forcibly displaced and stateless people in 2025, while available funding covered 37% of total needs. Available resources fell by $1.246 billion, and the workforce was reduced by more than 6,600 positions by January 2026. This links geopolitical conflict and displacement to donor allocation, operational reach, staffing, and service continuity.

The report also shows why “assistance” is not the endpoint: protection services, legal aid, documentation, work access, cash, national education and health systems, resettlement, and local integration are different conversion stages. Tightly earmarked funding reached 44% of the portfolio, which can preserve specified priorities while reducing flexibility for under-covered or newly emerging crises. These are institutional and aggregate signals—not individual service receipt, respondent-level data, or proof of durable protection, adequate income, safe return, or equal access.

Rotation finding: displacement should be tracked from conflict and movement through donor resources, operational capacity, legal status, work and service access, host institutions, and durable outcomes. The open arrow is whether formal protection capacity becomes practical, sustained room for displaced people and host communities.

Trade governance: flexibility is becoming a strategy for managing fragmentation

The WTO World Trade Report 2026 record adds a market-and-institutional route to the atlas. The report describes a trade system with more dispersed economic power, more diverse membership, complex frictions, regional and targeted agreements, rising digital services, and AI as both an opportunity and a governance stressor. Low- and middle-income economies' share of global trade rose from 23% in 1995 to 45% in 2024, while more than 380 regional trade agreements have been notified to the WTO.

The report's modeled scenarios make the institutional stakes visible: a geopolitically fragmented world is associated with a 5.1% global GDP decline and an 18.6% export decline, while an FTA-only scenario is associated with larger modeled losses. These are counterfactual simulations, not forecasts or realized losses. The broader signal is that safeguards, waivers, regional agreements, and special treatment can preserve cooperation under pressure but can also raise prices, divert trade, or weaken predictability if disconnected from capacity and need.

Rotation finding: trade trends should be followed from rule design through firm and sector exposure, prices, technology access, worker and consumer room, development space, and geopolitical alignment. The open arrow is whether flexibility widens participation and bargaining capacity or becomes a pathway to fragmented standards, concentrated leverage, and unequal gains.

Macro-fiscal resilience: geopolitical shocks narrow the room to respond

The World Bank Global Economic Prospects June 2026 record adds a fiscal-space and investment route. The World Bank projects global growth slowing to 2.5% in 2026 from 2.9% in 2025, with inflation at 4.0%, while a more severe disruption and financial-stress scenario reduces modeled growth to 1.3%. Regional exposure differs with energy dependence, strategic reserves, policy buffers, food and fertilizer prices, and fiscal capacity. These are forecasts and scenarios, not realized household or firm outcomes.

The deeper trend is institutional room: developing-economy government debt has risen from under 40% of GDP in 2010 to over 70%, and the World Bank associates rising debt with higher sovereign spreads and domestic-currency yields. That can narrow the room for infrastructure, health, education, jobs, and social protection precisely when shocks increase demand for them. Private investment and AI adoption are therefore not standalone growth stories; they depend on finance, infrastructure, institutions, and the ability of public systems to absorb risk.

Rotation finding: macro shocks should be followed from energy and food prices through inflation, debt service, fiscal buffers, public support, firm finance, investment, jobs, and household room. The open arrow is whether stabilization preserves practical capacity for people and firms or shifts the shock into future public-service and opportunity constraints.

Work inequality: employment form and opportunity shape the value of work

The ILO Inequalities in the World of Work record adds a structural labor-market route. The publication treats inequality as more than a headline wage gap: it separates vertical earnings inequality, horizontal differences across groups and labor markets, and inequality of opportunity tied to circumstances beyond individual control. It also identifies sector and employment form as major parts of the distributional mechanism.

The own-account and informality signal matters for the atlas because autonomy, entry, volatility, protection, and bargaining can coexist in the same work form. The ILO reports high earnings inequality in Sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America and substantial within-group inequality among own-account workers, especially in informal economies. These are comparative publication findings, not individual wage estimates, new microdata analysis, or proof that formalization alone improves household security.

Rotation finding: work trends should be followed from sector and employment form through earnings, protection, bargaining, time, household room, and institutional response. The open arrow is whether formalization and decent-work policies expand practical opportunity without eliminating flexible entry routes or shifting costs onto already exposed workers.

Education and digital learning: future-ready capability depends on foundations and context

The OECD PISA 2025 record adds a social-reproduction and institutional-capacity route. Across 91 systems, the OECD reports large declines in reading and mathematics performance, with one in five OECD 15-year-olds now low performers across science, mathematics, and reading. The socioeconomic science gap is 85 points on average, while 76% of students report feeling that they belong at school. These are published assessment aggregates, not new respondent-level analysis or later-life causal estimates.

The digital signal is more conditional than a simple “technology helps/hurts” story: 46% of OECD students report weekly-or-more AI chatbot use for learning, digital distraction is common, and performance patterns vary with the task and whether students are taught to assess AI-generated information. Almost two thirds reach the relevant computational problem-solving level, but only half also show basic proficiency in science, reading, and mathematics. AI therefore adds a capability and governance layer to education, while foundational skills, school climate, family resources, and teacher guidance remain complements.

Rotation finding: education trends should be followed from access and family resources through school capacity, learning, belonging, digital tools, AI guidance, future work, and civic capability. The open arrow is whether digital adoption expands practical learning room or amplifies pre-existing inequality when foundational and institutional complements are weak.

Care financing: aging and work-form change reshape the social-protection base

The OECD Financing of Social Protection record adds a social-reproduction and public-finance route. OECD and EU social- protection expenditure is about 23% of GDP; by 2045, pension spending is projected to rise by 1.1 percentage points of GDP in the OECD and health and long-term-care spending by 1.5 points. These are comparative projections, not individual care needs, benefit adequacy, or household outcomes.

The financing mechanism is unevenly tied to work: social-security contributions covered 43% of OECD social spending in 2023, down from 47% in 1995, while self-employed workers represented 14% of EU employment but only 4% of social- protection contributions. Under the report’s hours scenario, total hours worked fall by about 9% across the OECD and almost 20% across the EU between 2024 and 2060. That makes care, pensions, family benefits, and poverty prevention a question of coverage and financing architecture—not only benefit generosity.

Rotation finding: care trends should be followed from demographic change through work form, contributions, informal care, service access, public budgets, firms, and household time. The open arrow is whether broader financing bases expand protection without shifting costs onto caregivers, unstable workers, or families with the least room.

Health-workforce capacity: care access depends on where workers are and when they exit

The WHO National Health Workforce Accounts 2026 record adds a service-supply endpoint to the care map. WHO reports that health-worker density rose 52% from 2006 to 2025 to 67.9 per 10,000 population, with more than 70 million health and care workers globally. That aggregate improvement coexists with a 13-fold medical-doctor density ratio between the WHO European and African regions and a six-fold nursing/midwifery ratio. These are workforce and planning statistics, not patient-level access or quality measures.

The demographic pressure is two-sided: nearly one in four doctors is older than 55, the projected global shortage reaches 11.1 million health workers by 2030, and population aging is increasing demand. WHO also reports that more than 90% of Member States actively reported workforce data in 2025, nearly 20 times the availability when the accounts system launched. Better measurement is an important institutional capability, but it does not itself train, retain, finance, or redistribute workers.

Rotation finding: health trends should be followed from population need through training, migration, retention, workforce age, geographic distribution, service access, care burden, and outcomes. The open arrow is whether improved workforce intelligence becomes actual local capacity where patients and caregivers need it.

Purchasing power: energy shocks reach consumers through inflation and support design

The OECD September 2026 Interim Economic Outlook record adds a consumer/economic-behavior route. The OECD projects G20 headline inflation rising from 3.4% in 2025 to 4.1% in 2026 before easing to 3.6% in 2027, while global growth is projected at 2.9% in 2026 and 3.0% in 2027. The shock has been partly absorbed through alternative supply routes, inventory drawdowns, strategic reserves, additional production, and lower oil demand. These are macro forecasts and mechanisms, not household-specific price or consumption outcomes.

The social signal is the policy tradeoff: support needs to be targeted and temporary enough to protect exposed households while retaining incentives for energy savings, and public finances face pressure as long-term yields rise. Meanwhile, rapid AI investment supports trade and growth but increasingly relies on external financing, creating a concurrent market-correction risk if expected returns fail to materialize. Consumer room is therefore shaped by prices, wages, transfers, firm costs, energy behavior, and public support together.

Rotation finding: price trends should be followed from geopolitical shock through energy costs, inflation, wages, substitution, support take-up, firm pricing, savings, and household participation. The open arrow is whether stabilization preserves practical purchasing power or simply delays and redistributes the burden.

Political voice: formal representation does not guarantee safe or equal power

The IPU-UN Women Women in Politics 2026 record adds a political-participation route. Women hold 27.5% of parliamentary seats and 22.4% of cabinet posts globally, while only 28 countries are led by a woman and 101 have never had a woman leader. Parliamentary gains are slow and women Speakers fell to 19.9%; these are institutional aggregates, not proof of policy influence.

The access-to-power conversion is also about safety and rules: 76% of surveyed women parliamentarians reported public intimidation or violence versus 68% of men, while IPU identifies well-designed and implemented quotas as a decisive mechanism in several 2025 renewals. This is a bounded publication synthesis of institutional counts and the cited parliamentarian survey, not a new microdata analysis.

Rotation finding: political trends should be followed from electoral rules and party selection through candidacy, representation, leadership, safety, agenda control, policy response, and later trust or participation. The open arrow is whether formal inclusion becomes safe, durable, and consequential political power.

Cultural production: digital reach is expanding faster than creator security

The UNESCO Re|Shaping Policies for Creativity 2026 record adds a cultural-production route. UNESCO reports that 85% of reporting countries include cultural and creative industries in development plans, but only 56% set specific cultural objectives. Cultural goods trade reached $254 billion in 2023, yet developing countries accounted for just over 20% of cultural-services trade. The route therefore connects culture to trade, state capacity, and unequal access to digital markets—not only taste or identity.

Digital reach also changes the creator bargain: digital revenues rose to 35% of creators’ income from 17% in 2018, while UNESCO projects 2028 revenue losses of 24% for music creators and 21% for audiovisual creators from generative-AI outputs. These are publication indicators and projections, not realized individual outcomes. Skills, mobility, and protection remain uneven: essential digital skills are reported for 67% of people in developed countries versus 28% in developing countries; only 38% of developed countries facilitate inward artistic mobility from developing nations; and only 61% of countries maintain independent artistic-freedom monitoring bodies.

Rotation finding: cultural trends should be followed from public recognition and education through creation, licensing, platform distribution, mobility, income, safety, audience access, and cultural participation. The open arrow is whether digital expansion produces a broader creative public or concentrates value and visibility in a smaller set of platforms, markets, and creators.

Housing and place: urban access is a linked system, not a shelter count

The UN-Habitat World Cities Report 2026 record adds a place-and-access route. UN-Habitat estimates that up to 3.4 billion people lack secure, safe, and adequate housing, including more than 1 billion in informal settlements and slums. The global housing deficit rose from 251 million units in 2010 to 288 million in 2023, while an estimated 64 million people were evicted between 2003 and 2023. These are global estimates, not a city-specific rent series or individual household panel.

The mechanism is broader than shelter: affordability, displacement, informality, resilience, sustainability, and liveability interact with transport, public services, health, employment, public space, and local implementation. Climate planning is beginning to acknowledge that route: UN-Habitat finds well-developed urban content in 80% of 142 third-generation national climate plans, up from 49% in the prior cycle, with housing and informal settlements a priority in nearly half and concrete urban delivery mechanisms in roughly three-quarters.

Rotation finding: place trends should be followed from land and tenure through rents, housing quality, transport, service proximity, climate exposure, displacement, social networks, and local delivery. The open arrow is whether national housing and climate commitments become usable, affordable, and durable urban access for residents.

Democracy under pressure: legitimacy depends on conversion into results

The UNDP Democracies Under Pressure 2026 record adds a regional institutional route. UNDP describes Latin America and the Caribbean as the most democratic developing region, with more than four in five people living in democracy, but emphasizes that democratic access alone is not the endpoint. Democracy, the State, and human development form a connected triangle: political inequality, weak representation, and fragmented state capacity can reinforce one another.

The pressure stack includes questioning of elections, weakened electoral authorities, personalist concentration of power, weaker checks and balances, polarization, changing information systems, organized crime, human mobility, and the triple planetary crisis. These are aggregate institutional findings, not a new analysis of the report’s optional public quiz or citizen responses.

Rotation finding: political legitimacy should be followed from electoral integrity through representation, economic-power constraints, state control, deliberation, institutional checks, public delivery, development, and trust. The open arrow is whether formal democracy can turn pressure into renewal and public promises into visible, legitimate results.

Acute food crises: conflict and response capacity convert shocks into hunger

The FAO-WFP Global Report on Food Crises 2026 record adds a crisis-escalation route distinct from the existing healthy-diet affordability record. The 2026 assessment finds 266 million people in 47 countries and territories facing high acute food insecurity in 2025, or 22.9% of the analyzed population; about 1.4 million faced the most severe level. Acute hunger has approximately doubled over the past decade, and two famines were confirmed in parts of Gaza and Sudan during 2025.

The mechanism is not food supply alone: conflict, displacement, economic shocks, weather extremes, market disruption, access constraints, and financing gaps concentrate risk. Ten countries account for roughly two-thirds of the assessed acute-hunger population, while 35 contexts have appeared in every report for nine years. Funding and data availability have weakened, increasing the importance of prevention, agricultural livelihoods, early warning, negotiated access, and resilience alongside emergency assistance. These are aggregate crisis classifications and response signals, not individual consumption data.

Rotation finding: food-crisis trends should be followed from conflict and climate shock through displacement, markets, livelihoods, acute food access, nutrition, humanitarian reach, financing, and recovery capacity. The open arrow is whether early action and resilient local systems can interrupt repeated crisis cycles before acute hunger becomes famine.

The generational economy: hidden care and transfers shape fiscal room

The UN DESA generational-economy record adds a life-course accounting route. UN DESA defines the generational economy as the social institutions, markets, public transfers, time transfers, caregiving, production, consumption, and savings through which people receive and provide support over their lives. Conventional GDP does not fully reveal these flows.

Demographic change alters the balance: declining fertility and expanding working-age populations can create a dividend when human-capital investment and employment are sufficient, while ageing increases demand for health and long-term care and pressures pensions and public finance. The measurement route is therefore substantive, not merely statistical: National Transfer Accounts, National Time Transfer Accounts, and National Inclusion Accounts can expose age, time, care, and socioeconomic-status differences in resource flows.

Rotation finding: intergenerational trends should be followed from age structure through education, paid work, unpaid care, taxes, transfers, pensions, health, household support, gender, and public budgets. The open arrow is whether better accounting becomes fairer care, durable fiscal planning, and stronger social cohesion rather than a new way to pit generations against one another.

AI markets: capability diffusion and firm power can move together

The OECD Artificial Intelligence Markets 2026 record adds a firm-power route. OECD’s assessment is mixed: foundation-model segments have shown dynamism over the past three years, while structural risks persist across the value chain. AI deployment reshapes business performance, cost structures, and strategic advantage, so the relevant endpoint is not simply adoption but who can enter, switch, innovate, and capture value.

The concentration risk is especially visible in hardware and data, where incumbent positions may become entrenched. This complements the World Bank’s capability-and-dependency route: infrastructure and model access can expand capacity while still leaving firms and governments dependent on bottleneck providers. These are aggregate competition findings, not firm-level market-share estimates or consumer microdata.

Rotation finding: AI trends should be followed from compute and data through models, cloud infrastructure, applications, entry, interoperability, cost structures, labor control, consumer choice, public procurement, and competition enforcement. The open arrow is whether AI lowers capability barriers broadly or converts technical bottlenecks into durable firm and geopolitical power.

Climate and firms: heat is becoming a productivity, wage, and trade mechanism

The World Bank MENAAP climate-risk record adds a firm-and-worker climate route. Across the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan, roughly three in ten firms operate in extreme heat for more than 100 days a year. The World Bank reports that 17 additional hot days are associated with a 6% sales decline, a 4% decline in labor productivity, and an 8% decline in wages in its firm-level analysis. These are study estimates, not universal constants or household heat-stress outcomes.

The mechanism extends beyond local weather: smaller and financially constrained firms face greater adaptation barriers, while EU and UK carbon-border measures reshape export competitiveness, investment, and sector access. Adaptation can also create a double dividend through finance, energy efficiency, green production, and a projected $46 billion sustainable-cooling opportunity, though cooling itself can increase energy demand and affordability pressure if it is not efficient and broadly accessible.

Rotation finding: climate trends should be followed from temperature and water exposure through firm size, finance, energy, work conditions, sales, productivity, wages, trade rules, adaptation, and worker security. The open arrow is whether climate policy distributes adaptation capacity or amplifies the gap between firms and workers that can protect themselves and those that cannot.

Fragility and poverty: shock exposure becomes durable exclusion through weak capacity
