The OECD States of Fragility 2025 record adds a state-capacity route. OECD identifies 61 high- or extreme-fragility contexts containing 25% of the world’s population but 72% of the world’s extreme poor in 2024. By 2040, as much as 92% of the world’s extreme poor could live in those contexts under the report’s projection. This is a context-level projection, not a household forecast.

The mechanism is cumulative: organized violence, low growth, food insecurity, forced displacement, gender inequality, weak institutions, limited FDI, and service-delivery constraints reinforce one another. More than 100 million refugees and internally displaced people originate in high- or extreme-fragility contexts, while those contexts received 5% or less of global net FDI inflows in 2023. The relevant response is therefore not only crisis aid but institutional recovery, social protection, gender-responsive services, peacebuilding, and better data.

Rotation finding: fragility trends should be followed from political and security shocks through state capacity, public services, markets, poverty, displacement, gender exposure, financing, and recovery. The open arrow is whether early institutional investment interrupts the poverty-fragility loop before crisis concentration becomes a durable global geography.

Spatial opportunity: place converts infrastructure into usable access

The World Bank People, Jobs, and Places record adds a place-to-opportunity route. The central signal is that national labor and welfare averages can conceal persistent differences between neighborhoods, rural and urban places, and people facing different transport, safety, infrastructure, and hazard conditions. Access to jobs is therefore not only a question of job supply or worker skills; it is also a question of where people live and what surrounds them.

The practical mechanism runs through travel time, housing, local firms, services, information, safety, migration, and mobility. World Bank GeoE3 work shows how combining labor-market and geographic information can identify location-specific constraints and support targeted employment interventions. That precision is useful but not automatically just: spatial data can improve allocation while also stigmatizing neighborhoods or enabling surveillance, so resident voice and data rights remain part of the policy route.

Rotation finding: spatial trends should be followed from land and housing through transport, travel time, safety, services, local firms, worker access, migration, wages, and neighborhood governance. The open arrow is whether place- sensitive policy expands usable opportunity or merely maps inequality more precisely without changing it.

Institutional justice: formal progress does not guarantee usable voice

The UN SDG 16 2026 record adds a publication-level institutional route across violence, justice, public information, human-rights oversight, and political representation. The report shows a mixed pattern: violence indicators have improved in aggregate, while progress remains uneven; access-to-information laws have spread but compliance is inconsistent; bribery exposure is sharply unequal across income groups; and the growth of fully compliant national human-rights institutions has slowed.

The cultural and political signal is that institutional form and institutional use are different trend layers. A law, accreditation, or appointment can widen formal capability without ensuring timely information, effective remedy, independent oversight, or influence over high-consequence decisions. Women and young people remain underrepresented in influential roles, especially as conflict, climate, economic insecurity, and technological disruption reshape public choices.

Rotation finding: follow institutional change from legal adoption through enforcement, public-service access, civic space, representation, trust, and lived remedy. The open arrow is whether formal institutional expansion becomes usable voice and protection for people facing unequal exposure, rather than remaining a paper capability.

Creative labor: cultural participation depends on work conditions

The UNESCO creative-industries skills and employment record adds a culture-to-work route. The publication treats music, fashion, film, heritage crafts, and related fields as economically important but labor-market fragile: 40 percent of workers are reported to earn below their national minimum wage, while informality, precarity, gender disparities, curriculum lag, and weak measurement limit who can sustain creative work.

The mechanism is broader than training alone. Changing tools and industry needs raise the value of adaptable skills, but fragmented policy, outdated qualifications, teacher shortages, and uneven access to learning can shift the cost of adaptation onto workers. Microcredentials, intergenerational learning, and public-private partnerships may widen entry, yet they do not automatically improve pay, bargaining power, protections, or control over distribution.

Rotation finding: follow cultural production from training and digital infrastructure through pay, informality, gender, platform dependence, labor rights, and cultural participation. The open arrow is whether skills investment creates sustainable creative livelihoods or simply supplies more precarious labor to expanding cultural markets.

Poverty and protection: the consumption floor is exposed to compound shocks

The UN SDG 1 2026 record adds a current poverty-and-consumption route. The UN estimates that about 826 million people, or 10 percent of the world population, remain below the $3.00 per-day extreme-poverty line in 2026. Social assistance has expanded, reaching 37.3 percent of vulnerable people, but coverage is incomplete; at the same time, poverty-reduction aid grants fell 8.7 percent from 2023 to 2024.

The mechanism is a buffer problem rather than a single-income problem. Rising living costs, conflict, climate shocks, inequality, and weak labor-market opportunity can push households below a consumption floor, while transfers, public services, work, remittances, and savings may protect recovery. Coverage statistics therefore need to be followed through adequacy, timing, take-up, service access, and the ability to rebuild after a shock.

Rotation finding: follow poverty from prices and work through transfers, care, public services, climate and conflict exposure, household buffers, and recovery. The open arrow is whether social protection converts formal coverage into durable consumption security when multiple shocks arrive together.

Drug markets and public health: harm follows access and institutional pathways

The UNODC World Drug Report 2026 record adds a social-behavior and institutional-response route. The report shows a wide market footprint—cannabis cultivation is reported in at least 155 countries—and a sharp expansion in reported coca cultivation, while drug-related deaths continue to rise in total even as population-adjusted growth is slower. Opioids remain the most common substance in direct drug-related deaths in the available toxicology data, with cocaine ranking second.

The key social trend is not prevalence alone. Treatment coverage remains low and varies sharply by region; referral routes and intervention types differ, with criminal-justice systems playing a larger role in some regions and self/family referral more common in others. This connects market structure to stigma, care access, institutional trust, public safety, work disruption, and community harm. Limited reporting also means that the most visible data may overrepresent people who reach formal services.

Rotation finding: follow drug-market change from production and trafficking through exposure, mortality, stigma, referral, treatment, recovery, and local institutional capacity. The open arrow is whether public-health systems reduce harm equitably or whether unequal access and enforcement pathways deepen it.

Platform attention: convenience is becoming the gateway to civic interpretation

The Reuters Institute Digital News Report 2026 record adds a missing encounter-to-interpretation route. Across 48 markets, social media and video networks became the most widely used route to online news, used by 54 percent of respondents, ahead of news organisations' own sites and apps. The shift is not only substitution: 12 percent now use only social/video networks for news, casual or passive users have grown, and younger audiences are especially platform-first.

The important mechanism is the convenience-trust tension. Overall trust in news fell to 37 percent, while trust in news encountered on social media and through AI chatbots was lower; concern about fake or misleading news reached 62 percent. People may therefore rely on a convenient default channel while treating it as less reliable, creating an open middle between exposure, interpretation, discussion, and action. The report does not establish that platform use causes polarization or political behavior, which remains the next empirical bridge.

Rotation finding: follow platform exposure through attention, source selection, trust, misinformation interpretation, identity, discussion, and collective action. The open arrow is whether platform convenience expands civic access or produces a thinner, more distrustful information environment.

Time poverty: care is a hidden allocation system for work and participation

The UN Women time-use and social-inequality record adds the missing social-reproduction route. Across ten countries, the report uses harmonized time-use measures to show how paid work, unpaid domestic and care work, leisure, mobility, multitasking, and well-being combine into social and economic inequality. Its central contribution is to make time poverty a measurable dimension rather than treating time as an unobserved personal constraint.

The mechanism runs through household composition and care continuity. Living with children is identified as a key driver of time inequality, while multitasking and mobility reveal pressures conventional employment statistics miss. Those pressures can reduce paid-work access, rest, social participation, and political voice, but the same time pattern can also reflect support, meaning, and chosen family arrangements. Better indicators expose the route; services, leave, schedules, and responsibility-sharing determine whether it changes.

Rotation finding: follow care from household composition and unpaid time through work schedules, services, mobility, rest, social participation, and well-being. The open arrow is whether care policy redistributes time and continuity or simply records unequal burdens more precisely.

Digital consumer agency: transparency is not the same as usable choice

The OECD digital-markets consumer-policy record adds the consumer-power middle between market conduct and effective recourse. The OECD describes personalized pricing, recommendation systems, data-driven targeting, interface design, drip pricing, tying, and AI-generated deceptive claims as practices that can implicate both competition and consumer law.

The central mechanism is consumer agency: understanding alternatives, making an informed choice, acting on preferences, and switching when appropriate. A market can provide nominal options while algorithms, lock-in, information asymmetry, or weak remedies make those options difficult to use. The same conduct can affect consumer welfare, privacy, trust, entry, innovation, and market power, which is why the report emphasizes coordination between competition and consumer authorities while preserving distinct mandates.

Rotation finding: follow digital conduct from interface and pricing through understanding, comparison, switching, complaint, remedy, and market response. The open arrow is whether consumer-protection capacity produces real agency or merely more disclosure inside increasingly powerful intermediaries.

Civic space and global rules: state power changes the cost of participation

The CIVICUS State of Civil Society 2026 record adds a geopolitical/state-response route. Its central claim is that civic space, multilateral rules, and technology governance are being contested at the same time: activists and journalists face rising costs of dissent, civil-society funding is under pressure, powerful states weaken or selectively use global institutions, and AI creates new surveillance, disinformation, military, and gendered-abuse risks.

The report also documents the counterforce. Civil society uses litigation, fact-checking, early-warning systems, secure platforms, community documentation, and decentralized youth organizing to contest state and corporate power. This is an external-response mechanism, not just an attitude endpoint: whether rules are accepted, enforced, resisted, or bypassed depends on civic capacity, resources, technology, institutional trust, and the ability to build coalitions across borders.

Because CIVICUS is an advocacy organization, the record preserves its normative standpoint and does not treat the report as a neutral causal index. The open arrow is whether adaptive resistance can convert civic participation into durable accountability when states and firms control more of the legal, financial, and technological environment.

Online literacy: confidence, attention, and ability are separating

The Ofcom adult media-use record adds a platform middle beyond reach and news choice. In the UK, overall online confidence is high, but confidence in judging accuracy and recognizing advertising exceeds performance on some scenario tests. Social participation is also becoming more passive: posting, sharing, or commenting has declined, while read-only use and reduced exploration of new sites remain substantial.

The consumer and social signal is a divergence between access and meaningful control. People can be online yet rely on one device, lack confidence, miss scams or sponsored content, spend more time than intended, or experience the social environment as unkind and mentally costly. At the same time, online access can broaden understanding, support learning, connect people, and enable public-service or civic action. The relevant trend is therefore not simply screen time; it is how platform design, skills, household resources, and institutional literacy shape the quality of participation.

Rotation finding: follow online use from access and exposure through attention, recognition, safety behavior, consumer choice, well-being, and public digital-literacy response. The open arrow is whether literacy and safety capacity convert platform access into agency rather than passive, unequal, or harmful participation.

Socioeconomic voice: trust is shaped by whether institutions feel reachable

The OECD trust and political-agency record adds a public-institutions middle route. The 2026 OECD report links trust gaps to partisan alignment, financial concerns, perceived discrimination, education, interpersonal trust, and whether people feel that people like them have a say in government decisions. In the comparable survey waves, the average partisan gap in trust in national civil services widened from 10 percentage points in 2021 to 15 points in 2025.

The mechanism is reachability and agency, not attitude alone. Groups with less material security or weaker perceived representation may trust institutions less and participate less, making it harder for policy to reach them and for public agencies to learn from their experience. The same route now extends to public-sector AI: automated services can improve consistency or access, but skepticism, transparency, human oversight, and recourse determine whether they enhance or erode legitimacy.

Rotation finding: follow socioeconomic exposure through service encounters, perceived voice, participation, responsiveness, AI-mediated administration, and institutional trust. The open arrow is whether public systems convert formal access into felt influence and credible fair treatment across groups.

Gender parity and the next economy: representation does not automatically become power

The WEF Global Gender Gap 2026 record adds a cross-cutting gender-and-transition route. The index finds the global gender gap 69.2 percent closed in 2026, but the remaining gaps are concentrated in economic participation and opportunity and especially political empowerment. Professional and technical representation is substantially closer to parity than the representation of legislators, senior officials, and managers.

The forward-looking mechanism runs through the jobs and capital shaping the next economy. Across 57 economies, women’s representation falls from 46 percent at entry level to 23 percent at the C-suite. The report also tracks women’s participation in AI-related roles and financial markets, where growth can remain concentrated in less technical or lower-paid segments. This links care, training, hiring, promotion, capital allocation, technology, and political voice rather than treating a headline parity score as equal power.

Rotation finding: follow gender gaps from care and education through skills, technical work, hiring, leadership, capital, AI transition, and political representation. The open arrow is whether new growth sectors widen agency and mobility or reproduce old hierarchies inside new occupations and institutions.

Child platform life: exposure becomes a time, safety, and consumer system

The Ofcom Online Nation 2025 record adds a child-focused platform route. UK children aged 8-14 spend almost three hours online per day on average, with YouTube and Snapchat together accounting for a large share of time; a material portion of use occurs late at night. The same environment supports friendship, schoolwork, well-being, and learning, while creating questions about sleep, family routines, attention, and safety.

The route also reaches action and consumption. Ofcom reports that many children encounter harmful content and that a substantial share take action through reporting, blocking, dislike tools, or telling an adult. Children also spend money across games and social platforms, often after prompts from customization, advertising, recommendations, or influencers, with notable regret and uncertainty about what was purchased. These findings connect platform design to care responsibilities, consumer agency, safety governance, and children’s own capacity to respond.

Rotation finding: follow child platform use from exposure and time through family routines, harmful-content response, digital literacy, spending, remedy, and agency. The open arrow is whether safety and consumer systems protect children without removing useful connection, learning, and participation.

Gender inequality across systems: exposure, access, and power compound

The UN Women and UN DESA Gender Snapshot 2025 record adds an SDG-wide route that complements the WEF parity index. It links the gendered distribution of poverty, conflict exposure, food insecurity, digital access, unpaid care, work, rights, and institutional decision-making. The report projects 351 million women and girls could remain in extreme poverty in 2030 if current trends continue, while a closed gender digital divide is modeled as a potential source of broad economic and poverty gains.

The key mechanism is compounding exposure rather than a single gap. Conflict, food insecurity, care burdens, weak services, and limited digital access can reduce time, income, safety, information, and voice simultaneously. Formal commitments or representation can therefore coexist with weak implementation and limited lived power. The source is a global indicator and scenario synthesis, not a respondent-level explanation of individual outcomes.

Rotation finding: follow gendered exposure from poverty, conflict, food, care, and digital infrastructure through work, services, representation, financing, and implementation. The open arrow is whether cross-sector policy capacity converts formal equality commitments into durable access and power.

Risk perception: geopolitical shocks are being read through social fragility

The WEF Global Risks Report 2026 record adds an institutional risk-framing route. In the report's expert survey, geoeconomic confrontation and state-based armed conflict together account for nearly one-third of selections for the leading material global crisis risk in 2026. Geoeconomic confrontation also ranks first over the two-year horizon, while misinformation and disinformation remain near the top.

The broader signal is convergence: the report places inequality, economic downturn, polarization, trust, disinformation, technology, climate, and geostrategic change in one interacting risk landscape. This is not a forecast or an objective probability estimate. It is evidence about how expert and business institutions are prioritizing threats and linking them to social stability, markets, public legitimacy, and state capacity.

Rotation finding: follow perceived geopolitical risk from conflict and trade confrontation through prices, supply chains, information, polarization, institutional trust, and preparedness. The open arrow is whether risk framing improves coordinated prevention or reinforces narrow elite threat narratives.

Financial access: mobile connectivity is becoming part of household resilience

The World Bank Global Findex 2025 record adds a consumer and infrastructure route. The database links mobile-phone and internet access to account ownership, digital merchant payments, mobile-money saving, borrowing, digital safety, and financial resilience across 141 economies. Account ownership and digital use are expanding, but gaps remain by gender, income, phone ownership, and geography.

The mechanism is not “technology equals inclusion.” A phone and account can reduce payment friction or create a saving channel, yet effective control also depends on affordability, identity, literacy, privacy, safety, product quality, and recourse. Financial resilience remains connected to employment, transfers, health costs, social networks, and public systems. The source is survey-based aggregate evidence, not transaction-level behavior or causal welfare analysis.

Rotation finding: follow connectivity from device and account access through payments, saving, borrowing, safety, gendered control, consumer protection, and shock response. The open arrow is whether digital finance becomes durable household room or simply shifts risk and dependency into new infrastructures.

Social justice: formal protection and lived power remain separate

The ILO State of Social Justice 2025 record adds a rights-to-lived-outcomes route. The report places declining progress in social justice alongside persistent poverty, wealth concentration, informality, weakening collective-bargaining rights, and a gap between legal protections and workers’ reported experiences of exclusion or neglect. It also frames climate, technology, and demographic change as transitions whose distributional effects must be governed rather than assumed to be fair.

The mechanism is institutional reach and bargaining power. Growth or formal rights can coexist with insecure work, weak voice, and low trust if enforcement, representation, and social protection do not travel into everyday employment and transition decisions. The report’s interview evidence is treated as a qualitative publication synthesis, not as respondent-level prevalence or a causal worker panel.

Rotation finding: follow social-justice commitments from poverty and legal rights through informality, bargaining, trust, services, and fair-transition implementation. The open arrow is whether labour and social institutions adapt quickly enough to distribute new risks and opportunities credibly.

Democracy under conflict pressure: institutional erosion becomes a security route

The International IDEA Global State of Democracy 2026 record adds a democracy-to-conflict route. Across 173 countries, the report finds that 57 percent declined in at least one key democratic indicator between 2020 and 2025, with especially broad deterioration in Rule of Law, Rights, credible elections, legislative effectiveness, expression, press freedom, and access to justice. It also examines how partial democratic procedures without real competition or enforceable rights can coexist with heightened conflict risk.

The mechanism is institutional, not simply attitudinal. Weakened checks, unreliable elections, restricted expression, and poor access to justice can reduce peaceful channels for contestation while concentrating executive power. But the report also identifies fragile improvements through transitions and civil-society mobilization. The conflict relationship is treated as comparative association, not an individual-level causal forecast.

Rotation finding: follow institutional decline from representation and rights through trust, civic participation, executive constraint, conflict risk, and international security. The open arrow is whether democratic renewal and civic capacity can restore nonviolent channels before institutional erosion hardens into security crisis.

Freedom and rights: democratic status is also lived civic space

The Freedom House Freedom in the World 2026 record adds an independent political-rights and civil-liberties lens to the IDEA democracy assessment. Freedom House reports a twentieth consecutive year of global freedom decline in 2025: 54 countries deteriorated and 35 improved. Its longitudinal framing highlights armed conflict, coups, institutional erosion, and authoritarian crackdowns as recurring pathways affecting media freedom, expression, due process, and civic space.

The cross-source signal is not simply that democracy scores fall. Rights and freedoms shape whether people can contest power, organize, access information, seek remedy, and reverse institutional deterioration. The assessment also records resilience: most countries rated Free in 2005 remained Free, and some Partly Free countries improved through competitive elections, judicial independence, and stronger rule of law. This remains an expert-coded country index, not respondent-level rights histories or causal repression evidence.

Rotation finding: follow political status from formal classification through expression, media, due process, elections, civic organization, conflict, and reform resilience. The open arrow is whether institutional safeguards create real room for civic action before rights erosion becomes normalized.

Planetary health: environmental risk becomes a production, consumption, and justice problem

The UNEP Global Environment Outlook 7 record adds a systems-level climate and environmental route. GEO-7 links climate, nature and biodiversity loss, land degradation, pollution, food, energy, materials, finance, health, poverty, and economic development rather than treating them as separate issue silos. Its transformation scenarios project large long-run gains, but also emphasize up-front costs and difficult choices.

The cultural and consumer mechanism matters: behavior, production, lifestyles, Indigenous and Local Knowledge, procurement, infrastructure, and finance all shape environmental outcomes. Individual “green choices” cannot substitute for changes in prices, systems, corporate incentives, public investment, and distributional protection. The source is a scientific assessment and scenario framework, not household behavior data or a deterministic forecast.

Rotation finding: follow environmental pressure from energy, food, land, materials, and consumption through health, poverty, culture, infrastructure, finance, and public governance. The open arrow is whether whole-system policy can convert planetary risk into equitable transformation rather than shifting costs onto exposed households and communities.

Biodiversity and livelihoods: protection expands while ecological security erodes

The UN SDG 15 2026 record adds a more specific biodiversity-to-livelihoods route beneath GEO-7’s broader planetary-health frame. The SDG assessment reports expanding biodiversity targets, environmental accounting, and protected-area coverage, while more than 48,600 species face extinction, forests continue to shrink, and coral risk has risen. These changes reach people through fisheries, tourism, coastal protection, food systems, water cycles, climate buffering, and cultural value.

The open issue is implementation and distribution. A law, target, accounting system, or protected-area designation can improve governance without ensuring effective stewardship, local consent, ecological connectivity, or livelihood security. Conversely, community management and restoration can create gains that global indicators register slowly. This is aggregate SDG evidence, not individual livelihood histories or local causal ecological analysis.

Rotation finding: follow biodiversity loss from species, forests, reefs, and key sites through food, water, work, tourism, culture, coastal safety, and conservation governance. The open arrow is whether expanding formal protection becomes effective, locally legitimate ecosystem security.

Tourism and cultural mobility: recovery is broad, but access and value remain uneven

The UN Tourism International Tourism Highlights record adds a global demand-and-cultural-mobility route alongside the OECD tourism resilience record. International travel recovered to roughly 1.4 billion arrivals in 2024, with visitor spending also recovering strongly, and early 2025-2026 monitoring shows continued demand. Tourism therefore connects consumer spending, transport, services exports, cultural exchange, work, destination infrastructure, and place-based development.

The important qualification is unevenness. Aggregate recovery can hide price barriers, visa and connectivity differences, conflict-affected destinations, resident pressure, external ownership, and weak local value retention. Tourism can support cultural economies and mutual understanding while also producing overcrowding, commodification, housing pressure, and dependency. These are sector-level publication signals, not individual travel motives or resident sentiment data.

Rotation finding: follow travel demand from mobility, prices, and air connectivity through cultural participation, service work, destination income, resident pressure, geopolitical shocks, and local agency. The open arrow is whether tourism recovery broadens shared cultural and economic benefits or concentrates them in firms, places, and travelers with the most access.

Oceans and coastal livelihoods: governance milestones meet physical stress

The UN SDG 14 2026 record adds a marine route distinct from the terrestrial biodiversity and GEO-7 records. Ocean governance is advancing through the BBNJ Agreement, fisheries subsidy rules, and expanded protected coverage, while ocean heat, acidification, overfishing, and uneven monitoring continue to pressure marine ecosystems.

The social and consumer link runs through food, coastal work, tourism, cultural value, climate buffering, and the fiscal and political position of small-island and coastal economies. Formal protection or treaty membership is not the same as effective stewardship: implementation, research capacity, benefit sharing, local participation, and enforcement determine whether ocean governance reaches dependent communities.

Rotation finding: follow ocean change from treaties, protection, and monitoring through fisheries, food security, coastal work, tourism, culture, and community resilience. The open arrow is whether new marine rules convert global legal milestones into durable, locally shared ocean security.

Consumption systems: throughput and waste outrun governance

The UN SDG 12 2026 record adds a consumer-to-infrastructure route. Global domestic material consumption rose substantially between 2015 and 2022, while higher-income populations accounted for most global material use. At the same time, food waste, electronic waste, and fossil-fuel subsidies continue to expand or remain structurally large despite growing circular-economy, sustainable-consumption, and procurement frameworks.

The mechanism is institutional as much as behavioral. Product design, prices, subsidies, procurement, storage, repair, recycling, infrastructure, and corporate accountability determine what consumers can realistically do. The large gap between monitoring sustainable contracts and monitoring actual outcomes shows why policy adoption is not the same as transformed production or consumption. These are aggregate SDG indicators, not household purchase or waste microdata.

Rotation finding: follow material demand from extraction and energy pricing through products, food, e-waste, public procurement, household costs, labor, and environmental justice. The open arrow is whether governance changes the material system or merely asks consumers to compensate for upstream incentives.

Water services: access gains meet local capacity and financing gaps

The UN SDG 6 2026 record adds a public-service route across drinking water, sanitation, hygiene, rural and conflict inequality, water stress, quality monitoring, basin cooperation, community participation, and local finance. Global coverage has improved, but least developed and conflict-affected countries remain far behind, while water stress and service reliability remain uneven.

The mechanism is institutional reach. A national plan or improved monitoring does not automatically produce safe, affordable, continuous service when local and basin authorities lack revenue, data, maintenance capacity, or community voice. Water also links time, health, care, food, energy, migration, conflict resilience, and household room. These are aggregate service and governance indicators, not individual health outcomes or household service histories.

Rotation finding: follow water insecurity from coverage and infrastructure through time, care, health, food, work, stress, public finance, and local participation. The open arrow is whether global access commitments become reliable, locally governed service systems under climate and conflict pressure.

Energy access: the transition is also a household and regional-security problem

The UN SDG 7 2026 record adds a household-energy route alongside the IEA policy and energy-system records. Global electricity and clean-cooking access are expanding, but the remaining exclusion is concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa, remote rural areas, low-income settings, and fragile or conflict-affected places. Renewable capacity is growing, yet energy efficiency and reliable service remain uneven.

Energy is a time, care, health, work, cost, and political-capacity issue. A connection or installed renewable asset is not the same as affordable, continuous, safe, locally maintainable service. Clean cooking can change household labor and exposure, while energy costs and transition investment shape consumer room and public legitimacy. These are aggregate SDG indicators and projections, not household energy diaries or causal policy effects.

Rotation finding: follow energy exclusion from electricity and cooking access through health, care, time, work, prices, distributed infrastructure, finance, and conflict resilience. The open arrow is whether the clean-energy transition reaches households as reliable agency and security rather than capacity without service.

Decent work and youth transition: low unemployment does not equal secure work

The UN SDG 8 2026 record adds a global labor route alongside the ILO records. The report shows how historically low unemployment can coexist with widespread informality, youth disconnection from employment and education, weak productivity, child labour, and deteriorating freedom of association and collective bargaining.

The mechanism is job quality and institutional voice. Macro resilience does not automatically translate into real wages, secure work, bargaining power, or household room. Young people and informal workers experience transitions through skills, care, digital and green work, energy costs, migration, and social protection. The record uses aggregate SDG indicators and report synthesis, not individual employment histories or respondent-level analysis.

Rotation finding: follow labor-market resilience from unemployment through informality, youth pathways, productivity, wages, child labour, bargaining, social protection, and transition capacity. The open arrow is whether growth and new sectors create secure agency or reproduce exclusion behind a healthy headline employment rate.

Migration and mobility: development assets operate under disruption

The IOM World Migration Report 2026 record adds a mobility route across migrant stocks, work, displacement, remittances, skills, climate mobility, regular pathways, disability, and community action. The report places migration inside a period of geopolitical, environmental, technological, and demographic disruption: international migration remains a minority experience, while internal movement and displacement are much broader parts of the mobility system.

The mechanism is institutional access under unequal exposure. Migration can support development through work, remittances, investment, knowledge, skills, and civic engagement, but those channels depend on safe pathways, rights, financial systems, local capacity, and durable responses to displacement. Climate stress does not mechanically cause migration; adaptation, livelihoods, infrastructure, networks, and public choices shape whether people move, stay, or return. This record uses aggregate stocks and thematic report analysis, not individual migration histories or respondent-level attitudes.

Rotation finding: follow mobility from work and remittances through displacement, climate exposure, regular pathways, disability inclusion, local response, and origin/destination power. The open arrow is whether migration systems convert movement into agency and shared development or reproduce insecurity through blocked access and unequal protection.

Trade, energy, and industrial capacity: geopolitical shocks become household and development constraints

The UNCTAD Trade and Development Foresights 2026 record adds a macro-to-lived-conditions route across trade, shipping, energy, finance, clean investment, AI-linked industrial production, and development capacity. The report projects a sharp slowdown in world merchandise trade growth after 2025 and describes how geopolitical conflict can transmit through energy markets, financial conditions, and critical maritime routes.

The mechanism is unequal exposure plus infrastructure dependence. Renewable generation can be cost-competitive while investment remains concentrated away from places with strong resource potential. AI and critical-component investment can support industrial resilience, but it can also deepen supply, finance, and technology dependence when productive capacity and bargaining power are uneven. This record uses aggregate macro indicators and report analysis, not household price panels, firm histories, or causal AI employment estimates.

Rotation finding: follow geopolitical shocks from trade and shipping through energy prices, finance, industrial investment, work, and household room. The open arrow is whether clean and digital transition investment broadens productive agency or reproduces concentration behind a resilient headline.

Youth voice and education governance: formal consultation is not influence

The UNESCO 2026 Youth Report record adds a youth-participation route across education governance, institutional feedback, representation, legitimacy, skills, and intergenerational change. Its central signal is a gap between formal consultation mechanisms and genuine influence over education policy. That gap matters because education systems shape work transitions, identity, opportunity, and trust in public institutions.

The mechanism is voice-to-implementation. Mapping youth and student organizations makes participation infrastructure visible, but organization counts do not establish membership, representativeness, policy access, or outcomes for marginalized young people. This record uses government and organization-level survey analysis and institutional mapping, not raw respondent-level attitudes or individual student histories.

Rotation finding: follow youth voice from formal consultation through agenda setting, implementation, monitoring, education-to-work transitions, and public legitimacy. The open arrow is whether institutions convert being heard into shared decision power or preserve participation as symbolic access.

Meaningful connectivity: access is progressing, but digital agency remains uneven

The ITU ICT Development Index 2026 record adds a digital-infrastructure route across affordability, Internet use, network quality, platform dependence, public services, work, and cultural participation. The index reports continued global progress toward universal and meaningful connectivity across 159 economies, while persistent disparities remain in affordability, use, and quality.

The mechanism is access-to-agency conversion. A connection is not the same as affordable, reliable, safe, high-quality participation; digital development depends on devices, electricity, skills, institutional design, and user control. Expanded connectivity can widen work, learning, culture, and public-service access while also increasing platform, data, attention, and misinformation dependencies. This record uses an economy-level index, not respondent-level Internet diaries or individual transaction data.

Rotation finding: follow digital development from coverage through price, quality, devices, skills, platform power, public services, work, and cultural life. The open arrow is whether connectivity creates durable agency and public capacity or access without meaningful control.

Generative culture and consumer meaning: acceleration creates a counter-demand for grounding

The Dentsu Creative Generative Realities 2026 record adds a commercial-cultural route across generative technology, cultural production, craft, fandom, connectivity ambivalence, and the search for escape, grounding, and reconnection. Its signal is not simply that consumers adopt new technology: rapid synthetic production may increase the value of visible human effort, difference, embodied experience, and meaningful participation.

The mechanism is attention and identity under saturation. Constant connectivity can expand discovery, belonging, and creative opportunity while also producing exhaustion, sameness, privacy concerns, and difficulty distinguishing authentic from synthetic work. The report uses published cross-market consumer research and strategist synthesis, not raw respondent-level data, clinical measures, or causal forecasts of behavior.

Rotation finding: follow generative technology from production speed through attention, authenticity, fandom, craft, offline experience, consumer value, and cultural participation. The open arrow is whether AI-mediated abundance creates more agency and meaning or drives a premium market for human texture and escape.

Urban housing and public space: city growth does not equal shared urban access

The UN SDG 11 2026 record adds a comparable urban-indicator route across informal settlements, housing, public space, transport, services, disaster resilience, and local data. It complements the narrative World Cities Report by showing how housing and urban form condition access to work, health, education, mobility, safety, and social life.

The mechanism is spatial exposure and local delivery. A city can grow while secure housing, public space, transport, and basic services remain uneven; aggregate land or coverage measures do not establish safety, accessibility, tenure, or resident agency. This record uses SDG indicators and city comparisons, not individual housing histories, resident sentiment, or causal commute and health estimates.

Rotation finding: follow urban inequality from housing and informal settlements through transport, public space, services, climate exposure, local finance, data, and participation. The open arrow is whether urban growth converts density into shared opportunity or reproduces exclusion by place.

Financial stability and trust in money: AI-led resilience carries public and household risks

The BIS Annual Economic Report 2026 record adds a central-bank route across AI investment, inflation, public debt, non-bank finance, supply shocks, digital money, and monetary trust. It helps connect the macro headline of resilience to the institutional mechanisms that determine whether shocks become higher prices, tighter credit, weaker public capacity, or new forms of financial access.

The mechanism is fiscal-financial and technological transmission. AI investment can support growth while raising questions about valuation and sustainability; high public debt and non-bank participation can amplify stress; digital money can expand convenience while testing trust, privacy, oversight, and the boundary between public and private payment systems. This record uses system-level policy analysis, not household financial diaries, individual portfolios, or causal AI employment estimates.

Rotation finding: follow financial resilience from AI investment and public debt through inflation, energy and supply shocks, non-bank markets, household room, payment systems, and trust. The open arrow is whether innovation expands productive capacity and public legitimacy or shifts risk into less visible financial and consumer channels.

Digital infrastructure and climate accountability: AI growth creates a measurable environmental load

The ITU/WBA Greening Digital Companies 2026 record adds a company-to-system route across digital infrastructure, electricity, Scope 1–3 emissions, AI, climate commitments, transition plans, and public accountability. It makes the environmental cost of digital expansion visible alongside the benefits of connectivity, optimization, and climate applications.

The mechanism is infrastructure dependence and distributed exposure. Digital firms can procure clean energy and improve efficiency while increasing demand for electricity, hardware, water, land, and network capacity. Disclosure and transition plans matter because communities, utilities, workers, users, and public institutions may bear costs not visible in a company's operational footprint. This record uses company-level comparisons and disclosed aggregates, not user behavior or causal AI climate estimates.

Rotation finding: follow digital growth from connectivity and AI demand through electricity, emissions, supply chains, local infrastructure, climate claims, procurement, regulation, and community burden. The open arrow is whether digital expansion aligns private innovation with public decarbonization and resilience or shifts environmental costs downstream.

Technology diffusion: frontier invention is not the same as broad adoption

The WIPO World Intellectual Property Report 2026 record adds a diffusion route across invention, adoption, innovation ecosystems, skills, finance, infrastructure, work, consumers, and governance. Its central distinction is that new technology raises productivity only when it is widely adopted and used—not simply because it exists at the frontier.

The mechanism is ecosystem capacity and control. Firms, universities, finance, skills, intellectual-property systems, infrastructure, and public policy shape who can adopt, adapt, and benefit. Late adoption can mean exclusion, but it can also support leapfrogging or locally appropriate design. This record uses comparative report analysis, not respondent-level technology diaries, individual employment histories, or causal productivity estimates.

Rotation finding: follow technology from invention through diffusion, adoption, skills, work, consumer use, cultural participation, competition, and public governance. The open arrow is whether innovation ecosystems broaden agency or concentrate frontier gains among firms and places already closest to the frontier.

Trust and insularity: economic anxiety turns difference into a social boundary

The Edelman Trust Barometer 2026 record adds a cross-cultural trust route across intergroup difference, economic anxiety, optimism, income-based trust gaps, social-media intermediaries, and institutional collaboration. Its headline signal is not simply low trust: trust is retreating toward familiar circles, making shared facts, cross-group cooperation, and collective problem-solving harder.

The mechanism is material insecurity plus identity and information sorting. The published survey reports aggregate patterns in 28 countries, but it does not explain which experiences cause distrust or prove that influencer trust changes behavior. This record uses published aggregate survey results, not raw respondent-level records or reweighted microdata.

Rotation finding: follow trust from income and future expectations through difference, social media, employers, institutions, public facts, and collective action. The open arrow is whether institutions can broker credible contact across social boundaries or whether economic and technological pressure hardens insularity into durable political and cultural fragmentation.

Cyber resilience under geopolitical fragmentation: digital dependence makes skills and readiness public issues

The PwC Global Digital Trust Insights 2026 record adds an organizational-readiness route across geopolitical risk, critical infrastructure, supply chains, AI defense, quantum readiness, data governance, and cyber skills. It shows how geopolitical fragmentation is being translated into changes in infrastructure location, operating policy, cyber investment, and vendor relationships.

The mechanism is infrastructure dependency plus capability gaps. Organizations can increase cyber budgets while remaining exposed through legacy systems, supply chains, weak data controls, skills shortages, and uneven post-quantum preparation. These weaknesses can spill into public services, work, consumer trust, and everyday access. The record uses published executive-survey aggregates, not respondent-level records, technical audits, or incident microdata.

Rotation finding: follow geopolitical tension from cyber investment through critical infrastructure, vendors, AI defense, data governance, quantum readiness, skills, public services, and user trust. The open arrow is whether security spending builds shared resilience or merely relocates risk across opaque supply chains and less-capable institutions.

Family formation and care: demographic change reflects room to realize choices

The UNFPA Demographic Futures Survey record adds a family-formation route across partnership, parenthood, housing, financial security, stable employment, emotional readiness, reproductive agency, and future expectations. It shifts demographic interpretation away from population targets and toward the social conditions under which young adults can realize the lives and families they want.

The mechanism is household room plus institutional support. Partnership and parenthood aspirations coexist with housing and economic constraints; work, care, health services, and social protection shape whether preferences become feasible choices. The report's data are comparative findings from Internet- connected young adults and are not nationally representative. This record uses published aggregates, not raw respondent-level data or individual fertility histories.

Rotation finding: follow demographic change from aspirations through housing, work, care, reproductive services, social protection, conflict, inequality, and future trust. The open arrow is whether institutions expand reproductive agency and family choice or leave demographic outcomes to material constraint.

Cultural unease and consumer meaning: technology, fracture, nostalgia, and uncertainty reshape demand

The Ipsos Global Trends 2026 record adds a commercial-cultural route across technology sentiment, social fracture, nostalgia, individualism, uncertainty, identity, and consumer meaning. It complements the Dentsu record by broadening the signal beyond generative culture: people may simultaneously want technological progress, fear who controls it, retreat toward familiar values, and use consumption to recover personal agency.

The mechanism is meaning under instability. Geopolitical, financial, and technological uncertainty can change what people seek from products, brands, communities, and institutions—immediacy, control, belonging, difference, or escape. The report uses published 38-market aggregate survey and macro-force synthesis, not respondent-level records, individual purchase histories, causal attitude models, or clinical outcomes.

Rotation finding: follow cultural change from technology sentiment through fragmentation, immigration and inequality, nostalgia, identity, consumption, trust, and collective life. The open arrow is whether markets and institutions convert anxiety into shared meaning and connection or monetize retreat into insular, individual solutions.

Industrial futures: green and digital upgrading must become broad productive capacity

The UNIDO Industrial Development Report 2026 record adds a production-side route across manufacturing, green transition, AI, reconfigured value chains, demographics, food systems, jobs, poverty, and social inclusion. It connects the macro question of industrial divides to the consumer, work, energy, and geopolitical systems already in the atlas.

The mechanism is capability conversion. Green technology, digitalization, and new value chains create opportunity only when countries and firms have skills, finance, infrastructure, institutions, and bargaining capacity to adopt and retain value. Industrial growth can reduce poverty and strengthen food security, but can also shift pollution, insecurity, and transition costs onto workers and communities. This record uses report-level analysis, not firm microdata, individual employment histories, or household food diaries.

Rotation finding: follow industrial change from technology and energy through value chains, jobs, food systems, demographics, local value retention, worker voice, and environmental burden. The open arrow is whether future-ready industry creates shared productive agency or reproduces industrial divides behind green and digital investment headlines.

Food systems and household room: productivity gains remain exposed to shocks and unequal capacity

The OECD–FAO Agricultural Outlook 2026–2035 record adds a food-system route across agricultural production, farm income, fertilizer and energy shocks, emissions, dietary change, trade, rural work, and household food security. The outlook shows how productivity can expand supply and income while geopolitical disruption and unequal infrastructure still translate into different food and consumption choices across households and countries.

The mechanism is production-to-consumption transmission. Fertilizer, energy, trade, storage, transport, and income conditions shape whether projected gains become affordable nutritious food or higher exposure to price and availability shocks. Diet diversification also changes environmental and labor pressures. This record uses OECD–FAO model projections and market analysis, not household food diaries, individual farm histories, or causal price estimates.

Rotation finding: follow food resilience from productivity and inputs through trade, rural income, diet change, emissions, infrastructure, household room, and geopolitical shocks. The open arrow is whether agricultural growth broadens affordable healthy choice or leaves lower-income households carrying volatility.

Food security and nutrition: modest global improvement can coexist with high healthy-diet costs

The SOFI 2026 record adds a food-security route across hunger, moderate or severe food insecurity, healthy-diet affordability, regional divergence, gender and age disparities, rural exposure, and multisector public response. It links aggregate nutrition outcomes to household purchasing room without treating a global estimate as an individual diet history.

The mechanism is affordability and unequal exposure. Food prices, incomes, markets, logistics, health, social protection, and local food systems shape whether modest aggregate progress becomes a healthy diet for particular groups. This record uses UN estimates and report synthesis, not respondent-level data, household food diaries, individual medical histories, or causal food-price estimates.

Rotation finding: keep the food route open from global hunger trends through healthy-diet cost, regional divergence, women and children, rural communities, food-system structure, and public intervention. The open arrow is whether aggregate improvement converts into equitable healthy choice under unequal income and infrastructure conditions.

Development progress: place, work, infrastructure, and digital access move unevenly

The World Bank Atlas of Global Development 2026 record adds a cross-domain route across development speed, gender and work, poverty geography, water quality, electricity, Internet use, and digital capability. It keeps the analysis broad: the same country-level development gap can surface as constrained household room, weaker work options, thinner infrastructure, and less access to digital opportunity.

The mechanism is place-mediated capability. Starting points, public investment, care burdens, skills, service reliability, and affordability shape whether headline progress becomes usable capacity. This record uses World Bank indicator comparisons and synthesis, not respondent-level records, individual income histories, household time diaries, or causal infrastructure estimates.

Rotation finding: follow development from aggregate progress through place, poverty, gendered work, infrastructure, digital access, and institutional delivery. The open arrow is whether faster national progress becomes practical capability for groups starting further behind.

Human capital: homes, neighborhoods, and workplaces shape who can convert effort into capability

The World Bank Human Capital Report 2026 record adds a settings-based route across stalled learning, family resources and care, neighborhood opportunity, workplace learning, informal work, and gendered labor participation. It connects cultural and social reproduction to material room, service quality, place, and later work without treating any one setting as the whole explanation.

The mechanism is capability formation across settings. Home care, neighborhood schools and safety, workplace learning, childcare, and job quality determine whether education and effort become durable skills and earnings. This record uses World Bank cross-country evidence and synthesis, not respondent-level data, individual child histories, household time diaries, or individual employment panels.

Rotation finding: follow human capital from home and care through place, school and clinic quality, workplace learning, gendered participation, and later economic opportunity. The open arrow is whether policy connects these settings or leaves people carrying the cost of fragmented systems.

War and technology: headline growth can mask divergent exposure to prices, work, and public capacity

The IMF July 2026 WEO update record adds a macro route across global growth, war, energy importers, technology value chains, AI demand, stalled disinflation, fiscal space, and household purchasing room. It complements the source map by connecting geopolitical shocks to the different buffers and opportunities available across economies and groups.

The mechanism is uneven transmission. Energy dependence, technology integration, skills, market access, fiscal space, and policy credibility determine whether the same global shock becomes higher prices, weaker work options, or a technology tailwind. This record uses IMF forecasts and macro synthesis, not respondent-level data, household price diaries, firm microdata, or causal AI productivity estimates.

Rotation finding: follow the war-and-technology cross-current from global forecasts through energy, inflation, value chains, work, fiscal buffers, and public response. The open arrow is whether policy can convert technology momentum into broad capability while containing unequal shock exposure.

External imbalances: trade and financial adjustment become household and political exposure

The IMF External Sector Report 2026 record adds a geoeconomic route across current-account divergence, China and US drivers, external positions, trade barriers, exchange rates, capital flows, and coordinated rebalancing. It connects international macro structure to domestic purchasing room and policy capacity without reducing a surplus or deficit to a moral story.

The mechanism is external-to-domestic transmission. Adjustment can reach import prices, export demand, investment, employment, exchange rates, financial markets, and public policy room, but the burden depends on institutions, buffers, sector, and place. This record uses IMF external-balance assessments and macro synthesis, not respondent-level data, household expenditure diaries, firm microdata, or causal political-behavior estimates.

Rotation finding: follow global imbalance from current accounts through trade, capital, prices, work, financial risk, domestic policy, and public legitimacy. The open arrow is whether rebalancing is coordinated enough to avoid shifting macro adjustment costs onto already exposed households and regions.

Financial stability: geopolitical shocks can become household exposure through markets, leverage, and liquidity

The IMF April 2026 GFSR record adds a systemic-finance route across war, energy prices, inflation expectations, market repricing, sovereign rollover, nonbank leverage, emerging-market capital flows, private credit, AI concentration, and supervisory capacity.

The mechanism is amplification. A geopolitical or energy shock can move through rates, bonds, currencies, credit, funds, asset values, and public borrowing costs before reaching household purchasing room or work conditions. This record uses IMF financial surveillance and risk synthesis, not respondent-level data, household financial diaries, individual portfolio histories, or causal market predictions.

Rotation finding: follow financial stress from conflict and energy through inflation, leverage, liquidity, capital flows, household credit, and public oversight. The open arrow is whether buffers and supervision interrupt the chain before market volatility becomes durable social and political damage.

Aquatic food systems: production and trade gains can coexist with ecological and livelihood inequality

The FAO SOFIA 2026 record adds an aquatic-food route across fisheries, aquaculture, nutrition, trade, livelihoods, value-chain resilience, resource health, and community participation. It broadens the food system beyond terrestrial production and keeps the link open between global output, local affordability, ecological limits, and control over coastal and inland resources.

The mechanism is production-to-consumption and governance transmission. Processing, storage, transport, trade rules, prices, resource management, labor conditions, and community voice determine whether higher aquatic production becomes nutritious local access or concentrated export value. This record uses FAO aggregate sector statistics and synthesis, not respondent-level data, individual fisher histories, household seafood diaries, or causal price estimates.

Rotation finding: follow aquatic food from production and stocks through nutrition, trade, cold chains, livelihoods, ecological sustainability, and local control. The open arrow is whether Blue Transformation produces resilient and inclusive food systems or shifts ecological and social costs onto exposed places.

Research and innovation careers: technology capacity depends on the people and working conditions behind it

The OECD Research and Innovation Careers Observatory 2026 record adds a labor-and-technology route across R&D workforce growth, doctoral and STEM composition, doctorate earnings, fixed-term work, international mobility, and career evidence gaps. It treats innovation as a social labor system rather than only a firm, patent, or infrastructure output.

The mechanism is talent formation and retention. Education, sector pathways, working conditions, contracts, mobility, care, and institutional funding shape who can enter and remain in research and innovation careers—and therefore who controls future technical capacity. This record uses OECD comparative indicators and synthesis, not respondent-level career histories, individual earnings panels, or causal education-return estimates.

Rotation finding: follow innovation from degrees and skills through contracts, mobility, sector transitions, gender and care constraints, research institutions, and downstream firm or public capacity. The open arrow is whether expanding technical talent also expands durable and broadly accessible agency.

Digital education: generative AI can raise visible performance while weakening learning if cognitive work is outsourced

The OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026 record adds an education-and-technology route across teacher use, task performance, durable learning, academic integrity, teacher agency, infrastructure, privacy, safety, and equity. It gives the corpus a sharper cultural signal about what counts as learning, authorship, effort, and legitimate assistance.

The mechanism is cognition-and-governance transmission. A tool can improve a student's output without building transferable knowledge; pedagogy, teacher control, assessment, access, and platform design determine whether convenience becomes learning or displacement of cognitive work. This record uses OECD indicators and research synthesis, not respondent-level student histories, individual learning trajectories, or causal AI effects.

Rotation finding: follow GenAI from teacher practice through student effort, academic integrity, learning outcomes, devices, connectivity, privacy, and school governance. The open arrow is whether educational AI expands human capability or turns visible performance into a substitute for durable skill.

Health progress: aggregate gains can coexist with crisis scars and a visibility gap

The WHO World health statistics 2026 record adds a health-system route across progress toward health-related SDGs, pandemic excess mortality, life-expectancy and healthy-life-expectancy recovery, and civil registration and cause-of-death capacity. It connects public health outcomes to the ability of institutions to see, classify, and respond to harm.

The mechanism is measurement-and-capacity transmission. Health indicators can move in the right direction while the pace remains insufficient for 2030 goals; pandemic disruption can leave recovery uneven; and weak mortality registration can hide who is dying and why. This record uses WHO indicators and modelled estimates, not respondent-level medical histories, patient records, or individual treatment effects.

Rotation finding: follow health shocks from mortality and care disruption through recovery, inequality, registration, public planning, and resource allocation. The open arrow is whether better visibility and system capacity convert aggregate health progress into durable, equitable protection.

Employment geography: strong headline labour markets can conceal place-based loss of income and mobility

The OECD Employment Outlook 2026 record adds a place-based labour route across employment resilience, real wages, young entrants, regional structural change, skills, non-compete constraints, and employment protection. It keeps jobs connected to place, firms, infrastructure, technology, and household purchasing room rather than treating unemployment as the whole labour-market story.

The mechanism is shock-to-place transmission. Trade, AI, digitalisation, energy transition, and local institutions reshape which regions attract jobs, which workers can move or retrain, and which households retain income and bargaining room. This record uses OECD indicators and comparative regional synthesis, not respondent-level employment histories, individual wage panels, or causal AI displacement estimates.

Rotation finding: follow structural shocks from firms and regions through wages, skills, mobility, employment protection, household room, and local institutional response. The open arrow is whether place-based policy converts labour-market resilience into broadly shared security rather than concentrated regional advantage.

Education and justice: rights literacy is a capability only when institutions can receive and remedy claims

The UNESCO/Namati Education and justice record adds an institutional route across everyday legal needs, access to justice, rights literacy, legal empowerment, justice-system professional capacity, trust, democracy, peace, crime reduction, and social cohesion. It gives education a political meaning beyond enrollment or labor-market skill: the ability to understand rights and navigate institutions.

The mechanism is capability-to-remedy transmission. Education and community support can make rights legible and claims actionable, but fair outcomes still depend on accessible, trusted, funded, and accountable institutions. This record uses UNESCO/Namati synthesis, not respondent-level legal histories, case files, court outcomes, or causal education estimates.

Rotation finding: follow people from rights awareness through navigation, representation, institutional response, remedy, trust, and collective voice. The open arrow is whether education expands practical civic power or merely teaches rights that inaccessible systems cannot honor.

Public employment services: labor-market resilience depends on the delivery systems between policy and people

The IDB/OECD/WAPES World of Public Employment Services 2026 record adds a delivery route across public-employment-service organization, digital maturity, shock response, migrant transitions, social-economy partnerships, and support for people facing the greatest difficulty finding work. It makes the intermediary institution visible between labor-market policy and household employment outcomes.

The mechanism is policy-to-service transmission. Matching, training, information, digital tools, human support, partnerships, and local context shape whether a public promise becomes an accessible transition path. This record uses comparative survey and policy information, not respondent-level job-search histories, placement case files, or causal service evaluations.

Rotation finding: follow a worker from shock or job search through service contact, matching, training, mobility, employer response, and durable work. The open arrow is whether public employment services reduce unequal transition costs or digitize an already uneven access structure.

Social protection: coverage expansion does not guarantee adequate or shock-responsive security

The World Bank State of Social Protection Report 2025 record adds a route across social-protection coverage, benefit adequacy, crisis response, delivery infrastructure, gender disparity, labor programs, and household resilience. It connects public systems to the practical room households have to absorb shocks, preserve health and education spending, and navigate work or care transitions.

The mechanism is protection-to-room transmission. Databases, digital payments, case management, financing, benefit design, and labor programs determine whether formal coverage becomes timely, sufficient, and usable support. This record uses aggregate World Bank indicators and synthesis, not respondent-level benefit histories, individual case files, consumption panels, or causal transfer effects.

Rotation finding: follow a shock from exposure through registration, payment, benefit adequacy, work or care adjustment, and recovery. The open arrow is whether expanded social protection creates durable household room or merely counts nominal access while people remain unable to absorb the next crisis.

Gendered ageing: longer lives can expand contribution while reproducing health, care, and income inequality

The UN DESA Gender matters in an ageing world record adds a demographic route across the growth of older women’s populations, longevity, later-life health, interrupted careers, pensions, unpaid care, and participation. It makes ageing a distributional and cultural question rather than only a dependency-ratio or fiscal question.

The mechanism is life-course-to-late-life transmission. Earlier inequality in work, earnings, health, care, and legal or financial access accumulates into older women’s security and autonomy, while longer survival increases the value of care and civic contribution. This record uses UN DESA estimates and policy synthesis, not respondent-level ageing histories, health records, or care diaries.

Rotation finding: follow women across work, care, health, income, pensions, living arrangements, and voice over the life course. The open arrow is whether gender-responsive institutions turn demographic longevity into autonomy and contribution or merely extend unequal care and financial burdens.

Peace and fragmentation: conflict is spreading through a more plural power system while local peace capacity remains decisive

The IEP Global Peace Index 2026 record adds a geopolitical route across global peacefulness, state-based conflict, external involvement, conflict deaths, militarisation, middle powers, economic costs, and Positive Peace. It connects international order to household and community exposure without treating a country ranking as a complete account of lived safety.

The mechanism is geopolitical-fragmentation transmission. Conflict, arms, finance, ideology, displacement, and power redistribution can move across borders, while institutions, social trust, and local resilience mediate whether external pressure becomes durable violence. This record uses an IEP composite index and synthesis, not respondent-level safety histories, event-level conflict microdata, or causal geopolitical forecasts.

Rotation finding: follow a conflict signal from power competition through militarisation, civilian exposure, displacement, economic strain, institutional response, and local peacebuilding. The open arrow is whether Positive Peace and public capacity interrupt fragmentation before it becomes normalized insecurity.

Terrorism and borderlands: aggregate declines can hide concentrated, networked, and youth-linked risk

The IEP Global Terrorism Index 2026 record adds a terrorism route across global incident and death trends, regional concentration, conflict linkage, borderlands, youth radicalisation, online pathways, governance gaps, and employment conditions. It sharpens the distinction between a global count and the places and social systems where risk is actually concentrated.

The mechanism is conflict-to-recruitment transmission. Border authority gaps, state abuse, unemployment, social isolation, algorithmic pathways, and conflict can combine into different recruitment routes across regions. This record uses IEP index measures and report synthesis, not respondent-level radicalisation histories, individual victim files, or causal platform effects.

Rotation finding: follow a terrorism signal from conflict and border control through youth exposure, online contact, recruitment, civilian harm, displacement, and prevention. The open arrow is whether trusted institutions, opportunity, and community support interrupt recruitment before security responses deepen the same grievances that sustain it.

Fragility and state capacity: repeated shocks become durable poverty when institutions cannot absorb or sequence recovery

The World Bank Fragile and Conflict-Affected Situations record adds a route across persistent fragility, overlapping shocks, conflict scarring, poverty, food insecurity, health, education, infrastructure, debt, and state capacity. It makes institutional weakness a transmission mechanism rather than a label attached after conflict has already occurred.

The mechanism is shock-to-capacity transmission. Conflict, disasters, commodity swings, debt, and global downturns interact with fiscal room and service capacity; the resulting losses in health, education, food, and work can then reduce the ability to recover from the next shock. This record uses aggregate World Bank analysis, not household respondent histories, individual service records, or causal conflict forecasts.

Rotation finding: follow a shock from fiscal and institutional exposure through services, poverty, food, human capital, debt, and recovery. The open arrow is whether state capacity and external support break the reinforcing cycle or whether each crisis narrows the options available for the next one.

Built environment: the climate transition is also a housing, labor, materials, and affordability transition

The UNEP/GlobalABC Buildings and Construction 2025-2026 record adds a route across the sector's economic footprint, future building stock, energy performance, green certification, affordable living, resilience, and investment. It makes buildings a transmission system between climate policy, household costs, work, materials, and urban quality of life.

The mechanism is built-stock lock-in. Construction, renovation, codes, finance, materials, and building operations determine whether future growth reduces or reinforces emissions, energy costs, and exposure to climate risk. This record uses aggregate UNEP and GlobalABC sector analysis, not respondent-level housing histories, individual utility bills, property records, or causal forecasts.

Rotation finding: follow a building signal from construction and materials through energy performance, jobs, household affordability, resilience, finance, and local implementation. The open arrow is whether standards and investment make efficient, resilient buildings broadly affordable or leave transition benefits concentrated in premium stock.

Renewable deployment: rapid capacity growth can coexist with concentrated technology, geography, and energy-security gains

The IRENA Renewable Capacity Statistics 2026 record adds a route across renewable capacity expansion, solar and wind concentration, regional distribution, off-grid systems, and energy security. It separates the visible buildout from the harder question of who receives reliable, affordable, and resilient energy.

The mechanism is deployment-to-security conversion. Capacity growth changes the physical energy system, but the gains depend on grids, storage, finance, supply chains, ownership, prices, and local implementation. This record uses aggregate IRENA capacity statistics, not respondent-level energy histories, individual utility bills, plant-level operating records, or causal forecasts.

Rotation finding: follow an energy signal from deployment through technology and regional concentration, grids, supply chains, finance, jobs, household costs, and local legitimacy. The open arrow is whether rapid buildout diffuses energy security or reproduces a new geography of dependence and exclusion.

Hydrological overshoot: water crises become durable governance problems when natural capital cannot return to baseline
