The UNESCO common-good consultation record adds an education and public-purpose technology layer. UNESCO’s discussion paper and consultation ask how education systems can exercise agency as AI diffuses, and organize the governance problem around sovereignty, age appropriateness, learner safety, procurement, total cost of ownership, and the right to an explanation. The consultation also foregrounds human agency, equity, inclusion, safety, ethics, evidence, and implementation.

The broader signal is that education institutions are being asked to govern the purposes and conditions of AI—not simply purchase or adopt tools. This is a normative discussion-paper and consultation record, not a learner-level dataset, adoption survey, learning-outcome evaluation, representative opinion measure, or proof of equitable implementation. The open arrow is from AI diffusion through institutional agency, procurement, cost, safety, explanation, teacher and learner voice, public trust, and realized educational value.

Education is being imagined as everyday infrastructure for multilateral habits and cooperation across difference

The UNESCO multilateralism think-piece record adds a qualitative cultural-institutional layer. The essay frames classrooms as multilateral forums where students and teachers negotiate different histories, values, languages, knowledge traditions, and imagined futures; it connects curriculum, local communities, international cooperation, non-WEIRD research, intellectual humility, and civic capability.

The broader signal is that education is being asked to build a common world without requiring consensus: identities and knowledge are treated as relational, and local questions are meant to travel into global conversations and back into local life. This is an IdeasLAB think piece whose authors’ views are not necessarily UNESCO’s official position, not a classroom observation, learning-outcome study, survey, or causal evaluation. The open arrow is from educational encounter through difference, knowledge authority, trust, identity, cooperation, civic agency, and realized democratic or social cohesion outcomes.

Climate action is being linked to social-protection design, insurance coverage, livelihood security, and the conditions of a just transition

The ILO-AFD social-insurance record adds a climate-labor-household layer. The report treats social protection as a way to address climate impacts and the social consequences of climate policy, emphasizes that more than half the world’s population still lacks basic coverage, and gives particular attention to contributory social insurance as an underexamined route for protecting livelihoods and managing transitions.

The ILO Cambodia digital-platform-workers record adds a platform-labor layer: digital work creates access to income while algorithmic ratings and penalties, unpaid waiting, operating costs, injury exposure, contractor classification, and weak worker voice distribute insecurity across workers and public systems. The source is a Phnom Penh diagnostic and is not nationally representative.

The WHO AI-health-research ethics record adds an AI-health governance layer: the key trend is movement from one-time project approval toward lifecycle oversight involving ethics committees, funders, publishers, regulators, data power, public trust, local participation and benefit sharing. It explicitly frames data colonialism and ethics dumping as risks in low- and middle-income settings; it is a governance framework, not an implementation or outcome study.

The OECD homelessness and housing-exclusion record adds a household-security layer: housing loss is treated as a pathway assembled from poverty, housing costs, eviction, institutional exits, relationships, health, employment and social support, while temporary stays with family or friends reveal a large hidden layer beyond visible street counts. The source is a review and cross-national survey synthesis, not a harmonized current prevalence estimate.

The OECD climate-sentiment and just-transition record adds a climate-legitimacy layer: concern about climate change is widespread, but action support depends on perceived effectiveness, household and sectoral economic exposure, fair distribution of adjustment costs, transparent compensation, and credible public communication. The source is descriptive public-attitudes evidence, not a causal forecast of policy support.

The W3C Identity & the Web record adds a digital-identity layer: credentials are not merely authentication tools but infrastructure shaping recognition, access, privacy, trust, cultural meaning, human rights, surveillance, interoperability and vendor dependence. The source is an exploratory W3C Team document, not a standard, membership consensus or deployment study.

The Government of Canada AI and Culture Summit record adds a cultural-production layer: AI adoption is being negotiated through copyright and creator livelihoods, trust, co-design, Indigenous and linguistic sovereignty, domestic compute and data infrastructure, literacy and institutional readiness. The source is an organizer synthesis of a 314-person summit, not representative opinion or formal consensus.

The Circle 2026 Community Trends record adds a community-culture layer: amid AI-generated content and algorithmic noise, connection and belonging are being positioned as higher-value than attention alone, while creators and brands treat community as business infrastructure. The source is a commercial public summary with disclosed limitations, not representative population evidence or a causal evaluation.

The OECD critical-risk governance record adds a state-capacity and geopolitical-risk layer: governments are broadening risk governance toward compound threats, anticipation, whole-of-society coordination and critical dependencies, but preparedness investment, accountability, systematic learning and international cooperation remain uneven. The source is a comparative governance review, not a causal resilience evaluation, incident census or proof of realized public safety.

The WEF TradeTech Paradox record adds a trade-infrastructure layer: geopolitical fragmentation is pulling parts of the trade system apart while digital tools connect institutions, regulators, logistics, finance and enterprises across borders. The report’s central implication is that technology can improve visibility, liquidity, compliance and coordination, but only when paired with collaborative governance, cross-layer partnerships, human capacity, ethics and interoperable data infrastructure. This is a strategic insight report with case studies, not a causal technology evaluation, firm census or proof of inclusive resilience.

The SVR Germany housing and participation record adds a place-and-status layer: housing is not only shelter but an access condition for education, work, local services, social interaction and participation in an immigration society. The report separates ethnic concentration from rising income segregation, identifies arrival neighbourhoods as potential resources rather than automatic barriers, and shows how affordability, discrimination and legal accommodation rules shape different routes through housing and belonging. This is Germany-specific annual-report evidence, not a U.S. estimate, respondent-level panel or causal neighbourhood evaluation.

The UNESCO–IEP intercultural-dialogue record adds a cultural and civic-capacity layer: dialogue is framed as measurable infrastructure connecting structures, processes and values to inclusion, human rights, conflict prevention, resilience and peace. The public UNESCO release draws on more than 160 countries, comparative data, regional trends and case studies, but the underlying report is from 2022; this is not new 2026 outcome data or proof that dialogue alone causes peace.

The World Bank social-cohesion record adds a measurement-to-intervention layer: social cohesion is separated into bonding within communities, bridging across groups and linking between people and institutions with power. That distinction matters because a program can improve internal solidarity without improving intergroup trust or citizen-state accountability. The 2023 working paper emphasizes that effects are conditional on diagnosis and implementation; it is not a current global prevalence estimate or causal program result.

The World Bank process-legitimacy record adds the institutional mechanism upstream of that cohesion route: development change is more durable when affected groups, especially those who lose, perceive the process as fair, represented and contestable. The paper identifies legitimacy contests between societal groups, elite factions, local and national authorities, and national and global actors, then points to negotiation and shared understanding as possible responses. This is a 2025 analytical framework, not a legitimacy survey or causal project result.

The World Bank generative-AI use record adds a technology-capability layer: GenAI web use is growing rapidly, but the observed capability frontier is highly unequal across country income groups, platforms and local ecosystems. The study reports roughly 25% ChatGPT penetration among internet users in high-income countries versus 0.3% in low-income countries, while noting that traffic is only a proxy and that some underlying data are proprietary. The open arrow is from connectivity and affordability through platform access, skills, language, work use, bargaining power and realized economic participation.

The UK Creative Industries AI Adoption Plan record adds a sectoral cultural-labour layer: creative industries report higher AI use than the wider economy, but adoption varies sharply by subsector and firm size and remains concentrated in operational work before public-facing creative workflows. The plan frames the unresolved route as AI adoption through trust, rights, skills, worker voice, entry-level pathways, cost, regional infrastructure and human creative control. This is UK policy and cited business evidence, not a causal workforce study or U.S. estimate.

The ITU Protection through Online Participation record adds a child-agency and protection layer: digital environments are being designed as both spaces where risks arise and entry points where children can report harm, seek help and reach protection services. The signal shifts child online safety upstream from content removal alone toward accessible reporting, trusted response, referral, platform accountability and public or community capacity. This is global guidance with child consultations and multi-stakeholder input, not an implementation audit or child-outcome evaluation.

The ITU AI and ageing record adds a life-course digital-inclusion layer: AI is being evaluated through health, economic security, participation and connectivity, while age, gender, geography, affordability, skills and trust shape who can benefit. The open arrow is from demographic ageing and digital systems through service access, care capacity, household security, agency, privacy and realized later-life wellbeing. This is global policy and practice synthesis, not a representative older-person survey or outcome evaluation.

The World Bank international risk-sharing record adds a macro-household buffer layer: international shocks are absorbed through different mixes of government saving, private saving, remittances, transfers and investment income, with fiscal space and capital-account openness shaping which channel is available. The open arrow is from global volatility through public capacity and household self-insurance to consumption room, political protection and unequal exposure. This is aggregate accounting evidence, not respondent-level data or a household welfare evaluation.

The World Bank housing robustness record adds a built-environment resilience layer: poverty constrains the first step of removing fragile housing, while governance and hazard-specific institutional learning shape later improvement. The open arrow is from household material room and housing systems through repeated disaster feedback to infrastructure safety, unequal exposure and realized resilience. This is cross-country aggregate evidence, not an event-damage audit or household causal evaluation.

The World Bank disaster-poverty record adds an adaptive-protection layer: disaster-related poverty and well-being losses create a policy choice between reaching more people and supporting each beneficiary more intensely, with lower-income countries benefiting more from early coverage expansion. The open arrow is from hazard exposure through poverty, targeting, delivery capacity and benefit intensity to household recovery, legitimacy and unequal resilience. This is modeled scenario evidence, not a disaster-loss census or implementation audit.

The OECD AI and skills record adds a work-transition layer: skills shortages constrain AI adoption, while adoption raises demand for high-level, digital, data, managerial and human capabilities. Training is associated with better reported outcomes, but algorithmic-management signals also raise questions about empathy, social interaction and job quality. This is OECD survey synthesis with underlying data no newer than late 2024, not a causal training evaluation or forecast.

The PwC Voice of the Consumer record adds an everyday-health consumer layer: health is being organized through recurring occasions—sleep, food, stress, weight, fitness, longevity and appearance—and connected to apps, wearables, diagnostics, coaching, pharmacies and AI. The open arrow is from household routines and resources through data, trust, commercial platforms and human guidance to health choices and unequal participation. This is commercial survey and market-insight evidence, not clinical or causal evidence.

The UN Women Generation Equality record adds an institutionalization layer: gender-equality ambition becomes durable when financing is integrated into public systems, accountability supports learning and decision-making, and feminist, youth and local actors exercise shared leadership. The open arrow is from commitments through power, resources, convening, data and civic space to policy implementation and durable social change. This is program learning synthesis with selected cases, not a causal evaluation or beneficiary census.

The UN Women Pacific Gender Data Outlook Index record adds a data-infrastructure layer: gender data are not merely descriptive inputs but part of the institutional chain from visibility to priorities, resource allocation and accountability. The open arrow is from enabling laws and financing through production and accessibility to data use, policy judgment and unequal recognition. The Index covers 11 of 22 Pacific jurisdictions, omits comparable data-use indicators from the final score and is diagnostic rather than causal or outcome evidence.

The Belonging Forum UK Belonging Barometer record adds a social-infrastructure layer: belonging is shaped by the practical conditions of People, Place, Power and Purpose—relationships, shared spaces, economic and housing security, services, voice and meaningful contribution. The open arrow is from cost, time, health, place and institutional responsiveness through participation and recognition to trust, wellbeing and social cohesion. This is a nationally weighted cross-sectional survey and descriptive trend comparison, not causal evidence.

The DataReportal Digital 2026 Mid-Year record adds a global digital-systems layer: internet access, mobile ownership, social platforms and AI are becoming a combined everyday infrastructure for information, advice, learning, entertainment and connection. The open arrow is from connectivity and platform design through attention, data, skills, affordability and geopolitical infrastructure dependence to household agency, work and social participation. The source combines partner estimates and surveys, so aggregate users are not unique people and causal welfare effects remain open.

The Public First AI Global 2026 record adds a legitimacy-and-power layer: AI adoption is broadening, but sentiment, sophistication, data trust, model origin, sovereignty and infrastructure politics remain uneven. The open arrow is from technical capability through workflow design, income, education, organizational support, privacy, national control and cultural meaning to who benefits, who resists and who can govern the transition. This combines public-attitudes polling with economic modeling, not causal outcome evidence.

The NIQ Consumer Outlook 2026 record adds a household-consumption layer: economic recovery is cautious, with consumers protecting essentials, seeking additional income, adjusting category and channel choices, and valuing quality, responsiveness, local cultural fluency and autonomy. The open arrow is from prices, jobs, geopolitical concern and household room through trust, spending, private label, social commerce and physical retail to firm strategy and lived consumption. This combines survey and market-measurement evidence, not causal household welfare evidence.

The Capgemini consumer 2026 record adds a hybrid-value layer: consumers are not choosing between cheapness and technology in the abstract; they are testing whether price, quality, transparency, AI convenience, control and human support fit the moment. The open arrow is from inflation fatigue and household constraint through switching, indulgence, automation permissions, data trust, human assistance and social commerce to loyalty and perceived value. This is a 12-country survey with executive interviews, not transaction or causal evidence.

The Culturati Cultural Mosaic 5.0 record adds a cultural-decision layer: the public overview treats identity, lifestyle, shopping, media, creators, trusted voices and AI discovery as connected parts of the polycultural mainstream. The open arrow is from cultural meaning and group recognition through trusted intermediaries, platform attention and recommendation authority to product discovery, evaluation and choice. Because only the public overview is available, this is a scope and measurement signal, not evidence of subgroup effects or causal behavior change.

The CIVICUS 2026 State of Civil Society record adds a civic-geopolitical layer: democratic retreat, impunity, technology power, civic-space contraction and funding pressure are treated as mutually reinforcing conditions that produce distributed resistance across protest, mutual aid, documentation, litigation, education and migrant defense. The open arrow is from geopolitical and institutional power through civic space, technology, organizational autonomy and collective action to defensive wins and democratic legitimacy. This is an advocacy and analytical synthesis using selected cases, not a representative movement census or causal estimate.

The ILO Employment and Social Trends 2026 record adds a work-security layer: stable unemployment is separated from access to work, job quality, informality, working poverty, real-income recovery and productive convergence. The open arrow is from demographic, technological, trade and macroeconomic pressures through labour demand, productivity, wages, social protection and institutional capacity to household security and political legitimacy. These are ILO estimates and projections, not respondent-level or causal evidence.

The Circana Eating Patterns in America 2026 record adds an everyday consumption layer: the public overview treats food behavior as a system of occasions, in-home and away-from-home contexts, channels, preparation infrastructure and commercial decision points. The open arrow is from household money and time through food routines, discovery, channel choice, service and retail infrastructure to repeat consumption and firm strategy. Because only the commercial overview is public, this is a scope and measurement signal, not evidence of household inequality, food security or causal behavior change.

The Gallup Global Confidence in Institutions 20-Year Review record adds a legitimacy countertrend: confidence is not universally collapsing; it differs by institution, regime type, country and political position, with military and financial institutions often trusted more than governments, elections or courts. The open arrow is from institutional performance, political voice, regime context and information constraints through confidence, polarization and democratic legitimacy. This is a World Poll trend analysis using country medians and associations, not a causal trust or legitimacy estimate.

The World Bank Fragility at the Core of Global Poverty record adds a development-security layer: extreme poverty is increasingly concentrated in fragile and conflict-affected settings, and the source treats poverty and fragility as mutually reinforcing rather than independent outcomes. The open arrow is from conflict, displacement, institutional capacity and fiscal or service constraints through household assets, income, resilience and recovery to durable poverty reduction and political stability. The public source is a reproducibility catalog with some restricted inputs, not a complete causal intervention evaluation.

The JRC Climate Security, Migration and Fragility record adds a climate-mobility layer: climate stress is treated as a risk multiplier whose effects travel through existing political, economic and social vulnerabilities, while mobility, remittances, shock-responsive protection, safe pathways and inclusive urbanization can weaken negative dynamics. The open arrow is from climate exposure through conflict, mobility, settlement, services and institutional capacity to displacement risk or resilience. This is a policy brief, not a global causal event study.

The OCHA Global Humanitarian Overview 2026 record adds a humanitarian-capacity layer: conflict and climate shocks create needs, but funding and delivery capacity determine whether health, food, protection, cash, water and shelter lifelines continue. The open arrow is from geopolitical and climate shocks through humanitarian finance, coordination, service continuity and infrastructure to household survival, agency and recovery. These are planning estimates and system descriptions, not individual receipt, adequacy or durable recovery evidence.

The Deloitte Global Human Capital Trends 2026 record adds an organizational-AI layer: the public report frames AI adoption as a work-design and trust problem, not merely a technology purchase, emphasizing human–machine synergy, judgment, adaptability, cultural debt and role-specific perception gaps. The open arrow is from AI and market pressure through work redesign, leadership, worker voice, data trust and organizational culture to realized productivity, autonomy and job quality. This is executive and leader survey evidence, not causal worker-outcome evidence.

The ACCA Global Talent Trends 2026 record adds a professional adoption-and-legitimacy layer: AI use and confidence in learning are advancing, but hiring confidence, human review, agent deployment, hybrid time, promotion visibility, social impact and organizational support shape whether adoption feels legitimate. The open arrow is from AI-enabled recruitment and work redesign through skill access, decision authority, schedule control, career visibility, wellbeing and retention. This is aggregate accountancy and finance professional survey/report evidence, not a general workforce panel or causal outcome study.

The ITDF Human Purpose in Peril record adds a public meaning-and-agency layer: people are using LLMs as practical infrastructure for learning, shopping, health, work, finance, housing and social rehearsal while fearing weakened human connection, purpose and critical thought. The open arrow is from everyday AI availability through delegation, convenience, dependence, verification, social meaning and institutional guidance to autonomy, trust and human agency. This is a U.S. public-opinion survey with an LLM-user oversample, not a longitudinal behavioral or causal outcome study.

The More in Common/UCL Disagreeing Well record adds a civic-conversation layer: people can value open debate and understanding while withholding views, fearing labels, avoiding formal forums and observing political institutions model hostility. The open arrow is from identity conflict and reputational risk through silence, listening, venue choice, social contact and institutional example to participation, belonging and democratic legitimacy. This is a Britain-focused polling and focus-group synthesis, not a behavioral trace or causal polarization study.

The Rockefeller Foundation/Focaldata global cooperation record adds a geopolitical-legitimacy layer: worsening world perceptions coexist with demand for cooperation, especially when it delivers security, aid, national benefit and visible results. The open arrow is from conflict, economic pessimism and geopolitical leadership gaps through security priorities, aid framing, institutional trust and coalition design to cooperation, legitimacy and public consent. This is a 34-country survey with country medians and an information treatment, not observed foreign-policy behavior or causal geopolitical change.

The Potential Energy Fixing Climate Communications record adds a climate-consent layer: climate support is widened when communication connects pollution and climate impacts to health, household cost, fairness, protection and energy independence, while abstract net-zero and restriction language can narrow support. The open arrow is from climate exposure and household pressure through narrative framing, perceived solvability, ideological identity and policy consent to implementation legitimacy and durable action. This combines surveys, focus groups and randomized message tests, not durable behavior or climate-policy outcomes.

The Meta-Gallup Global State of Social Connections record adds a social-connection layer: most people feel connected, but loneliness is substantial, country variation is wide, young adults report more loneliness than older adults, and connection does not guarantee relief from loneliness. The open arrow is from household, community and social-contact conditions through emotional connection, loneliness, health, social capital and public-system support to resilience and belonging. This is representative 2022-2023 survey evidence published in 2023, not current monitoring or causal health evidence.

The 4Culture King County Culture and Communities record adds a cultural-infrastructure layer: participation is treated as everyday social infrastructure for connection, identity, learning, wellbeing and community quality of life, but cost, time, caregiving and accessibility constrain who participates deeply. The open arrow is from household room and leisure time through cultural access, welcome, representation and participation to belonging, health, civic connection and public investment. This is a regional program-baseline survey with self-reported outcomes, not a national census or causal impact study.

The broader signal is that climate policy is becoming a social-contract question: decarbonization and adaptation require protection against income, health, work, and lifecycle risks, while coverage gaps can make both climate shocks and policy transitions unequal. The source is an ILO-AFD literature review whose underlying analysis was conducted in 2022 and not updated, not a current coverage census, household panel, causal evaluation, or proof that contributory insurance reaches excluded workers. The open arrow is from climate exposure and policy through social protection, work transitions, household room, inequality, legitimacy, and realized resilience.

The OECD Slovak Republic well-being record adds a measurement-to-governance layer: governments are treating well-being dashboards as a way to connect material conditions, quality of life, relationships, sustainability, inequality and future resources to policy appraisal, strategy and budgeting. Slovakia’s mixed profile—improved selected material and life-satisfaction indicators alongside education, housing, poverty, debt and trust concerns—shows why aggregate progress cannot stand in for distribution or institutional legitimacy. The open arrow is from measurement choice and data visibility through cross-sector trade-offs, budget authority and accountability to realized well-being; the report does not establish that dashboard adoption causes policy change.

The OECD Slovak trust record adds the legitimacy check to the measurement story: national-government trust fell to 23% in 2025, political voice to 17%, perceived evidence use to 28%, intergenerational balancing to 24%, and data-use legitimacy to 38%. Confidence in government AI safeguards is also low. The open arrow is from service experience and decision visibility through fairness, voice, evidence, privacy and human oversight to trust and policy acceptance. This is representative survey and cross-country association evidence, not causal political behavior or an administrative service audit.

The UNESCO Voices of Courage record adds a gendered cultural-emergency layer: 69% report economic instability or livelihood loss, 59% trauma or burnout, 35% emergency displacement, and only 37% continued cultural work fully or significantly; yet women-led cultural work sustains heritage, solidarity and recovery. The open arrow is from conflict, disaster or health emergency through safety, care, funding, mobility and decision power to cultural continuity, community resilience and recovery legitimacy. This is a global survey with testimonies and case studies, not a complete crisis census or causal resilience study.

The WHO Economics of Health for All record adds a health-as-economic-system layer: health is linked to tax, trade, industry, labor, unpaid care, commercial practices, social protection, finance, climate and public participation. The open arrow is from economic rules and investment through household costs, worker conditions, service access, data and voice to health equity and prosperity. This is a draft global strategy and policy framework, not an implementation evaluation or causal health estimate.

The Pew American Dream record adds a cultural-economic mobility layer: 57% of Latino adults say their living standard is better than their parents’, 53% expect their children to be better off, yet 18% say the dream is out of reach and 27% say it does not exist. The open arrow is from household security, work, homeownership, family identity and opportunity through perceived fairness and structural constraint to intergenerational hope, consumer aspiration and political legitimacy. This is representative survey and open-ended coding evidence, not realized mobility or wealth data.

The Pew Latino identity record adds a belonging-and-opportunity layer: 61% say Hispanic identity is extremely or very important to how they see themselves, while 33% say it hurts their ability to get ahead and 34% report recent identity-related discrimination. Identity centrality, self-labels and linked fate shift across immigrant generations, but shared exposure does not automatically become collective responsibility or action. The open arrow is from language, identity and institutional treatment through belonging, perceived opportunity, safety and linked fate to participation and legitimacy. This is representative survey evidence, not an administrative discrimination census or causal political-behavior study.

The Pew Muslim Americans record adds a religion-and-civic-visibility layer: population, mosque infrastructure and political representation have expanded since 9/11, yet 59% of Muslim Americans report a lot of discrimination and 59% say news coverage is often unfair, while public views of Muslims and Islam remain sharply polarized. The open arrow is from demographic visibility and post-9/11 memory through media framing, discrimination, institutional representation and political sorting to belonging, civic voice and legitimacy. This is a mixed survey, administrative-count and secondary-estimate essay, not a complete discrimination census or causal time series.

The Swedish SOU 2026:53 record adds a social-exclusion systems layer: the inquiry links segregation, discrimination, institutional distrust, informal routes for housing, dispute resolution, information or finance, and rights constraints, while insisting that cultural diversity and community organisation are not themselves the problem. The open arrow is from socioeconomic and spatial exclusion through trust, institutional reach, informal systems, gendered power and rights access to integration, participation and social resilience. This is a government inquiry and policy framework, not a national prevalence census or causal evaluation.

The TASC Ireland AI and Inequality record adds a distributional-AI layer: 63% of Irish jobs are estimated to be exposed to AI, while risk and benefit are distributed through occupational complementarity, gender, skills, algorithmic management, governance, ownership and global supply chains. The open arrow is from AI adoption and infrastructure through task change, bargaining power, digital access, discrimination, worker voice and environmental externalisation to wages, time, inclusion and democratic legitimacy. This is an independent think-tank synthesis using secondary evidence, not a worker panel or causal forecast.

The TASC State We Are In 2026 record adds a material-baseline layer: Ireland’s tax-and-transfer system compresses market-income inequality, but real median household disposable income barely rose from 2022 to 2025, renters and no-work households face concentrated risk, and emergency accommodation has expanded sharply. The open arrow is from wages, ownership, housing, work, transfers and essential services through household purchasing power, deprivation, time and security to political legitimacy and room for future transitions. This is an independent think-tank synthesis of official and secondary evidence, not a new panel or causal evaluation.

The CDC Youth Health in Focus 2025 record adds a US youth-health layer: mental-health and dietary indicators improved from 2023 to 2025, but only 24% of students got at least eight hours of sleep, activity and daily physical education did not improve, and risky digital behavior remains common. The open arrow is from school, family, food, activity, sleep and digital environments through health, attention, safety and social connection to longer-term wellbeing and institutional response. This is national YRBS evidence summarized by CDC, not a causal intervention evaluation.

The TruStage What Matters Now 2026 record adds a US consumer-reality layer: 46% say salary is not enough and a hustle is needed, while financial worry is uneven by race, generation and neurodivergence. Family and friends, mobile/social discovery, app experience and community relevance shape how financial institutions are encountered and judged. The open arrow is from income pressure and identity through household security, digital access, cultural relevance and institutional choice to consumer behavior and legitimacy. This is commissioned Ipsos/TruStage research, not objective financial data or a causal evaluation.

The Social Connection in America 2026 record adds a US social-infrastructure layer: about four in ten adults report moderate or severe loneliness, nearly 70% see loved ones no more than once or twice a month, and time is the leading reported barrier. Weak club, volunteering, religious and cross-background participation coexists with skepticism that virtual contact is an in-person substitute. The open arrow is from time, distance, institutions and digital mediation through social connection, belonging, health and civic capacity to community resilience. This is a public summary of a new RAND–Connection Institute tracking initiative, not a causal evaluation.

The Equimundo State of American Men 2026 record adds a US young-men culture layer: 74% say financial security is harder for their generation than their fathers’ generation, while 78% use AI, 35% have used prediction markets, restrictive “Man Box” attitudes have risen, and democratic commitment coexists with deep institutional distrust. The open arrow is from economic mobility, digital influence and community space through masculinity, purpose, social connection and institutional fairness to political receptivity and legitimacy. This is a mixed-method YouGov/Equimundo/YMRP study, not a causal or population-wide account of young men.

The Annenberg Civics Knowledge 2026 record adds a civic-literacy layer: 65% can name all three branches, 9% can name all five First Amendment protections, and knowledge is stronger for some constitutional procedures than for the full rights system. The open arrow is from education, communication and political salience through constitutional literacy, rights recognition, institutional judgment and democratic capacity. This is a nationally representative knowledge survey, not a measure of legal competence, political behavior, or democratic performance.

The Annenberg Data Centers 2026 record adds an AI-infrastructure legitimacy layer: local data-center opposition rose to 61% from 49% in spring, crossing party lines and peaking among adults under 30, even as broad AI expectations and regulatory demand stayed stable. The open arrow is from AI adoption and infrastructure through privacy, jobs, energy, land use and neighborhood exposure to local legitimacy and public regulation. This is public-opinion evidence, not an assessment of realized data-center effects or causal opposition.

The Annenberg Heat and Health 2026 record adds a climate-as-household-life layer: 76% report extreme heat affecting daily activities, 82% report heat affecting electricity bills, 56% report impacts on sleep and exercise, and 65% do not know where to find a cooling center. The open arrow is from climate exposure through energy costs, routines, health knowledge, unequal adaptation and public cooling capacity to household room and wellbeing. This is nationally representative public-health survey evidence, not clinical outcome or adaptation-effectiveness data.

The TFAH Underfunded and Under Strain 2026 record adds a public-health-capacity layer: governmental public health received about 3% of national health expenditures in 2024, CDC staffing fell roughly 28% from FY2024 to May 2026, and workforce, grant administration, technical assistance and data systems determine whether appropriations become protection. The open arrow is from fiscal design and institutional continuity through public-health capacity, prevention, emergency response and community security to household health and economic resilience. This is nonprofit policy analysis, not a causal national health evaluation.

The PH WINS Pulse Check 2026 record adds a worker-experience layer to that system story: 35% report worsening burnout, 47% say outside politics negatively affect their work unit, 41% say their budget is worse than in 2024, and 31% of workers age 35 and younger plan to leave within a year. The open arrow is from funding uncertainty and political conditions through worker well-being, advancement, retention and institutional continuity to public-health delivery. This is a follow-up workforce pulse, not a census, causal retention evaluation, or community health outcome measure.

The Nature Human Behaviour political-health polarization record adds a deeper public-judgment mechanism: political identity may be becoming a social determinant of health through trust in medical professionals and willingness to seek or follow care. Add Health shows no significant liberal–conservative biomarker or mortality gap before the 2010s but worse health and higher mortality among conservatives during the 2010s and by the 2020s; the authors treat contemporary medical-engagement differences as evidence consistent with, not proof of, the mechanism.

The JCHS State of the Nation’s Housing 2026 record adds a material-life-course mechanism: high prices, payments, insurance, and rent burdens are suppressing household formation and mobility while narrowing entry into homeownership and shrinking the low-cost rental stock. The open arrow runs from housing-market structure through household timing, place attachment, intergenerational support, and public-capacity pressure; the report does not provide a same-household causal panel.

The Commonwealth Fund coverage-denials record adds a healthcare-institution mechanism: a coverage denial can turn a recommended service into a household choice among delay, out-of-pocket payment, debt, appeal labor, or non-use. Among privately insured working-age adults who experienced denials, the report documents reported effects on care timing, health worsening, household costs, debt, anxiety, remedy delays, and trust. These are conditional survey and focus-group findings, not adjudicated causal outcomes.

The Belonging Barometer 2026 record adds a civic-life distinction that matters for the wider trend map: people can feel psychologically safe, socially connected, and locally rooted while still feeling unable to influence local decisions. Stronger belonging is associated with age, income, and local-news use, but the study does not establish that those factors cause belonging or translate into institutional power.

The Federal Reserve Worker Perspectives 2026 record adds the lived mechanism behind labor-market headline resilience: cost pressure can turn employment from a route to mobility into a survival anchor. Participants describe staying in imperfect jobs, using side work to bridge costs, treating flexibility and advancement as aspirational, and encountering AI-mediated screening as a new gate. The evidence is qualitative and bounded to LMI focus groups, but it explains how household room, time, confidence, and job choice interact.

The Berkeley Labor Center security guard record adds a public-safety infrastructure mechanism: a workforce of roughly 1.3 million guards is asked to de-escalate conflict, manage emergencies, and respond to mental-health crises, yet median pay is $18.70 per hour, annual turnover reached 89%, and training standards are uneven. The report’s central connection is that job quality is also service capacity—churn and weak preparation can reduce the reliability of the safety layer the public experiences.

The RAND State of the American Teacher 2026 record adds an education-capacity mechanism: nationally representative teacher data show well-being pressure relative to similar workers, 18% intending to leave, and 30% holding outside jobs averaging 13 hours a week. The open arrow runs from working conditions and financial/time pressure through retention and staffing continuity to school learning and student-support capacity; the source does not estimate those downstream outcomes causally.

The Luminate 2026 Midyear record adds a commercial-cultural mechanism: entertainment consumption is not converging on one digital model. U.S. streaming expands alongside Spanish-language discovery, genre diversification, physical CDs, nostalgia, library viewing, younger theater use, fandom, and creator-side AI experimentation. The signal is that culture is becoming more hybrid and cross-border in consumption while platform economics remain concentrated.

The ReFED American Households 2026 record adds a food-as-household-routine mechanism: price pressure becomes deal seeking, brand switching, smaller or bulk purchases, meal planning, freezing, and leftover management. Lower-income households face the same nominal grocery increase with far less room to absorb it, and fewer reported behavior changes despite greater potential benefit. The source does not equate lower waste with food security or improved health.

The Purdue mobile-dependent households record adds a digital-infrastructure mechanism: the United States can reduce outright non-use while increasing a narrower form of participation through cellular data and smartphones alone. The open arrow runs from affordability, fixed-network quality, device constraints, disability, housing, and place through the practical ability to use work, education, health, commerce, and civic systems. The study is tract-level and cross-sectional, so it does not estimate individual service failure or causality.

The Financial Health Pulse 2026 record adds a household-protection mechanism: financial vulnerability is reversing while insurance confidence, bill payment, debt manageability, planning, and essential-cost confidence weaken together. The open arrow runs from prices, debt, income, insurance design, and public-policy conditions through household room, risk absorption, and trust in protection. The report is a recurring survey-based trend measure, not a causal panel, claims audit, or default series.

The Climate Central heat-illness record adds a climate-to-care mechanism: warming is no longer only an exposure or perception signal but a modeled contributor to emergency-care demand. Climate change accounted for 27% of the US warm-season heat-related emergency-department visit rate in 2018–2025, with southern/western concentration and extreme-event spikes. The open arrow runs through heat exposure, illness, hospital capacity, household cost, insurance, and public-health response; the attribution is modeled and not an individual causal series.

The America’s Health Rankings 2026 Senior Report record adds an aging-capacity mechanism: demographic growth is being met by some care-workforce expansion, but capacity is geographically uneven while food insecurity and several behavioral-health risks worsen among older adults. The open arrow runs from population age structure through family and paid care, food support, clinical access, household room, and public-service demand. The report combines indicators with different denominators and does not establish causality or care adequacy.

The Freedom House United States 2026 record adds an institutional-legitimacy mechanism: formal democratic protections and electoral competition coexist with assessed declines in legislative functioning, executive-legislative balance, anticorruption safeguards, and political-expression protections. The open arrow runs from institutional conflict and oversight capacity through public trust, civic voice, media space, policy continuity, and state legitimacy. The source is an expert-coded assessment with cited events, not a causal political-behavior series.

The CBO Budget and Economic Outlook 2026–2036 record adds a macro-geopolitical mechanism: domestic policy is transmitted through tariffs, supply chains, immigration, aging, AI capital formation, labor supply, deficits, inflation, and the dollar. The open arrow runs from policy choice and external exposure through firm adjustment, prices, employment, household room, and political legitimacy. The source is a baseline forecast, so realized incidence and causal effects remain open.

The GAO public-library facilities record adds a material civic-infrastructure mechanism: libraries are simultaneously cultural spaces, technology access points, community-program venues, voting sites, and emergency centers, yet their physical systems and accessibility are often undermaintained. The open arrow runs from capital funding and building condition through usable public space, service continuity, inclusion, civic connection, and trust. The report does not estimate user-level or civic-behavior effects.

The NLC Municipal Infrastructure Conditions 2026 record adds a local-state-capacity mechanism: municipal leaders are directing scarce capital toward water, sewer, stormwater, roads, and treatment while funding availability, staff capacity, local cash, and federal grant access determine what can move. The open arrow runs from fiscal and administrative capacity through infrastructure reliability, household safety, economic opportunity, and local legitimacy. The source is a small self-reported municipal survey, not a national condition audit.

The Duke Cost of Keeping Cool record adds an energy-to-safety mechanism: electricity supports food, medical-device charging, heating, and cooling; rising temperatures and electricity costs compound existing energy insecurity; and support programs may under-recognize cooling access. The open arrow runs from county-level modeled energy burden and heat exposure through household tradeoffs, health protection, and public-system targeting. The source is a report synthesis, not a household-level or causal outcome study.

The EIA 2024 RECS housing-characteristics record adds a home-as-interface mechanism: streaming devices and smart speakers are expanding while legacy media peripherals decline; lighting is shifting toward LEDs; and housing form, appliances, cooking, and conditioned space remain regionally differentiated. The open arrow runs from housing and device infrastructure through energy demand, media attention, domestic routines, and household room. The release does not establish bills, time use, attention, privacy, or causal savings.

The Civic Life in America 2036 record adds a civic-imagination mechanism: participation-trust gaps, AI-mediated information and relationships, weak social connection, economic precarity, and polarization are translated into four possible futures—convenience without belonging, institutional hollowing, guarded rule-bound protection, and AI-mediated representation. The open arrow runs from present conditions through civic imagination, institutional design, unequal agency, and public participation. The source is a scenario synthesis, not evidence that any future is probable.

The Gallup influencer-audiences record adds a media-to-political-judgment mechanism: audiences of political podcasters and influencers diverge from party peers on protest rights, voting efficacy, and leader accountability. The open arrow runs from creator-mediated attention through norm interpretation, institutional skepticism, and possible political action. The source does not establish whether creators cause these differences or whether judgments become behavior.

The Gallup election-concerns record adds an election-legitimacy mechanism: concerns about political pressure, ballot security, intimidation, political finance, gerrymandering, and illegal executive action extend beyond election administration into the perceived fairness and accountability of democratic institutions. The open arrow runs from information and threat interpretation through confidence, vigilance, participation, and acceptance of outcomes. The source measures perceptions, not verified risk or realized behavior.

The MPI migration-diplomacy record adds a migration-as-statecraft mechanism: conflict, displacement, smuggling, aid cuts, visas, sanctions, tariffs, labor pathways, and bilateral bargaining are reshaping how states manage mobility and security. The open arrow runs from geopolitical disruption through migration governance, partner leverage, labor demand, humanitarian capacity, and domestic legitimacy. The source is a comparative policy synthesis, not proof of a particular U.S. causal effect.

The Business Economics immigration-policy record adds a policy-to-labor mechanism: reduced net migration can narrow the employment growth compatible with stable unemployment while immigrant-intensive industries, education composition, and fiscal incidence vary across sectors and government levels. The open arrow runs from immigration policy through labor supply, firm capacity, public finance, wages/prices, and household room. The source's public abstract does not establish effect sizes or causal outcomes.

The SAMHSA 2025 NSDUH record adds a behavioral-health transition mechanism: selected adolescent and young-adult indicators improve or hold steady while adult mental-health prevalence remains large, treatment receipt is lower among young adults with serious mental illness, and substance use has broad population reach. The open arrow runs from changing youth behavior and adult burden through care access, household time and cost, work capacity, and public-system demand. The survey does not establish the causes of the improvement, individual treatment need, or treatment quality.

The UF-UCL arts-engagement record adds a cultural-health transition mechanism: arts participation remains low but stable while creative activity shifts toward home and solitary settings, with only partial rebound in public/social contexts after the pandemic. The open arrow runs from cultural access and time allocation through shared space, social connection, identity, and possible health support. The study does not establish annual participation, unequal access mechanisms, or causal health effects.

The Pew teen summer-employment record adds a youth-work transition mechanism: summer employment has partly recovered but remains below historical norms, with age and race/ethnicity gaps and concentration in hospitality, retail, and logistics. The open arrow runs from access to first jobs through work socialization, household contribution, time allocation, sector exposure, and later opportunity. The BLS-based comparison does not establish causes, job quality, school tradeoffs, or long-run developmental effects.

The NCES Condition of Education 2025 record adds an education-capacity transition mechanism: public K-12 enrollment is lower across many states, at-home instruction remains elevated, undergraduate and postbaccalaureate enrollment diverge, achievement indicators are weaker than in 2019, and attainment remains associated with employment and earnings. The open arrow runs from demographic and delivery change through household time/cost, institutional capacity, learning, credentials, work access, and intergenerational opportunity. The indicator synthesis does not establish causes or causal returns to education.

The FHWA Our Nation's Highways 2026 record adds a mobility-infrastructure transition mechanism: motor vehicles dominate trips, roads organize commuting, family/personal, and social/recreational activity, arterials carry disproportionate VMT, local roads carry disproportionate access, and trucks move most domestic freight by weight. The open arrow runs from built mobility dependence through household time/cost, work access, social participation, energy exposure, and supply-chain capacity. The infrastructure description does not establish household burdens, safety, emissions, or unequal access effects.

The DOE National Transmission Needs Study record adds a grid-capacity transition mechanism: AI data centers, manufacturing, electrification, storms, congestion, and interregional reliability are converting transmission into a national growth and affordability planning problem. The open arrow runs from technology and industrial demand through interconnection, congestion, public investment, rate allocation, land/use governance, and household service. The draft does not establish a project, household rate effect, reliability gain, or realized consumer benefit.

The National Academies drought-assessment record adds a climate-governance transition mechanism: more frequent and longer-lasting drought, aridification, groundwater decline, wildfire, and flash drought are making historical baselines less reliable. The open arrow runs from changing hazard conditions through indicators, impact data, early warning, water management, infrastructure, public authority, and long-term adaptation. The consensus report does not establish a regional loss estimate or prove that its framework produces effective or equitable outcomes.

The Knight-NORC public-library record adds a shared-institution transition mechanism: libraries retain broad perceived legitimacy because they combine information, internet and technology access, classes, job and public-service navigation, and space outside home or work. The open arrow runs from common institutional provision through access, social infrastructure, local legitimacy, and perceived community loss under budget cuts. The survey does not establish usage, service quality, fiscal return, or causal trust.

The AARP/National Alliance for Caregiving sandwich-generation record adds a life-course care transition mechanism: nearly 17 million caregivers are raising children while caring for an adult, and similar weekly hours can conceal greater medical-task and daily-care intensity. The open arrow runs from overlapping family obligations through compressed time, work disruption, physical strain, financial pressure, clinical recognition, and demand for formal support. The survey does not establish causality, adequacy of care, or durable household trajectories.

The Pew 250th-anniversary national-mood record adds a legitimacy-and-future-imagination transition mechanism: Americans report a sour present and concern about political division, yet selected expectations for 2050 have improved since 2023, with party control and age organizing the interpretation. The open arrow runs from material and institutional experience through national mood, identity, future narratives, political judgment, and possible legitimacy or mobilization. The survey does not establish causes, behavior, institutional performance, or future outcomes.

The AAM Museums & Public Opinion 2026 record adds a cultural-institution transition mechanism: museums retain broad perceived value as educational, economic, informational, and civic assets, with support for public funding and limited support for censorship. The open arrow runs from cultural provision through information trust, identity, community legitimacy, elected-official incentives, public funding, and participation. The public summary does not establish access, usage, learning, local economic effects, or causal trust.

The UMass corruption and economic-attribution record adds a public-power transition mechanism: people broadly agree that corruption exists and that certain abuses are corrupt, but partisan identity redirects blame across the presidency, bureaucracy, Congress, and other institutions while household price perceptions feed national-direction judgments. The open arrow runs from public-power conduct and material pressure through attribution, trust, partisan identity, accountability demand, and possible institutional remedy. The poll does not establish actual corruption, causal price responsibility, enforcement, or political behavior.

The Pew U.S. role in the world record adds a domestic-opinion-to-geopolitics transition mechanism: partisan publics disagree over whether U.S. power is respected, peaceful, attentive to other countries, or strengthening, while 83% say the U.S. interferes in other countries' affairs. The open arrow runs from domestic identity and administration context through perceived global legitimacy, intervention judgment, superpower narratives, and potential support for external action. The survey does not establish foreign-policy conduct, partner response, or geopolitical outcome.

The Pew Hispanic identity and counting record adds a cultural-demographic transition mechanism: population growth is filtered through Census categories, racial self-identification, ancestry, generation, Afro-Latino identity, intermarriage, and institutional coding. The open arrow runs from demographic change through classification, identity, family formation, cultural continuity, consumer and electoral interpretation, and public-system recognition. The synthesis does not establish a unified population experience, market, electorate, or assimilation path.

The Pew data-center public-opinion record adds an AI-infrastructure transition mechanism: growing awareness is accompanied by more negative perceptions of environmental, home-energy, nearby quality-of-life, jobs, and tax effects, with broad discomfort toward local siting. The open arrow runs from AI and electricity demand through infrastructure buildout, rate and land-use exposure, local information, community consent, political oversight, and public legitimacy. The survey does not establish realized impacts, causal opinion change, or durable consent.

The Pew supplements record adds a consumer-health transition mechanism: supplement use is widespread, but product mix and perceived importance vary by age, income, gender, race/ethnicity, education, and wellness culture. The open arrow runs from health concern and information through product choice, household spending, self-management, identity, commercial influence, and clinical or public-health systems. The survey does not establish efficacy, safety, medical need, spending burden, or care substitution.

The Pew 9/11 memory and generational-transmission record adds a cultural-memory transition mechanism: vivid direct recollection persists while younger adults increasingly receive national trauma through school, family, friends, media, and inherited narratives. The open arrow runs from historical shock through memory, education, identity, security meaning, intergenerational transmission, and possible political interpretation. The survey does not establish memory accuracy, trauma, shared meaning, or causal political effects.

The Pew working-class identity record adds a class-language transition mechanism: working-class identity reaches beyond low income or blue-collar work, including many financially comfortable and non-blue-collar adults, while party differences remain visible inside the same economic categories. The open arrow runs from work and material position through status language, group belonging, political representation, attribution, and possible collective action. The source does not define class, establish hardship, or show that identity produces policy preference or behavior.

The Gallup employee data-use record adds a workplace-control transition mechanism: employees distinguish between data used to support development or team effectiveness and data that may shape evaluation, staffing, or scheduling, while communication about monitoring is associated with both more trust and more concern. The open arrow runs from digital measurement through transparency, managerial mediation, worker voice, perceived fairness, engagement, and bargaining power. The publication does not establish actual surveillance, causal effects, or durable worker action.

The Gallup-Pivotal women's health record adds a care-to-capacity transition mechanism: dismissal, misdiagnosis, diagnostic delay, and treatment barriers are linked in reported experience with constrained work, family care, relationships, and civic participation, while menopause concentrates the pattern at a life stage. The open arrow runs from health-system encounter through recognition, diagnostic time, usable care, role capacity, and public participation. The survey does not establish clinical causality, provider intent, employer accommodation, or durable economic and civic outcomes.

The KFF women's health affordability record adds a care-cost transition mechanism: even insured women report delaying needed care, skipping recommended services, altering prescription use, and reducing spending on food, clothing, or electricity to cover healthcare. The open arrow runs from coverage and price exposure through treatment choice, medication adherence, household room, and unequal health capacity. The survey does not establish clinical harm, causal insurance effects, or total household budgets.

The Pew woman-president skepticism record adds a gender-representation transition mechanism: perceived likelihood of a woman president has weakened while most people frame presidential gender as irrelevant, creating a gap between symbolic importance, institutional expectation, and partisan meaning. The open arrow runs from representation and recent political experience through hope, skepticism, identity, legitimacy, and possible political action. The survey does not establish electoral behavior, candidate viability, or causal gender bias.

The Pew South Korea-U.S. relationship record adds an external-legitimacy transition mechanism: South Korean favorability toward the U.S., perceived reciprocity, reliability, and peace contribution have weakened even while the U.S. remains the most important ally and North Korea remains the central threat. The open arrow runs from U.S. policy and dependence through partner voice, perceived respect, trade and security judgments, alliance legitimacy, and strategic room. The source does not establish government action, military effectiveness, or causal responsibility for opinion change.

The Pew race and social-media health-information record adds a mediated-care transition mechanism: racial and ethnic groups differ in how often they use social media for health information, how accurate they perceive it to be, which source qualities they value, and whether influencers help them ask questions they do not want to ask a doctor. The open arrow runs from access, cultural fit, and clinical communication through platform discovery, source authority, disclosure, and possible care decisions. The source does not establish misinformation exposure, clinical substitution, algorithmic causality, or health outcomes.

The Pew AI chatbots for health record adds an AI-mediated care transition mechanism: chatbot use combines speed, low cost, symptom interpretation, lab and diagnosis translation, sensitive questions, and care-seeking decisions, while users find it helpful but remain divided about sharing health data and the public is more skeptical of chatbots for loneliness or depression support. The open arrow runs from cost, access, and information friction through AI navigation, privacy, clinical handoff, emotional support, and care legitimacy. The source does not establish accuracy, clinical outcomes, privacy protection, or substitution for professionals.

The Pew AI concern and young-adult jobs record adds an AI-legitimacy transition mechanism: concern has become the dominant public orientation, young adults have moved sharply away from early excitement, and job-loss expectations have spread across age groups. The open arrow runs from visible technological change through work security, generational expectation, creativity and connection, public trust, and the legitimacy of adoption. The source does not establish actual employment effects, AI exposure, or why concern is rising.

The Urban families, core cities and suburbs record adds a family-mobility transition mechanism: fertility and child retention are related but distinct processes, and their local correlates differ between core cities and suburbs. The open arrow runs from housing, child care, schools, amenities and commute patterns through family formation, child retention, migration, labor-market access and metropolitan fiscal capacity. The analysis does not establish causal effects, individual preferences, or that one geography is universally family-friendly.

The CSSP family care arrangements record adds a care-portfolio transition mechanism: families do not simply choose one child-care product but combine and sequence parental, formal and kin/community arrangements as costs, trust, culture, availability, leave and work conditions change. The open arrow runs from household resources and institutional design through care portfolios, parental time, work continuity, child development conditions and family policy legitimacy. The report does not establish national prevalence, causality, or child outcomes.

The Stanford CEO activism and consumer response record adds a corporate-voice transition mechanism: public acceptance of executive speech depends on issue, generation, political identity and perceived corporate role, while reported recall and purchasing response make CEO speech part of market legitimacy. The open arrow runs from firm authority through public voice, issue alignment, consumer trust, identity, wallet response and corporate governance. The public summary does not establish transaction effects, employee behavior, or political outcomes.

The Capita-Book Harvest home literacy record adds a household-cultural-capacity transition mechanism: parents value books, but cost, home-library supply, cultural fit, reading time and work strain shape whether children have sustained access to stories and literacy routines. The open arrow runs from household resources and time conditions through cultural exposure, identity, language, learning capacity and civic agency. The survey does not establish causal educational or democratic effects.

The UNU–UN Youth Office youth mental-health record adds an ecosystem transition mechanism: mental health is being reframed from an individual clinical problem toward the conditions in which young people grow, learn, work, connect, and make meaning. The open arrow runs from housing, education, decent work, digital exposure, climate, peace, culture, sports, governance, and youth voice through care, connection, belonging, prevention, and possible resilience. The flagship is a global policy framework with cited evidence and reported partnership reach, not a new prevalence survey, causal model validation, or proof of equal effects across places.

The Google U.S. Future Report record adds a digital-readiness transition mechanism: teen AI adoption is moving faster than shared school norms, while young people are developing their own practices of verification, questioning, creative use, and boundary-setting. The open arrow runs from AI access through learning support, productive friction, source judgment, trusted adults, school governance, family guidance, and youth agency. The sponsor-backed study does not establish behavioral-trace usage, causal learning gains, or that reported verification produces reliable outcomes.

The Freedom Forum First Amendment record adds a civic-expression transition mechanism: constitutional support remains high while practical knowledge, speech confidence, surveillance concerns, online verification and government-platform distrust complicate everyday participation. The open arrow runs from rights awareness and institutional conflict through perceived risk, self-censorship, media legitimacy, protest and political-group participation, and democratic capacity. The proprietary online-panel survey does not establish actual censorship, legal correctness, observed behavior or causal participation effects.

The Chamber Foundation Civic and Economic Literacy record adds an optimism-to-practice transition mechanism: teens and adults see political division and value listening, government understanding and local business, but civic and economic knowledge and perceived listening performance lag those ideals. The open arrow runs from concern and civic aspiration through knowledge, low-friction practice, workplace and community settings, agency, and possible participation. The Chamber Foundation/RXN publication does not establish causal effects, independent test validity, or durable civic behavior.

The Nuffield–Ada Lovelace youth digital-experience record adds a platform-agency transition mechanism: digital spaces can supply connection and support while their design, surveillance, commercial incentives and harmful content reduce control and shift safety work onto young people. The open arrow runs from digital infrastructure through access, algorithmic exposure, identity, privacy, self-safeguarding, mental-health pressure, AI/work concerns, regulation and youth voice. The peer-led qualitative research does not establish prevalence, causal harm, legal liability or intervention effects. The IRENA–ILO renewable-energy jobs record adds a transition-distribution route. Global renewable employment reached 16.6 million in 2024, but grew only 2.3% while installations hit a new peak. The conversion from capacity to work is being shaped by scale, automation, manufacturing overcapacity and grid bottlenecks—not by deployment volume alone. China’s integrated manufacturing and deployment position shows how energy transition gains can be geographically concentrated, while the report’s focus on women’s advancement, disability inclusion, training and domestic supply chains makes inclusion and local value capture part of energy policy rather than an afterthought. The source is a global employment estimate and policy synthesis, not worker-level data or a causal job-creation evaluation.

The UNDP Peoples' Climate Vote 2024 record adds a public-legitimacy route to the energy and just-transition chain. Across 77 countries representing 87% of the world's population, 80% want stronger climate action, 72% want a faster move away from fossil fuels, 69% say climate change has affected major life decisions, and 86% want countries to set aside geopolitical differences and cooperate. The deeper signal is not simple consensus: support for direction coexists with unresolved questions about affordability, policy instruments, household exposure, adaptation responsibility, and delivery credibility. The source is cross-country attitude evidence, not respondent-level causal proof or a forecast of implementation.

The European Commission energy Eurobarometer record adds the household-control layer that the global climate-attitude evidence leaves open. In EU surveys, affordability is the dominant meaning attached to energy policy; leading preferences include helping energy-poor households, reducing consumption and self-production. Consumers also prioritize protection for vulnerable households, clearer bills, prevention of unfair practices, access to energy data and easier provider switching. The signal is that transition legitimacy is experienced through the everyday interface of bills, housing, providers and usable control—not only through climate targets. These are reported attitudes and behaviors, not meter data or causal savings estimates.

The European Commission Citizens' Energy Package record adds the response architecture. The Commission combines household bill relief, energy-poverty protection, supplier switching and transparent contracts with EIB-backed clean-energy finance, grids, homegrown technology supply chains and strategic autonomy. The deeper pattern is that energy policy is no longer separable into climate, consumer, industrial and geopolitical lanes: the same infrastructure and financing decisions are being asked to lower costs, reduce external dependence, create skilled work and preserve political legitimacy. These are announced measures and policy rationales, not proof of delivery or savings.

The World Bank Women, Business and the Law 2026 record adds a law-to-capability route that sharpens the gender and work themes. Across 190 economies, women have about two-thirds of men’s legal rights on average, while supportive policies and institutions score 47/100 and perceived enforcement 53/100; only 4% of women live in economies close to full legal equality. The important finding is the gap between formal permission and usable opportunity: safety, childcare, entrepreneurship, courts, administrative capacity, finance and enforcement determine whether rights become work, income, voice and economic agency. The report is a benchmark, not lived-experience or causal outcome data.

The World Bank W-LEX record supplies the missing practice-level check. In a pilot of nationally representative samples in Bangladesh, Brazil and Nigeria, W-LEX combines first-person experience with perceptions of broader norms across 10 economic-opportunity topics. Brazil illustrates the gap: its formal legal-framework score is 82/100, yet only 31.8% of women versus 45.7% of men say women receive equal pay. The implication is not that perception alone proves discrimination; it is that legal benchmarks need lived-experience measures to show where rights are not being felt, understood or enforced in everyday economic life.

The World Bank gender-and-fiscal-policy record adds a state-finance mechanism beneath the law-to-practice gap. The pilot covers gender dimensions of tax systems in 81 economies and gender-responsive budgeting in 50. The report’s most useful move is to treat fiscal design as behavior-shaping infrastructure: joint filing, thresholds, eligibility rules, administrative burden and invisible care can alter women’s work incentives and benefit access, while sex-disaggregated data and gender-responsive budgets can make public spending more accountable. The source is a framework and pilot indicator set, not household incidence data or proof of reform effects.

The UK Social Connection Framework record adds a youth-belonging route that links social life to institutional design. The framework treats loneliness among boys and young men as connected to stigma, school engagement, NEET status, lack of close friends, transport, clubs, trusted adults, libraries, sports, creative spaces and online harms. Its practical insight is that connection is a form of social infrastructure: people need places, time, safety and credible intermediaries to build belonging and re-enter education or work. The framework is guidance informed by mixed evidence and 58 youth responses, not a causal program evaluation.

The UK NatCen boys and young men loneliness record provides the empirical backbone. Across Understanding Society and MHCYP, chronic loneliness is a minority experience but intermittent loneliness is common: 36% reported feeling lonely some of the time in Understanding Society and 45% occasionally or some of the time in MHCYP. Among young men 16–21, chronic loneliness was 31% for those with no close friends versus roughly 9–11% for those with three or more; it was 9% among those meeting friends daily or several times a week versus 21% among those meeting less than weekly. The report explicitly warns these are associations, not causal effects, and notes that mental health, bullying and stigma may both shape reporting and underlying experience.

The UK Offload and Movember pilot evaluation record adds the intervention bridge. Across Wigan and Wakefield, two community-sport programmes engaged more than 1,400 participants: Movember Ahead of the Game targeted boys and young men aged 11–18 plus trusted adults, while Offload used a six-week model for NEET young men aged 16–24. Public summaries describe encouraging improvements in connection, wellbeing and aspirations, but do not provide enough accessible comparison, attrition or effect-size detail to claim causality. The durable theme is the delivery mechanism: sport can be an engagement hook, but scale requires trusted adults, local organizations, transport, safeguarding and pathways into education or work.

The UNDP Bosnia and Herzegovina SCORE 2025 record adds a comparative social-cohesion case. The assessment finds moderate cohesion, relatively functional everyday intergroup relations, strong local cooperation and a durable inclusive civic identity, yet widespread pessimism about political instability, economic uncertainty, social progress and the country’s direction. The deeper pattern is a coexistence–future-pessimism gap: local life can remain workable while system-level distrust reduces civic engagement and creates room for divisive narratives. This is a weighted national diagnostic, not a causal polarization model or proof that local resilience will persist.

The WHO social determinants of health equity record adds a structural-health route.
